messages.content: I'm building an AI Day Planner web app in Jac and I need a login/signup form component. It should keep its own username, password, and error state and have a toggle to switch between signing in and creating a new account. On sign in, call the login helper and show an error if the credentials are wrong. On sign up, first check the fields aren't empty and the password is at least 4 characters, register the account, then log the user in automatically. While a request is running, show a loading state and disable the submit button. When login or signup succeeds, call an onAuth callback so the parent can flip the app into its logged-in state.

Build a self-contained AuthForm(onAuth) client component. Owns local state: isSignup, username, password, error, loading. Sign-in path validates non-empty fields, awaits jacLogin, calls onAuth() on success else sets an error. Sign-up path requires non-empty fields plus password length >= 4, awaits jacSignup, and on success immediately jacLogin to establish a session before onAuth(). Disable submit and show a processing label while loading; provide a sign-in/sign-up mode toggle that clears the error.
Write a header component for my AI Day Planner app. It should show the app title and a short subtitle, plus a Sign Out button on the right that calls a logout callback passed in as a prop.

```jac """App header with title, subtitle, and sign-out button.""" def:pub Header(onLogout: Callable[[], None]) -> JsxElement { return

AI Day Planner

Task management with AI-powered meal planning

; } ```

Presentational IngredientItem(ing: ShoppingItem): render name, quantity + unit, a conditional 'Carbs' badge when ing.carby, and cost formatted as $X.XX.

Build the shopping-list column for my AI Day Planner. It should own the ingredient list and load the saved list when it mounts. Give it a text input where the user describes a meal and a Generate button that calls the AI to turn that description into a list of ingredients, showing a 'Generating...' state while it works. Render each ingredient as a row, show the running total cost at the bottom with a Clear button, and show a friendly message when the list is empty. Pressing Enter in the input should also generate.

Write a presentational component for a single to-do task row. It shows a checkbox reflecting whether the task is done, the task title (styled/struck through when complete), a category tag when the category is set and isn't just 'other', and a delete button. The toggle and delete actions should be passed in as callbacks.

TaskItem(task, onToggle, onDelete) presentational row: a done checkbox bound to onToggle, the title with a done style when task.done, a category chip shown only when category is set and != 'other', and a delete button wired to onDelete.

I need the tasks column for my AI Day Planner. It owns the list of tasks, loads them on mount (showing a loading message first), and lets the user add a task by typing and pressing Enter or clicking Add. Each task can be toggled done or deleted. Show an empty message when there are no tasks, render each one, and display a count of how many tasks are still remaining with correct singular/plural wording.

TasksPanel component with tasks / taskText / tasksLoading state. On mount await get_tasks() then clear the loading flag. addTask trims the input, awaits add_task, and appends the result; toggleTask and deleteTask await their endpoints and update the list by jid. Enter or the Add button triggers add. Render a loading message, an empty state, a TaskItem per task, and a footer counting incomplete tasks with singular/plural wording.

Wire up the top-level client app for my AI Day Planner. On startup, check whether the user is already logged in. If not, show the auth form. Once logged in, show the app: a header with a sign-out button and a two-column layout with the tasks panel and the shopping-list panel. Handle a brief 'Loading...' state while the auth check runs, and update the view when the user logs in or signs out.

Top-level app component with isLoggedIn / checkingAuth state. On entry set isLoggedIn from jacIsLoggedIn() and finish the auth check. Render a loading placeholder while checking; the AuthForm (wired to a handler that flips isLoggedIn) when logged out; and when logged in a Header whose onLogout calls jacLogout and resets state, above a two-column layout of TasksPanel and ShoppingPanel. Import the stylesheet.

Build a complete single-file AI Day Planner app in Jac, both backend and UI. On the server: model tasks and shopping items as persistent graph nodes, and use LLM-powered functions to categorize a task from its title and to generate a shopping list of ingredients (name, quantity, unit, estimated cost, and whether it's high-carb) from a meal description. Expose endpoints to add, list, toggle, and delete tasks and to generate, get, and clear the shopping list. On the client: a two-column layout with a tasks column (add, toggle, delete, remaining count) and a shopping column (describe a meal, generate ingredients with a loading state, show each ingredient with a carb badge and cost, a running total, and a clear button).

Single-file full-stack Jac AI Day Planner. Server side: Task and ShoppingItem nodes on root; llm-delegated categorize(title)->Category and generate_shopping_list(meal)->list[Ingredient] with sem annotations on the Ingredient fields and functions; public functions add_task (categorize then persist), get_tasks, toggle_task, delete_task, generate_list (clear existing items then regenerate), get_shopping_list, clear_shopping_list. Client side in a cl block: presentational TaskItem and IngredientItem, a TasksColumn and ShoppingColumn that own their state and fetch on mount, composed by an app component in a two-column layout.

I have server-side walkers for my shopping list, one to get the current list, one to generate a list from a meal description, and one to clear it. Write the client shopping-panel component that drives them: load the list on mount by spawning the get walker, generate ingredients from the typed meal description by spawning the generate walker (with a loading state), and clear everything with the clear walker. Read the results back from each walker's report, render the ingredient rows, show the total cost with a Clear button, and let Enter trigger generation.

ShoppingPanel client component backed by walkers. On mount, root spawn GetShoppingList() and take ingredients from reports[0]. Generate: root spawn GenerateShoppingList(meal_description=mealText) behind a generating flag, reading ingredients from reports[0]. Clear: root spawn ClearShoppingList() and reset local state. Render IngredientItem rows, an empty prompt, a summed total, and a Clear button; the Enter key triggers generate.

Write the shopping-list panel component for my meal-planner UI. It manages the ingredient list and a meal-description input. On mount it should load any existing list; a Generate button turns the meal text into ingredients (with a 'Generating...' indicator) and fills the panel, and a Clear button empties it. It talks to the backend by spawning walkers and reading their reports. Render each ingredient, a footer with the total cost and a Clear button, and an empty-state message when there's nothing yet. Enter in the input should also generate.

Rebuild my AI Day Planner's backend in Jac's object-spatial style using walkers instead of plain functions. Keep the graph model of task and shopping-item nodes hanging off root, and keep the LLM helpers that categorize a task and generate a meal's ingredients. Implement each operation as a walker: add a task (categorizing it first), list all tasks, toggle a task's done state by id, delete a task by id, generate a fresh shopping list from a meal description (clearing the old items first), get the current shopping list, and clear it. The client side just renders the existing frontend app.

Walker-based full-stack AI Day Planner. Keep the Category/Unit enums, the Ingredient obj with sem annotations, the llm categorize / generate_shopping_list functions, and the Task / ShoppingItem nodes. Implement each operation as a private walker traversing from Root: AddTask (categorize, attach, report), ListTasks (visit children, collect Tasks, report on Root exit), ToggleTask and DeleteTask (match by jid, mutate or del, disengage), GenerateShoppingList (clear existing ShoppingItems, generate, attach, report), GetShoppingList, and ClearShoppingList. The cl block re-exports the frontend app component.

I'm building Little-X, a decentralized social app in Jac, and I need a polished auth screen. Make a fully controlled login/signup form where all the values, the error, the loading flag, and every handler come in as props. Use the shadcn-style Card, Field, Input, and Button pieces. On large screens show a split layout with branding (logo, the LITTLE-X wordmark, and a tagline) on one side and the form card on the other; on small screens just show the card. Swap the title, description, button label, and the toggle prompt depending on whether we're in sign-up or sign-in mode, and show an inline error banner with an icon when there's an error.

Build the Channels tab for my Little-X social app. It has two views. The list view shows every channel with its name, description, and member count, plus a 'Joined' badge if I'm a member, and a Create Channel button that opens a dialog asking for a name and optional description. Clicking a channel opens the detail view: a header with the channel name, member count, description, and a Join or Leave button; a post composer if I've joined; and the channel's posts rendered as tweet cards with like, comment, delete, and repost. Show loading skeletons while channels load and friendly empty states when there are no channels or no posts. All the data and actions come in as props.

I'm building the Explore tab for a small Twitter-style app called Little X, and I need a client component that shows a scrollable list of everyone a user could follow. Each row should have the person's avatar (falling back to their initial if the image doesn't load), their display name and @handle derived from the username, and a short bio line. Show a Follow button next to anyone I'm not already following, but hide it for my own profile; for people I already follow, show a button that reads Following normally and flips to Unfollow on hover. While the profile list is still loading, render a handful of placeholder skeleton rows, and if there's genuinely nobody to show, display a friendly empty state with an icon and a short message. The component receives the full profile list, my following ids, my own id, and follow/unfollow callbacks as props.

Explore-tab component (.cl.jac). Props: allProfiles, followingIds, myProfileId, onFollow, onUnfollow. One row per profile - avatar with initial fallback, name + @handle split from username, bio or 'No bio yet'. Row action: Following->Unfollow on hover when already followed; Follow when not and not self; nothing for own profile. Null list -> 5 skeleton rows; empty list -> icon empty-state ('No one to show'). Fade-in rows, hover highlight.

Create the home feed screen for a Twitter-like app. At the very top, optionally show a dismissible welcome banner for first-time users, then a composer box for writing a new post (with the user's avatar, a placeholder, a character ring, and a Post button). Below that comes the feed itself: while it's loading show shimmer skeleton placeholders, if there are no posts show an empty state telling the user to follow people or post something, and otherwise render each post as a tweet card. It takes all the state and callbacks as props - the composer text and its change/post handlers, the loading flag, the tweet list, and the like/comment/delete/repost handlers.

FeedTab .cl.jac. Compose in order: optional <WelcomeBanner> (showWelcome), <Composer> (avatar/placeholder/value/onChange/onPost, char ring, 3 rows), then feed body. feedLoading -> 4 skeleton rows; empty tweets -> icon empty-state; else map tweets -> <TweetCard> keyed by jid with onLike/onComment/onDelete/onRepost + myUsername. Purely presentational, all state and callbacks via props.

I need the main feed component for my social app. It should stack a welcome banner (only when a flag says to show it), a post composer wired to the current draft text and a post action, and then the list of posts. Handle three feed states cleanly: a loading state with placeholder rows, an empty state with a helpful message when there's nothing to show, and the normal state that maps every tweet to a card. Pass the interaction handlers for liking, commenting, deleting and reposting straight through to each card.

Build FeedTab: conditional banner + composer + tweet stream. Three-way branch on load/empty/populated - skeleton rows, empty placeholder, or a TweetCard per tweet keyed by jid. Forward like/comment/delete/repost plus the viewer's profile identity down to each card. Stateless component, everything driven by props.

Write a mobile bottom navigation bar for a social app. It should be pinned to the bottom of the screen, only visible on small screens, and hold four icon buttons: home/feed, explore, channels, and profile. Highlight whichever tab is currently active in the accent color and leave the rest muted, invoke an onNavigate callback with the tab name when one is tapped, and show a small numeric badge over the profile icon whenever there are unread notifications.

Mobile bottom nav (.cl.jac, md:hidden, fixed bottom, backdrop blur). Four icon tabs: feed/explore/channels/profile. Active tab -> primary color, rest muted (compose via cn()). onNavigate(tab) on click. notifCount > 0 -> small count badge over the profile icon. Props: activeTab, notifCount, onNavigate.

Build the profile screen for a Twitter-style app. Show a gradient cover banner, a large avatar overlapping it (with an initial fallback), and the user's display name and @handle. Include a bio area that flips into an editable textarea with Save/Cancel buttons when editing is toggled on, and otherwise just shows the current bio text. Underneath, display following / followers / posts counts with correct singular-plural labels, then list all of the user's own posts as tweet cards. The profile bundle, whether the bio is being edited, the bio draft, and the various post-interaction callbacks all arrive as props.
ProfileTab .cl.jac. Layout: gradient cover strip, avatar overlapping (-mt-12) with initial fallback, display name + @handle. Bio region: editingBio ?

I need a component that renders someone's own profile page. Give it a colored header strip, an avatar sitting over it, the name and handle, and a bio section that can switch between read mode and an edit mode with a textarea plus save and cancel actions. Show three stat counts - following, followers and post count, pluralized properly - and then render the person's posts below using the tweet card component. Everything, meaning the profile data, edit state, bio text, and the like/comment/delete/repost handlers, is passed in.

Own-profile view component: cover banner + overlapping avatar + name/handle. Toggleable bio editor (textarea with save/cancel vs static paragraph). Following/followers/posts counters with correct singular/plural. Below, the user's own tweets rendered as TweetCards. All state and handlers via props; guard the count derivations against a null profile bundle.

Create the right-hand sidebar for a Twitter-like app. It needs a rounded search input with a magnifier icon and a clear (X) button that runs a search when the user presses Enter. Below it, a Trending card listing hashtag tags with their post counts (shown only when there are any), each clickable to filter by that tag. Then a Who to follow card showing up to five suggested profiles - avatar, name, handle, a Follow button, and a hover card previewing their bio - with a Show more link if there are more than five. Finish with a small about card describing the app and a few hashtag badges. It's sticky, desktop-only, and takes the search/trending/suggestion data and their callbacks as props.

I need a tweet card component for a Twitter-like app. Given a single tweet plus the current user's username, show the author's avatar, display name, handle, and a relative timestamp (now, minutes, hours, days, or a plain date for old posts). Render the post text, and an action row with reply, repost, and like buttons that show counts - the like button fills in and turns colored when the viewer has liked it. If the tweet belongs to the current user, show a delete button that opens a confirmation dialog before deleting. Tapping reply expands an inline thread listing existing comments plus an input to post a new reply on Enter or via a send button. Ownership and liked-state should be computed purely from data the client already holds. Like, comment, delete and repost callbacks are passed in.

TweetCard .cl.jac. Props: tweet, myUsername, onLike/onComment/onDelete/onRepost. Local has-state: showComments, commentText. Derive is_mine (author == myUsername, guard empty), is_liked (myUsername in likes), like/comment counts, and a relative date_str (now/m/h/d/date). Render avatar+initial, name/@handle/dot/time, content, action row (reply toggles thread, repost prefills composer, like fills when liked). Own tweet -> AlertDialog delete confirm. Expanded thread: list comments + reply input (Enter or Send, disabled when blank).

Put a small X button in the corner that calls an onDismiss callback so the user can close it.

I want a reusable icon component for the web build of my Jac app, wrapping Lucide (lucide-react). Set up a name-to-icon lookup for the glyphs I use — home, search, bell, user, heart, comment, repeat, edit, logout, lock, at-sign, a spark/star, calendar, close, send, image — and expose an Icon function taking a name plus size, color, stroke width, and a fill flag. When fill is on it should paint the glyph solid in its own color (for an active like or a brand mark); otherwise render it outlined. Keep the exact same <Icon name=.../> API that the native build uses so call sites don't change.

```jac
"""Icon set — WEB variant (Lucide via `lucide-react`, real DOM SVG).

The compiler picks `icon.native.cl.jac` (which uses `lucide-react-native`) for
the react-native target instead of this file, so the same `<Icon name=.../>`
call renders crisp Lucide vector icons on both platforms. `lucide-react` renders
plain `<svg>` and needs no `react-native-svg`, so the web bundle stays clean.
"""

cl {
    import from "lucide-react" {
        House,
        Search,
        Bell,
        User,
        Heart,
        MessageCircle,
        Repeat2,
        SquarePen,
        LogOut,
        Lock,
        AtSign,
        Star,
        Calendar,
        X,
        Send,
        Image as ImageIcon
    }

    # name → Lucide component. Same keys exist in icon.native.cl.jac.
    glob LUCIDE = {
             home: House,
             search: Search,
             bell: Bell,
             user: User,
             heart: Heart,
             comment: MessageCircle,
             repeat: Repeat2,
             edit: SquarePen,
             logout: LogOut,
             lock: Lock,
             at: AtSign,
             spark: Star,
             calendar: Calendar,
             close: X,
             send: Send,
             image: ImageIcon
         };

    """Render a Lucide icon by name. `fill` paints it solid in its own color
    (active like / brand mark); `width` is the stroke weight."""
    def:pub Icon(
        name: str, size: int, color: str, fill: bool, width: float
    ) -> JsxElement {
        Glyph = LUCIDE[name];
        return
            <Glyph
                size={size}
                color={color}
                fill={(color if fill else "none")}
                strokeWidth={width}
            />;
    }
}

```

The 'none' mode is our enforced no-GC build, so compile it with the enforce-nogc / assert-no-rc flags, and if any enforced build still contains RC or trace machinery, print a loud error to stderr and exit non-zero. Aggregate median/min/max/stdev ns + max RSS per cell. Demonstrate the arithmetic operators, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, remainder, exponent, and grouping with parentheses, printing the sum, the product, and a parenthesized expression.

```jac
with entry {
    # Basic math
    sum = 5 + 3;        # Addition: 8
    difference = 10 - 4; # Subtraction: 6
    product = 6 * 7;     # Multiplication: 42
    quotient = 20 / 4;   # Division: 5.0

    print(sum);         # Shows: 8
    print(product);     # Shows: 42

    # More operations
    remainder = 17 % 5;  # Modulo (remainder): 2
    power = 2 ** 3;      # Exponent: 8 (2³)

    # Combined operations
    total = (5 + 3) * 2;  # Use parentheses like in math: 16

    print(total);
}
```

    print(numbers[2:5]);   # [2, 3, 4]

f-string width and alignment specs: :10, :>10, :^10, :<10, plus fill chars like :*>10 and :-^10.

```jac
def example() {
    name = "Alice";
    # Width specification
    f"{name:10}";           # "Alice     " (10 chars, left-aligned)
    f"{name:>10}";          # "     Alice" (right-aligned)
    f"{name:^10}";          # "  Alice   " (centered)
    f"{name:<10}";          # "Alice     " (left-aligned, explicit)

    # Fill character
    f"{name:*>10}";         # "*****Alice" (fill with *)
    f"{name:-^10}";         # "--Alice---" (centered with -)
}
```

Show the numeric formatting options available in Jac f-strings: integer bases (decimal, binary, octal, hex in both cases), zero-padding, fixed-point and scientific float formatting with precision, percentages, and thousands separators.

```jac
def example() {
    n = 42;
    pi = 3.14159265;

    # Integer formats
    f"{n:d}";               # "42" (decimal)
    f"{n:b}";               # "101010" (binary)
    f"{n:o}";               # "52" (octal)
    f"{n:x}";               # "2a" (hex lowercase)
    f"{n:X}";               # "2A" (hex uppercase)
    f"{n:05d}";             # "00042" (zero-padded, width 5)

    # Float formats
    f"{pi:f}";              # "3.141593" (fixed-point, 6 decimals default)
    f"{pi:.2f}";            # "3.14" (2 decimal places)
    f"{pi:10.2f}";          # "      3.14" (width 10, 2 decimals)
    f"{pi:e}";              # "3.141593e+00" (scientific notation)
    f"{pi:.2e}";            # "3.14e+00" (scientific, 2 decimals)
    f"{pi:g}";              # "3.14159" (general format)

    # Percentage
    ratio = 0.756;
    f"{ratio:.1%}";         # "75.6%"

    # Thousands separator
    big = 1234567;
    f"{big:,}";             # "1,234,567"
    f"{big:_}";             # "1_234_567" (underscore separator)
}
```

Profile(user_id) component: render the async child inside an <article>, with a try/awaiting suspense fallback showing a loading paragraph until it resolves.

Write a simple App component that renders a heading and a plain button, and leave an inline note in the markup reminding us to swap that button out for a custom Button component later. The note should be a JSX comment, not a rendered element.
App component: <h1> plus a placeholder <button>, with a JSX-embedded comment flagging the button as a TODO to replace with a custom component.
I want an app component that pulls in a Button from a local components folder and renders it with a label of "Click" and an onClick handler. The handler can be an empty inline function for now.
Import Button from ./components/Button and render it with label="Click" and a no-op onClick lambda.

Show me how to bring in modules using the project's configured path aliases instead of long relative paths - for example a Button from a components alias, a formatDate helper from a utils alias, and shared constants from a shared alias.
Client import block resolving three symbols through path aliases: Button from @components, formatDate from @utils, constants from @shared.

Build a custom "install the app" prompt for a PWA. Use the install hook to find out whether the app can currently be installed, and only when it can, show a button that triggers the native install flow when clicked.
Custom PWA install UI via usePwaInstall: destructure canInstall/triggerInstall, and conditionally render an install button that fires the trigger on click.

Create a small form component with a controlled text input that keeps its value in state, submits when the user presses Enter inside the field, and also has a Submit button that runs the same submit action when clicked.
Controlled-input form: sync value on change, call submit() on the Enter keypress, and wire a Submit button click to the same handler.
Component exercising conditional rendering: if/else to choose content, boolean-and for optional output, and a keyed list comprehension mapping items to <li> elements.
Wrap the main part of my app in an error boundary so that if something inside crashes, the user sees a friendly "Oops! Something went wrong." message instead of a broken screen.
Guard the main app subtree with the runtime error boundary, using a simple "something went wrong" fallback.
I have an expensive widget that occasionally fails to load. Wrap it in an error boundary that shows a styled error message if the widget throws.
Error-boundary an ExpensiveWidget with a custom styled fallback div for load failures.

Set up an app layout with a header, main content, and footer, but isolate failures: put an outer error boundary around the whole app and a second inner one just around the main content, each with its own fallback message, so a crash in the content doesn't take down the header and footer.
Nested error boundaries: an app-level boundary wrapping header/content/footer, plus an inner boundary scoped to the main content, each with a distinct fallback.
Define a User node type that holds a name, then create one for "Alice" and explicitly persist it to the database by saving and committing it.
Declare a User node with a name field; instantiate User("Alice") and manually save() then commit() it to storage.
Declare module-level client globals: an initialized boolean defaulting to false and a nullable cache slot.
Write a walker that runs from the root and returns the list of users - for now it can just report an empty list as a placeholder implementation.
Root-entry walker get_users that reports an empty list.
I want a GET endpoint that lists users. Define it as a walker that triggers at the root and reports back a list (empty stub is fine for now).
Auto-generated users endpoint: walker with a Root entry ability reporting [].
Define a search walker that accepts a query string and an optional result limit, defaulting the limit to 10 when the caller doesn't provide one.
search walker with a required query field and a limit field defaulting to 10.
Create a walker to drive a search request - it should carry the search query and a maximum number of results, with the max defaulting to 10 if unspecified.
Search request walker: query: str, limit: int = 10.
Add request logging as a middleware-style walker. It receives the incoming request as a dict and, when it runs at the root, prints out the request's HTTP method and path.
_before_request hook walker holding the request dict; on Root entry, log its method and path.

Write an authentication middleware walker that inspects the incoming request headers. If there's no Bearer token in the Authorization header, it should report a 401 unauthorized error and stop; otherwise it proceeds and reports that the request is authenticated.
Public get_users walker pinned to HTTP GET via @restspec, reporting an empty list.
Expose a public walker as a GET endpoint but override the auto-generated route so it's served at a custom path of /custom/users.
list_users public walker: @restspec GET mapped to a custom path /custom/users.

Set up two public REST endpoints that read values out of the URL. One responds to GET /items/{item_id} and echoes back the item id from the path. The other responds to GET /users/{user_id}/orders, taking the user id from the path plus an optional status query parameter that defaults to "all".
Two @restspec GET walkers with path params: /items/{item_id} echoing item_id, and /users/{user_id}/orders binding user_id (path) plus a status query param defaulting to "all".

Build a pair of GET endpoints that pull parameters from the request URL: one that captures an item id from its path, and another that captures a user id from its path and also accepts a status filter as a query parameter with "all" as the default.
Path-parameterized GET endpoints: get_item on /items/{item_id}; get_user_orders on /users/{user_id}/orders with a defaulted status query param.

Add two public GET endpoints backed by plain functions rather than walkers: a health check that returns a healthy status, and an app status endpoint mounted at a custom /custom/status path that returns a running status plus a version string.
Show how to make a node publicly accessible to all users - grant everyone read permission on it, and separately grant everyone write permission.
Grant global READ and WRITE permissions on a node to everyone.
I want to share a node with one specific user rather than everyone. Grant that user's root read access to the node, and also grant them write access.
Grant a specific root READ and WRITE access to a node via allow_root.
Show me how to take back all the public access on a node - revoke every permission that was previously granted to everyone.
Remove a single user's access to a node - specifically, revoke the read permission previously granted to one particular root.
Disallow a specific root's READ access to a node.

Demonstrate the three access levels for walker endpoints: a default protected one that requires a valid JWT and returns whatever is connected to the root, a public one needing no auth that reports an ok status, and a private, per-user isolated one that also requires authentication.
Show the endpoint visibility tiers side by side: default protected (JWT) get_profile, :pub health_check, and :priv per-user internal_process.

Illustrate secure-by-default endpoints by defining three walkers with different exposure: one left protected so it needs a token, one marked public so anyone can hit it, and one marked private so it's authenticated and scoped to each user.
Three walkers contrasting endpoint auth: protected-by-default, :pub, and :priv (per-user isolated).

Write a webhook handler that receives payment notifications. It should accept a payment id, an amount, and a currency (defaulting to USD), and when invoked it processes the notification and reports back a success message that includes the payment details.
Webhook-protocol walker PaymentReceived: fields payment_id/amount/currency(=USD); on entry report a success payload echoing the payment.
Public async WebSocket walker EchoMessage: reflect message and client_id (default anonymous) back to the sender.

Build a public WebSocket chat room where a message sent by one client is broadcast to all connected clients. Each message has the text and an optional sender name defaulting to anonymous, and the async handler emits a message-typed payload with the sender and content.
Broadcasting async WebSocket walker ChatRoom: fan out each {sender, content} message to all connections; sender defaults to anonymous.

I have two Jac services. In a provider service, define a public Greet walker that takes a name and reports a greeting string. In a separate consumer service, import that walker and write a TriggerGreet walker that, given a name, invokes the remote Greet over HTTP and reports back its first result.

Show the different ways to get a storage instance using the built-in store() helper: a bare default one with no configuration, one pointed at a custom base path, and one that also creates the directories if they don't exist.
Three store() constructions: defaults, a custom base_path, and base_path plus create_dirs.

Show how to work with stored files: generate a temporary, time-limited access URL (a pre-signed URL on S3) that expires in ten minutes, and write a public download walker that checks whether a file exists, reporting an error if not, otherwise returning its contents and length.
Storage URL + download: mint a 600s-expiry get_url, and a download_file walker that 404s on missing paths else returns content and size.

Demonstrate the advanced way to obtain storage through the StorageFactory: one instance created explicitly as a local backend with a config dict specifying the base path and directory creation, and another obtained via the factory's default resolution that reads from jac.toml, env vars, or built-in defaults.
StorageFactory usage: explicit create("local", config) plus get_default() resolving from jac.toml/env/defaults.

Write an async walker that takes a list of items and processes them one at a time, awaiting an async per-item processing call for each and collecting the results, then reports the full list of results.
Async walker: iterate items, await process_item on each, accumulate and report results.
Show how to open direct connections to two different databases through the kvstore helper - one MongoDB store for the main app data and one Redis store used as a cache.
Open two kvstore handles: a MongoDB store and a Redis cache store.

Demonstrate MongoDB-style operations through a kvstore connection: insert a user document, look one up by name, query all admins, find users older than a threshold with an operator query, update a user's age, delete a user, and set a keyed value in a sessions collection.
Show how to query persisted graph nodes directly from a MongoDB-backed kvstore: fetch all User nodes younger than 30 using an operator query, and separately fetch all User nodes whose role is admin.
Via kvstore.find_nodes over 'User': pull nodes with age < 30 and, separately, role == admin.
I want to run filtered lookups against my stored User nodes using the database layer. Query for users under 30 with a less-than operator, and also query for users in the admin role.
find_nodes('User', ...) queries: age below 30 and role of admin.

Demonstrate common Redis operations through a kvstore cache: store a session object, set two keys with expirations (a short-lived token and a longer profile cache), increment a view counter, scan for all session keys by pattern, and set an expiry on an existing session key.
Redis kvstore ops: set a session, set_with_ttl for a token and a profile, incr a counter, scan_keys('session:*'), and expire a session key.

Write a helper that runs an operation on a repo while holding a distributed lock so no two pods act on the same repo at once. It should acquire a Redis lock with a unique fence token and a TTL, retrying for up to about 25 seconds before giving up with a contention error, run the protected operation, and always release the lock afterward using a safe compare-and-delete that no-ops if another pod has since taken it over.
Cross-pod mutex over Redis: fenced set_nx_with_ttl acquire with ~25s retry/timeout, run the guarded op, and release via compare-and-delete (delete_if_equals) in a finally.

Write a function that ensures a periodic task runs at most once across the whole cluster within a time window. Using a Redis set-if-not-exists key with a 60-second TTL as a debounce, run the task and return true only if this pod won the race; otherwise return false because another pod already ran it recently.
Cluster-wide debounce: set_nx_with_ttl a 60s key; run the task and return true on win, else false (already ran).
Write a walker that, when an order is placed, publishes an event to the message broker on an "orders.placed" topic carrying the order id and amount, along with a trace id.
place_order walker: on entry, publish an Event to 'orders.placed' with order_id/amount payload and a trace_id.
Set up a push-style event subscriber that reacts to "orders.placed" events. Register a handler that receives each event and prints its type and data.
@subscribe('orders.placed') handler printing the event type and data.
I want to replay the entire history of a topic. Subscribe to "orders.placed" but start consuming from the earliest available event, and have the handler print each event's id as it replays.
@subscribe('orders.placed', start_from='earliest') replay handler printing each event id.

Write a pull-based consumer function that drains a batch from the broker. Given a broker, it should consume up to 10 messages from "orders.placed" with a 2-second timeout, process and acknowledge each one, and return how many it handled.
drain(broker): consume up to 10 'orders.placed' messages (2s timeout), ack each, return the count.
Add a basic health-check walker that runs at the root and reports back a healthy status.
health walker reporting {status: healthy} on Root entry.
I need a simple health endpoint for the service. Implement it as a walker that reports a healthy status when hit at the root.
Health endpoint walker returning a healthy status.

Write a readiness-check walker that verifies the app's dependencies before declaring it ready. It should check the database and the cache, report a ready status only if both are up, and otherwise report a not-ready status that includes the individual database and cache states.
readiness walker: probe database and cache; report ready only if both pass, else not_ready with each subsystem's state.
Show how to retrieve every root in the system - all the roots currently held in memory or the database - using the built-in helper.
Fetch all roots via allroots().
Show how to flush in-memory changes to durable storage by committing the current memory state to the database.
Persist in-memory state to the database with commit().

Show how to obtain a sandbox instance through the SandboxFactory two ways: one using the default configuration from jac.toml, and one created explicitly as a Kubernetes backend with a config specifying the namespace, base image, memory limit, TTL, and a domain template for preview URLs.
SandboxFactory: get_default() from config, plus create("kubernetes", {...}) with namespace/base_image/memory_limit/ttl_seconds/domain_template.

Show how to spin up a new sandbox for a user's project by supplying the user id, project id, and a path to the project files, then, if creation succeeded, print out the sandbox's access URL and its id.
sandbox.create(user_id, project_id, code_path); on success print the URL and sandbox_id.

Demonstrate managing the sandbox lifecycle: check a sandbox's current state, list all of a user's sandboxes and print each one's id, state, and URL, stop a sandbox, destroy one to free its resources, and clean up any sandboxes that have exceeded their TTL, printing how many were cleaned.

Show the file operations available on a sandbox: write a file with given contents, read a text file back and print it, read a binary file such as an image (which comes back base64-encoded with a mime type), delete a file, and list all files in the sandbox.
Sandbox file ops: write_file, read_file (text and base64 binary), delete_file, and list_files.
Show how to run a shell command inside a sandbox with a timeout and print its standard output - for example listing the contents of a directory.
sandbox.exec_command(id, 'ls -la /app', timeout=30) and print stdout.
Show how to fetch a sandbox's logs starting from a byte offset and print the returned content, noting that the response also carries the next offset so you can keep streaming further logs.
Read sandbox logs from offset 0 and print content; response includes the next-read offset for streaming.

Build a complete little full-stack app in a single Jac program: define a Todo node with a title and done flag, a public server function that seeds a few todos under the root and returns them as plain dicts, and a client app component that on mount fetches the todos and renders each one as a row with a checkbox reflecting its done state.
Single-file fullstack todo: Todo node (title, done); a :pub server fn seeding todos on root and returning them; a client app that awaits them on entry and renders checkbox rows.

Model a small social graph and walk it. Define Person nodes with names and Friend and Family edges, where a Person announces when a walker visits and the Family edge announces when it's traversed. Build a graph of a few people linked by friend and family relationships, then write a FriendFinder walker that starts at the root, moves to the first person, then explores that person's connections and family edges, printing who it finds as friends-of-friends or family. Finally spawn the walker from the root and print the result.

Graph with Person nodes plus Friend/Family edges (node and edge abilities that announce on FriendFinder visits); build a friend/family network and a FriendFinder walker that hops root->person, then traverses outgoing and Family edges reporting friends-of-friends/family; spawn from root and print.

Create a graph traversal example over a social network. Set up Person nodes and Friend/Family edge types (with node and edge abilities that print when the walker arrives), wire several people together with friend and family edges, and write a FriendFinder walker that begins at the root, steps into the graph, and follows connections including family edges to surface friends-of-friends and family members, then run it from the root and print the outcome.

Traverse a friends/family graph: Person nodes and Friend/Family edges with visit-triggered abilities, and a FriendFinder walker that starts at root, descends, and walks outgoing plus Family edges to report friends-of-friends/family; spawn on root.
Spec: declare a Person node holding a name string, plus a Friend edge type for linking people in a social graph.

I'm setting up a graph traversal to locate friends. Can you declare a walker named FriendFinder that keeps a boolean flag, defaulting to false, so it can remember whether it has already started running?
Declare a FriendFinder walker with a single boolean state field `started` initialized to false.
Write an ability that runs whenever a walker lands on a Person node and prints that person's name followed by 'is a friend'.
Ability on Person entry: print '<name> is a friend'.

I need a small people-graph. Define a Person node with a name, plus Friend and Family edge types. Then, at program start, create three people (John, Susan, Mike), hang John off the root, link John to Susan as a friend, and connect Susan to both John and Mike as family.
Set up a Person node and Friend/Family edges; in an entry block create John, Susan, Mike, attach John to root, add a Friend edge John->Susan and Family edges from Susan to [John, Mike].
Create a walker that, when it starts at the graph's root, moves out to every node directly connected to it. Then kick it off by spawning it on the root.
Walker triggered on Root entry that visits all outgoing neighbors; spawn it from root in an entry block.
Define a Family edge type and a walker that, starting from the root, first queues up every outgoing node and then separately queues only the nodes reached through Family edges.
Family edge plus a Visitor walker: on Root entry, visit [-->] then visit only the Family-typed outgoing edges.
Build a traversal that begins at the root and visits both all of its outgoing connections and, as a separate step, just the ones linked by Family edges. Include the Family edge definition.
Walker over a graph with a Family edge; from Root, dispatch to all neighbors and to Family-edge neighbors specifically.

I want to mix regular Jac with a performance-critical native section in one file. Write a program with an ordinary function that filters a list of dicts down to the active ones, plus a native (machine-compiled) block containing a checksum routine and a recursive Fibonacci function, and an entry point that calls the native checksum on [1,2,3,4,5] and fibonacci(30).
Single-file Jac: standard `def process_data` filtering active items; a native `na {}` codespace with compute_checksum (rolling hash mod 1e9+7) and recursive fibonacci; entry calls both.

Model people who know each other, then walk the graph to greet each one. Define a Person node (name, age) and a Knows edge recording the year the acquaintance began. Add a walker that starts at root, hops to each person, and prints 'Hello, <name>!'. Wire up Alice and Bob (Alice knows Bob since 2020) and run it.
Person(name, age) node and Knows(since) edge; a Greeter walker printing 'Hello, <name>!' at each Person while fanning out via [-->]. Build Alice->Bob (Knows since 2020) under root and spawn Greeter.

Write a graph-walking greeter: from the root it visits everyone reachable and prints a hello with their name. Set up a Person/Knows schema and a small graph of Alice and Bob to demonstrate it, expecting 'Hello, Alice!' then 'Hello, Bob!'.
Greeter walker traversing outward from root, greeting each Person by name; scaffold Person/Knows types and an Alice->Bob graph.

I need to visit and print every person reachable from the root of my graph. Define Person and Knows types, connect Alice and Bob, and have a walker traverse outward greeting each person it reaches by name.
Traverse root's reachable Person set via outgoing edges, printing a per-node greeting; Person/Knows schema with an Alice-knows-Bob sample graph.
Person node: name, age=0, and a greet ability on Visitor entry printing 'Hello from <name>'. Plus a data-less Waypoint node.

Create a SecureRoom node that reacts differently depending on which walker visits it. It should run a generic handler for any walker on entry, run a clearance check only for Inspector walkers (denying access and stopping if their clearance is too low), respond specifically when a Root-type walker arrives, fire a handler when an Inspector leaves, and share one handler for either of two other walker types.

SecureRoom(clearance_required) node with entry/exit abilities: a generic entry, an Inspector-typed entry doing a clearance gate plus disengage, a Root-typed entry, an Inspector exit, and a Walker1|Walker2 union entry.

Show how a node can filter its entry and exit abilities by the type of walker visiting it. Build a SecureRoom that handles a plain entry, an Inspector-only clearance check with early stop, a Root-walker case, an Inspector exit, and a shared handler for two walker types.
Demonstrate walker-type dispatch on a node: SecureRoom with generic entry, typed Inspector entry (clearance check, disengage on fail), Root entry, Inspector exit, and a Walker1|Walker2 union entry.
Set up node inheritance: a base Entity node that carries a created_at timestamp, and a User node that extends it while adding username and email fields.
Entity base node (created_at); User(Entity) subtype adding username and email.

Define a few edge types: a Friend edge that records the year it started and a strength defaulting to 1.0, a plain Follows edge with no data, and a Weighted edge that holds a weight and exposes a method returning that weight normalized against a supplied maximum.
Edges: Friend(since, strength=1.0); empty Follows; Weighted(weight) with get_normalized(max_weight)->float returning weight/max_weight.
Create a Road edge that knows its distance, and whenever a Traveler walker crosses it, add that distance onto the traveler's running total.
Road edge(distance) with a Traveler-entry ability accumulating self.distance into visitor.total_distance.
Show the difference between directed and undirected connections in Jac. Make two Item nodes, link them one-way, and then also link them both ways.
Two Item nodes; create one directed edge (a ++> b) and one undirected edge (a <++> b).

Write a walker that gathers values from data nodes as it traverses, but stops collecting once it has grabbed a set maximum. It should announce when it starts, then walk outward from the root, appending each DataNode's value to its list until the cap is hit.
Collector walker: items list, max_items=10; on Root entry print and fan out, on DataNode entry append here.value while under the cap, continue via [-->].

I need a traversal that collects up to N node values. Define a walker holding a results list and a limit, printing a start message at the root, then visiting each node and storing its value until the limit is reached.
Bounded-collection walker over DataNodes: append value while len < max_items, keep visiting outgoing neighbors.

Build a walker that counts how many nodes it visits. Define a DataNode type, have the walker increment its counter at the root and at every data node while continuing outward, then set up a chain of two data nodes under root and print the total (which should be 3).
DataNode(value); Counter walker with a count field incremented on Root and each DataNode entry; build root->DataNode(1)->DataNode(2), spawn, print 'Counted 3 nodes'.
Write a graph traversal that tallies every node it lands on, including the root, and reports the count afterward. Demonstrate it on a two-node chain hung off the root so it reports 3.
Node-counting walker with an accumulator field, incrementing at Root and DataNode entries over a root->A->B chain; print the resulting count.
Make a walker that, on reaching an Item node, fans out in every direction: to nodes it points to, to nodes that point at it, and to nodes in both directions.
Item node; Visitor walker on Item entry visiting [-->], [<--], and [<-->].
Show how a walker can follow edges outbound, inbound, and in both directions at once. Define an Item node and a walker whose Item-entry ability queues all three.
Walker traversing outgoing, incoming, and bidirectional neighbors from each Item node.
Person node, Friend edge(since=2020); Visitor filtering visits by node type [?:Person], by Friend edge, and by Friend edge with since>2020.
I want a traversal with several filter styles. From a Person node, have the walker visit only Person neighbors, only Friend-edge neighbors, and only Friend-edge neighbors added after 2020.
Filtered walker over a Person/Friend graph: node-type filter, edge-type filter, and edge-attribute predicate (since>2020).
Create a walker that tries to move to its outgoing nodes, but if there are none to go to, prints 'No outgoing edges' as a fallback.
Show the else-clause on a visit: a walker should continue to its outgoing neighbors, and when the graph has no such neighbors, run a fallback branch that logs a message.
Walker using visit-else to print a message when [-->] yields nothing.
Visitor walker with an optional target field; on Item entry `visit here` and `visit self.target`.
Walker directing traversal to `here` and to a node held in a walker field.
Item node; Visitor using indexed visits (`visit :0:`, `:-1:`, `:2:`) to insert outgoing nodes at the front/back/position in the queue.
I want to influence whether my traversal behaves like DFS or BFS. Create a walker that can push newly discovered nodes onto the front of its queue, onto the end, or at an arbitrary index.
Walker controlling queue-insertion position for outgoing nodes to switch between DFS and BFS ordering.

Build a walker that collects data from the graph and returns it to the caller. It should visit each DataNode, report that node's value, and keep going. After spawning it, the caller reads the accumulated values from the walker's reports list.
DataNode(value); DataCollector reporting here.value at each node and continuing; caller reads result.reports after spawn.
Write a traversal that reports each node's value as it goes without halting, so that after it finishes the spawn result exposes all reported values as a list.
Report-collecting walker over DataNodes; harvest result.reports post-spawn.

Write a data-collecting walker whose reported values are typed. Give it a reports field declared as a list of ints, start it at the root, and have it report each DataNode's value (checked against that int type) while continuing outward.
DataCollector walker with `has reports: list[int]`; report here.value (int-checked) per DataNode and fan out via [-->].
Create a walker that traverses data nodes and reports their integer values, with the reports collection explicitly typed as list[int] for type checking.
Typed-report walker: list[int] reports, reporting each DataNode value during outward traversal.
Searcher walker(target): on Person entry, if the name matches, report the node and disengage; otherwise visit [-->].
Create an auditing walker that walks a chain of accounts and reports each balance, but skips over any account that isn't active without processing it or continuing from it.
Auditor walker: on Account entry, `skip` when not active; otherwise report the balance and visit [-->].

Show the different ways to launch a walker. Define an Item node with a value and a walker that reports each item's value as it traverses; build a three-node chain under root, then spawn the walker both with default parameters and with a parameter supplied, and print the collected reports.
Item(value) chain root->1->2->3; MyWalker(param) reporting each value; spawn via `root spawn MyWalker()` and `MyWalker(param=10)`, then print result.reports.

I want to demonstrate spawning a walker with and without arguments and reading back its results. Have a walker collect item values along a chain of three nodes, spawn it two ways, and print the reports list.
Value-reporting walker over a 3-item chain; illustrate parameterless and parameterized spawn plus result.reports access.

Build the backend for a simple todo list on a graph. Define a Todo node with a title and a done flag, a walker that creates a new todo hanging off the root and reports it, and another walker that lists all todo nodes attached to the root.
Todo(title, done=False) node; add_todo walker creating `root ++> Todo(title)` and reporting it; list_todos walker reporting all [-->][?:Todo].
Two todo-API walkers: create-and-report a Todo off root, and enumerate/report root's Todo children.

Demonstrate walker inheritance and method overriding. Write a base visitor walker that logs each node it visits and keeps traversing, then a subclass that overrides the logging to print the node's type name instead.
BaseVisitor walker logging `here` per node; DetailedVisitor(BaseVisitor) overriding the entry ability to log the node's type name.

Illustrate the special references available inside nodes and walkers. Build a SecureRoom node that, on an Inspector's entry, uses `visitor` and `self` to grant access when the inspector's clearance meets the room's required level. Pair it with an Inspector walker that uses `here`, `self`, and `root` to report room details and traverse from the root.
SecureRoom(required_level) using visitor/self in a clearance check; Inspector walker(clearance, name) using here/self/root, inspecting SecureRoom nodes and starting from root.

Show how `here`, `self`, `visitor`, and `root` are used across a node and a walker. The Inspector walker reports the room it's on and starts traversal at root; the SecureRoom checks the visiting inspector's clearance against its required level.
Show a couple of ways to create nodes. Define a Person node with a name and age, instantiate two people as local variables, and also create a third person inline while attaching it to the root.
Person(name, age); construct two standalone instances and one created inline within a `root ++> Person(...)` connection.

Demonstrate the edge-creation variations between two people. Define Person, Friend (with a since year), and Colleague (with a department) types, then link Alice and Bob with a plain untyped edge, a typed Friend edge, and a bidirectional typed Colleague edge.

Show how to build a graph chain in a single expression. Define an Item node and Start/Next/End edge types, then create four items and connect them into a chain off the root two ways: once with plain edges and once with the typed Start/Next/End edges.
Item nodes plus Start/Next/End edges; build root->a->b->c->d in one chained expression, both untyped and with typed edges.

Show how to remove nodes and edges from a graph. Link Alice and Bob with a Friend edge, then delete that specific edge and delete Bob. Also include a Cleanup walker that, when it lands on a completed Todo, captures the node's id, deletes the node, and reports what was removed.

Demonstrate deletion in Jac, including from inside a walker. After building an Alice-Bob friendship, delete the edge and then a node. Then write a Cleanup walker that deletes any completed todo it visits and reports its id.

Write a private walker that deletes a todo and all of its children. Given a parent id, it should traverse from the root and delete any Todo node that either is the target or lists the target as its parent.
Private cascade-delete walker(parent_id): from Root visit children and delete each Todo whose jid==parent_id or whose parent_id matches.
Demonstrate the built-in graph utility functions. Create a few Person nodes, then get one node's persistent id, save it, and print the graph starting from the root.
Person nodes; call jid() for a node's id, save() to persist it, and printgraph(root).
Show usage of Jac's built-in graph helpers: after creating some Person nodes, obtain a node's unique id, persist it, and dump the whole graph from the root.
Exercise jid/save/printgraph over a set of Person nodes rooted at root.

Write a walker that traverses a graph of people breadth-first. Starting at the root it announces its position, then at each Person node it prints the name and queues that person's outgoing neighbors for later.
BFSWalker: on Root entry print the start and visit [-->]; on Person entry print the name and queue outgoing neighbors.

Illustrate how node exit abilities fire in reverse order after a depth-first descent. Define a Step node with a label and a Logger walker that prints 'ENTER: <label>' on the way in and 'EXIT: <label>' on the way out, so that along a root->A->B->C chain the exits print C, then B, then A.
Step(label) node; Logger walker printing ENTER on Step entry (then descending) and EXIT on Step exit, demonstrating LIFO deferred exits over a linear chain.

Show a walker whose entry and exit handlers bracket each node. On a linear chain of Step nodes it should log entering each in order and then log exiting them innermost-first, demonstrating deferred exits.
Entry/exit-logging walker over Step nodes showing exits run in reverse (deferred) order relative to entries.
Person(age)/Friend(since); FilteredWalker visiting by node type [?:Person], by Friend edge, and by Friend edge with since>2020 to Person nodes.

I need a traversal demonstrating node-type, edge-type, and combined filtering. Have the walker start at root and, at each person, branch to Person neighbors, Friend-edge neighbors, and Friend-edge-since-2020 Person neighbors.
Filtered traversal walker combining node-type, edge-type, and edge-predicate filters over a Person/Friend graph.
Define a Room node that prints 'Entering room' whenever a Visitor walker arrives and 'Exiting room' when that visitor leaves.
Room node with a Visitor-entry ability printing 'Entering room' and a Visitor-exit ability printing 'Exiting room'.

Put together a reference showing the edge-query syntax in Jac. In a walker over Person nodes, collect all outgoing, incoming, and bidirectional neighbors; neighbors reached via a specific edge type; neighbors filtered by an edge attribute; result nodes filtered by node type; and the edge objects themselves, both untyped and typed.

Traverser walker enumerating edge-reference forms: [-->], [<--], [<-->]; typed [->:EdgeType:->]; an edge-attribute filter; a [?:Person] node filter; and edge-object forms [edge -->] / [edge ->:Friend:->].

Write a walker that demonstrates every way to reference edges and neighbors from a node: outgoing/incoming/both, by edge type, by edge condition, filtering results by node type, and retrieving edge objects rather than nodes.
Walker covering the full edge-reference grammar: direction forms, typed edges, attribute predicates, node-type result filter, and edge-object retrieval.
Graph-query cheat sheet in a walker: neighbor directions, typed traversals, edge conditions, node-type filter, and edge-vs-node selection.

Write a walker that filters connections by attribute. Define a User node (age, status, verified) plus Friend (since) and Link (weight) edges, then from a user gather adult neighbors, active-status neighbors, friends made after 2020, and strongly-weighted links.

User(age, status, verified) plus Friend(since)/Link(weight); Filter walker selecting neighbors by node attribute ([?age>=18], [?status=='active']) and by edge attribute (Friend since>2020, Link weight>0.8).
Create a traversal that applies both node-attribute and edge-attribute filters: pick out adult users, active users, recent friends, and strong links from a user's connections.

Show how to filter graph queries by the attributes of nodes and edges. Given users with age/status and Friend/Link edges carrying since/weight, retrieve adults, active users, post-2020 friends, and high-weight links.
Query patterns filtering on node attributes (age, status) and edge attributes (Friend.since, Link.weight) from a User node.

Write a walker that runs multi-hop and mixed-edge graph queries. From a Person, compute friends-of-friends by chaining two Friend hops, a path that goes across a Friend edge and then a Colleague edge, and a filtered query for friends made before 2020 that land on Person nodes older than 30.

Model a social graph — a Person node with an age, a Friend edge carrying a since-year, and a plain Colleague edge — plus a walker that demonstrates multi-hop chained traversal, mixed edge-type paths, and combined edge/node filtering.

I'm working with a small social graph of people linked by Friend and Colleague edges. Can you write a walker that, starting from a person, gathers their friends-of-friends across two Friend hops, follows a Friend-then-Colleague path, and also pulls people reachable through older Friend edges who are over 30?

Walker over a Person/Friend/Colleague graph: compute friend-of-friend sets via chained Friend hops, traverse mixed Friend->Colleague paths, and filter edges by since<2020 combined with a Person age>30 node filter.
I want to model an animal hierarchy in Jac — a base Animal node with a name, plus Dog and Cat as subtypes — and a walker that greets each animal differently depending on whether it's a dog or a cat.
Define an Animal base node (name) with Dog and Cat subclasses; add a walker whose ability uses per-subtype context blocks to emit a dog-specific and a cat-specific message.
Walker on an Animal-subtype graph (Dog/Cat inherit Animal): dispatch on runtime subtype using typed entry blocks, printing a distinct greeting per subtype.
Create two simple node types that each hold an integer value, plus a walker that can process either kind on entry and print the value it finds.
Two int-valued node types (Node1, Node2); walker with a single ability bound to the union Node1 | Node2 that prints each node's value.

I have two different node types that both carry an integer field. I'd like one walker ability that handles either type when entered and prints its value, instead of writing a separate ability per node type.
Walker ability triggered on a union entry type (Node1 | Node2), reading the shared value field off whichever node it lands on.

Define a data node that carries an integer value and reacts to any walker that visits it by printing which walker type arrived and its current value. Also include a couple of walker types — a plain reader and a writer that carries a new value.
DataNode with an int value and an anonymous entry ability that logs the visiting walker's class name plus the node value; plus Reader and Writer (new_value field) walkers.

In Jac, how do I make a node run the same reaction for every walker that lands on it? I want a node holding a value that, whenever any walker enters, prints the visitor's type and its value — with example reader and writer walkers to trigger it.
Node-side generic entry hook: DataNode reacts to any visitor with a print of type(visitor) and self.value; supply Reader and Writer walker archetypes.

I'm building a shopping-cart traversal. Write a walker that walks over Product nodes and, for each one, prints details specific to its subtype — books show title and author, magazines show title and issue number, electronics show name and warranty — while accumulating the total price and continuing to the next connected product.
Cart walker over Product nodes: per-subtype detail print (Book title/author, Magazine title/issue, Electronics name/warranty), sum price into self.total, then visit forward neighbors.

I need a full CRUD set of walkers for managing Item records attached to the root node: one to create a new item by name, one to list all items, one to update an item's name by its id, and one to delete an item by id. Each should report its result.
Private CRUD walkers for Item under root: create (return new node), list (gather all children), update-by-jid (rename), delete-by-jid (del + confirm), each reporting.

Set up a searchable item catalog: an Item node with a name, a relevance-scoring helper, and a walker that takes a search query, finds items whose name contains it (case-insensitive), scores each match, and reports them sorted by score.
Item node (name) + relevance helper; private SearchItems walker: case-insensitive substring match over child items, build {id,name,score} records, sort desc by score, report.

Write a walker that searches all Item nodes hanging off root for ones whose name contains a given query string (ignoring case), computes a relevance score for each hit, and returns the matches ordered from most to least relevant.
SearchItems walker: traverse root children, filter Items by case-insensitive query substring, attach relevance score, sort matches descending, report on root exit.
I want a full-text-ish search over my Item nodes. Given a query, gather every item whose name includes that text regardless of case, rank them by a relevance score, and hand back the ranked list.
Write a walker that scans all Todo nodes connected to root and reports summary statistics — the total count, how many are completed, how many are still pending, and the completion percentage.
Stats walker over Todo children: tally total and completed, report totals plus pending and completion_rate (guard divide-by-zero).
Using Jac's client-side syntax, create two small UI components: a Greeting that displays 'Hello, <name>!' from its props, and a Counter button that increments a count each time it's clicked.
Client components: Greeting(props) rendering an h1 from props.name; Counter with local int state and an onClick lambda that increments, shown in a button.
Show me how to put both a server-side and a client-side function in the same Jac file — for example a simple add(a, b) that runs on the server and a greet(name) that runs on the client.
Single codespace: server def add(int,int)->int, plus a client-marked def greet(str)->str returning a greeting.
Build a minimal todo API in Jac: define a Todo node with a title and a done flag, then expose public walkers to add a todo, list all todos, and a health check.
Todo node (title, done=False); public walkers: add_todo (create + report), list_todos (filter Todo children), health (status ok).
I need public endpoints for a todo app: one that creates a todo from a title, one that returns all todos, and a simple health check. Include the Todo node definition.
Public walker endpoints over root: add_todo(title), list_todos returning title/done dicts, and health — backed by a Todo node.
Create a task-management backend: a Task node with a title and done status, plus public walkers to fetch all tasks (with their ids) and to add a new task.
Task node (title, done); public walkers get_tasks (list id/title/done) and add_task(title) attaching to root.
Public endpoints: get_tasks (map Task children to id/title/done) and add_task(title) -> new Task on root, reporting the created record.
Define a public search endpoint walker for users that accepts a search query along with pagination parameters — a result limit and a page number with sensible defaults.
Public search_users walker declaring query plus paginated limit (default 10) and page (default 1) parameters.
I just need the signature for a user-search endpoint: it should take a query string and support paging via a limit and a page number, defaulting to 10 per page starting at page 1.
Paginated query endpoint stub: search_users(query, limit=10, page=1) as a public walker.
Write a public walker that looks up a single user by id among the users connected to root, returning their id, name and email — or an error object if no user matches.
get_user(user_id) walker: linear scan of User children, return id/name/email on match else {error: not found}.
Two walkers: save_state dumps User/Post node dicts to state.json via json; load_state reads it, rebuilds User nodes on root, catching FileNotFoundError.
Write a walker that reads configuration from environment variables and reports it — the database URL (with a sqlite default), an API key, and a debug flag parsed as a boolean.
Public health walker returning {status: healthy}.
Readiness walker: probe database and cache; report ready if both ok else not_ready with per-dependency booleans.

Build a complete user-management API in Jac. Define a User node holding name, email and a creation timestamp, then provide public endpoints to list users, get one by id, create a user, update a user's name/email, delete a user, and a health check.
User node (name/email/created_at) with full CRUD public walkers — list, get-by-id, create (timestamped), update (partial), delete — plus a health endpoint using datetime.

I need a full set of user endpoints backed by the graph: list all users, fetch a single user by id, create a new one with a timestamp, update an existing user's fields, delete by id, and a health check. Each should return JSON-friendly data.
CRUD walker suite over User children of root: list_users, get_user(id), create_user(name,email)+timestamp, update_user (partial name/email), delete_user(id), health.
Define a simple Task node type that stores a name and a priority level.
Node schema: Task { name: str; priority: int }.
Declare a Task node carrying a name and an int priority.

Write the main module for a task app that imports a models module and a utils module. It should have a walker that validates a given title, and if valid creates a Task node, generates a description for it, and prints both — otherwise warns the title is too short. Kick it off from an entry block.
Entry-point module importing models/utils: TaskCreator(title) walker — validate title, on success attach models.Task and print the generated description, else warn; spawn from with entry.
Define a Task node with a title and a done flag that defaults to false, and give it a docstring.
Documented Task node: title (str), done (bool, default False).

I have legacy Python validation logic I want to keep verbatim. Show me a Jac app that embeds that Python inline — functions to validate a title and return a sample task — alongside a Jac description generator and a walker that uses the inline Python functions to validate and create a task.
App mixing an inline ::py:: block (legacy validate_title + get_sample_task) with a Jac generate_desc; TaskCreator walker calls the inline Python to validate then create a models.Task.

Write the main Jac module for a task app that imports a Python models module and a Python validators module. The walker should validate the incoming title through the validators module, and on success create a Task, generate a description, and print the result; otherwise warn the title is too short.
Entry module importing Python models + validators: TaskCreator(title) calls validators.validate_title, then creates models.Task and prints generate_desc output, else warns.
Create a Jac module that defines a Task node with title and done, a walker that creates a task and prints it, and a helper that generates a task description from a title.
Module: Task node (title, done); TaskCreator(title) walker attaching a Task and printing it; generate_desc(title) helper.
I want a walker that takes a title, creates a Task node connected to the current node, and prints a confirmation — plus the Task node definition and a description-generating helper function.
TaskCreator walker: create Task(title) via here ++>, print confirmation; include the Task node and a generate_desc helper.
Set up a small graph module with a Task node, a walker that adds a new task off the current node and confirms it, and a function that produces a description string for a title.
Graph module with Task node + TaskCreator walker (attach + print) + generate_desc(title) function.

Build a complete single-file full-stack todo app in Jac with AI categorization. Define a Todo with a title, category and done flag plus a Category enum, use an LLM to categorize each new todo, expose server functions to add and fetch todos, and render a client component with a text input, an Add button, and the list of todos showing their category.
One-file full-stack AI todo: Todo node + Category enum, categorize(title) by llm(), add_todo/get_todos server defs, and a cl app component (input + Enter/Add handlers + rendered list with category).

Show me how to let an LLM decide which tools to call. I have a get_weather function and a search_web function; I want an answer_question function whose body is handled by the LLM, free to invoke either tool as needed to answer.
LLM tool-use: expose get_weather and search_web, then define answer_question(question) by llm(tools=[get_weather, search_web]).
Define a Todo node with a title and a done flag, and in an entry block attach one to root so it's automatically persisted.
Todo node (title, done=False); entry block connecting a persisted Todo('Learn Jac') to root.
Write a client component that reads an API URL from a Vite environment variable and displays it in a div.
Client app component rendering import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL inside a div.
Client import block: react hooks (useState/useEffect/useCallback), @tanstack/react-query (useQuery, useMutation), lodash (debounce, throttle), axios default.
Define a Counter node holding a count and a walker that increments it by a configurable amount as it traverses. Include tests verifying the default increment of one and a custom amount.
Counter node (count) + Incrementer walker (amount=1) incrementing on Counter entry; add tests for the default and amount=5.

Write a walker that walks from root to a Counter node and adds a configurable amount to its count, defaulting to one. Add a couple of tests confirming it increments correctly for the default and a custom amount.
Incrementer walker (amount, default 1): visit root children, add amount to Counter.count; include tests asserting count==1 and count==5.
Define a Person node with a name and age, and a walker that reports everyone aged 18 or over. Include a test that sets up a few people and checks only the adults are returned.
Person node (name, age) + FindAdults walker reporting age>=18; test asserting two adults from a three-person setup.
FindAdults walker reporting Person children with age>=18; test verifies report count and adult names, excludes the minor.
Model rooms connected by doors — a Room node with a name and a Door edge — and write a test that builds a kitchen-living-bedroom chain and verifies the connections and reachability between rooms.
Room node + Door edge; test wiring kitchen->living->bedroom, asserting per-node out-degree and Door reachability.
Connectivity test: Room/Door graph in a linear chain; assert [node -->] counts and membership via [x ->:Door:->].
Illustrate test-naming conventions in Jac — show a couple of tests with clear, descriptive names alongside examples of vague, cryptic names to avoid.
Contrast readable test names with poor ones: empty tests demonstrating good descriptive naming vs vague names like 't1'/'thing'.
Show the difference between good and bad test names in Jac — write a few empty test blocks with descriptive names and a few with unclear names as examples of what not to do.
Test-naming style demo: descriptive test titles vs cryptic ones (t1, thing) as an anti-pattern.
Write tests for a process() function covering the key cases — an empty list, a single-element list, and a large thousand-element list — asserting the expected output size for each.
Tests for process(): empty list -> empty, single item -> len 1, 1000-item list -> len 1000.
Define a Person node with a name, age, and a greet() method, then in an entry block create a couple of people and use them like ordinary objects — calling greet() and reading fields.
Person node with name/age and a greet() method; entry block instantiating two Persons and using them as plain objects (method call + field access).
Create a few Person nodes and wire up a small graph — connect a couple of them to root, and connect one person to another.
Define a Person node and a typed Knows edge that records the year two people met and how close they are, then connect two people with it.
Person node + Knows edge (since:int, strength:str); connect alice->bob with Knows(since=2020, strength='close').

Show the basic graph queries in Jac — build a small graph of people connected to root and to each other, then query the nodes connected to root, the ones connected to a specific person, and filter results by node type.
Person graph: root->alice, alice->bob/carol; demonstrate [root -->], [alice -->], and type-filtered [root -->][?:Person] queries.

I'm learning graph traversal queries. Set up people connected to root and to each other, then show how to get everything connected to root, everything connected to one person, and how to keep only the Person nodes.
Neighbor-query patterns over a Person graph: forward connections from root and from a node, plus [?:Person] type filtering.

Put together a reference of Jac's graph query syntax — using Person nodes and a Knows edge, show forward, backward and bidirectional connection queries, filtering by node type and by edge type, and a chained friends-of-friends traversal.
Person/Knows schema with a function cataloguing query forms: -->, <--, <-->, [?:Person], ->:Knows:->, combined edge+node filter, and chained two-hop traversal.

Give me a rundown of the different ways to query a graph in Jac. With people linked by Knows edges, demonstrate outgoing, incoming and both-direction queries, type filtering on nodes and edges, and a two-hop friends-of-friends chain.
Enumerate graph-query patterns: directional (-->/<--/<-->), node type filter, Knows-edge filter, edge+node combined, and chained ->:Knows:-> ->:Knows:->.

Define a Person node with a name and a visited flag, and a Greeter walker that starts at root, visits connected people, greets each by name and marks them visited. Set up a small graph and spawn the walker.
Person node (name, visited=False) + Greeter walker: from root visit neighbors, greet each Person and set visited=True; entry builds alice->bob and spawns.

Write a walker that begins at root, travels to the connected people, prints a greeting for each, and flags them as visited. Include the node definition and an entry block that builds the graph and runs the walker.
Greeter walker: root entry visits children, Person entry prints greeting and marks visited; entry wires a two-node chain and spawns at root.
Define a Room node and an Explorer walker that walks through connected rooms, counting how many it has visited and printing a running tally as it goes.
Room node + Explorer walker (rooms_visited counter): on each Room increment, print progress, then visit forward neighbors.
