Write a walker that explores a series of connected rooms, keeping a count of how many rooms it has entered and printing which room it's in along with the running total, continuing to the next room each time.
Explorer walker traversing a Room chain: increment rooms_visited per entry, print current room + count, recurse via visit [-->].

Define a Person node with a name and age, and a walker that traverses from root through the connected people, reporting everyone 18 or older. In an entry block, create a few people, run the walker, and print how many adults were found along with their names.

I want to keep a small set of people in a graph and then pull out all the adults. Each person has a name and an age. Write a walker that starts at the root, visits every connected person, gathers the ones who are 18 and up, and then reports back how many adults there were and lists their names.
Given Person nodes (name, age) hung off root, implement a traversal that reports each person whose age is at least 18; the driver should print the adult count and their names.

Suppose several people are connected to the root, each with a name and age. I need a walker that searches through them and stops the moment it finds the first adult (18 or older), reporting only that one person, then prints that first adult's name.
Person(name, age) nodes off root; walk them in order and return only the first adult (age >= 18), halting traversal immediately on the match. Print that person's name.
Traversal over root's Person children that short-circuits on the first node with age >= 18, reporting it and disengaging. Driver prints the found name.

I'm learning how walkers react to different node types. Create a walker that behaves differently depending on where it is: one message when it's spawned at the root, another when it lands on a Person node (printing that person's name), and a fallback for any other kind of node it visits, continuing to move outward through the graph in every case.

Walker with three entry abilities — Root entry announcing start, Person entry printing the name, and a catch-all default entry for any other node type — each continuing outward via visit. Include a Person node with name/age and a data field on the walker.

Show me how a single walker can have separate handlers per node type: one that prints a message when it starts at root, one that prints the person's name when it reaches a Person, and a generic one for any node type it doesn't specifically handle, all while continuing to traverse.

Build a tiny social graph where users follow each other. Each user has a username and an optional bio, and a follow relationship records the year it started. I need two walkers: one that, starting from a given user, finds everyone who follows them, and another that finds their mutual follows (people they follow who follow them back). Set up a few users with one-way and two-way follows, then print Alice's followers and her mutual follows.

User(username, bio) nodes with a Follows(since) edge. Provide two User-entry walkers: one reporting inbound followers, one reporting mutuals (intersection of outbound and inbound follows). Seed alice/bob/carol with mixed follows and print alice's followers and mutuals.

Model a follow-based social network and write the traversal logic to answer two questions about any user: who follows them, and which of those are mutual. Users have a username and bio; follow edges carry a start date. After wiring up a small example, print one user's follower list and their mutual connections.

Show me how a walker collects multiple reported values. Write a private walker that runs at the root and reports two separate strings, then spawn it and print the full list of everything it reported so I can see them come back in order.
Private root-entry walker that emits two reports; spawn it and print the resulting reports list to show ordered accumulation.

I have Task nodes each with a title and a done flag. Write a walker that takes a task id, searches out from the root for the matching task, flips its done status, and reports the updated task back, using a typed report channel so the caller receives a real Task object. Once found, it should stop searching.

Task(title, done) nodes; walker parameterized by task_id with a typed reports: list[Task] channel. Search from root, match on jid(here), toggle done, report the node, disengage. Consumer reads reports[0] as a Task.

Write a walker that toggles a single to-do item's completion by its id. It should walk out from the root, locate the task whose id matches, invert its done field, hand the updated task back as a typed result, and quit once it's handled that one.
Typed toggle traversal: given a task_id, find the Task by jid, flip done, report the typed node into a list[Task] channel, and disengage on the match.

I need a walker that grabs all the Task nodes hanging off the root in one step and returns them as a typed list, reporting the filtered collection at once, and shows pulling that list back out of the result type-safely.
Root-entry walker reporting [-->][?:Task] in a single shot; consumer extracts reports[0] as list[Task].

Given a set of Item nodes each holding a string, write a walker that gathers every item's data into one list as it traverses, then reports that whole list a single time when it finishes back at the root, ending up with one clean report rather than many small ones.
Item(data) nodes; accumulation walker that appends each item's data during traversal and emits a single typed report of the full list on Root exit.

Show the accumulate-then-report pattern: as the walker visits each Item node it should stash the item's string into an internal list, and only once it's finished walking should it report the complete list in one go.
Single-report collection walker: buffer Item.data across the traversal into an instance list, then report it once at Root exit as list[str].

I want a search walker over Item nodes, where each item has a name. Given a search term, the walker should visit all the items and report each one whose name contains that term (one report per match) so the caller gets back a typed list of matching items.
Item(name) nodes; walker taking a search_term with a typed list[Item] reports channel, reporting each item whose name contains the term, one report per match.

Write a walker that filters items by a substring: it takes a search string, walks all the Item nodes off root, and reports each item individually whenever its name includes that string, returning the matches as a typed list.
Report-per-node search: for each Item entry, if search_term is a substring of name, report the typed node; results accumulate into list[Item].

I need a walker that creates a new Item node with a given name, attaches it to the current node, and then reports the freshly created item back as a typed Item so it can be read directly off the result.

Write a walker that performs a create operation and returns the result: given a name, make a new Item node connected to where it starts, and report that new item so whoever spawned it receives the created object.
Operation-plus-result walker: create Item(name) off root and report the created node, typed for hydration on the client side.

Show me how one walker can spawn another and use its results. Write an outer walker that, when it runs at the root, creates and spawns an inner walker, lets the inner one compute a value into its own attribute, and then reports a combined result that pulls in that inner walker's data.
Nested spawn pattern: OuterWalker spawns InnerWalker at root, then reads inner.result off the instance and reports a dict combining outer and inner data.

I'd like a walker that does some processing and returns both the detailed results and a summary. It takes an input string, runs it through a helper that produces a list of results, reports those raw results first, and then reports a second summary object with the count and a status. Show reading each report back separately.
Walker emitting two ordered reports: first the raw list from a processing helper, then a summary dict of count and status. Consumer indexes reports[0] and reports[1].

Show me the safe ways to read a walker's reports without crashing on missing data. After spawning a simple walker that reports a value, demonstrate defensively pulling out the first report with a fallback, guarding index access when expecting more than one report, and iterating over all reports even when the list might be empty.
Illustrate defensive .reports access: guarded single-report read with a default, length-checked multi-report access, and safe iteration over a possibly-empty reports list.
Show the anti-pattern versus the fix for returning a created node: manual dict construction that drops typing, versus reporting the typed object and letting the runtime serialize it.

Demonstrate why a server endpoint should return a typed object instead of a hand-assembled dict. Show a get_task function written the bad way, packing the task's fields into a dict, next to the good version that simply returns the Task itself so the client receives a properly hydrated instance.
Contrast dict-return versus typed-return for a public get_task endpoint: a manual id/title/done dict versus returning the Task so the client gets a hydrated instance.

Show the difference between reporting inside a loop and accumulating first. Given Item nodes with data, contrast a walker that reports each item separately (producing lots of tiny reports) with a better one that collects all the items into a list as it traverses and reports that list just once when it exits at the root.
Anti-pattern versus fix over Item nodes: per-node report producing N reports, versus accumulate-into-a-list and a single report on Root exit.

Illustrate why accumulating beats reporting in a loop. Write two walkers over the same Item nodes: a bad one that fires a report for every node, and a good one that appends each node's data to an internal list and reports the whole thing only once at the end.

I have a walker that reports a list of items and then a metadata object as two separate reports. Show me how to consume those results clearly: instead of relying on bare magic indices, document what each report position means and read them defensively with sensible defaults when a position might be missing.

Put together a minimal full-stack Jac slice for todos: a persistent Todo node on the server with a title and done flag, a public server function that creates a new todo off the root and returns its id and title, and a client component with an Add button that awaits that server call and appends the returned todo to its local list.
Server Todo(title, done) node plus a public add_todo(title) endpoint returning id and title; client component with an Add button that awaits add_todo and appends the result to reactive state.

Show the different ways to query nodes connected to the root: grab everything connected from root as a list, then narrow to only nodes of a particular type (Task), and finally filter further to Tasks that aren't done yet.
Root outbound queries: all children as a list, type-filtered to Task, and field-filtered to Task where done == False.
Give me a few examples of reading the graph from the root: collecting all connected nodes, keeping only the Task nodes, and then keeping only the pending (not done) tasks.
Demonstrate progressive edge-query filtering off root: unfiltered, by node type Task, and by the Task done == False predicate.

Define a typed edge that carries scheduling info (a time and a priority), connect the root to a task through it, and then query for the urgent tasks by filtering on that edge's priority being at least 3.
Scheduled(time, priority) edge; connect root to a Task through it and query Tasks reachable via Scheduled edges where priority >= 3.

I want to attach extra data to my graph connections and query on it. Create an edge type holding a time and a priority, link a task off the root using it, and then pull back only the tasks reached through high-priority (3 or above) scheduled edges.
Filter a traversal by edge attribute: query Task nodes across Scheduled edges constrained to priority >= 3.
Write a simple object type called Foo that holds an integer field defaulting to zero and has a method taking an integer and returning it plus one.
obj Foo with an int field defaulting to 0 and a method(val: int) -> int returning val + 1.
Create a walker that, whenever it enters one of your custom nodes, reports that node's value and then keeps walking outward to the nodes connected from it.
Walker with an ability on MyNode entry that reports here.value and continues via visit [-->].
I need a walker that traverses a graph reporting each node's value as it goes: on entering a node it should report the node's value field, then move on to whatever that node connects to.
obj Foo declaration: an int field defaulting to 0 plus an unimplemented method signature my_method(val: int) -> int, with the body deferred to an impl file.
Write an object type Foo with an integer field, and give it a constructor that takes an int, calls the parent initializer, and stores the value into the field.
obj Foo with an int field and a def init(x) that calls super.init() then assigns self.x.
Write a function that takes a list and appends the number 42 to it, mutating the caller's list in place.
Function modify(data: list) -> None appending 42 to the passed list, mutating it in place by reference.
Give me an object type with a static method that takes no arguments and just returns 42.
obj with a static def bar() -> int returning 42.
Write a plain top-level function named bar that takes nothing and returns the integer 42.
Module-level def bar() -> int returning 42.
Create a basic walker whose ability fires when it enters a node and simply continues on to all the nodes connected outward from it.
Walker with a Node-entry ability that just visits [-->].
Define an edge type that carries a floating-point weight, defaulting to 1.0.
edge MyEdge with a float weight field defaulting to 1.0.
Nodes A(value: int) and B(label: str); instantiate one of each and link a to b with a default edge.
Two node archetypes (A with an int value, B with a str label); build instances and connect them with the default edge operator.
Write a client-side component called Greeting that takes props and renders an h1 saying hello to the name passed in through those props.
Client Greeting(props) component rendering an h1 greeting props.name, inside a cl block.
In a client file, write a Greeting component that accepts props and displays a level-one heading greeting the provided name.
In a .cl.jac file, a public Greeting(props) component returning an h1 that greets props.name, with no explicit cl block needed.
Build a counter button component: it should keep a count in reactive state starting at zero, show the current count as its label, and increment that count each time it's clicked.

Write a todo list component that manages its items in reactive state, where adding an item creates a brand-new list with the entry appended and removing an item builds a new filtered list, so that reassigning the list reference triggers a re-render each time.
TodoApp with reactive has todos; add by building a new list with the item appended and remove via a filtering comprehension, always replacing the list immutably to trigger re-render.

Create a timer component that counts up every second. When it mounts it should start an interval that bumps a seconds counter, when it unmounts it should clear that interval, and it should display the current seconds count.
Timer component using can with entry to start a 1-second setInterval incrementing seconds and can with exit to clearInterval; renders the seconds value.

Write a client component that loads and displays a user's tasks on mount. It should import the server-side get_tasks walker, spawn it against the root when the component mounts, pull the task list out of the reports, and render each task's title as a list item.
Client TaskList: on async mount, invoke the imported get_tasks walker via root() spawn, take reports[0] into reactive tasks, and render each title as a list item.

I need an async click handler on the client that adds a new task. It should call the imported add_task walker via root() spawn with a title, and if the walker reports back a created task, append that task to the current list.
Async handler invoking the add_task walker with root() spawn and a title, appending reports[0] to the tasks list when present.
Write a public walker endpoint named get_tasks that fetches all the Task nodes connected to the root and reports them.
Expose a public server endpoint as a walker that, when run, gathers every Task hanging off the root and returns them to the caller.
walker:pub get_tasks reporting the root's Task children.
Write a private walker named create_task that takes a title, creates a new Task node off the root with that title, and reports the created task.
Private walker create_task(title): connect a new Task off the current node and report it.
Create a private, per-user server endpoint (a walker) that accepts a task title, adds a corresponding Task node under the root, and returns the newly created task.
walker:priv create_task with a title field; create a Task off root and report the new node.

Show the difference between a public and a private server function: one that anybody can call returning a simple status object, and one that's private so each user automatically only ever sees their own data.
Two endpoints: a public get_status() returning an ok status, and a private get_user_data() that is per-user isolated.
I want a pair of server endpoints: a public health-check-style function returning an ok status, and a private one that returns user-specific data with automatic per-user isolation.
def:pub get_status returning a status object alongside def:priv get_user_data returning per-user data.
Write a public create_task walker where the title field is filled in automatically from the incoming request body, and whatever it reports (the newly created Task node) becomes the response body.
Public create_task walker: the title has-field is bound to the request body, and the reported new Task becomes the response.
Create a private walker that returns the current user's tasks. Since it's private, querying the Task nodes off the root should automatically be scoped to just that logged-in user's data.
walker:priv get_my_tasks reporting the root's Task children, relying on automatic per-user data isolation.
Add an About page to a file-based-routed client app: a page component that renders a heading reading About Us.
File-routed pages/about.jac exporting a page() component that renders an h1 reading About Us.
Write a layout component for a routed app that renders shared chrome like a nav bar and then drops in the current child page using the Outlet component from the runtime.
Layout component importing Outlet from @jac/runtime; renders a nav plus the Outlet element for child pages.

Write a Person object with a name, an age, and an optional email. Give it a method that returns a friendly greeting including the name and age, and another that reports whether the person is an adult. Then create a person and print both the greeting and their adult status.
obj Person with name, age, and an optional email field; add greet() -> str and is_adult() -> bool (age >= 18), then instantiate one and print both.

Model cities connected by roads as a graph (each city has a name and population, each road a distance), then write a walker that explores outward from the root, recording and printing each city it visits along with its population. Build a small chain of a few cities linked by roads and run the explorer over it.

City(name, population) nodes joined by Road(distance) edges; an Explorer walker that logs visited city names and prints each with its population while traversing outward. Seed a 3-city chain and spawn from root.
Graph-traversal walker over a City/Road network that accumulates visited city names and prints name and population per node; demo on a seeded 3-city chain.

Build a graph of cities and roads (cities with a name and population, roads with a distance) and write a walker that walks it from the root, visiting each connected city, noting its name, and printing the city with its population.

Set up the data model and initial graph for a social network: a User node with a username and bio, a Follows edge that records when the follow began, and a Blocks edge with a reason. Create a few users and wire up several follow relationships between them, each with its start date.

Model a social graph in Jac: a User node holding a username and an optional bio, plus two typed edge kinds — Follows, which records the date the follow began, and Blocks, which records a reason. Seed three users and wire a handful of dated follow relationships between them.

I want to set up a small social network in Jac. Define a user type that stores a username and an optional bio, add relationship kinds for following (recording when it started) and blocking (with a reason), then create a few sample users and connect some of them as followers.

Sketch a follower-graph seed script in Jac: a User archetype with username/bio fields, separate Follows and Blocks edge types, and an entry block that instantiates alice, bob and carol and links them together with dated follow edges.

Show me the different ways to write import statements in Jac — pulling specific names out of a package or module, importing a whole module by itself, grabbing things from the Python standard library, and doing a relative import from a sibling submodule.

Reference snippet covering every Jac import form: selective `import from` off a package, the same against stdlib modules (os/pathlib/typing/collections), a plain whole-module import, and a relative import from a submodule.

Create a couple of enums in Jac — one for colors where each member has an explicit string value, and one for compass directions with plain auto-valued members — and write a function that takes a color and returns a sentence describing it using that member's value.
Demonstrate Jac enums: a string-valued Color enum, a bare-member Direction enum, and a helper that formats a given Color through its `.value`.

I need a small client component in Jac: a counter with a text input. Track the input's value in state, and give it a plus button that bumps the count. Show 'Start clicking!' before any clicks and 'Clicks: N' afterward, and reset the count once when the component first mounts.

Build a client component for a single book entry that shows its title next to a delete button. It receives the book's id, its title, and a delete callback as props, and clicking the button should invoke that callback with the book's id.
BookCard component — props are bookId, title, and an onDelete callback; render the title plus an X button whose handler calls onDelete(bookId).
ItemList(items): early-out empty state when the list is empty, otherwise an <h2> followed by an enumerated <li> per item, each keyed by index and class-toggled on its done flag.

Write a reusable state hook in Jac for managing a list of items, and define the Item node it works with. The hook should hold the items and a loading flag, flip loading off when it mounts, expose a handler that appends a new item, and return the items, the loading state, and that add handler bundled together.
Define an Item node (name field) plus a `useItems` hook returning {items, loading, handleAdd}: an items list and a loading flag, a mount effect clearing loading, and an append-only add handler.

Set up two page components for a Jac client app: a login page with a button that programmatically navigates to the dashboard, and a dashboard page that is protected — if the visitor is not logged in, redirect them to the login route instead of rendering.

Two routed pages using @jac/runtime helpers: a LoginPage with an imperative useNavigate handler to /dashboard, and a guarded DashboardPage that redirects to /login via <Navigate replace> when jacIsLoggedIn() is false.
cn utility: variadic `*inputs`, returns twMerge(clsx(inputs)); pulls clsx and tailwind-merge in as npm imports.

Wire up the top-level client entry for a Jac app: import the shared API types and server functions from the recipe service, then inside a client block pull in the global stylesheet and the AppShell component and expose an `app` component that just renders AppShell.
App root: import the recipe service's types and endpoints, then in a `cl` block import the global CSS and AppShell and export `app()` returning <AppShell/>.

Show how to call a native C library from Jac: declare the foreign functions from a raylib shared object (window init, the should-close check, the vertex and color calls, and window close) with their C signatures, then open an 800x600 window and run a render loop until it is asked to close.

FFI against libraylib.so — declare InitWindow/WindowShouldClose/rlVertex3f/rlColor4ub/CloseWindow with typed C signatures, then an entry block driving the usual open-window, render-loop, close sequence.

Using Jac's graph features, create Person nodes joined by a Follows edge, connect a few people, then demonstrate the ways to query outgoing connections: every outgoing node, only those reached through a specific edge type, results filtered by node type, and results filtered by a node-field value — printing the names from each.

Person/Follows graph demo exercising the edge-reference query forms: unfiltered `[-->]`, edge-typed traversal, a `[?:Person]` node-type filter, and a `[?name == ...]` field predicate — print the names from each.

Show the import section for a Jac page that uses shadcn-style UI components — buttons, cards, dropdown menus, dialogs and tables from the local components folder — plus the cn helper from lib/utils and a set of icons pulled in as npm client imports.

Give me a few examples of using icons with the jac-shadcn buttons: an inline icon on its own, an icon-only button, and applying button styling directly to a Radix dropdown trigger via buttonVariants without a forwardRef.
Three hugeicons usage patterns: a standalone <HugeiconsIcon>, an icon-only <Button size="icon">, and a DropdownMenuTrigger styled by calling buttonVariants({variant, size}) directly.
Write a tiny client component that renders a warning banner, using the project's semantic warning color tokens for its background and text.
WarningAlert component — a div styled with the bg-warning and text-warning-foreground tokens.

Build an events listing page for a Jac app. While data is loading show a centered spinner; once loaded, render a header with a 'New Event' button that opens a create-event dialog, and below it a card holding a table of events with their name and a status badge, looping over the events to fill the rows.

EventListPage: a loading→Spinner guard, then a header with a Dialog-wrapped 'New Event' button and a Card>Table of events (name plus a status Badge) rendered from an events list; the async mount effect flips loading off.

Show the difference between public and per-user data in Jac by writing Todo endpoints: a public one that counts every Todo hanging off the shared root, and private ones — scoped to the calling user's own graph — that list that user's todos and add a new one.

I am trying to understand data scoping in a Jac backend. Define a Todo type, then give me an endpoint returning the total number of todos everyone shares alongside login-scoped endpoints that only see the current user's todos and let them create one.
Contrast shared versus per-user roots on a Todo node: a public total-count endpoint plus private per-caller list and create endpoints.

Write a full set of CRUD endpoints in Jac for a todo-style Item (a title plus a done flag): public functions to list all items, add one, toggle an item's done state by id, and delete by id; a login-required function returning the current user's items; and an internal helper kept off the API by its leading underscore.

I need server functions for managing items in a Jac app, where each item has a title and a done flag. Expose public operations to fetch the list, create an item, flip its completion by id and remove it by id; add a private endpoint for a logged-in user's own items; and include a helper that must not become a callable endpoint.
Backend endpoints over an Item node: public read/create/toggle/delete keyed by jid, one authenticated per-user list, plus a non-exported `_`-prefixed helper.

Build a mini social backend in Jac. Give each user a Profile and let them post Tweets, connecting each tweet to the profile with a Posted edge and granting it connect permission so other users can read it. Then add an endpoint that assembles a global feed by scanning every user's root and collecting the tweets they have shared.

Add a simple role check to a Jac backend: an Account node carrying a role, a private helper reporting whether the current user is an admin, and a privileged endpoint that refuses to run for non-admins and otherwise proceeds with its work.
Role gate: an Account(role) node, an `is_admin()` helper checking the caller's account, and an admin-only endpoint returning 'forbidden' unless is_admin() passes.

Model a blog in Jac with User and Post nodes joined by a Wrote edge, and write endpoints covering the whole lifecycle: create a post authored by a given user, list the posts a user wrote by traversing those edges, filter to only the published ones, count all posts, and publish a post by id.
User/Post/Wrote blog endpoints: create (typed Wrote edge), read posts-by-user via edge traversal, a published-only field filter, a count, and a publish-by-jid update.

Write a Jac walker that searches a graph for nodes matching a target name. Set up an Item node that greets any arriving search walker, and a Finder walker that starts at root, visits outward, collects the items whose name matches its target, and reports them — then spawn it and print the matches.

Item node (name) with a Finder-triggered ability, plus a Finder walker (target, matches) that fans out from root, collecting and `report`ing name-matching items; the entry block spawns it and prints the matches.

I want to see how walkers traverse a graph in Jac. Create some Item nodes under root, then write a walker that carries a target name, walks the outgoing nodes, gathers every item whose name equals the target into a list and emits them as reports — and have the node print a greeting whenever the walker arrives.

Graph-search walker: from Root visit the neighbors, and on each Item compare here.name against the walker's target, appending and reporting the matches; the node ability prints on visit. Spawn from root and inspect `.matches`.

ActivityFeed(events, status): fold the event stream into think/tool/event rows — consecutive reasoning merged into one live-by-default collapsible, each tool call into a closed-by-default row filled by its following tool_result, phase/error as terminal rows — with per-row expand toggles, a live dot on the trailing think block, and auto-scroll to bottom.

Create the chat panel for an agent app in Jac. Derive its message list from the shared event feed — the user, answer, system and error events — so it stays in sync with the rest of the UI. Stream the agent's answer in token by token with a live cursor on the reply still in progress, show a status badge (working / stopping / done / idle), and give it a composer textarea that sends on Enter but not Shift+Enter and offers a Stop button while a turn runs.

Conversation pane: filter events down to user/answer/system/error messages and render them as bubbles with a live cursor on the last streaming answer, a status Badge (working/stopping/done/idle), and a composer that sends on Enter (Shift+Enter for a newline), swapping Send for Stop/Stopping while busy.

I need a panel that displays an agent's session ledger — the durable cross-phase memory it writes. It receives a ledger object holding a list of phase change summaries and a list of free-form notes. Render each change as a row with its phase and summary, each note as its own row, show an entry count in the header, fall back to an empty message when there is nothing yet, and auto-scroll to the latest entry as it grows.

Write a client component that shows an agent's running ledger. Given an object with a `.changes` list of phase/summary pairs and a `.notes` list of strings, list every change and note, display how many entries there are, handle the empty case gracefully, and keep the view scrolled to the newest row whenever the count changes.

Give me a scrollable ledger pane for an agent session. It takes the ledger — which may be missing — pulls out its change summaries (each tagged with a phase) and its plain-text notes, renders both as labeled rows under a header that counts them, shows a placeholder when empty, and scrolls to the bottom as new entries arrive.
Ledger panel component: map a nullable ledger's `.changes` and `.notes` into keyed rows, show the total entry count, provide an empty fallback, and auto-scroll on growth.

Build a phase-inspector panel for an agent's state graph. Given the list of graph nodes, the id of the selected one, and that phase's fetched context, find the selected node and display its role prompt, its description, the tools it exposes, and the messages from its captured context (each with a role, a body, and any tool calls). Show a prompt to pick a node when nothing is selected, and a 'no context yet' note when the phase has not run.

PhaseInspector(nodes, selected, context): look up the selected GraphNode and render its description, role (sem) and tools, then its PhaseContext messages (role, content, tool-call chips); include empty states for no-selection and no-captured-context, guarding every field on a possibly-None context.

I want a detail panel that inspects one node of an agent's phase graph. It should locate the node whose id matches the current selection, then lay out that phase's role/system prompt, its short blurb, the tool names it can use, and the conversation messages it last worked with — handling both the no-node-selected and the phase-never-ran cases.

State-inspector component: match the selected id against the traced nodes, surface the role prompt, description and exposed tools plus the fetched context messages (role, pre-formatted body, tool-call chips); render distinct empty states with every read None-guarded.

Create a component that shows everything about one selected phase in an agent's graph — its role instructions, a description, the tools it offers, and a transcript of the messages it accumulated on its last run. It gets all the nodes, the selected id, and the per-click context object (which can be absent), and needs sensible fallbacks for the unselected and never-run cases.

Phase detail pane: from (nodes, selected, context) find the node, print its sem/desc/tools and the context.messages transcript with per-message tool chips; guard the nullable context and cover both the no-selection and no-context states.

I need a draggable divider component in Jac for resizing panes. It reports a cumulative drag delta to its parent via an onResize callback — the horizontal delta when it sits between side-by-side panes, the vertical delta when between stacked ones. Measure the delta from the pointer's position at mousedown, attach the move/up listeners to the window so dragging keeps working past the thin gutter, and suppress page text selection while dragging.

ResizeHandle(vertical, onResize): on mousedown capture the start clientX/Y, add window mousemove/mouseup listeners reporting the cumulative delta (X when vertical, else Y) to onResize, toggle a body 'resizing' class, and remove the listeners on mouseup.

Create a footer stats bar for an agent UI that summarizes the latest turn, matching the numbers the CLI prints: the active phase, elapsed time, a tool count broken into reads/writes/runs, files changed, token usage in and out (compacting big counts like 12400 to '12.4k'), cost, generation throughput, and a project-health chip — each piece appearing only when it has data, with a 'no turns yet' hint before the first run.

Build a live token-usage panel showing one row per model call, newest last. For each call display the phase it belongs to, input tokens with a magnitude bar scaled against the largest call this turn so an oversized prompt stands out, output tokens, cache read/created counts, and latency. Compact large token counts, let a row be clicked to select it for detail, mark the panel live while running, and auto-scroll to the newest row.

TokenStream(events, live, selected, onSelect): filter to 'call' events and render a row per call — phase chip, input tokens with a bar normalized to the turn's max, output, cache read/create, latency — k-compacting the counts, highlighting the click-selected row, showing a live dot, and scrolling to the end on new calls.
Write a small badge primitive in Jac — a status pill that shows a label, optionally takes a style variant, and optionally renders a little pulsing dot before the label to signal live activity.

I need a reusable button primitive for a Jac client app, styled through the global CSS .btn classes. It takes a label, a click handler, a variant that switches between the primary and ghost look, and a disabled flag.
Button(label, onClick, variant='primary', disabled=False): a shadcn-style button whose class is 'btn' for primary and 'btn ghost' otherwise, forwarding onClick and disabled.

Set up the top-level entry file for a Jac AI web app that ties the frontend to the backend. Import the client app from the frontend module and expose an `app` client component that renders it — the server endpoints it calls do not need re-importing here because the frontend's `sv import` already registers those bindings.

App entry combining the agent backend and the frontend: `cl import` the frontend's app and expose `cl def:pub app` returning <ClientApp/>; server endpoints auto-register through the frontend's sv import, so there is no re-import here.

Define the foundational types for declaring Jac CLI commands: an enum for the kinds of argument (positional, option, flag, multi, remainder), an enum for registration priority (core/plugin/user), an Arg object holding a full argument definition with a factory constructor, a CommandSpec object carrying a command's metadata plus methods to gather its args and add hooks and extensions, and a HookContext object passed to the pre/post hooks.

```jac
"""Core types for CLI command definitions.

This module provides the foundational types for declaring CLI commands
with structured metadata that enables auto-documentation and plugin extension.
"""

import from typing { Callable }

"""Kind of command-line argument."""
enum ArgKind {
    POSITIONAL = 1,  # jac run <filename>
    OPTION = 2,  # jac run --session foo
    FLAG = 3,  # jac run --verbose (bool, no value)
    MULTI = 4,  # jac check file1.jac file2.jac
    REMAINDER = 5,  # jac enter main args...
}

"""Priority levels for command registration."""
enum CommandPriority {
    CORE = 100,  # Built-in commands
    PLUGIN = 200,  # Plugin-provided commands
    USER = 300,  # User-defined commands (highest priority)
}

"""Definition of a command-line argument with full metadata.

Provides structured argument definitions that enable:
- Auto-generated help documentation
- Type-safe argument parsing
- Plugin argument extension
"""
obj Arg {
    has name: str,  # Parameter name
        kind: ArgKind = ArgKind.OPTION,  # Argument kind
        typ: any = str,  # Python type for conversion
        `default: any = None,  # Default value
        help: str = "",  # Help text for this argument
        short: str | None = None,  # Short flag, e.g., "-s" for "--session"
        choices: list[any] | None = None,  # Valid choices
        required: bool = False,  # Whether argument is required
        dest: str | None = None,  # Override destination variable name
        metavar: str | None = None,  # Display name in help
        source: str = "jaclang";  # Source plugin that added this arg

    static def create(
        name: str,
        kind: ArgKind = ArgKind.OPTION,
        typ: any = str,
        `default: any = None,
        help: str = "",
        short: str | None = None,
        choices: list[any] | None = None,
        required: bool = False,
        metavar: str | None = None
    ) -> Arg;
}

"""Complete specification for a CLI command.

Contains all metadata needed to:
- Generate help documentation
- Build argparse configuration
- Execute the command with hooks
"""
obj CommandSpec {
    has name: str,  # Command name
        help: str,  # One-line description
        description: str = "",  # Detailed description (multi-line)
        args: list[Arg] = [],  # Base arguments
        examples: list[tuple[str, str]] = [],  # (command, description) pairs
        group: str = "general",  # Command group for help menu
        priority: CommandPriority = CommandPriority.CORE,
        source: str = "jaclang",  # Source package/plugin
        handler: Callable | None = None,  # Implementation function
        # Plugin extensions (populated at runtime)
        extra_args: list[Arg] = [],  # Arguments added by plugins
        pre_hooks: list[tuple[Callable, str]] = [],  # (hook, source) pairs
        post_hooks: list[tuple[Callable, str]] = [];  # (hook, source) pairs

    def get_all_args -> list[Arg];
    def add_extension_arg(arg: Arg, source: str) -> None;
    def add_pre_hook(hook: Callable, source: str) -> None;
    def add_post_hook(hook: Callable, source: str) -> None;
}

"""Hook context passed to pre/post hooks.

Provides a mutable context for:
- Accessing command arguments
- Passing data between pre and post hooks
- Storing plugin-specific state
"""
obj HookContext {
    has command_name: str,  # Name of the command being executed
        args: dict[str, any],  # Parsed command arguments
        data: dict[str, any] = {};  # Mutable context for hook communication

    def get_arg(name: str, `default: any = None) -> any;
    def set_data(key: str, value: any) -> None;
    def get_data(key: str, `default: any = None) -> any;
}

```

Define the `jac code` CLI command — compiler-backed code intelligence for agents that answers the structural questions grep cannot, like where a symbol is defined and used, its type, and which walkers traverse it. Register it with positional action and target arguments, a --text flag for human-readable output instead of the default JSON, and a --depth option for slice queries, along with a set of usage examples, in the analysis group.

```jac
"""The `jac code` command group: compiler-backed code intelligence for agents.

Where `grep` answers "which lines contain this string", `jac code` answers
"where is this symbol defined, everywhere it is used, what type it has, and
which walkers traverse it" -- the structural questions a text search cannot.
It is grep's structural successor: a thin, JSON-by-default shim over the
compiler's `CodeIntelligence` facade, built for terminal-driven AI agents.

Output is machine-readable JSON by default (every payload carries a
`schema_version` so consumers can pin a shape); pass `--text` for the
human-readable rendering. Exit codes are stable: 0 = ok, 1 = usage/runtime
error, 2 = nothing found for the query.
"""

import from jaclang.cli.command { Arg, ArgKind }
import from jaclang.cli.registry { get_registry }

glob registry = get_registry();

"""Ask the compiler about your code -- grep's structural successor."""
@registry.command(
    name="code",
    help="Query code structure via the compiler (grep's structural successor)",
    args=[
        Arg.create(
            "action",
            kind=ArgKind.POSITIONAL,
            default="",
            help="symbol | uses | map | walkers | slice | diag"
        ),
        Arg.create(
            "target",
            kind=ArgKind.POSITIONAL,
            default="",
            help="Symbol name, node type, archetype-kind filter, or file path"
        ),
        Arg.create(
            "text",
            kind=ArgKind.FLAG,
            typ=bool,
            default=False,
            help="Human-readable text instead of the default JSON"
        ),
        Arg.create(
            "depth",
            typ=int,
            default=1,
            help="Type-dependency depth for `slice` (default 1)",
            short="d"
        ),

    ],
    examples=[
        ("jac code symbol User", "Definition(s) of a symbol plus where it is used"),
        ("jac code uses make_user", "Every read/write of a symbol, def/use-precise"),
        ("jac code map", "Structural overview: nodes, walkers, edges, objs"),
        ("jac code map walker", "Only walker archetypes"),
        ("jac code walkers User", "Walkers whose entry points traverse a node type"),
        ("jac code slice Profile --depth 2", "Typed neighbourhood for prompt assembly"),
        ("jac code diag", "Structured compiler errors and warnings"),
        ("jac code symbol User --text", "Same query, human-readable output"),

    ],
    group="analysis"
)
def code(
    action: str = "", target: str = "", text: bool = False, depth: int = 1
) -> int;

```

```jac
"""Eject command: convert a Jac project to standalone Python + JavaScript.

            default="",

            short="o"

            default=False,
            help="Overwrite output directory if it already exists",
            short="f"

    ],
    group="project"
```

```jac
"""Shared guide store -- the single source of truth for Jac reference guides.

A "guide" is a curated reference document (Markdown body + YAML frontmatter)
for writing correct, idiomatic Jac. The guides are hand-edited and live in
`jaclang/cli/skills/<name>.md`, so they ship inside the jaclang wheel and need
no build step.

Every consumer reads guides through this module -- the `jac guide` CLI command
(including `jac guide --export`, which writes them out as Claude Code Agent
Skills), the compiler's diagnostic hints, and the jac-mcp server -- so there is
exactly one copy of the content and one frontmatter parser.
"""

import from pathlib { Path }

"""A single reference guide: parsed frontmatter plus its markdown body."""
obj Guide {
    has name: str,  # Stable identifier, e.g. "jac-types"
        description: str,  # One-line summary from frontmatter
        body: str,  # Markdown body with frontmatter stripped
        path: str;  # Absolute path to the backing .md file
}

"""Absolute path to the bundled guides directory inside the jaclang package."""
def guides_dir -> Path;

"""Parse a guide markdown file (frontmatter + body) into a Guide.

Returns None when the file is missing or unreadable.
"""
def parse_guide(path: Path) -> Guide | None;

"""Return every bundled guide, ordered by name. Empty when none are bundled."""
def list_guides -> list[Guide];

"""Return a single guide by name, or None when it is not bundled."""
def get_guide(name: str) -> Guide | None;

"""Return guides whose name, description, or body contains `query` (case-insensitive)."""
def search_guides(query: str) -> list[Guide];

"""Map a compiler diagnostic to the guide that explains how to fix it.

`code` is a diagnostic code like "W0064"; `category` is the lowercase
diagnostic Category value (e.g. "type"). Returns a guide name only when that
guide is actually bundled, so callers never emit a dangling hint.
"""
def guide_for_diagnostic(code: str, category: str = "") -> str | None;
```

```jac
"""Scoped-style annex support for the `cl` (client) target.

A `.style.css` file that shares a base name with a `.cl.jac` module
(e.g. `card.style.css` alongside `card.cl.jac`) forms one logical module
with auto-scoped CSS classes. The compiler:

  1. Hashes every class selector declared in the annex with a per-module
     digest (`blake2s(module_path + class_name)`, truncated to 8 hex
     chars), producing names like `card-1a2b3c4d`.
  2. Rewrites the annex CSS so each declared selector uses the hashed
     form, leaving `:global(...)` selectors verbatim (the wrapper is
     stripped, the inner selector preserved).
  3. Exposes the hashed names so the ECMAScript pass can rewrite JSX
     `className`/`class` literals in the module that reference a declared
     class to the same hashed form.

The rewritten CSS is emitted as a sidecar artifact (`Module.gen.css`) and
a side-effect `import "./<base>.css";` is injected into the compiled JS so
the styles load with the component -- framework-neutral, no bundler config.

This subsystem is self-contained: annex discovery + CSS parse + selector
hashing all live here; the ECMAScript pass only consumes the resulting
`class_map` and `scoped_css`.
"""

import from hashlib { blake2s }
import from jaclang.jac0core.bccache { discover_style_annex }

"""A loaded, scoped `.style.css` annex for one client module.

    Construct via `load_style_annex`; `postinit` parses `source_css`,
    populating `class_map` (bare name -> hashed name) and `scoped_css`
    (the selector-rewritten stylesheet).
    """
obj ScopedStyleSheet {
    has module_path: str,
        css_path: str,
        source_css: str,
        class_map: dict[str, str] = {},
        scoped_css: str = '';

    def postinit -> None;
    """Rewrite a JSX `className`/`class` value, hashing each declared token.

        The value is split on whitespace; tokens that name a class declared
        in the annex are replaced with their hashed form, others are kept
        verbatim. Original inter-token spacing is collapsed to single
        spaces (semantically irrelevant for a class list).
        """
    def rewrite_class_value(value: str) -> str;
}

"""Hash a single class name with the module-scoped digest.

    Returns the scoped name `<class_name>-<8 hex>`. Deterministic for a
    given (module_path, class_name) pair, so the CSS selector rewrite and
    the JSX `className` rewrite agree.
    """
def hash_class_name(module_path: str, class_name: str) -> str;

"""Rewrite a CSS selector prelude, hashing declared class tokens.

    Class tokens (`.name`) are replaced with `.name-<hash>` and recorded in
    `class_map`; `:global(...)` regions are unwrapped and preserved
    verbatim; comments, strings, and attribute selectors are passed through
    untouched.
    """
def scope_selector(selector: str, module_path: str, class_map: dict[str, str]) -> str;

"""Rewrite a full stylesheet, scoping the class selectors of style rules.

    Walks rules with brace tracking: style-rule preludes are scoped via
    `scope_selector`; grouping at-rules (`@media`, `@supports`,
    `@container`, `@layer`, `@scope`) are descended into; other at-rules
    (`@keyframes`, `@font-face`, ...) and all declaration blocks are copied
    verbatim. Mutates `class_map` in place and returns the rewritten CSS.
    """
def scope_stylesheet(css: str, module_path: str, class_map: dict[str, str]) -> str;

"""Load and scope the `.style.css` annex for a module, or None if absent.

    `module_path` is the head module's source path (variant suffix is
    handled by `discover_style_annex`).
    """
def load_style_annex(module_path: str) -> (ScopedStyleSheet | None);

"""Advance past a CSS string literal. `i` is the opening quote; returns the
    index just after the matching close quote (backslash escapes honored)."""
def _skip_string(s: str, i: int) -> int;

"""Consume a brace-delimited block verbatim. `start` indexes the opening
    `{`; returns the block text (braces included) and the index after the
    matching `}`. Strings and comments inside are not brace-counted."""
def _consume_braced_block(css: str, start: int) -> tuple[(str, int)];

"""True if a rule prelude is a grouping at-rule whose block holds nested
    rules (`@media`, `@supports`, `@container`, `@layer`, `@scope`) rather
    than declarations."""
def _grouping_at_rule(prelude: str) -> bool;

glob __all__ = [
         'ScopedStyleSheet',
         'load_style_annex',
         'hash_class_name',
         'scope_selector',
         'scope_stylesheet'
     ];

```

```jac
"""Semantic Token Manager module."""
import from typing { List, Optional, Tuple }
import logging;

import jaclang.jac0core.unitree as uni;
import from jaclang { JacRuntimeInterface as Jac }
import from jaclang.langserve.utils {
    find_surrounding_tokens,
    get_token_start,
    get_line_of_code
}
import jaclang.lsp.types as lspt;

# Semantic token flat array field offsets.
# Each token occupies TOK_STRIDE (5) consecutive ints:
#   [line_delta, col_delta, length, token_type, token_modifier]
glob TOK_LINE_DELTA = 0,
     TOK_COL_DELTA = 1,
     TOK_LENGTH = 2,
     TOK_TYPE = 3,
     TOK_MODIFIER = 4,
     TOK_STRIDE = 5,
     logger = logging.getLogger("jaclang.langserve.sem_manager");

"""Semantic Token Manager class."""
obj SemTokManager {
    has ir: uni.Module,
        hub: dict = {},
        sem_tokens: List[int] by postinit,
        static_sem_tokens:
            List[Tuple[(lspt.Position, int, int, uni.AstSymbolNode)]] by postinit;

    def postinit -> None;
    def collect_resolved_nodes(ir: uni.Module) -> list;
    def gen_sem_tokens(ir: uni.Module) -> list[int];
    def gen_sem_tok_node(
        ir: uni.Module
    ) -> List[Tuple[(lspt.Position, int, int, uni.AstSymbolNode)]];

    def update_sem_tokens(
        content_changes: lspt.DidChangeTextDocumentParams,
        sem_tokens: list[int],
        document_lines: List[str]
    ) -> list[int];

    static def handle_multi_line_delete(
        self: SemTokManager,
        sem_tokens: list[int],
        next_token_index: int,
        nxt_tok_pos: tuple[(int, int, int)],
        change_start_line: int,
        change_end_line: int,
        change_start_char: int,
        change_end_char: int,
        prev_tok_pos: tuple[(int, int, int)],
        is_next_token_same_line: bool
    ) -> list[int];

    static def handle_single_line_delete_between_tokens(
        self: SemTokManager,
        sem_tokens: list[int],
        next_token_index: int,
        is_next_token_same_line: bool,
        change: lspt.TextDocumentContentChangeEvent_Type1,
        change_start_line: int,
        change_end_line: int
    ) -> list[int];

    static def handle_single_line_delete(
        self: SemTokManager,
        sem_tokens: list[int],
        next_token_index: int,
        prev_token_index: int,
        is_next_token_same_line: bool,
        change: lspt.TextDocumentContentChangeEvent_Type1
    ) -> list[int];

    static def handle_single_line_insertion(
        self: SemTokManager,
        sem_tokens: list[int],
        next_token_index: int,
        is_next_token_same_line: bool,
        change: lspt.TextDocumentContentChangeEvent_Type1,
        tokens_on_same_line: bool,
        nxt_tok_pos: tuple[(int, int, int)],
        change_start_line: int,
        line_delta: int
    ) -> list[int];

    static def handle_multi_line_insertion(
        self: SemTokManager,
        sem_tokens: list[int],
        next_token_index: int,
        nxt_tok_pos: tuple[(int, int, int)],
        change_start_line: int,
        change_end_line: int,
        change_end_char: int,
        prev_tok_pos: tuple[(int, int, int)],
        tokens_on_same_line: bool,
        changing_line_text: tuple[(str, int)],
        line_delta: int
    ) -> list[int];

    static def handle_insert_inside_token(
        self: SemTokManager,
        change: lspt.TextDocumentContentChangeEvent_Type1,
        sem_tokens: list[int],
        prev_token_index: int,
        changing_line_text: tuple[(str, int)],
        line_delta: int,
        prev_tok_pos: tuple[(int, int, int)],
        change_start_char: int,
        change_end_char: int,
        is_token_boundary_edit: bool,
        nxt_tok_pos: tuple[(int, int, int)]
    ) -> tuple[list[int], bool, tuple[(int, int, int)], Optional[int]];
}
```

Declare a template-loader module for file-based project templates. One function loads a template from a directory whose jac.toml carries a [jacpack] section (returning a strongly-typed ProjectTemplate), another bundles a template directory into a single distributable .jacpack JSON file, a third loads a template back from that bundled JSON, and a fourth resolves a post-create hook given as a 'module.path:function' string. Signatures and docstrings only.

```jac
"""Template loader for file-based project templates.

This module provides functions to:
- Load templates from a directory with a jac.toml containing [jacpack] section
- Bundle a template directory into a single JSON file for distribution
- Load templates from bundled JSON files

Templates are defined using a single jac.toml file. To make a project packable
as a template, add a [jacpack] section with name and description fields.
All other sections (project, plugins, dependencies, etc.) become the config
for created projects.
"""

import from typing { Callable }
import from pathlib { Path }
import from jaclang.project.template_registry { ProjectTemplate }

"""Load a template from a directory containing jac.toml with [jacpack] section.

The jac.toml should have:
- [jacpack]: Metadata with name, description, jaclang version, plugins
- [jacpack.options]: directories, files patterns, gitignore entries
- All other sections: Become the created project's jac.toml config

Returns a strongly-typed ProjectTemplate object.
"""
def load_template_from_directory(
    template_dir: Path, post_create_hook: Callable | None = None
) -> ProjectTemplate;

"""Bundle a template directory into a single JSON file.

Reads all files in the template directory and embeds their content
in a JSON file for easy distribution.

Args:
    template_dir: Path to the template directory with jac.toml
    output_path: Path for the output .jacpack file (e.g., fullstack.jacpack)
"""
def bundle_template(template_dir: Path, output_path: Path) -> None;

"""Load a template from a bundled JSON file.

The JSON file should contain all template metadata and file contents
as produced by bundle_template().

Returns a strongly-typed ProjectTemplate object.
"""
def load_template_from_json(
    json_path: Path, post_create_hook: Callable | None = None
) -> ProjectTemplate;

"""Resolve a post_create hook from a string like 'module.path:function_name'.

Used when loading templates from JSON where the hook is specified as a string.
"""
def resolve_post_create_hook(hook_path: str) -> Callable | None;

```

Write the query planner that chooses an execution strategy for a graph QueryPlan across three layers — native backend pushdown, the root topology index, and bulk batch_get. Expose an execute_plan entry point that runs a QueryPlan against a memory (applying any post-filter and returning empty for trivial plans), an execute_path that runs an ObjectSpatialPath through the pushdown/mixed/floor ladder and returns NodeAnchors in edge order or None to signal fallback, and plan_chain / plan_chain_ordered helpers that resolve a hop chain on a root's topology index to a candidate UUID set.

```jac
"""Query planner — picks the execution strategy for a QueryPlan.

The planner is the only place that knows about all three layers:

  1. Backend native pushdown (`Memory.execute_plan`, declared via
     `Memory.capabilities()`). Fastest when the backend can handle the plan
     because it bypasses the topology_index entirely.
  2. Root topology_index (`TopologyIndex.resolve_chain[_ordered]`). The
     universal in-process narrowing path. Always available when the index is
     enabled and the relevant root carries one.
  3. `batch_get` (every backend has this). The bulk-load primitive used after
     narrowing to materialize anchors → archetypes.

Strategy selection:

  * `pushdown`  — `plan.needs() <= backend.capabilities()`. Hand the whole
                  plan to the backend; iterate its generator.
  * `mixed`     — topology_index resolves the chain to a candidate UUID set,
                  the planner attaches that set as `plan.id_in`, and the
                  reduced plan (now needing `id_in` + maybe `field_pushdown`)
                  goes to the backend if it covers those needs. Otherwise the
                  planner falls through to `floor`.
  * `floor`     — topology_index → `batch_get`. Pure in-process. Always
                  works as long as the index is populated.

The planner is also the one place that observes `JAC_QUERY_TRACE` to log
which strategy fired for which plan — invaluable when debugging unexpected
fallbacks or perf cliffs in CI.
"""

import os;
import logging;
import from collections.abc { Generator }
import from uuid { UUID }

import from jaclang.jac0core.archetype { Anchor, NodeAnchor }
import from jaclang.runtimelib.query_plan { QueryPlan }

glob logger = logging.getLogger(__name__),
     __all__ = ['execute_plan', 'execute_path', 'plan_chain', 'plan_chain_ordered'];


"""Top-level entry point: execute a QueryPlan against a memory.

Returns an iterable of NodeAnchor results. Applies `plan.post_filter` if set.
Trivial plans (no chain, no filters, no narrowing) return empty — callers
should use `Memory.query()` directly for unfiltered scans.

The signature deliberately accepts `any` for `mem` so the planner can be
called from the bootstrap-compiled runtime layer without a circular import on
the Memory type.
"""
def execute_plan(mem: any, plan: QueryPlan) -> list[any];


"""High-level entry point: execute an `ObjectSpatialPath` against a memory.

This is what the runtime's `refs()` calls. Builds the QueryPlan from the
path's destinations, walks the strategy ladder (pushdown / mixed / floor),
applies the final node filter post-narrowing, and returns the result as
NodeAnchors in canonical edge-walk order (single-hop) or arbitrary order
(multi-hop set narrowing).

Returns None to signal "no fast path applies" — the caller should fall back
to the legacy edge-walk via `edges_to_nodes`. This happens when:
  * the path has predicate filters the index can't express
  * the origin isn't persistent (no root → no topology_index)
  * the chain has no useful filter (full walk anyway)
  * topology_index is disabled and no backend pushdown applies
"""
def execute_path(
    mem: any, path: any, slc: (slice | None) = None
) -> (list[any] | None);


"""Resolve a chain on a given root's topology_index to a `set[UUID]`.

Used internally by `execute_path` (and available to callers that want the
candidate set without materializing anchors). Returns None when no fast
path applies (index disabled, root has no index, or origin not persistent)."""
def plan_chain(
    root_anchor: any,
    origin_ids: set[UUID],
    chain: list[tuple[(str | None), (str | None), int]]
) -> (set[UUID] | None);


"""Compatibility helper: resolve the final hop in canonical edge-insertion
order with `slc` applied. Returns None when no ordered fast path applies."""
def plan_chain_ordered(
    root_anchor: any,
    origin_ids: set[UUID],
    chain: list[tuple[(str | None), (str | None), int]],
    slc: slice
) -> (list[UUID] | None);

```

```jac
import from 'react' { useState as reactUseState, useEffect as reactUseEffect }

# PLATFORM DETECTION
# =============================================================================
```

Define the storage-neutral query-plan IR that sits between the runtime planner and the pluggable storage backends. Write a HopSpec record for one path hop (optional edge type, optional node type, direction) and a QueryPlan record capturing the root id, the hop chain, MongoDB-style field predicates, an optional narrowed id set, an optional slice, a final node-type filter, and an opaque post-filter callable — with method declarations for is_trivial, needs, and repr — and document the backend capability strings and the execute_plan contract.

```jac
"""QueryPlan IR — the contract between the runtime planner and storage backends.

A QueryPlan describes a graph query in storage-neutral terms so the planner can
either hand it to a backend's native `execute_plan` (e.g. MongoDB compound index
+ `_id $in` pushdown, Postgres jsonb GIN) or fall back to the universal floor
(root topology_index → set narrowing → `batch_get`).

The IR captures only the shapes we can actually optimize today; complex
predicate lambdas stay on the slow path. Anything not representable as a
declarative dict belongs in the post-filter the runtime applies above.

Capability strings backends declare via `Memory.capabilities()`:

  - `'type_pushdown'`   — backend can filter by archetype type natively
                          (e.g. an `arch_type` index in Mongo/Sqlite).
  - `'field_pushdown'`  — backend can apply declarative field predicates
                          on archetype data without loading rows
                          (e.g. Mongo `data.archetype.*` filter dict,
                          Postgres jsonb path ops).
  - `'id_in'`           — backend can filter by `_id IN (...)`; required
                          when the topology_index narrows to a candidate set
                          and we want the backend to materialize that subset.
  - `'slice'`           — backend can apply `(offset, limit)` natively
                          (otherwise the planner slices the result list).

A backend's `execute_plan(plan)` returns:
  - `Generator[Anchor, ...]`  when it fully handled the plan
  - `None`                    to opt out and let the planner use the floor

The planner trusts the backend's claim — if a plan needs `'field_pushdown'`
and the backend declares it, the result is taken as authoritative. Mixed
strategies (narrow with the index, materialize via backend `id_in`) are
composed by the planner, not by the backend.
"""

import from collections.abc { Callable }
import from uuid { UUID }
import from jaclang.jac0core.archetype { Anchor }

glob __all__ = ['HopSpec', 'QueryPlan'];


"""One hop in a path expression: `[edge_type? -[direction]-> node_type?]`.

`edge_type` / `node_type` are bare archetype class names (no module prefix);
the topology_index resolves them via MRO fan-out so subclass matches "just
work". `direction` mirrors `EdgeDir`: 1=IN, 2=OUT, 3=ANY.
"""
obj HopSpec {
    has edge_type: (str | None) = None,
        node_type: (str | None) = None,
        direction: int = 2;
}


"""Declarative query plan handed to backends or executed by the floor.

Fields are populated by `planner._build_plan_from_path` (the IR builder)
from the runtime's `ObjectSpatialPath`. None of these is required — a plan
with only `chain` and a `root_id` is the common case for `[root -->]`.

Field reference:

  - `root_id`         the root anchor that owns the subgraph. Used both as the
                      adjacency origin for the topology_index and as the
                      access-control scope for backends that partition by root.
  - `chain`           ordered list of HopSpec. Empty chain = "match anchors in
                      this root with no traversal" (e.g. for `query_by_type`-
                      style scans).
  - `field_predicates` archetype-field constraints, keyed by bare field name
                      with MongoDB-style operator values:
                          `{'age': {'$lt': 28}, 'status': 'active'}`
                      Backends prefix field names with whatever path they use
                      (`data.archetype.<f>` in Mongo, jsonb path in PG).
                      Operators understood across backends: `$eq`, `$ne`,
                      `$lt`, `$lte`, `$gt`, `$gte`, `$in`, `$nin`. Anything
                      else is backend-specific.
  - `id_in`           when the planner has already narrowed to a candidate
                      set (typically via the topology_index), this carries
                      that set so the backend can do a single `_id IN (...)`
                      lookup. None means "no candidate narrowing applied".
  - `slc`             optional slice. The planner sets this when the user
                      wrote `[-->][0:50]` and the chain is pushdown-eligible.
                      Backends without `'slice'` capability should ignore it;
                      the planner slices afterwards.
  - `node_type_final` archetype class name to match on the final result set.
                      Distinct from chain hops because it can be checked
                      directly via the `arch_type` index without graph
                      traversal — the cheap path when chain is empty.
  - `post_filter`     opaque callable from the runtime; the planner applies
                      it AFTER any backend execution. Not pushdown-eligible.
"""
obj QueryPlan {
    has root_id: (UUID | None) = None,
        chain: list[HopSpec] = [],
        field_predicates: dict = {},
        id_in: (set[UUID] | None) = None,
        slc: (slice | None) = None,
        node_type_final: (str | None) = None,
        post_filter: (Callable[[Anchor], bool] | None) = None;

    def is_trivial -> bool;
    def needs -> set[str];
    def repr -> str;
}

```

Write the maintenance hooks that keep each root's topology index in sync with graph mutations — all no-ops when the topology-index flag is off. Provide an enabled check (an env var overriding the toml flag), helpers to find a node's owning root, to get an archetype's type name and its user-defined MRO chain, and to index and unindex an edge into a given root, plus the event callbacks on_edge_created, on_edge_destroyed, on_node_saved, and on_node_destroyed.

```jac
"""Topology index maintenance hooks.

These functions keep root topology indices in sync with graph mutations
(edge create/destroy, node save/destroy). All are no-ops when the
topology_index config flag is disabled.

Query planning lives in `jaclang.runtimelib.planner` — this module only
mutates the index in response to runtime events. The cleanup boundary is
explicit: anything that *reads* the index for a query goes through the
planner; anything that *writes* the index in response to a graph mutation
stays here.
"""

import from uuid { UUID }

"""Check if topology_index is enabled. The `JAC_TOPOLOGY_INDEX` env var
overrides the toml flag (truthy: 1 / true / yes / on)."""
def _is_enabled -> bool;

"""Get the root NodeAnchor that owns this anchor."""
def _get_root_anchor(anchor: any) -> any;

"""Get the archetype class name."""
def _type_name(`obj: object) -> str;

"""Get the user-defined MRO chain for a node/edge archetype, stopping at the
runtime base archetypes (Node/Edge/Walker/Archetype/object). Concrete type
appears at index 0."""
def _get_type_mro(`obj: object) -> list[str];

"""Record an edge in the given root's topology index. Used by
`on_edge_created` to mirror cross-root edges into the indexes of both
endpoint owners (otherwise reverse queries from the target side would
miss the edge entirely)."""
def _index_edge_into(root_anchor: any, source: any, target: any, `edge: any) -> None;

"""Remove an edge from the given root's topology index. Mirror of
`_index_edge_into` used by `on_edge_destroyed`."""
def _unindex_edge_from(root_anchor: any, source: any, target: any, `edge: any) -> None;

"""Called after an edge is created between source and target."""
def on_edge_created(source: any, target: any, `edge: any) -> None;

"""Called when an edge is destroyed."""
def on_edge_destroyed(source: any, target: any, `edge: any) -> None;

"""Called when a node is saved/persisted. Ensures it's in the root's index."""
def on_node_saved(node_anchor: any) -> None;

"""Called when a node is destroyed."""
def on_node_destroyed(node_anchor: any) -> None;

```

Gallery (.cl.jac), prefix-scoped, sv-imports list_galleries / gallery_images. On mount: load dir list, filter by prefix, auto-open first. Dir chips → responsive image grid (base64 data-URIs, dashed stub for skipped/unreadable) → click-to-zoom fixed overlay (click to close). Empty + loading fallbacks.

I want a read-only image browser component in Jac that surfaces the training and eval figures already saved to disk in the repo. Fetch the available figure folders from a server endpoint, list them as clickable chips with counts, and when one is picked lay its images out in a grid from their base64 payloads. Clicking a thumbnail should open a zoomed lightbox that closes on click. Support an optional path prefix so a section only sees its own figures, plus loading and no-figures fallbacks.

Spec: repo-figure viewer .cl.jac component, prop prefix. On entry pull the gallery dir list (server) filtered by prefix and auto-open the first; render dir chips + responsive grid from server {name, mime, b64}; oversize/unreadable → dashed stub; thumbnail click → fixed zoom overlay. Handle no-dirs and loading.

Write a log viewer component for the Jac app that shows monospace text newest-line-first. Split the incoming text into lines, reverse them, and render each, coloring error / traceback / ✗ lines and lines starting with >>> differently from ordinary output. Accept the text and a max-height, and keep it scrollable.
LogView (.cl.jac): props text, maxH. Split on newline, reverse (newest first), flex-col-reverse scroll box. Per-line class: error/traceback/✗ → foreground, >>> prefix → foreground/80, else muted.

I need a single-line chart component for our Jac dashboards, with an option for a second overlaid line. Data arrives as lists of {x, y} points; merge the primary and secondary series by x while keeping x order so the line doesn't zigzag. Draw it with recharts (grid, axes, tooltip), let a flag format the Y axis as exponents for the learning-rate panel, and let another flag mark the latest point with a reference dot on live runs. Show a NO SIGNAL placeholder when there's no data.

MonoChart (.cl.jac) over recharts. Props: title, data / secondary (list[{x,y}]), live, accent, expY. Merge secondary into primary by x preserving monotonic order (insert in place); solid primary line + dashed secondary; expY → Y tickFormatter to one-sig exponent; live → ReferenceDot on the last point; animations off; empty data → NO SIGNAL box.

Create a multi-line chart component in Jac for overlaying several runs on one plot. It gets a title, a list of row dicts each keyed by x plus one key per run name, and the list of names. Draw one recharts line per name in a distinct color, add a matching color-coded legend underneath, and show a NO SIGNAL placeholder when there are no rows.

Build a reusable bordered card component for the Jac UI with a floating micro-label notched into its top border. It takes the label text, children, optional extra classes, and a labelBg prop that masks the border behind the label — background color for page-level panels, card color when the panel is nested inside another card surface.

Panel (.cl.jac): bordered rounded card + floating micro-label absolutely positioned over the top border. Props: label, className, labelBg (default bg-background), children. labelBg masks the border behind the label.

Spec: stateless RowBrowser + RowDetail (.cl.jac), no has-state. Parent passes files/path/rows/offset/total/expanded + onOpen/onToggle/onPrev/onNext. Render file chips, a 6-col row grid (idx/name/kind/diff/source/preview) with click-to-expand RowDetail, and a centered pager with range readout. RowDetail: CodeBlock panes for python/jac/chosen/rejected chosen by kind, else raw <pre>.

Write a simple section-header bar for the Jac app — the top bar every section was hand-rolling. It takes a title and a right slot, both accepting arbitrary elements, and lays them out at opposite ends with a bottom border and horizontal padding.
SectionHeader (.cl.jac): title + right slots (any elements), justify-between, bottom border, px-4 py-2.5.
