Design-system module shared by the whole app: it declares no components, only public tokens and the compiled stylesheet. `C` holds the OLED-black color palette (`bg`, `surface`, `accent`, `like`, `rt`, `danger`, and friends), `S` the spacing scale, `R` the radii, and `F` the font sizes; `styles` is the `StyleSheet.create` result covering every screen region — splash, auth card, header, tab bar, composer, tweet `card`, comment modal, search, notifications, and profile. The module is platform-agnostic (no `.native` variant needed), so `main.jac` imports all five globs directly. Re-skinning the entire app is a matter of editing the token globs; nothing here has side effects or touches the graph.

IR-audit harness: verifies the zero-RC contract by counting reference-counting and collector machinery in the LLVM IR emitted per (kernel, mode) cell. `mode_flags` maps a memory `mode` to nacompile flags — the "none" mode adds `--enforce-nogc` and `--assert-no-rc`. `audit` compiles one cell with `JAC_DUMP_IR` pointed at a .ll file and returns a `dict` of counts: `rc_symbol_refs`, the sorted `rc_symbols` list, `trace_fns`, and `collector_refs`. `parse_opts` reads the `--kernels`, `--modes`, and `--out` options with defaults drawn from the `KERNELS` and `MODES` globs, and `main` audits every requested cell, prints a per-cell summary, and writes the census JSON to the output path. Side effects: temporary binaries (unlinked after use), IR dumps under results, and the census file; the process exits nonzero if an enforced "none" build shows any RC machinery.

`erase` deletes every ownership annotation from kernel source `text`, the executable counterpart of the paper's erasure function: own-typed declarations lose their qualifier, borrow types on parameters and locals collapse to bare types, and call-site borrow markers are stripped. Parameter: `text`, the full kernel source as a `str`. Returns the erased source as a new `str`; the function is pure — a chain of `re.sub` rewrites with no I/O and no graph effects. The transform is exact only for kernels authored in the constrained style described in the module header and is not a general-purpose Jac rewriter. The `with entry` block wraps it as a CLI filter that reads the file named by the single argument and writes the erased source to stdout, exiting with status 2 on wrong usage.

Measurement harness for the ownbench kernels: it compiles and times every requested (kernel, mode) cell and enforces the differential-identity oracle. The `KERNELS`, `MODES`, and `SIZES` globs define the matrix and per-kernel argument sets; `mode_flags` picks nacompile flags per memory mode (adding `--enforce-nogc` and `--assert-no-rc` for "none"); `compile_kernel` builds one binary and exits loudly on failure; `run_once` performs a single timed invocation, extracting the kernel's internal ns= timing line, max RSS via /usr/bin/time, and a sha256 `digest` of the remaining stdout; `parse_opts` handles the CLI, including `--invocations`, `--sizes`, and `--skip-compile`. `main`, invoked from `with entry`, aggregates `median_ns`, min/max/stdev, and `max_rss_kb` per cell, prints progress lines, writes the results JSON, and fails the run if any kernel produces nondeterministic output across invocations or differing digests across modes.

Driver for the osp_regions benchmark experiments: compiles the four region kernels and measures them across GC modes while enforcing digest identity within each configuration. `compile_src` builds a source under a given gc mode; `run_once` performs one invocation, splitting stdout into the identity digest, the internal ns= timing, and parsed m: metric lines, plus max RSS; `measure` repeats it `invocations` times, asserts a single digest, and aggregates medians and `max_rss_kb`; `make_bare` generates the managed baseline of the `reg_graph` kernel by running `rerase.jac`; `parse_opts` reads `--invocations`, `--quick`, and `--out`. `main` sequences the four experiments — `reg_graph` over region/bare variants x `MODES` x acyclic/cyclic configs, `reg_wspawn` walker-spawn reclamation, `reg_transfer` across `TRANSFER_SIZES` with move/copy/serial strategies, and the `reg_overhead` allocation micro — printing per-cell results, writing the results JSON, and exiting nonzero on any digest mismatch.

`rerase` produces the managed baseline of a region kernel: given kernel source `text`, it walks the lines deleting region annotations — standalone Region-handle declarations are dropped, the opening and closing lines of in-blocks are removed while their bodies are dedented one level (tracked by an indent `stack`) — and returns the rewritten source as a `str` with a trailing newline. It is pure (no I/O, no graph effects) and exact only for kernels following the load-bearing style constraints spelled out in the module header; it is not a general Jac rewriter. The `with entry` block turns it into a CLI filter: it reads the kernel file named by the single argument and writes the erased source to stdout, exiting with status 2 on wrong usage. On the native backend the erased program pins managed nodes immortal, so zero drops and growing RSS in the bare variant are expected measured findings, not erasure bugs.

Histogram micro-kernel used as a benchmark workload. `fill_round` runs one round: it steps a linear-congruential generator from `seed`, distributes `n` values across `buckets` bins of a hash map, tracks distinct reduced values in the `seen` set, and folds the bucket counts into a single integer `digest` modulo 1000000007. `run` repeats this for `reps` rounds with varying seeds and accumulates the running total. The `with entry` block is the entry point and CLI: positional arguments override `n` (default 100000) and `reps` (default 20), the workload is timed with `time.perf_counter_ns`, and two stdout lines are emitted — the hist: digest line consumed by the differential-identity check and the ns= timing line consumed by the measurement harness. Pure compute; no graph interaction.

Vector dot-product micro-kernel. `build_vec` deterministically fills a `list[float]` of length `n` from a linear-congruential generator seeded with `seed`, producing values in [0, 1). `dot` takes two borrowed vectors (typed `&list[float]`) and returns their inner product as a `float` without taking ownership. `run` performs `reps` rounds, building a fresh vector pair per round and accumulating `dot(&a, &b)` into the returned total. The `with entry` block reads optional positional overrides for `n` (default 10000) and `reps` (default 100), times the whole computation with `time.perf_counter_ns`, and prints the dot: result line plus the ns= timing line for the benchmark harness. Pure compute with no side effects beyond stdout.

Walker-spawn reclamation kernel: measures whether walker and resource objects are actually dropped after each spawn. `Spot` nodes carry a value `v` and a visit `stamp`; `build_graph` chains `n` of them into a linear path and returns the head. The `Serve` walker owns a `Res` resource (an `obj` with an `fd` field whose `drop` hook increments the global `rdrops`), walks the chain summing `v` into `total` while writing `cur` into each node's `stamp` to avoid revisits, and has its own `drop` hook incrementing `wdrops`. The `with entry` block builds the graph (CLI overrides for `n` and `reps`), spawns `Serve` on the entry node once per request with a fresh `Res`, and prints the accumulated total, the m:wdrops= and m:rdrops= metric lines, and the ns= timing — the metric lines are what the region benchmark harness parses to verify reclamation behavior.

Three public walker endpoints (`walker:pub`, no authentication) back this todo desktop app, each invoked by spawning. `create_todo` — spawned on `root` — takes one field, `text` (`str`), attaches a new `Todo` node (fields `text` and `done`, the latter defaulting to `False`) under the root, and reports the created node; `text` has no default, so omitting it is a request error. `toggle_todo` — spawned on a `Todo` node id — takes no fields, flips `done`, and reports the updated node; spawned on a non-`Todo` anchor it matches no ability and reports nothing. `read_todos` — spawned on `root` — visits every connected `Todo` and reports on exit, so the response reports carry the full list. The bundled `cl` component `app` shows the calling convention: `root spawn read_todos()` on mount, `create_todo` spawned on `root` with the input text, and `id spawn toggle_todo()` per item, with node identity carried in `_jac_id`.

Backend smoke-test module for the todo_app desktop example: it boots `main.jac` through the same `inprocess_dispatch` path the native desktop host uses, so the walkers are exercised with no webview. `_backend_available` gates every test on the scale backend being importable (tests print a skip line otherwise). `_call` lazily boots the app once — `boot` against a temp graph directory, tracked by the `_BOOTED` flag — then routes a JSON envelope (walker `kind`, `name`, anchor `node`, and `fields`) through `dispatch` and returns the parsed reply; `_first_todo` digs the first todo out of a reply's nested reports. The three `test` blocks cover the walker surface end-to-end: `create_todo` persists a todo with the right `text` and `done` defaults, `read_todos` returns previously created todos, and `toggle_todo` — dispatched with the created node's `_jac_id` as anchor — flips `done` on the node.

Illustrates Jac's typed filter comprehensions. `example` takes `animals`, an untyped `list`, and shows four selection forms: `dogs` keeps only `Dog` instances via a type-only filter; `indoor_cats` combines the `Cat` type test with a field condition (`indoor==True`); `people` applies the `Person` type filter to nodes reached by an outgoing graph traversal; and `adults` layers a field condition (`age > 21`) on top of that traversal filter. The `node` declarations — `Dog` with `name`, `Cat` with `indoor`, `Person` with `age` — exist to give the filters something to match. No return value and no mutation; the traversal forms only read the current node's neighborhood.

Demonstrates Jac's bulk-assignment comprehension. `example` takes `people` (`list[Person]`) and `items` (`list[Item]`) and mutates them in place: the first form sets `verified` to `True` on every `Person`; the second chains a filter with an assignment, granting `can_vote` only to people matching `age >= 18`; the third sets multiple fields at once on every `Item` — `status` to "processed" and `processed_at` to the value returned by the `now` helper. Nothing is returned; the side effect is the field mutation on every targeted node, which for persisted nodes writes through to the graph.

Answers a natural-language `question` by delegating to an LLM that may call the `get_current_time` tool, which returns the current timestamp formatted via `datetime`. The `answer` function takes `question` (`str`) and returns the model's reply as a `str`. It has no graph side effects; its only external interactions are the model call and reading the system clock through `get_current_time`.

`solve_math` delegates a natural-language math `problem` (`str`) to an LLM equipped with three tools: `add` and `multiply`, which perform exact integer arithmetic on operands `a` and `b`, and `get_pi`, which returns the constant 3.14159 as a `float`. Returns the model's worked answer as a `str`. Purely computational, with no graph mutations or other side effects.

`query` routes a user `question` (`str`) to an LLM that can invoke two lookup tools: `search_database`, which returns matching record strings for a `query` string up to `limit` (default 10, capped at 3 simulated results), and `get_user_info`, which returns a `dict` with `id`, `name`, and `email` keys for a `user_id`. Returns the model's synthesized answer as a `str`. Both tools are simulated and read-only, so the call has no persistent side effects.

`research` answers a compound `question` (`str`) by letting an LLM reason with three tools: `search_web` (simulated web lookup for a `query`), `calculate` (evaluates a math `expression` via `eval` and returns a `float`), and `get_date` (today's ISO date). The `sem` string attached to `research` steers the model toward multi-step reasoning with tools. Returns the final answer as a `str`. No graph side effects, though `calculate` executes arbitrary expressions with `eval`, which is unsafe on untrusted input.

This module models a stateful, LLM-driven calculator. The `Calculator` `obj` keeps a running `memory` value (`float`, starting at 0) and exposes four deterministic methods that read or mutate it: `add`, `subtract`, `clear`, and `get_memory`, each returning the updated `memory`. The `calculate` method ties the pieces together: declared `by llm` with the four instance methods as tools, it lets the model interpret free-form `instructions` and execute them as a sequence of tool calls against the instance's state, while the `sem` annotation on `Calculator.calculate` tells the model to work step by step. The entry block is the demo entry point: it constructs a `Calculator`, runs a chained instruction through `calculate`, and prints both the model's answer and the final `memory`.

Defines a retrieval-and-summarize agent over `Document` nodes. Each `Document` carries `title`, `content`, and a mutable `summary` field. `search_documents` does a case-insensitive substring match of `query` against each document's `content` in `docs` and returns the matching titles. The `DocumentAgent` `walker`, entered on `Root`, gathers all connected `Document` nodes, filters them through `search_documents` using its `query` field, then calls the LLM-backed `summarize` function on each relevant document's `content`. Side effects: it writes the generated text into each matched node's `summary` field and emits a `report` for every match containing the `title` and `summary`.

Entry point that seeds the graph and runs the document agent. It attaches three `Document` nodes (each with a `title` and `content`) directly to `root`, then spawns `DocumentAgent` with `query` set to "AI" on `root`. The walker's collected `reports` are iterated to print each matched document's `title` and generated `summary`. Graph side effects: three new `Document` nodes are created under `root`, and the matched ones have their `summary` fields populated by the agent.

`support_agent` answers a customer `question` (`str`) using an LLM whose context is enriched via `incl_info` with the global `company_info` block (company name, products, support hours, contact email), passed under the `company_context` key. A `sem` annotation frames the function as a product-and-services Q&A assistant. Returns the grounded answer as a `str`; read-only, with no graph or global-state mutations.

`sales_agent` turns a free-form customer `request` (`str`) into tool-driven actions against an in-memory catalog held in the globals `products`, `prices`, and `inventory`. The LLM can call `list_products`, `get_price` (formatted price for a `product`, or a not-found message), `check_inventory` (stock status with remaining quantity), and `place_order`, which validates availability and decrements `inventory` by `quantity` on success. Returns the agent's reply as a `str`. Side effect: successful orders mutate the global `inventory` map; the other tools are read-only.

`describe_image` sends an `Image` to a vision-capable LLM and returns a natural-language description of its contents as a `str`; the docstring doubles as the model instruction. Parameter: `img`, a `byllm` `Image` wrapper (constructed here from a local file path). No side effects beyond the model call.

`get_person_info` performs structured extraction from a photo: given `img` (an `Image`), the LLM returns a fully typed `Person` with `full_name` (`str`), `year_of_death` (`int`), and `personality`, a `Personality` enum whose `INTROVERT` and `EXTROVERT` members carry `sem` descriptions that guide the classification. Returns the populated `Person` object; the call has no side effects.

Demo entry block cataloguing the accepted ways to construct a `byllm` `Image`: from an in-memory `BytesIO` buffer after saving a `PILImage`, from raw bytes obtained via `getvalue`, directly from a PIL image object, and from remote sources — an HTTPS URL or a Google Cloud Storage path. Nothing is returned or persisted; the block exists purely to illustrate the `Image` constructor's input types.

`explain_video` submits a `Video` to a multimodal LLM and returns a prose description of what happens in it as a `str`. The `Video` is constructed with a file `path` and an `fps` sampling rate (1 frame per second here), which controls how many frames the model sees. Parameter: `video`. No side effects beyond the model call.

Entry block illustrating the `fps` knob when constructing a `Video` for LLM analysis: `fps=1` samples one frame per second (sufficient for most content), while `fps=2` doubles the sampling density for finer temporal detail at higher cost. Both examples load the same file via `path`; nothing is returned or persisted.

`parse_receipt` extracts structured data from a receipt photo: given `img` (`Image`), the LLM returns a `Receipt` containing `store_name`, `date`, a `total`, and `items` — a `list` of `LineItem` objects each holding a `description`, `quantity`, and `price`. The typed return shape constrains the model's output so downstream code can iterate `items` and read fields directly, as the entry block does. No side effects.

`solve_math` reads a math problem from an image and returns a `MathSolution` object: `problem` restates the recognized question, `steps` is a `list` of worked reasoning steps, and `answer` holds the final result as a `str`. Parameter: `img`, an `Image` of the problem (e.g. a photo or screenshot). Purely functional — the LLM call produces the structured solution with no side effects.

`analyze_video` runs multimodal analysis over a `Video` (constructed with a `path` and an `fps` sampling rate) and returns a `VideoAnalysis` object carrying a prose `summary`, a `list` of `key_events`, a `duration_estimate`, and a classified `content_type`. Parameter: `video`. The structured return type lets callers consume the analysis field by field; there are no side effects.

`find_similar_products` is a vision-plus-tools agent: it shows `img` (an `Image` of a product) to the LLM, which may call the `search_products` tool — a simulated text search returning matching product strings for a `query` — to ground its recommendation. Returns the result text as a `str`. The tool is read-only, so the call has no persistent side effects.

`translate2french` sends `text` (`str`) to an LLM and returns the French translation as a `str`. The function body is fully delegated via `by llm`, and the attached `sem` string supplies the actual instruction. Stateless, with no side effects beyond the model call.

A tour of the four `sem` attachment points for steering LLM-backed code. A `sem` on the `translate` function supplies its instruction; `translate.text` documents an individual parameter; `Product.price` describes a `has` field of the `Product` `obj` (price in USD) so structured extraction fills it correctly; and `Priority.HIGH` gives an enum member classification guidance. None of these declarations execute anything — they attach semantic strings that the LLM sees at call time.

`summarize` condenses an `article` (`str`) into a short summary via an LLM; the attached `sem` string pins the output format to 2-3 bullet points. Returns the summary as a `str`. Stateless and side-effect free — the entry block simply prints the result for a sample article.

`generate_code` asks an LLM to produce a Python function from a natural-language `description` (`str`), as directed by its `sem` instruction. Returns the generated source code as a plain `str` — it is not executed or validated, so callers should review the emitted code before use. No side effects.

`translate2spanish` delegates translation of `text` (`str`) to an LLM and returns the result as a `str`. The entry block shows the recommended error-handling pattern: because the model call can fail at runtime (network, provider, or parsing errors), it is wrapped in a try/except that catches `Exception` and prints the failure instead of crashing. The function itself has no side effects.

Unit-testing pattern for LLM functions using `MockLLM`. The global `llm` is a `MockLLM` configured with a fixed `outputs` list, so each call to the delegated `translate` function returns the next canned string instead of hitting a real model. The `test` block asserts that calling `translate` with "Hello" yields "Mocked response 1", making the test deterministic and network-free. `translate` takes `text` (`str`) and returns a `str`; with the mock installed there are no external side effects.

`classify_priority` maps a free-text support `ticket` (`str`) onto the `Priority` enum (`LOW`, `MEDIUM`, `HIGH`, `CRITICAL`) via an LLM constrained to return one of the enum members. Returns the selected `Priority`, suitable for direct comparison or routing logic. No side effects; the entry block triages a batch of sample tickets and prints each verdict.

`get_status` asks an LLM to map a natural-language `response_description` (`str`) onto the `HttpStatus` enum, whose members carry real status codes: `OK` = 200, `NOT_FOUND` = 404, `SERVER_ERROR` = 500. Returns the chosen `HttpStatus` member. Stateless with no side effects; useful for normalizing fuzzy descriptions into concrete status values.

`get_status` classifies a `response_description` (`str`) into the `HttpStatus` enum via an LLM. Because the enum is declared with an explicit `int` base (`HttpStatus: int`), the returned member compares directly against integers — the entry block checks the result with `== 404` rather than naming the member. Members: `OK` = 200, `NOT_FOUND` = 404, `SERVER_ERROR` = 500. No side effects.

Extracts structured company information from free-form text using an LLM-backed function. `extract_company` takes a single parameter `text` (`str`) containing unstructured prose and returns a `Company` object whose `name`, `industry`, and `headquarters` fields are populated by the LLM via `by llm()`. The nested `headquarters` field is an `Address` object with `street`, `city`, and `country` fields, so the LLM must produce a fully nested structure. The function is pure with respect to the graph: it performs no node or edge mutations, only an LLM call. The entry block demonstrates usage by parsing a description of Apple Inc. and printing the extracted `name`, `industry`, and the `city`/`country` of the `headquarters`.

Extracts a to-do list from unstructured text. `extract_tasks` accepts `text` (`str`) and returns `list[Task]`, delegating the parsing to an LLM via `by llm()`. Each `Task` carries a `title` (`str`) and a `priority` (`str`) inferred from cues in the text such as "urgent" or "low priority". There are no graph side effects; the function only invokes the LLM. The entry block runs it on a bulleted note, prints the task count with `len(tasks)`, and lists each task as `priority`/`title` pairs.

Parses contact details out of a sentence of free text. `extract_contact` takes `text` (`str`) and returns a `Contact` populated by an LLM via `by llm()`. The `Contact` object has required `name` and `email` fields plus an optional `phone` field typed `str | None` with a default of `None`, so input that mentions no phone number (like the second example) yields `None` for `phone` rather than a fabricated value. The function has no graph side effects. The entry block shows both cases: one input with a phone number and one without.

Converts raw resume text into a fully structured `Resume` object. `parse_resume` takes `text` (`str`) and returns a `Resume` via `by llm()`, with the LLM filling scalar fields (`name`, `email`, and optional `phone` typed `str | None`), a flat `skills` list (`list[str]`), and two nested collections: `education` as `list[Education]` (each with `degree`, `institution`, and `year`) and `experience` as `list[Experience]` (each with `title`, `company`, `years`, and `description`). No graph mutations occur. The entry block parses a sample resume and iterates over `resume.education` and `resume.experience` to print each entry.

Assigns an LLM-derived priority to every `Ticket` node reachable from the root. `analyze_priority` takes `title` and `description` (both `str`) and returns a `Priority` enum value (`LOW`, `MEDIUM`, or `HIGH`) via `by llm()`. The `PrioritizeTickets` walker starts at the root (its `with Root entry` ability visits all outgoing nodes with `visit [-->]`), and its `prioritize` ability fires on each `Ticket`: it overwrites `here.priority` with the result of `analyze_priority(here.title, here.description)`, reports the mutated node with `report here`, and continues traversal. Side effects: every visited `Ticket` node's `priority` field (default `Priority.MEDIUM`) is updated in place, and each node is appended to the walker's report stream.

Entry point that seeds the graph and runs ticket prioritization. It attaches three `Ticket` nodes to `root` with the `++>` connect operator, each given a `title` and `description`. It then spawns the `PrioritizeTickets` walker on `root` via `root spawn PrioritizeTickets()` and captures the walker result in `result`. Side effects: three new `Ticket` nodes and their root edges are created, and the walker mutates each ticket's `priority` field during traversal. Finally it iterates `result.reports` and prints each ticket's `priority` and `title`.

Extracts strictly typed values from text. `extract_data` accepts `text` (`str`) and returns a `StrictData` object via `by llm()`. The return type enforces primitive types on each field: `count` must be `int`, `ratio` must be `float`, and `active` must be `bool`, so the LLM output is coerced/validated into these exact types rather than returned as free-form strings. The function has no graph side effects.

Entry block illustrating Jac's mandatory statement terminators. Unlike Python, every statement must end with a semicolon: the block assigns `x = 5;` and calls `print(x);`, and the commented-out variants without semicolons show code that would fail to parse. All top-level executable code must also live inside a `with entry` block rather than at module scope. No parameters, return value, or graph side effects — the only effect is printing the value of `x`.

Demonstrates Jac's brace-delimited blocks in place of Python's colon-and-indentation syntax. `do_something` takes no parameters, returns `None`, and simply prints "done"; its body is enclosed in braces. The `with entry` block sets `condition = True` and shows the correct conditional form with a brace-delimited body — the commented Python-style `if condition:` would not parse. The only side effect is console output; nothing touches the graph.

Illustrates the distinction between instance state and local variables in a Jac `obj`. `Example` declares `field` with the `has` keyword and a default of `0`, making it a typed instance variable accessible as `self.field`. Inside `method`, `local = 5` creates an ordinary local variable — no `has` and no type annotation required — which exists only for the duration of the call. `method` copies `local` into `self.field`, so its only side effect is mutating the instance's `field`; the graph is untouched.

Demonstrates that `visit` queues destinations rather than traversing immediately. The `Example` walker's `traverse` ability runs on each `Item` node: it prints "Visiting", calls `visit [-->]` to schedule all outgoing neighbors, then prints a second line. Because `visit [-->]` only enqueues nodes, the second print executes before any child node is entered — the walker moves on to queued nodes only after the current ability finishes. The `Item` node carries a single `name` field (`str`, default empty). No graph mutations occur; the only side effects are console output and walker movement.

This module is a minimal demonstration of walker control-flow semantics in Jac's Object-Spatial Programming model. It defines one node type, `Item`, holding a single `int` field `value` (default `0`), and one walker, `Example`, whose `collect` ability fires on each `Item` it enters. The ability shows the three key control primitives in sequence: `report here.value` emits the current node's value to the walker's report stream without interrupting execution; `visit [-->]` enqueues all outgoing neighbors for later traversal and likewise continues; and `return` immediately ends the ability, which is how a walker halts early. The entry point is spawning `Example` on any graph of `Item` nodes; the walker walks outward from its start node, reporting each `value` it encounters.

Increments a module-level counter. The module declares `counter` with `glob` as a global `int` initialized to `0`. `increment` takes no parameters and returns `None`; because it assigns to a global from inside a function, it must first declare `global counter` — without that declaration the assignment would be treated as a new local and the module-level value would not change. Side effect: each call adds 1 to the shared `counter`. No graph state is involved.

Defines a simple data-holding `obj` with a method. `Person` declares two required typed fields via `has`: `name` (`str`) and `age` (`int`). Its `greet` method takes no parameters and returns a `str` greeting built from `self.name` using an f-string. Construction uses keyword arguments, as shown in the entry block with `Person(name="Alice", age=30)`; `obj` instances live in memory only and create no graph nodes or edges.

Adds two integers. `add` takes `a` and `b`, both typed `int`, and returns their sum as an `int`. It is a pure function — no state is read or written and the graph is untouched. The fully annotated signature (parameter types and `-> int` return type) is the required style for Jac function declarations.

Entry block demonstrating Jac's conditional chain syntax. It assigns `x = 1` and branches with `if x > 0`, `elif x < 0`, and `else`, printing "positive", "negative", or "zero" respectively; with `x` set to 1 the first branch runs. Each branch body is brace-delimited rather than indentation-based. The block takes no input and has no side effects beyond console output.

Document this Jac code:

```jac
enum Status {
    PENDING = "pending",
    ACTIVE = "active"
}
```

Declares a string-valued enumeration. `Status` defines two members, `PENDING` bound to the value `"pending"` and `ACTIVE` bound to `"active"`. Assigning explicit string values makes the members serialize to stable, human-readable strings (useful for APIs and persistence) rather than auto-assigned integers. The declaration itself has no runtime side effects.

Module entry point. The `with entry` block runs when the module is executed directly and does exactly one thing: call `main()`. This mirrors Python's main-guard idiom — all program logic is expected to live in a `main` function defined elsewhere in the module, keeping top-level code to a single dispatch call. Any side effects are whatever `main` performs.

Demonstrates Jac's exception-handling syntax. `divide` takes `a` and `b` (both `int`) and returns the floor-division result `a // b` as an `int`. The entry block wraps a call to `divide(10, 0)` in a `try` block; the `except ValueError as e` clause prints the error if a `ValueError` is raised, and the `finally` block prints "Done" regardless of outcome. Note the handler is specific to `ValueError` — exceptions of other types propagate past it, though `finally` still executes. No graph state is involved.

Entry block contrasting Jac's two assignment styles. The first group relies on type inference — `name`, `age`, `pi`, and `active` get their types from the literal values, as in Python. The second group repeats the same bindings with explicit annotations (`str`, `int`, `float`, `bool`), the recommended style for clarity and type-checking. The block produces no output and has no graph side effects; it exists purely to show both forms compile.

Entry block surveying Jac's built-in collection types with generic annotations. `numbers` is declared as `list[int]` and grown with `numbers.append(6)`; `person` is a `dict[str, any]` mapping string keys to heterogeneous values; `unique` is a `set[int]` built with brace literal syntax; and `point` is a fixed-shape `tuple[int, int]`. Literal syntax and mutation methods match Python's, with Jac's required semicolons and optional-but-recommended type annotations. No output or graph effects.

Formats a greeting with an optional salutation. `greet` takes `name` (`str`) and `greeting` (`str`, defaulting to `"Hello"`) and returns the composed `str` via an f-string. Callers may omit the second argument to get the default — `greet("Alice")` yields "Hello, Alice!" — or override it, as `greet("Bob", "Hi")` yields "Hi, Bob!". The function is pure with no side effects.

A minimal stateful accumulator object. `Calculator` holds one field, `value` (`int`, default `0`), declared with `has`. `add` takes `n` (`int`), adds it to `self.value` in place, and returns the updated running total as an `int`. `reset` takes no arguments, returns `None`, and sets `self.value` back to `0`. Both methods mutate only the instance; no graph nodes or edges are involved. The entry block shows two chained `add` calls accumulating 5 and 3 to leave `value` at 8.

Classifies an integer by sign. `classify_number` takes `n` (`int`) and returns a `str`: "negative" when `n < 0`, "zero" when `n == 0`, and "positive" otherwise, using an `if`/`elif`/`else` chain where every branch returns. The function is pure — no state or graph side effects. The entry block exercises all three branches with -5, 0, and 10.

Entry block demonstrating Jac's three common `for`-loop forms. It iterates directly over a list literal printing each `item`; loops over `range(5)` to count 0 through 4; and pairs indices with values using `enumerate(names)`, destructuring each pair into `(i, name)` — note the parenthesized tuple pattern in the loop header. Bodies are brace-delimited. The only side effect is console output.

Entry block demonstrating a basic `while` loop. It initializes `count` to 0 and loops with `while count < 5`, printing the current value and incrementing with `count += 1` each iteration, producing the numbers 0 through 4. The loop body uses Jac's brace syntax and semicolon-terminated statements. Console output is the only side effect.

Maps an integer onto a size label using structural pattern matching. `describe` takes `value` (`int`) and returns a `str` via a `match` statement: `case 0` returns "zero", the or-pattern `case 1 | 2 | 3` returns "small" for any of those three values, and the wildcard `case _` catches everything else, returning "medium". Every arm returns, so the function is total and pure. The entry block exercises all three arms with 0, 2, and 50.

A mutable person record with behavior. `Person` declares `name` (`str`) and `age` (`int`) as required fields and `email` (`str`) with a default of the empty string, so it may be omitted at construction. `introduce` returns a `str` self-description built from `self.name` and `self.age` with no side effects. `have_birthday` returns `None` and increments `self.age` by 1, mutating the instance in place. The entry block constructs `Person(name="Alice", age=30)`, prints the introduction, then shows `age` becoming 31 after one `have_birthday` call.

Demonstrates inheritance and method overriding between `obj` archetypes. The base `Animal` declares a `name` field and a `speak` method that returns a placeholder string; `Dog` and `Cat` both inherit from `Animal` and override `speak` to return their own sounds, with `Dog` adding a `breed` field defaulting to "Unknown". The entry block constructs a `Dog` and a `Cat` using keyword arguments (fields declared with `has` are auto-initialized) and prints each pet's `name` together with the result of calling `speak`. Takes no external input, returns nothing, and has no graph side effects — output goes to stdout via `print`.

Defines two enumerations and shows how they are used. `Color` is a plain enum with members `RED`, `GREEN`, and `BLUE` (auto-assigned values), while `Status` maps each member — `PENDING`, `ACTIVE`, `COMPLETED` — to an explicit string value. The entry block assigns `Color.RED` and `Status.ACTIVE` to locals, compares an enum member with `==` to drive a conditional, and reads the underlying string of a member through its `value` attribute (printing "active"). No parameters, return values, or graph side effects.

Shows typed enums whose members behave as their base type. `HttpStatus` is declared with base `int` (members `OK` = 200 and `NOT_FOUND` = 404), so `HttpStatus.OK == 200` compares directly as `True` and arithmetic like `HttpStatus.OK + 1` yields 201. `Tag` is declared with base `str` (members `OPEN` and `CLOSE`), so `isinstance(Tag.OPEN, str)` is `True`. The entry block prints each of these three results; there are no parameters, returns, or graph side effects.

`divide` computes the quotient of two `float` parameters `a` and `b`, raising `ValueError` with the message "Cannot divide by zero" when `b` is 0 instead of letting a runtime division error occur; otherwise it returns `a / b`. The entry block demonstrates structured error handling: it calls `divide(10, 0)` inside a `try` block, catches the `ValueError` in an `except` clause (bound as `e` and printed), and runs a `finally` clause that prints "Done" regardless of outcome. No graph side effects.

Demonstrates importing Python standard-library modules directly into Jac with plain `import` statements. `math`, `json`, and `os` are imported at module level; the entry block calls `math.sqrt(16)` (printing 4.0) and `os.getcwd()` to print the current working directory. `json` is imported but not used in the entry block. No parameters, return values, or graph side effects — output is written to stdout.

Shows selective importing from a Python module using the `import from` form: `Counter` and `defaultdict` are pulled from `collections` by name. The entry block builds a `Counter` over a list of strings and prints `counts["a"]`, which is 3 because "a" occurs three times. `defaultdict` is imported but unused here. No parameters, returns, or graph side effects.

Demonstrates cross-module imports between Jac files. In `utils.jac`, `helper` is a zero-argument function returning the `str` "I'm a helper". In `main.jac`, the declaration `import from utils { helper }` brings that function into scope by name, and the entry block calls it and prints the result. No parameters beyond none, no graph side effects; the pattern illustrates how one Jac module consumes another's public functions.

Illustrates a type-only import: `import type from billing { Invoice }` makes the `Invoice` archetype available purely for type annotations. `total` accepts a single parameter `inv` typed as `Invoice` and returns its `amount` field as an `int`. The function has no side effects and performs no graph operations; it simply projects one field from the passed-in object.

Declares a module-level global with `glob`: `config` is a `dict[str, any]` holding a "debug" flag and a "version" string. `get_version` takes no parameters and returns the "version" entry coerced through `str`, giving "1.0.0". The entry block prints that result. The global is read-only in this snippet — nothing mutates `config` — and there are no graph side effects.

`Greeter` is a `node` archetype carrying a single `has` field `name` of type `str`. Its ability `greet` is declared `with entry`, meaning it fires automatically whenever a `walker` enters a `Greeter` node during traversal; the ability prints a greeting interpolating `self.name`. The node itself takes `name` at construction time, the ability returns nothing, and its only side effect is writing to stdout.

Contrasts the three endpoint visibility levels for server functions. `def:pub add_task` (taking `title` and returning a `dict`) is public: it auto-generates an HTTP API callable without authentication. `def:priv get_tasks` (returning a `list`) requires an authenticated user and operates on that user's isolated data. `def:protect helper` is not exposed over HTTP at all — it is only accessible within the module. Bodies are elided (`...`), so the snippet documents the access-control surface rather than behavior.

Demonstrates typed local variable declarations inside a `with entry` block: `name` (`str`), `version` (`int`), `rating` (`float`), and `ready` (`bool`) are annotated explicitly, while `greeting` shows that the type can be inferred from its f-string value. The block prints the interpolated `greeting`. No parameters, no return value, and no graph side effects — the snippet exists to show annotation and inference syntax.

Document this Jac code:

```jac
# This is a line comment

#* This is a
   block comment *#
```

Shows Jac's two comment forms and nothing else: a single-line comment introduced with `#`, and a multi-line block comment delimited by `#*` and `*#`. The snippet contains no executable code, so it has no parameters, return values, or side effects.

Two small pure functions plus a demo entry block. `greet` takes `name` (`str`) and returns a personalized morning greeting built with an f-string. `add` takes `int` parameters `a` and `b` and returns their sum. The entry block calls `greet("Alice")` and `add(2, 3)` (printing 5). Both functions are side-effect free with no graph interaction; only the entry block writes to stdout.

`categorize` classifies a `fruit` name into a botanical category using a `switch` statement. The parameter `fruit` (`str`) is matched against literal cases: "apple" returns "pome"; "banana" or "plantain" (combined in one `case` with the `|` alternative syntax) return "berry"; the `default` arm returns "unknown" for anything else. The function is pure — it always returns a `str` and has no side effects.

`describe` maps a `value` of type `any` to a descriptive string using a `match` statement. A literal `case` returns "zero" for 0, an or-pattern (`1 | 2 | 3`) returns "small number", and the wildcard `case _` catches everything else, returning "something else". The function is pure, always returns a `str`, and has no graph side effects.

`describe_point` classifies a 2-element `tuple` using `match` with destructuring patterns. `(0, 0)` returns "origin"; `(x, 0)` and `(0, y)` capture the nonzero coordinate and report a point on the x- or y-axis respectively; the general `(x, y)` pattern reports both coordinates; and the wildcard `_` handles non-point values, returning "not a point". The parameter `point` is not mutated and the function is pure, returning a `str` in every branch.

`Animal` is an `obj` archetype declaring two `has` fields, `name` and `sound`, in a single comma-separated declaration. Its method `speak` — written without a parameter list, since `obj` methods receive `self` implicitly — returns an f-string combining both fields. The entry block shows the auto-generated keyword constructor (`name="Rex"`, `sound="Woof"`) and prints the result of `speak`, "Rex says Woof!". Pure in-memory object; no graph interaction.

`Task` is a `node` archetype — a graph-persistable entity — declaring two fields with `has`: a required `title` of type `str` and a `done` flag of type `bool` defaulting to `False`. Constructing one takes `title` (and optionally `done`) as keyword arguments; declaring the node has no side effects until instances are connected into a graph.

Defines the `Task` node type — a required `title` plus a `done` flag defaulting to `False` — and populates the graph in the entry block. Three `Task` nodes are created and attached to the built-in `root` node with the `++>` connect operator, then a confirmation line is printed. Side effect: the graph gains three `Task` nodes edged from `root`, which persist for later queries; nothing is returned.

Demonstrates Jac's filter comprehension syntax on an ordinary in-memory `list`. Two `obj` types, `Dog` and `Cat`, each carry `name` and `age` fields; `pets` mixes three instances. Three filters are shown: `pets[?:Dog]` selects elements by type, `pets[?age < 4]` selects by a field condition across both types, and `pets[?:Dog, age < 4]` combines a type check with a field condition. Each result is printed. The list itself is never modified and no graph operations occur — the filters return new lists.

Shows how to read back graph data attached to `root`. The entry block first connects two `Task` nodes with `++>`, then demonstrates three query forms: `[root-->]` collects every node one hop from `root` (bound to `everything`), appending `[?:Task]` narrows the result to `Task` nodes, and `[?:Task, title == "Buy groceries"]` adds a field-equality condition (bound to `grocery_tasks`). The loop prints each task's `done`-dependent status label and `title`. Side effects: two `Task` nodes are created under `root`; the queries themselves are read-only.

`Scheduled` is an `edge` archetype, meaning connections made with it carry their own data. It declares two `has` fields: `time`, a required `str`, and `priority`, an `int` defaulting to 1. Use it when linking nodes where the relationship itself needs scheduling metadata; declaring the edge type alone has no side effects.

A complete minimal task-manager backend. The data model is a single `node` type, `Task`, holding a `title` and a `done` flag defaulting to `False`; every task is stored in the graph as a child of the user's `root` node. Four public endpoints (`def:pub`) form the CRUD surface: `add_task` creates a `Task`, connects it to `root` with `++>`, and returns it; `get_tasks` returns all tasks via the `[root-->][?:Task]` query; `toggle_task` looks a task up by comparing `jid(task)` against the passed `id`, flips its `done` field, and returns the task or `None` if no match; `delete_task` removes the matching task with `del` and returns `{"deleted": id}`, or an empty `dict` when the `id` is unknown. The endpoints are the module's only entry points — there is no entry block — and all state lives in the graph under `root`.

`app` is a client-side component: the `cl` prefix marks it as browser code and `def:pub` exposes it as a mountable page, returning a `JsxElement` render tree. It declares two pieces of reactive component state with `has`: `tasks`, a `list` initialized empty, and `task_text`, a `str` initialized to the empty string — updating either triggers a re-render. The methods and render tree are elided in this snippet, so only the component's state shape and signature are documented here.

`app` is the public client entry component (`def:pub`) returning a `JsxElement`; it is rendered in the browser rather than exposed as a JSON endpoint, so there is no route, auth requirement, or request body. It declares two `useState` pairs: the `tasks` list, updated only through `set_tasks`, and the `task_text` input string, updated through `set_task_text`. As written it performs no server calls and renders nothing, so there are no error cases; all state changes must go through the two setters.

Mount-time entry ability: runs once when the component is first rendered. It awaits the server call `get_tasks` and stores the result in the component's `tasks` state, triggering a re-render with the loaded data. No parameters, no return value; its side effects are the network fetch and the `tasks` assignment.

Creates a task from the current input. If `task_text` is non-empty after trimming, `add_new_task` awaits `add_task` with the trimmed title, appends the returned `task` to the `tasks` list, and clears `task_text`. Blank or whitespace-only input is silently ignored. No return value; side effects are one server call and two state updates.

A single-component day-planner client. The entire UI lives in `app`, which holds two `has` state fields: `tasks` (the loaded task list) and `task_text` (the controlled input value). An entry ability awaits `get_tasks` on mount to populate `tasks`; `add_new_task` sends trimmed input to the server via `add_task`, appends the created task, and resets the input. The render tree ties these together: the input binds `task_text` and submits on Enter or the Add button, and the list is a comprehension over `tasks` keyed by `jid` that displays each task's `title`. Persistence is entirely server-side; the component only mirrors it locally.

Top-level day-planner component `app`. State: `tasks` (task records) and `task_text` (input value); `tasks` loads on mount via `get_tasks`. `add_new_task` creates a task from trimmed input through `add_task`; `toggle` awaits `toggle_task` and swaps the updated record into `tasks` by matching `jid`; `remove` awaits `delete_task` then filters the entry out locally. It derives `remaining` as the count of tasks whose `done` flag is unset and renders the input row, one checkbox/delete row per task, and a remaining-count footer. Every mutation round-trips through the server before local state is patched.

Task CRUD API plus its consuming client. All four endpoints are `def:pub`, so no authentication is required. `add_task` takes `title` (`str`), attaches a new `Task` node to `root` (with `done` defaulting to `False`), and returns it. `get_tasks` takes no arguments and returns `list[Task]`. `toggle_task` takes `id` (`str`, a `jid` value), flips the matching task's `done` flag, and returns the updated `Task` -- or `None` when nothing matches. `delete_task` takes `id` and returns `dict[str, str]`: a mapping with key "deleted" echoing the `id` on success, an empty `dict` on a miss. The `app` component calls these endpoints and mirrors results into its `tasks` state.

Module-level LLM configuration: imports `Model` from `byllm.lib` and binds the global `llm` to a locally served model via `model_name` "local:gemma-4-e4b". Any function in this module delegated through `llm` routes its calls to that local instance, so no remote API key is involved. The `Model` is constructed once at module load.

Persistent graph `node` representing a to-do item. `title` (`str`, required) holds the user-entered text; `done` (`bool`, default `False`) tracks completion; `category` (`str`, default "other") stores a category label. Instances live in the graph, so tasks survive across requests and sessions.

`add_task` is a public endpoint (`def:pub`, no authentication) that creates a task with an AI-assigned category. Request shape: a single `title` string. It runs the LLM-backed `categorize` on the title, lower-cases the final segment of the resulting enum into `category`, attaches a new `Task` node to `root`, and returns the created `Task` as the response body. There is no explicit error handling: an LLM failure inside `categorize` surfaces as a server error, and empty titles are not rejected.

`Unit` enumerates the measurement units an ingredient may use: `PIECE`, `LB`, `OZ`, `CUP`, `TBSP`, `TSP`, and `BUNCH`. `Ingredient` is a plain `obj` (not graph-persistent) describing one shopping-list entry: `name` (`str`), `quantity` (`float`), `unit` (a `Unit` member), `cost` (`float`), and `carby` (`bool`, whether the item is carbohydrate-heavy). Every field is typed, making the object a good structured target for LLM generation.

Persistent graph `node` for one stored shopping-list entry. Fields: `name` (`str`), `quantity` (`float`), `unit` (`str` -- the unit is stored as a plain string here rather than an enum), `cost` (`float`), and `carby` (`bool`). All fields are required at construction; because instances live in the graph, the list survives across sessions.

Three public (`def:pub`, unauthenticated) shopping-list endpoints operating on `ShoppingItem` nodes attached to `root`. `generate_list` takes `meal` (`str`): it deletes every existing `ShoppingItem`, calls the LLM-backed `generate_shopping_list`, persists each returned ingredient as a `ShoppingItem` node (lower-casing the `unit` enum name into a string), and responds with the fresh `list[ShoppingItem]`. `get_shopping_list` takes no arguments and returns the current `list[ShoppingItem]`. `clear_shopping_list` deletes all items and returns `dict[str, bool]` with "cleared" set to `True`. Error cases: an LLM failure inside `generate_list` aborts after the old list has already been deleted, leaving it empty; the other two endpoints cannot fail on normal input.

Single-component client for an AI day planner with two side-by-side features. `app` owns all state: `tasks` and `task_text` for the to-do column; `meal_text`, `ingredients`, and `generating` for the shopping column. Top-level authenticated client shell. `app` tracks `isLoggedIn` and `checkingAuth`; on mount it queries the runtime with `jacIsLoggedIn` and clears the checking flag. `IngredientItem` renders one shopping-list row. Its single prop `ing` is a `ShoppingItem`; the component shows its `name`, `quantity` and `unit`, a carb badge only when `carby` is true, and `cost` formatted to two decimals. Purely presentational: no state, no effects, no callbacks.

`add_task` is a private endpoint (`def:priv`): callers must be authenticated, and the created data lands in the calling user's own graph. Request shape: one `title` string. It derives `category` by running the LLM-backed `categorize` on the title and lower-casing the enum's final segment, attaches a new `Task` node to `root`, and returns that `Task` as the response. Errors: unauthenticated calls are rejected before the body runs; an LLM failure inside `categorize` propagates as a server error; no validation is performed on `title`.

`AddTask` creates one task node. Its `title` field is supplied at spawn time; the `create` ability fires when the walker enters a `Root` node, derives a category by running the LLM-backed `categorize` on `self.title` and lower-casing the enum's tail, then attaches a new `Task` under `here` and reports the created node back to the spawner. Side effects: one LLM call and one persistent graph insertion per spawn.

`AddTask` walker with an explicitly typed `reports` field (`list[Task]`) so spawners get typed access to what the walker reports. Spawned with a `title`; on `Root` entry the `create` ability computes a category via the LLM-backed `categorize`, attaches a new `Task` under `here` carrying `self.title` and the derived `category`, and reports the new node. One LLM call plus one graph write per spawn.

`ListTasks` gathers every task reachable from the entry point. On `Root` entry the `start` ability queues all outgoing neighbors with `visit`; each `Task` the walker lands on triggers `collect`, which appends `here` to `self.results`; and `done`, bound to `Root` exit, reports the accumulated list once traversal finishes. The typed `reports` field exposes the result to the spawner. Read-only -- no graph mutation.

Private endpoint returning the caller's tasks. `get_tasks` takes no parameters and returns `list[Task]`: it reads the nodes directly connected to the authenticated user's `root` and filters them to `Task` instances. Read-only with no side effects; unauthenticated calls are rejected by the `def:priv` visibility.

`Task` node combining data with behavior. Fields: `title` (`str`), `done` (`bool`, default `False`), and `category` (`str`, default "other"). The `respond` ability runs whenever a `ListTasks` walker enters this node and appends `self` to the walker's `results` through `visitor` -- the node-side half of the collection pattern, letting tasks register themselves instead of the walker filtering by type.

`ToggleTask` flips one task's completion flag. Spawned with `task_id`; the `search` ability fans out from `Root` to all neighbors, and `toggle` fires on each `Task`, comparing `jid(here)` against the target. On a match it inverts `done`, reports the updated node, and `disengage` halts traversal so remaining nodes are never visited. If no task matches, the walker finishes silently with empty `reports`.

`DeleteTask` removes one task by id. Spawned with `task_id`; `search` queues all of `Root`'s neighbors, and `remove` fires per `Task`, deleting `here` when `jid(here)` matches, reporting a confirmation dict keyed "deleted", and stopping early with `disengage`. A non-matching id means no deletion and nothing reported. Side effect: permanent removal of the node from the graph.

`GenerateShoppingList` rebuilds the stored list from a meal description in one pass. On `Root` entry, `generate` first queues the existing neighbors with `visit` -- queued visits only run after the current ability finishes -- then calls the LLM-backed `generate_shopping_list` on `self.meal_description`, attaches each result as a `ShoppingItem` under `here`, and reports the `ShoppingItem` nodes connected to `here`. Afterward the queued visits fire and `clear_old` deletes each old `ShoppingItem` the walker enters. The ordering is the subtle part: generation runs before the clearing visits even though the `visit` call appears first.

Two companion walkers for the stored list. `GetShoppingList` fans out from `Root` (`collect`), appends each `ShoppingItem` it enters to `self.items` (`gather`), and on `Root` exit (`done`) reports the accumulated list through its typed `reports` field -- purely read-only. `ClearShoppingList` is the destructive counterpart: it visits the same neighbors and its `clear` ability deletes each `ShoppingItem`, reporting a "cleared" confirmation per deletion. Deletions are permanent graph mutations.

Walker-based AI day planner. The client block's `app` just renders `ClientApp` from `frontend`. The server block defines the `Category` and `Unit` enums, the `Ingredient` obj with `sem` hints, LLM delegations `categorize` and `generate_shopping_list`, and persistent `Task` and `ShoppingItem` nodes. Instead of function endpoints, every operation is a `walker:priv` archetype spawned on the authenticated user's graph: `AddTask`, `ListTasks`, `ToggleTask` (early exit via `disengage`), and `DeleteTask` for tasks; `GenerateShoppingList`, `GetShoppingList`, and `ClearShoppingList` for the shopping list. Each walker reports results through a typed `reports` field, and private visibility keeps every user's data under their own `root`.

`TasksPanel` is the client feature component (`def:pub`, returns `JsxElement`) that drives task CRUD by spawning private server walkers on `root`. On mount it spawns `ListTasks` and unpacks the first entry of `reports` (defaulting to an empty list) into `tasks`, clearing `tasksLoading`. `addTask` spawns `AddTask` with `title` and appends the reported node; `toggleTask` spawns `ToggleTask` with `task_id` and swaps in the reported update by `jid`; `deleteTask` spawns `DeleteTask` and filters locally without reading a response; `handleKeyPress` submits on Enter. Blank input is a no-op. A `ToggleTask` miss (empty `reports`) would raise on the index access. Authentication is implied by the walkers' private visibility -- each spawn acts on the logged-in user's own graph.

Shopping-list feature module for the walker-based planner. It imports `ShoppingItem` and the three server walkers (`GenerateShoppingList`, `GetShoppingList`, `ClearShoppingList`) plus the presentational `IngredientItem` row. `ShoppingPanel` holds `ingredients`, `mealText`, and `generating`; on mount it spawns `GetShoppingList` on `root` and unpacks the first entry of `reports`. `generateList` guards blank input, flags `generating`, spawns `GenerateShoppingList` with `meal_description`, and replaces the list from its reports; `clearList` spawns `ClearShoppingList` and resets local state; `handleKeyPress` maps Enter to generation. `totalCost` sums each ingredient's `cost` for the footer, and the render switches between a progress message, an empty-state prompt, and ingredient rows with total and clear controls.

Declares `classify_sentiment` as an LLM-delegated function: no body is written, because the signature is the whole specification. Given a `text` string it returns a sentiment label as a `str`; the model infers the intended behavior purely from the function name and the parameter and return types, as the usage shows (an enthusiastic sentence yielding "positive"). Each call performs one LLM request.

Document this Jac code:

```jac
sem classify = """
Analyze the emotional tone of the input text.
Return exactly one of: 'positive', 'negative', 'neutral'.
Consider context and sarcasm.
""";

def classify(text: str) -> str by llm;
```

Pairs a `sem` annotation with the LLM-delegated `classify` function. The semantic string is the behavioral contract the model sees: analyze emotional tone, return exactly one of 'positive', 'negative', or 'neutral', and account for context and sarcasm. This pins down an otherwise generic name -- `classify` alone underspecifies the task -- without changing the signature (`text` in, `str` out).

`summarize` delegates to whichever model the project's `jac.toml` declares as the default: delegating with no explicit model binding means no imports or globals are needed in this file. It takes `text` and returns a `str` summary; the entry block demonstrates calling it like any ordinary function and printing the result.

Overrides the default model for this file: it imports `Model` from `byllm.lib` and binds the global `llm` to "gpt-4o", so `summarize` -- delegated through this `llm` -- always runs on that model here. Scope is the point: the binding applies only where this global is in effect, leaving other files on their own configuration.

Routes different LLM tasks to different models by declaring three `Model` globals: `fast_model` (a mini model) backs the cheap `quick_label` call, `smart_model` backs the heavier `deep_analyze` (which returns a structured `dict`), and `summarizer` (a Claude model) backs `tldr`. Each delegated function names its model in its by-clause, so cost/quality trade-offs are made per function instead of globally.

Binds the global `llm` to a `Model` that talks to a custom or proxied endpoint: `config` supplies a `base_url` pointing at the alternate server and sets `proxy` to `True`, while `model_name` still identifies the underlying model. Functions delegated through this `llm` send their requests to that endpoint instead of the provider's default API.

Declares `llm` as a `ModelPool` instead of a single model: the `models` list holds the candidates, and `strategy` set to "fallback" means each is tried in order until one succeeds. The delegated `answer` function is unaffected by the pooling -- it takes a `question` and returns a `str` -- and callers never see which pool member actually served the request.

A concrete fallback pool: `ModelPool` wraps three `Model` entries tried in declaration order -- a Gemini flash model first, a mini GPT model if that fails, and a Claude model as the last resort. With `strategy` set to "fallback", a provider outage or error cascades transparently to the next entry. The pool binds to the global `llm` used by delegated functions.

Load-balances a single model across multiple API keys: the `ModelPool` lists three `Model` entries with the same model but different keys pulled from the environment via `os.getenv`, and `strategy` set to "simple-shuffle" picks among them per call. Useful for spreading traffic under per-key rate limits; the referenced environment variables must be set or the affected entries fail.

Zero-configuration LLM delegation: `greet` is declared with a by-llm clause using the builtin `llm`, so no imports or model globals are needed anywhere in the file. It takes a `name` and returns a generated `str` greeting; the entry block calls it like a normal function. Model selection falls back to the project or runtime default.

`respond` is an LLM-delegated chat turn with two invocation arguments: `system_prompt` fixes the assistant persona (a coding assistant answering in Jac), and `conversation` binds the caller-owned `history` list so prior turns are replayed on every call and new turns accumulate into it. Takes the user `msg`, returns the reply as a `str`; the shared `history` list is the side-effect channel that makes the exchange multi-turn.

Configures `Model` for a fully custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint. `config` carries `api_base` (the complete chat-completions URL), an inline `api_key`, `http_client` set to `True` to use the direct HTTP path, and `ca_bundle` controlling TLS verification -- `True` for default SSL, `False` to skip verification, or a path to a certificate file. The resulting `llm` global routes all delegated calls to that server.

The canonical shapes for an LLM-delegated declaration. The basic form is `function_name` with a typed `param` and return type and a by-llm clause in place of a body. The second form adds a `sem` line carrying a natural-language description -- recommended when the bare name is ambiguous, since the model derives behavior from the name, the types, and the `sem` text together.

Shows that an LLM-delegated method sees its object's state: `method_name` inside `MyClass` is declared with a by-llm clause, and the model receives the instance's fields -- here `attribute` -- as context alongside the method name and return type. This enables per-instance behavior without passing the fields as explicit parameters.

The recommended alternative to delegating a raw prompt string: declare a typed function `explain` with a by-llm clause and pass the subject as its `topic` argument. The entry block assigns the generated `str` to `response`. A typed signature gives the model a contract and gives callers checkable types, unlike inline prompt-expression delegation.

Four delegated functions demonstrating that primitive return types drive output coercion: `get_summary` yields a `str`, `count_words` an `int`, `is_positive` a `bool`, and `get_score` a `float`. Each takes the same `text` parameter; the declared return type alone tells the model what shape of answer to produce and lets the runtime convert and validate it.

Constrains LLM output to a closed set by returning an enum: `analyze_sentiment` takes `text` and must produce one of the `Sentiment` members -- `POSITIVE`, `NEGATIVE`, or `NEUTRAL`. The runtime converts the model's choice into an actual enum value, so callers get exhaustive, type-safe results instead of free-form strings.

Enum classification with per-member semantics: `classify_personality` maps a free-text `bio` to a `Personality` value. Each member carries a `sem` description -- `INTROVERT`, `EXTROVERT`, and `AMBIVERT` are each defined by how a person is energized -- and those descriptions are surfaced to the model, sharpening the decision boundary beyond what the bare member names convey.

Valued enums as LLM return types: `HttpStatus` binds members to `int` codes (`OK` = 200, `NOT_FOUND` = 404, `SERVER_ERROR` = 500) and `Tag` binds members to `str` values (`OPEN`, `CLOSE`). `get_status` maps a natural-language `description` to an `HttpStatus` member, so the caller receives a typed member whose value is the numeric status code.

Structured extraction into a typed object: `extract_person` reads free text and returns a `Person` with `name` (`str`), `age` (`int`), and `bio` (`str | None` -- optional, so the model may return null when no biography is present). The runtime instantiates and type-checks the object, turning missing or malformed fields into a conversion error rather than silent garbage.

A catalog of by-llm invocation parameters. `temperature` trades determinism for creativity (`generate_story` at 0.9 versus `extract_facts` at 0.0; provider ranges differ). `max_tokens` caps output length. Passing `tools` turns the call into a ReAct loop -- `calculate` may invoke `add` and `multiply`. `incl_info` injects extra context values computed at call time. `stream` set to `True` yields tokens incrementally, and adding `logging` upgrades the stream to structured `StreamEvent` objects, as in `smart_answer`. Finally, `conversation` binds the caller-owned `history` list for multi-turn use, combined with tools in `chat`.

The three levels of `sem` annotation. Object level: `Customer` is described as a CRM record. Attribute level: `Customer.id`, `Customer.name`, and `Customer.tier` each get precise semantics, including the closed set of tier strings. Enum-value level: `Priority.HIGH` gets an urgency definition. These strings travel with the types into every LLM call that touches them, steering extraction and classification without changing any runtime behavior.

Documents an LLM-delegated function through parameter-level `sem` entries: `analyze_code.code` describes the source input, `analyze_code.language` the language hint, and `analyze_code.return` the expected output structure. The function itself takes `code` and `language` and returns a `dict`; the `sem` lines are the only specification of what that dict should contain.

Structured output with an explicit return contract: `analyze` returns a `CodeAnalysis` object carrying `issues`, `suggestions`, a `complexity_score` on a 1-10 scale, and a one-paragraph `summary`. The `sem` annotation on `analyze.return` spells out each field's meaning, so the model fills the object deliberately instead of guessing from field names alone.

Three plain (non-LLM) functions written to serve as agent tools, each with a docstring the model will see. `get_date` returns today's date in YYYY-MM-DD form. `search_db` takes a `query` and an optional `limit` (default 10) and returns matching records as `list[dict]`. `send_email` takes `recipient`, `subject`, and `body` and reports success as a `bool`. Clear names, typed parameters, and docstrings are exactly what make functions usable as tools.

`answer_question` is an agentic LLM function: its `tools` list hands the model three callables -- `get_date`, `search_db`, and `send_email` -- and the runtime drives the resulting reason/act loop until a final `str` answer to the `question` is produced. Note that one of the tools sends email, so a call can have real side effects beyond computing text.

`Calculator` is a stateful tool-using agent object. It keeps a running `memory` value; `add` accumulates into it and `clear` resets it, both returning the new state. `calculate` is LLM-delegated with `tools` bound to the instance's own methods (`self.add`, `self.clear`), so the model manipulates this particular instance's `memory` while interpreting free-form `instructions`. Calls therefore mutate the object they run on.

Per-iteration control of an agent loop. `my_hook` receives an `IterationContext` and returns an `IterationAction`: it aborts outright past five iterations (`ABORT`), aborts with a summarized answer once `total_tokens` exceeds 10000 (`ABORT_WITH_SUMMARY`), and otherwise lets the loop continue (`CONTINUE`). Wiring the hook into `agent_task` via `on_iteration` bounds runaway tool loops by both step count and token budget.

`my_agent` enables concurrent tool execution: with `parallelize` set to `True`, when the model emits several independent calls to `search`, `fetch`, or `analyze` in a single step, the runtime executes them simultaneously instead of one after another, cutting wall-clock latency for fan-out workloads. Semantics are otherwise unchanged -- `query` in, `str` out.

Demonstrates parallel tool execution with a safety valve. The module binds `llm` to a `Model` and defines two tools: `get_weather`, which is slow (it sleeps a second per call, simulating I/O), and `save_log`, whose `sem` warns that it has side effects. `weather_agent` is delegated with both `tools` and `parallelize` enabled, so a question spanning three cities triggers three concurrent `get_weather` calls -- roughly one second total instead of three. The entry block calls `mark_serialize` on `save_log`, forcing any batch containing that tool to run sequentially: parallelism for the safe tool, ordering guarantees for the side-effecting one.

Document this Jac code:

```jac
# Per-call - highest priority
def my_agent(query: str) -> str by llm(
    tools=[search, compute],
    ctx_window=128000,
    threshold_ratio=0.75,
    keep_recent_iterations=5,
    compaction_model="ollama/llama3.2:1b",
    compaction_enabled=True,
    on_compaction=my_hook
);

# Per-object - applied to every call on this model instance
glob llm = Model(model_name="gpt-4o", ctx_window=128000);
```

Context-compaction configuration at two scopes. Per call, `my_agent` sets the full parameter surface: `ctx_window` (context size), `threshold_ratio` (fill fraction that triggers compaction), `keep_recent_iterations` (history kept verbatim), `compaction_model` (a cheap local model that does the summarizing), `compaction_enabled`, and `on_compaction` (a custom hook, here `my_hook`). Per object, a `Model` constructed with `ctx_window` applies that setting to every call routed through it; per-call values take priority over per-object ones.

`my_compactor` is a custom compaction hook: given the `messages` list and a `keep_recent` count, it preserves the first two entries (system message and original user task), condenses the tool-call history through `my_domain_summariser` into a single summary message, and re-appends the most recent turns. The returned list replaces the agent's context. Wired into `my_agent` via `on_compaction`, it lets domain knowledge decide what survives compaction instead of the default summarizer.

Document this Jac code:

```jac
# In jac.toml - applies globally
# [plugins.byllm.compaction]
# compaction_model = "ollama/llama3.2:1b"

# Per-call
def my_agent(query: str) -> str by llm(
    tools=[search],
    compaction_model="ollama/llama3.2:1b"
```
