Takes no parameters, performs no side effects, and returns a `JsxElement` fragment. Because this is a layout file, every page in the folder automatically renders inside it.

`app` declares the application's client-side routing table rather than an HTTP API. Inside a `Router` from "@jac/runtime", the `Routes` block holds three `Route` entries mapping `path` "/", "/about", and "/contact" to the `Home`, `About`, and `Contact` components through the `element` prop. All routes are public -- no auth gate is present. The "request" is the browser URL; the "response" is the matched component's `JsxElement`. Unmatched paths render nothing since no wildcard `Route` exists, and `Home`, `About`, and `Contact` must be defined elsewhere; `Link` is imported but unused.

A self-contained three-page client application built on the "@jac/runtime" router. It defines three stateless page components -- `Home`, `About`, and `Contact` -- each returning a static `JsxElement`, plus the `app` entry point that ties them together. `app` wraps everything in a `Router`: a persistent nav of `Link` elements provides navigation, while the `Routes` block maps "/", "/about", and "/contact" to their components through `Route` elements' `element` prop. Because the nav lives outside `Routes`, it stays visible on every page while only the routed content swaps. Everything sits in one `cl` block, so the entire module runs in the browser with `app` as the mount point.

`NavExample` demonstrates the two kinds of navigation in a client component: the `Link` component for internal, client-side route changes (here to "/about"), versus a plain anchor tag for external URLs (here "https://example.com"). Internal `Link` navigation swaps routes without a full page reload; the anchor performs a normal browser navigation. Returns a `JsxElement`; no parameters, state, or side effects. `Link` is used without an import in this snippet, so it must already be in scope.

File-based dynamic route reference: "pages/users/[id].jac" matches URLs like "/users/42" and exposes the bracketed segment through `useParams`. The public `page` component reads `params`, pulls the "id" key into `user_id`, and renders it in a profile view. No auth wrapper is present. The "request" is the URL path parameter; the "response" is a `JsxElement` echoing `user_id`. There is no validation or error branch -- any string in the segment renders as-is.

Defines a parameterized route and its consumer together. `UserProfile` calls `useParams`, reads `params`, and extracts the "id" key into `user_id` for display. `app` registers the mapping: a `Router` containing a single `Route` whose `path` "/user/:id" declares the dynamic segment, binding `UserProfile` via the `element` prop. Both functions return `JsxElement` values, hold no state, and have no side effects; the router re-renders `UserProfile` with fresh `params` whenever the segment changes.

`BlogPost` shows how a route with multiple dynamic segments surfaces its values: `useParams` returns one entry per placeholder, and the component reads the "category" and "postId" keys directly from `params`. As the trailing comments illustrate, a route of "/blog/:category/:postId" visited at "/blog/tech/123" yields a `params` mapping of "tech" and "123". Returns a `JsxElement` displaying both values; stateless with no side effects.

Layout route reference, not an HTTP endpoint. Placed at "pages/dashboard/layout.jac", `layout` wraps every child page under "/dashboard": an aside of `Link` items targeting "/dashboard", "/dashboard/settings", and "/dashboard/profile", plus a main area whose `Outlet` renders whichever child route is active. It must be `def:pub` for the router to mount it. No auth is enforced here -- any visitor reaches these routes unless a guard is added elsewhere. Returns a `JsxElement`; no parameters or error cases.

A nested-routing dashboard module. `DashboardLayout` provides the persistent shell: a sidebar of `Link` navigation plus a main region whose `Outlet` slot hosts the active child. Three leaf pages -- `DashboardHome`, `DashboardSettings`, and `DashboardProfile` -- are minimal heading-only components. `app` is the entry point: its `Router`/`Routes` tree declares a parent `Route` at "/dashboard" rendering `DashboardLayout`, with an `index` child for the overview and relative `path` children "settings" and "profile". The relationship is strictly compositional -- the layout never knows which child renders; the router injects it through `Outlet`.

`LoginForm` renders a controlled login form and redirects on success. Two reactive `has` fields, `email` and `password`, hold the credentials (only `email` is wired to an input in this snippet). Clicking Login runs the async `handle_login`, which awaits `do_login` with both values; on a truthy result it calls `navigate` (obtained from `useNavigate`) to send the user to "/dashboard". Side effects: the network call through `do_login` and the client-side route change. Returns a `JsxElement`. `do_login` must be defined elsewhere, and `password` currently has no corresponding input field.

Client navigation reference, not a server route. `NavExample` demonstrates the call signatures of the function returned by `useNavigate`, bound to `navigate` and wired to four button `onClick` handlers: a path string ("/home") pushes a new history entry; a path plus an options `dict` with "replace" set to `True` replaces the current entry (used for "/login" so Back cannot return to the pre-login page); and the integer forms -1 and 1 move backward and forward through history. Returns a `JsxElement`; no auth or error semantics -- unregistered paths are resolved by the router's own route table.

`ProtectedRoute` is a hand-rolled auth wrapper that renders its `children` only when the visitor is logged in. It queries `jacIsLoggedIn` for session state and, in its mount ability, calls `navigate` to "/login" with "replace" set to `True`, so the redirect does not pollute browser history. While unauthenticated it renders a "Redirecting..." placeholder instead of the protected content. Parameter: `children` (default `None`), the JSX to protect. Returns a `JsxElement`; the conditional client-side redirect on mount is the only side effect.

Client route driven by URL query parameters -- the "request" shape is the query string, e.g. "/search?q=hello&page=2". `SearchResults` reads the current location via `useLocation`, parses it with `URLSearchParams`, and extracts `query` (key "q", defaulting to empty) and `page` (key "page", defaulting to "1" and coerced with `int`). `updatePage` handles the Previous/Next buttons by calling `navigate` with a rebuilt "/search" URL, so pagination state lives entirely in the query string and survives reload/back. Previous is `disabled` when `page` is 1 or lower. No auth; the main unhandled error case is a non-numeric "page" value, which would make the `int` conversion throw.

`NotFound` is the fallback screen rendered when no route matches: a 404 heading, a message, and a `Link` home. `app` wires it in by registering a wildcard `Route` (`path` "*") after the concrete "/" and "/about" entries inside `Routes`, so the router falls through to it only when nothing else matches. Both functions are stateless and return `JsxElement` values; `Home` and `About` are referenced but defined elsewhere.

`Navigation` renders the site nav with active-link highlighting. It obtains the current `location` from `useLocation`; the nested helper `isActive` compares the location's `pathname` against a candidate `path` and returns a `bool`. Each `Link` builds its `className` from a base "nav-link" plus "active" when its own route matches, so exactly one link is highlighted per page. Returns a `JsxElement`; it re-renders on route changes and has no other side effects.

Full client routing table for a small storefront -- routes, not HTTP endpoints. `app` mounts a `Router` whose single parent `Route` at "/" renders `Layout`: a header nav of `Link` elements, an `Outlet` for the active page, and a footer. Children: an `index` route to `Home`; "products" renders `Products`, which maps a hard-coded `products` list into detail links; the dynamic "products/:id" renders `ProductDetail`, which reads `params` via `useParams` into `product_id` and offers a history-back button through `navigate`; "about" renders `About`; and the wildcard "*" routes to `NotFound` as the 404 fallback. Every route is public -- no auth guard anywhere. "Responses" are `JsxElement` trees; the wildcard route is the only error path.

Document this Jac code:

```jac
cl import from "@jac/runtime" {
    Link,           # Navigation link component
    useNavigate,    # Programmatic navigation
    useParams,      # Access URL parameters
    useLocation,    # Get current location info
    Navigate,       # Redirect component
    Outlet          # Render child routes (for layouts)
}
```

Import manifest for the "@jac/runtime" navigation toolkit, annotated inline: `Link` renders client-side navigation anchors; `useNavigate` returns a function for programmatic route changes; `useParams` exposes dynamic URL segments; `useLocation` reports the current location; `Navigate` is the declarative redirect component; and `Outlet` marks where a layout renders its child routes. Importing them at the `cl` level makes the router primitives available to every component in the module; the statement has no runtime behavior beyond binding these names.

A single-file fullstack module. On the server side, `Todo` is a persistent `node` with a `title` string and a `done` flag defaulting to `False`; the `get_todos` walker (exposed via `walker:pub`) has a `fetch` ability that fires on `Root` entry, filters the root's outgoing neighbors down to `Todo` nodes, and emits each one with `report`, so a caller receives the full todo list. On the client side, the `cl` block's `app` component currently stands alone: it renders a static `message` greeting and does not yet invoke `get_todos`. The walker endpoint is the seam where the two halves would connect.

Illustrates the server/browser split within one file. `api_endpoint` is a `walker` -- backend code: when spawned, its `visit` ability fires on `Root` entry and reports an empty `dict`, making it a stub API surface with no input fields and a single empty report as its response. `MyComponent`, declared `def:pub` inside the `cl` block, is frontend code that returns a static `JsxElement` and never touches the server. No auth requirement or error handling is defined in either half.

A minimal single-file fullstack skeleton showing where each concern lives in "main.jac". Backend: `User` is a graph `node` carrying a `name` field, and the `get_user` walker supplies the server behavior -- its `visit` ability fires on `Root` entry and reports an empty `dict` placeholder. Frontend: the `cl` block holds `app`, the public browser entry component, currently rendering a static div. The two halves share the file but run in different environments; the walker is the seam where the client would fetch server data. Entry points: `app` for the UI, `get_user` for the API.

`get_user` is a walker housed in "api.jac", a module that imports the `User` and `Todo` models from the `models` module. Its single `visit` ability fires when the walker enters the `Root` node and reports an empty `dict` -- a stub response, since neither imported model is used yet. It declares no `has` fields, so spawning it takes no parameters, and it performs no graph mutation.

Not an HTTP route -- this documents the client entry wiring in "main.jac". Inside the `cl` block, `Header` is imported from "./components/Header.cl.jac" (the extension marks that file client-side), and `app`, the required public root component, composes it above a main content area. `app` takes no props and returns a `JsxElement`. No auth, state, or error handling; failures here are compile-time only, such as a bad import path or a non-public `Header`.

`app` is a minimal stateful client entry point: a centered page showing a heading, the current `count`, and an Increment button. `count` is a reactive `has` field (an `int` starting at 0); the button's `onClick` lambda reassigns it, and that reassignment triggers a re-render so the display stays current. No parameters or external calls; returns a `JsxElement`.

Component reference, not a network endpoint. `Counter` is a public, prop-less client component whose only state is the reactive `has` field `count` (`int`, default 0). "Request": the user clicks the Increment button; "handler": the `onClick` lambda reassigns `count`, which re-renders the component; "response": the updated Count line. No auth or error cases -- all logic is local and synchronous.

This module models a self-contained contact form with purely local state. `Form` declares three reactive `has` fields: `name` and `email` mirror the two controlled inputs -- each `onChange` lambda copies the event target's value back into state -- and `submitted` flags completion. `handle_submit` is the single action: it prints the captured values and flips `submitted` to `True`, at which point the component short-circuits to a thank-you message instead of the form. There is no validation or server interaction; the print is the only side effect. Entry point: the public `Form` component.

`TodoApp` is a fully client-side todo list. State: `todos` (a `list` of id/text records) and `input_text` (the controlled input's value). `add_todo` guards against empty input, appends a new entry whose id comes from the current list length, and clears `input_text`; `remove_todo` filters out the entry whose "id" matches its `id` parameter. Both update state by building a new list, which triggers a re-render. The UI wires the Add button to `add_todo` and each item's X button to `remove_todo`. Returns a `JsxElement`; nothing persists -- the list resets on reload.

Component lifecycle reference rather than a route. `DataFetcher` loads remote data exactly once on mount: its async entry ability (async effect bodies are IIFE-wrapped automatically) awaits `some_async_operation`, stores the result in `data`, and clears `loading`. While `loading` is `True` it renders a Loading placeholder; afterwards it maps `data` into a list, keying each row on the item's `id` and displaying its `name`. No parameters; the "response" is a `JsxElement`. Errors are unhandled -- a rejected `some_async_operation` leaves the component stuck on the loading branch.

`Subscriber` pairs setup and teardown lifecycle abilities. On mount, the entry ability calls `subscribe_to_events` to begin listening; on unmount, the exit ability calls `cleanup_subscriptions`, preventing leaked listeners. The `events` state field backs the rendered count via `len`, though nothing in this snippet appends to it -- the subscription callback is expected to do that elsewhere. Returns a `JsxElement` showing the event count.

React-interop lifecycle reference. `Timer` keeps a `seconds` counter in a reactive `has` field and drives it with the raw `useEffect` hook imported from `react`: on mount the effect starts a one-second `setInterval` that increments `seconds`, and it returns a cleanup lambda calling `clearInterval` with the saved `intervalId`, so the timer is torn down on unmount. The empty dependency array makes the effect run exactly once. Renders the elapsed seconds; no props, auth, or error cases.

`DataFetcher` shows the minimal `useEffect` mount pattern inside a `cl` component: with an empty dependency array, the effect lambda runs once after first render and invokes `fetch_data` (defined elsewhere) to kick off loading. Results are expected to land in the reactive `data` field, though this snippet never assigns it. The effect lambda is annotated as returning `None`, meaning no cleanup function is registered. Returns a placeholder `JsxElement`.

`FocusableInput` demonstrates imperative DOM access through a ref. The `inputRef` field is a `Ref` typed to `HTMLInputElement` -- the comment notes it compiles to React's `useRef` -- and it is attached to the input through the `ref` prop. The `focus` helper guards on the ref's `current` value before calling the DOM focus method; the button's `onClick` triggers it, moving keyboard focus into the field. Returns a `JsxElement`; the imperative focus call is the only side effect.

Context-based state sharing, documented as a component API. `AppContext` is a module-level `glob` created with `createContext`. `AppProvider` owns the shared state -- `user` (default `None`) and `theme` (default "light") -- and publishes a `value` mapping bundling both plus "setUser" and "setTheme" updater lambdas; its `children` prop receives the nested JSX. Consumers call `useContext` with `AppContext`: `UserDisplay` branches on the context's `user` between a welcome message and "Not logged in", while `ThemeToggle` flips `theme` between "light" and "dark" through the shared setter. `app` composes both consumers inside the provider. Error case: rendering a consumer outside `AppProvider` yields the `None` default, so member access on the context would fail.

This module packages localStorage persistence as a reusable hook. `use_local_storage` is a custom hook holding a reactive `value` seeded from `initial_value`: one `useEffect` hydrates it from `localStorage` under `key` on mount (JSON-parsed when an entry exists), and a second effect, keyed on `value`, re-serializes and writes every change back. It returns a `tuple` of the current value and a setter lambda. `Settings` is the demo consumer: it destructures the pair into `theme` and `set_theme`, shows the current theme, and offers Dark/Light buttons that call the setter -- each click round-trips through the persistence effect, so the choice survives reloads. Entry point: `Settings`; the hook is the reusable piece.

Form-handling reference. `ContactForm` keeps its "request body" in `form_data`, a `dict` with "name", "email", and "message" keys, which `update_field` rebuilds immutably on each keystroke. `validate` is the gate: it requires a non-empty "name" and an "@" in "email", collecting failures into the `errors` dict and returning a `bool`. `handle_submit` proceeds -- setting `submitting` -- only when `validate` passes; the transmission itself is elided. Error "responses" surface inline: the name input renders its `errors` entry beneath it when present. Only the name field is wired up in this snippet.

Three minimal declarations illustrating Jac function signatures. `add` takes two `int` parameters, `a` and `b`, and returns their sum. `greet` interpolates its `name` argument into an f-string and returns the greeting as a `str`. `log` is a side-effect-only function: it prints `message` with a "[LOG]" prefix and declares a `None` return, signaling callers not to expect a value. All three are pure apart from the console output in `log`.

Demonstrates Jac docstring placement: a triple-quoted string at the top of the file documents the module, and a string literal immediately preceding a declaration documents that declaration -- here "Function docstring." attaches to `add` and "Object docstring." attaches to the `Person` `obj`. `add` itself returns the sum of its `int` parameters `a` and `b`; `Person` declares a single `name` field with `has`. The convention mirrors Python's, except the docstring sits above the construct rather than inside its body.

`complete_example` is a signature showcase exercising every parameter category in required order: `pos_only1` and `pos_only2` precede the slash marker, making them positional-only; `pos_or_kw` may be passed either way; `with_default` carries a fallback of 10; `*args` absorbs extra positional `int` values; `kw_only` and `kw_default` come after the variadic, so they must be named at the call site (the latter defaulting to `True`); and `**kwargs` collects any remaining keyword arguments and must appear last. The body only prints, so the function exists purely to document the ordering rules.

`greet` restricts its parameter to positional passing: the slash marker after `name` makes it positional-only, so the plain call in the entry block is legal while the commented keyword form would be an error. The function simply interpolates `name` into a greeting and returns the `str`. Positional-only parameters keep the name out of the calling convention, so it can be renamed later without breaking callers.

Three functions covering variadic parameters. `sum_all` gathers all positional arguments into `values` and returns their total via `sum`. `build_config` collects arbitrary keyword arguments into `options` and materializes them as a `dict`. `flexible` combines the forms: a leading `required` parameter, `*args` for overflow positionals, and `**kwargs` for overflow keywords, printing each group. The entry block's calls show the routing -- e.g. passing 1, 2, 3, and a keyword yields `required` 1, extra positionals (2, 3), and a keyword mapping for "name".

Demonstrates argument unpacking into `add`, which sums its three `int` parameters `a`, `b`, and `c`. A `list` such as `values` is splatted with a single star into positional arguments; a `dict` such as `params` is splatted with a double star into keyword arguments; and the final example mixes both forms in one call. Each variant produces the identical invocation, so `result` is the same every time. Unpacking fails at runtime if the sequence length or the dict keys do not match the signature.

`ListItems` is a collecting walker with an `items` accumulator declared via `has`. Its three abilities fire automatically based on where the walker is and the traversal phase: `collect` runs when the walker enters the `Root` node and queues all outgoing neighbors with `visit`; `gather` runs on each `Item` node reached, appending that node's `value` (accessed through `here`) to the walker's own list via `self`; and `report_all` fires on `Root` exit, reporting the accumulated `items` back to the spawner. The net effect is a one-hop scan: spawn it on `root` and receive every connected item value in a single report.

`Calculator` is a stateful accumulator object. Its single `has` field, `total` (a `float` starting at 0.0), persists across calls. `add` folds `value` into the running total through `self` and returns the new total, so sequential calls read naturally; `reset` zeroes the accumulator and returns `None`. No validation is performed -- negative or extreme inputs are accepted as-is.

`Counter` contrasts static and instance members. The static `count` field lives on the class itself and is shared by all instances. `get_count` is a static accessor returning that shared value, and `make` is a static factory returning a fresh `Counter`, keeping the return type explicit. `increment` is the only instance method, but note it bumps the class-level counter through the `Counter` name rather than `self` -- so calling `increment` on any instance advances the same shared value.

`Animal` models a named creature whose `sound` defaults to "..."; `speak` formats both fields into a description. `named` is a static factory that builds an `Animal` from just a `name`, leaving the default sound in place. `Dog` subclasses `Animal` and overrides only the `sound` default to "woof", inheriting `speak` unchanged. As the entry block shows, the factory-built `Animal` speaks with the placeholder sound while a `Dog` given the same name says woof -- inheritance by changing a field default, without redefining behavior.

`QueryBuilder` implements a fluent builder: `from_table` and `limit` each mutate the instance (`table` and `limit_val` respectively) and return `Self`, so calls chain left-to-right as in the entry example. `table` starts empty and `limit_val` at -1, the sentinel for "no limit". The `Self` return annotation keeps chaining type-correct even for subclasses. No validation occurs and no query executes -- the object only accumulates configuration.

`make_adder` is a closure factory: each call returns a new lambda that captures the `x` it was given and adds it to its own argument `y`. The entry block builds two independent adders, `add_five` and `add_ten`, and the printed results (15 and 20 for the same input) show that each closure keeps its own captured `x` -- Jac closures capture per-invocation environments rather than sharing state.

Shows an immediately-invoked lambda: the typed expression doubling `x` is defined and called in a single statement, so `result` receives 10 without the lambda ever being named. Useful for computing a value inline where a full function declaration would be noise -- the parenthesized lambda is a first-class value like any other.

An immediately-invoked function expression using `def` rather than a lambda: the anonymous function assembles `host` and `port` locals into a configuration `dict` -- including a derived "url" entry -- and is called on the spot, binding the finished mapping to `config`. The pattern gives multi-statement initialization its own scope, so the intermediate variables never leak into the surrounding entry block.

Combines a named function expression with immediate invocation: `make_adder` is defined inline, called instantly with 10, and only its return value -- a lambda closing over `x` -- survives as `adder`. The closure adds its captured 10 to `y`, so the subsequent call prints 15. The name `make_adder` exists only inside the expression; the surrounding scope sees just `adder`.

`Counter` is a minimal mutable counter `obj`: a required `count` field, `inc` to increment it through `self`, and `get` to read it back (both declared in the parenthesis-free method form). `make_counter` is a `glob` lambda factory producing a `Counter` seeded at `start`. The entry block seeds one at 10, applies `inc` three times, and prints 13 -- demonstrating that an object constructed through a lambda is ordinary mutable state.

Two decorator shapes. `decorator` is the plain form: it receives the function object as `func` and returns it unchanged, applied to `my_function` with a bare decorator line -- a no-op pass-through. `decorator_with_args` is a decorator factory: called first with its own arguments (`arg1`, `arg2`), it returns the actual decorating lambda, which again passes the function through untouched; it is applied to `another_function`. Both decorated functions keep their original behavior -- the snippet documents the wiring, not a transformation.

Documents Jac's three function access modifiers. `public_func` uses `def:pub`, the default visibility, callable from anywhere. `_private_func` is marked `def:priv`, restricting calls to the defining module. `_protected_func` uses `def:protect`, extending access to the module plus subclasses. The leading underscores are naming convention only -- the modifier is what the checker enforces. All three bodies are empty; the snippet exists to show the annotation syntax.

Three functions plus a driver block. `greet` returns a formatted greeting for `name`; `add` sums `a` and `b`. The interesting one is `apply`: it accepts `func`, typed as a `Callable` taking two ints and returning one, along with operands `x` and `y`, and simply invokes the callable -- a minimal higher-order function. The entry block exercises all three, passing a multiplication lambda into `apply` so the final line prints 30. Functions and lambdas share the same calling convention.

`Person` shows the `postinit` hook: fields declared with `has` (`name` and `age`) produce an automatic constructor, and `postinit` runs immediately after that constructor finishes -- here printing a creation message with the initialized `self` available. `greet` is an ordinary instance method returning an introduction. The entry block's keyword construction fires the hook before `greet` is ever called. Use `postinit` for derived setup that needs the declared fields already populated.

The corrected form of the dynamic-attribute mistake: `Person` declares both `name` and `height` in a single `has` clause, with `height` defaulting to 0, so construction can set them via keywords and the later read is valid. This is the Jac contract -- an `obj` has a closed field list, and every attribute an instance will ever carry must appear in `has`.

An anti-pattern illustration: `Dog` is declared with Python-style `class`, and both `rename` and `train` create attributes (`secret`, `trick`) by assigning through `self` inside method bodies instead of declaring them. The comments flag each line as dynamic assignment to avoid -- such attributes exist only after the corresponding method has run, invisible to the checker and to readers. The remedy is declaring the fields with `has` on an `obj`.

The declared-fields version of the dynamic-assignment anti-pattern: `Dog` is an `obj` whose `secret` and `trick` fields are declared together in `has` with empty-string defaults, so `rename` and `train` merely update existing state through `self`. All fields are visible in one place, the checker can verify every access, and instances keep a stable shape from construction onward.

An inheritance hierarchy demo. `Animal` is the base: a required `name` and a `speak` stub returning an empty string. `Dog` and `Cat` subclass it and mark `speak` with `override` -- `Dog` also adds a defaulted `breed` field -- each returning its own sound. `Trackable` is a mixin contributing a `tracked` flag. `Pet` demonstrates multiple inheritance from `Animal` and `Trackable`; as the comment notes, because a parent declares defaulted fields, every field `Pet` adds (`owner`, plus its redeclared `name`) must also carry defaults -- a dataclass ordering constraint inherited from Python.

Two enum styles plus usage. `Color` binds explicit string values to `RED`, `GREEN`, and `BLUE`; `Status` omits values, so `PENDING`, `ACTIVE`, and `COMPLETED` receive automatic ones. The entry block assigns members to variables and interpolates them like ordinary values. Use explicit values when the representation matters (serialization, display) and automatic values when only member identity does.

`Crate` is a typed enum: annotating the enum header with `Box` declares that every member's value is a `Box` instance, so `SMALL` and `LARGE` each carry their own `Box` (whose `size` field defaults to 0). The pattern gives enum members structured payloads instead of primitive values while keeping the closed, named-member semantics of an enum.

`HttpStatus` is an integer-valued enum (`OK` = 200, `NOT_FOUND` = 404) extended with behavior through an embedded Python block. Inside the `::py::` section, `is_success` tests whether the member's value falls in the 2xx range, and the `message` property maps known codes to reason phrases with an "Unknown" fallback. The pattern shows that enum members can carry methods and properties -- callers get the numeric value and semantic helpers from one type.

`Account` wraps its private `_balance` storage in a managed `balance` property declared inline. The `getter` returns the stored value; the `setter` validates that the incoming `value` is non-negative, raising `ValueError` before writing through; and the `deleter` resets the balance to 0.0 rather than removing the attribute. Callers interact only with `balance` -- the underscore field is the implementation detail the property protects.

The split-file variant of a managed property: inside `Account`, the `balance` declaration lists only the signatures of its `getter`, `setter`, and `deleter`, and each body is supplied separately in an `impl` block (e.g. `Account.balance.getter`). Behavior matches the inline form -- reads proxy `_balance`, writes reject negative values with `ValueError`, and deletion resets the balance to 0.0 -- but declaration and implementation can live apart, keeping the type's surface compact.

A combined enum-and-inheritance example. `Color` maps `RED`, `GREEN`, and `BLUE` to string values. `Animal` requires `name` and `sound` and formats them in `speak`; `Dog` extends it with a required `breed` and redefines `speak` to include the breed. The entry block constructs a `Dog` with all three fields, calls the overridden method, and reads the underlying string of a member via `Color.BLUE.value` -- showing enum value access alongside subclass behavior.

Separates a type's interface from its behavior. `Calculator` declares one stored field, `value`, plus semicolon-terminated signatures for `add` and `multiply` with no bodies. The two `impl` blocks supply those bodies: each folds its `x` argument into `self.value` (by addition or multiplication) and returns the running result. Callers see a complete type; the split keeps the declaration readable as an API summary while the implementations can live elsewhere, even in a separate file.

The implementation half of a split `Calculator` type: two `impl` blocks attach bodies to the previously declared `add` and `multiply` signatures. Each mutates the shared accumulator -- `add` adds `x` to `self.value`, `multiply` scales it -- and returns the updated total so results can be read straight from the call. The parameter name `x` comes from the declaration; the bodies reference it without restating the signature.

An interface-style declaration: `Circle` stores a required `radius` and announces an `area` method returning `float`, but supplies no body -- the trailing semicolon defers implementation to a separate block compiled alongside. Note the parameterless declaration form omits parentheses entirely. Until the matching implementation is linked, the type documents its contract only.

`Display` declares a minimal renderable contract: one required `label` field and a `render` method signature returning `str`, body omitted via the semicolon form (the parameterless declaration also skips parentheses). A companion implementation elsewhere fills in `render`; consumers depend only on this declared surface.

Implementation blocks completing two separately declared types. `Circle.area` computes the area from `self.radius` using a hard-coded pi approximation; `Display.render` prefixes `self.label` with "Displaying: ". Each `impl` restates the return type and reaches the archetype's fields through `self`. Keeping these bodies apart from their declarations lets the interface files stay signature-only.

Supplies the body for the `describe` method declared on `CircleService`: it returns the instance's `name` prefixed with "Service: ". The `impl` block restates the `str` return type and accesses the declared field through `self`; nothing else about the type is redefined here.

A native-compilation module (the `.na.jac` extension) linking directly against the system C math library: the import block binds `sqrt` and `pow` from "/usr/lib/libm.so.6" as foreign functions with `f64` signatures. `hypotenuse` computes the hypotenuse of a right triangle from sides `a` and `b`, summing their squares and delegating the root to the C `sqrt`; `pow` is bound but unused here. Compiled natively, the calls go straight into libm with no Python runtime involved.

A native Jac program binding a minimal slice of the raylib C API from "libraylib.so": window management (`InitWindow`, `CloseWindow`, `WindowShouldClose`), the frame lifecycle (`BeginDrawing`, `EndDrawing`), and rendering (`ClearBackground`, `DrawText`), each declared with native types such as `i32`. The entry block opens an 800x600 window and runs the classic game loop -- while `WindowShouldClose` returns 0 it clears the background and draws a title string each frame -- then closes the window on exit. Demonstrates driving a C graphics library from a `.na.jac` file with no wrapper layer.

The smallest runnable Jac program: a `with entry` block is a module's execution entry point -- the counterpart of Python's main guard -- and this one simply calls `print` with a greeting. Code outside an entry block only defines things; placing the statement here is what makes the module actually do something when run.

`Header` is a shared presentational component living in "components/Header.cl.jac" -- the `.cl.jac` extension marks the entire file as client-side, so no wrapper block is needed. It is declared `def:pub` so other modules can import it, takes no props, holds no state, and returns a static `JsxElement` header bar. A typical building block for a layout or root component to compose.

Access-modifier tour for callables. `helper` shows that an unadorned `def` is public by default; `api_function` makes that explicit with `def:pub`; and `internal_helper` uses `def:priv`, confining it to the module. The same modifiers carry extra weight on walkers: a `walker:pub` such as `GetUsers` is exposed as an HTTP API endpoint when the app is served, while `walker:priv` keeps `InternalProcess` invocable only from server-side code.

Shows server-only code sections. The plain `node` declaration of `User` (with its `email` field) is already server-side by default; the `sv` prefix makes the scoping explicit for single statements without needing a block -- one line imports `connect_db` from the local `database` module, another declares the `SecretData` node with its `value` field. Statements marked `sv` are excluded from the client bundle, so database wiring and secret-bearing types never reach the browser.

`GetUsers` is declared `walker:pub`, so serving the app exposes it as an HTTP endpoint -- per the trailing comment, POST /walker/GetUsers. Request: the walker declares no `has` fields, so the body carries no arguments. Behavior: the `get` ability fires on `Root` entry, filters the root's outgoing neighbors down to `User` nodes, binds them to `users`, and reports the list -- the response payload is that reported collection. Error cases: none are handled explicitly; on an empty graph the endpoint simply reports an empty list.

A minimal fullstack task app in one module, organized around typed data crossing the wire. `Task` is a persistent `node` with a `title` and a `done` flag. Two public server functions operate on the graph from `root`: `get_tasks` returns every attached `Task` as a typed `list`, and `create_task` attaches a new one and returns it. The `cl` block is the browser half: it imports both functions with `sv import`, and `app` awaits `get_tasks` on mount to fill `tasks`, while `addTask` awaits `create_task` and appends the result. Because the server returns typed objects, the client receives hydrated `Task` instances -- the JSX reads `title` and `done` as attributes, not dict keys. Entry points: `app` on the client and the two `def:pub` functions as the API.

`create_todo` is a public walker that persists a new task. Its `text` field is the request parameter, supplied when the walker is spawned. The `create` ability fires on `Root` entry: it connects a fresh `Task` -- with `title` taken from `self.text` -- to the current node via `here` using the `++>` connect operator, then reports the result. As the comment notes, the report carries a typed `Task` back to the caller rather than a raw `dict`. Side effect: one new node and connecting edge in the caller's graph.

An entry block sketching module introspection: `get_module_walkers` is expected to return the walkers defined in the module and `get_module_functions` the plain functions, with the results bound to `walkers` and `functions`. Neither helper is defined or imported in this snippet, so it documents the intent -- enumerating a module's callable surface at runtime -- rather than working code.

`app` is the canonical minimal client entry point: a public, parameterless component inside a `cl` block returning a static `JsxElement` -- a div wrapping a Hello, World! heading. The runtime looks for a `def:pub` component named `app` to mount as the application root, so this is the smallest complete Jac frontend.

The same minimal root component written with the section-header form: `to cl:` switches everything that follows in the file to client-side compilation, so no braces wrap the code. `app` itself is unchanged -- a public, parameterless component returning a static `JsxElement` heading -- and remains the mount point the runtime looks for. Prefer this form over a braced block when the entire remainder of a file is client code.

Single-statement client entry: prefixing the definition with `cl` scopes just this one declaration to the browser bundle, no block required. `app` must be `def:pub` to serve as the mount root. It holds one piece of reactive state -- the `has` field `count` (`int`, default 0) -- and renders it; nothing here updates the value, so the display stays at 0. Not an HTTP route: no auth, request shape, or error cases apply. Note the parameterless declaration omits parentheses.

Documents the visibility requirement on the client root: the runtime mounts a component named `app` only when it is declared `def:pub`, as the inline comment stresses -- a private `app` would leave the page blank. This instance simply delegates to an `App` component defined elsewhere, a common pattern that keeps the mount shim trivial while the real UI lives in its own component.

`Button` is a reusable presentational wrapper around the native button element. Props: `className` (`str`, default empty) is forwarded for styling; `onClick` (a `MouseEventHandler`, default `None`) is forwarded as the click handler; and `children` (default `None`) is the caller-supplied label or JSX rendered inside. It adds no state or behavior of its own -- its value is a typed, defaulted prop surface that composes cleanly into forms and toolbars. Returns a `JsxElement`.

Component API reference. `Card` renders a titled content container with the "card" `className`. Props -- its "request shape": `title` (`str`, required) becomes the heading; `description` (`str`, default empty) renders as a paragraph even when blank; and `children` (default `None`) is arbitrary JSX injected below the description. Response: a `JsxElement`. No auth or network concerns; the only misuse is omitting the required `title`, which fails at compile time rather than at runtime.

`app` demonstrates component composition: a `Card` receives "Welcome" as its `title` and a greeting description, with a `Button` nested as its child content -- the button's `onClick` lambda logs a message via `print`, and its own child text supplies the label. Neither `Card` nor `Button` is defined in this snippet; the code documents the consumer side, showing how props and nested children flow into reusable components. Returns a `JsxElement`.

`Form` illustrates the reference-identity rule for reactive collections. `name`, `items`, and `data` are `has` state fields, and `add_item` grows the list by concatenation -- building a new `list` instead of appending in place -- because reactivity triggers on assignment of a new reference, not on mutation of the existing one. In-place mutation would leave the UI stale; the same rule applies to the `dict` field. The render itself is a placeholder.

Lifecycle-ability reference for client components. `DataLoader` shows the mount/unmount pair: an async entry ability awaits `fetch_data` into `data` and clears `loading` once on mount (async bodies are IIFE-wrapped automatically), while the exit ability calls `cleanup_subscriptions` on unmount. `UserProfile` shows dependency-driven re-runs: listing `userId` in brackets makes the ability re-fire whenever that prop changes, refreshing `user` via `fetch_user`, and the tuple form declares multiple dependencies (`userId` together with `refresh`). No auth or error handling -- a rejected fetch surfaces as an unhandled promise.

`DataLoader` uses React's `useEffect` directly (imported from `react`) instead of Jac lifecycle abilities. Two registrations: one with an empty dependency array runs `fetch_data` once after mount, and one keyed on `some_dep` re-runs `refresh_data` whenever that value changes. Both lambdas return `None`, so no cleanup is registered. The `data` and `loading` fields are declared but not yet written by the fetches -- the snippet documents effect timing rather than the data flow.

A minimal context pattern for theme propagation. `AppContext` is created at module scope with `createContext`, defaulting to `None`. `AppProvider` owns the `theme` state (initially "light") and exposes it to descendants through the provider's `value`; its `children` prop is whatever JSX the caller nests inside. `ThemedComponent` retrieves the context with `useContext` and applies the theme string as its `className`, so components at any depth read the value without prop drilling. Nothing here updates `theme` -- in practice a setter would be added to the shared value.

Hook plus consumer, documented as an API. `use_local_storage` takes `key` and `initial_value` and returns a `tuple` of the current value and a setter lambda. Internally, a mount-time `useEffect` hydrates `value` from `localStorage` (via `JSON.parse`) when a stored entry exists, and a second effect keyed on `value` writes every update back serialized -- so the state survives reloads. `Settings` consumes it: destructuring into `theme` and `set_theme`, displaying the current value, and persisting "dark" through the setter on click. Failure mode: corrupted stored JSON would make `JSON.parse` throw during mount.

`TaskList` fetches server data by spawning a walker. On mount, its async entry ability spawns the imported `get_tasks` walker on `root`; the result's `reports` array is checked for content, its first element becomes `tasks`, and `loading` clears. While loading, a placeholder renders; afterwards tasks display as list items keyed on "id" and showing each "title". The `sv import` line pulls the walker in from the backend `main` module so the client can invoke it. Side effect: one network round-trip per mount.

`TaskManager` wires a full CRUD cycle to backend walkers pulled in with `sv import`. `handle_add` spawns `add_task` on `root` and appends the first report -- the created task -- to `tasks`. `handle_toggle` spawns `toggle_task` and, only when the report's "success" flag is set, immutably rebuilds the list, flipping the matching entry's "completed" field. `handle_delete` spawns `delete_task` and filters the removed "id" out on success. Every mutation rebuilds `tasks` with a new reference so the UI re-renders, and local state changes only after the server confirms -- keeping client and graph consistent.

Error-handling pattern for walker calls, as a component reference. On mount, `SafeDataView` sets `loading`, spawns `get_data` on `root` inside a try block, and stores the first entry of the result's `reports` into `data`; any raised `Exception` is caught and formatted into the `error` string instead of crashing the component. The render then branches like an HTTP client: a Loading placeholder while `loading` is set; on `error`, the message plus a Retry button wired to `location.reload`; on success, the data JSON-stringified. Pending, failed-with-retry, and success are the three response states.

`LiveData` polls the server every five seconds. `fetch_data` spawns the `get_live_data` walker on `root` and stores the first entry of `reports` into `data`; the async entry ability performs an immediate fetch on mount. A `useEffect` registration then starts a five-second `setInterval` re-invoking `fetch_data`, returning a cleanup lambda that calls `clearInterval` so polling stops when the component unmounts. As the comment warns, the effect lambda must not be annotated as returning `None` -- it returns the cleanup function, so that annotation would be a type error. Renders the last-updated "timestamp" whenever data exists.

Route-group guard reference. The file location "pages/(auth)/layout.jac" applies `layout` to every page in the "(auth)" group -- the parenthesized folder groups routes without adding a URL segment. `AuthGuard` performs the check: unauthenticated visitors are sent to the path in its `redirect` prop ("/login"), while authenticated ones reach `Outlet`, where the requested child page renders. In endpoint terms: every wrapped route requires a session, the "error response" is a client-side redirect, and no per-page auth code is needed.

`UserProfile` reads a dynamic route segment: mounted under a route with an ":id" placeholder ("/user/:id" per the comment), it calls `useParams` and extracts the "id" entry into `user_id` for display. The component is otherwise stateless with no side effects and returns a `JsxElement`; the router supplies fresh `params` whenever the URL segment changes.

Client-side login trigger, not a server route itself. `LoginForm` is a `def:pub` client component returning a `JsxElement`: a single Login button whose `onClick` invokes the async `handle_login` helper. `handle_login` awaits `do_login` (which performs the actual credential exchange and resolves to a truthy value on success); on success it calls `navigate` (obtained from `useNavigate`) to redirect the client to "/dashboard". On failure nothing happens -- no error state is set and the user stays on the current page. No request payload is constructed here; any auth details are handled inside `do_login`.

Two nested-layout components. `layout` is the root layout applied to every page: it returns a `JsxElement` wrapping a nav bar, a main region, and a footer, with the active page rendered wherever `Outlet` (imported from "@jac/runtime") is placed. `DashboardLayout` is a nested layout for dashboard routes: it renders a `Sidebar` next to a main region whose `Outlet` hosts the matched child route. Neither component takes parameters, and neither has side effects -- they only compose UI structure around routed content.

`LoginForm` renders a credential form and performs client-side authentication. It holds three pieces of reactive state via `has`: `username`, `password`, and `error` (all `str`, initially empty). The async handler `handleLogin` takes the submit event `e` (a `FormEvent`), suppresses the default form submission with `preventDefault`, and awaits `jacLogin` with `username` and `password`. `jacLogin` returns a `bool`: on `True` the component redirects to "/dashboard" through `navigate` from `useNavigate`; on `False` it sets `error` to "Invalid credentials". Returns a `JsxElement` form wired to `handleLogin` via `onSubmit`. No graph mutations occur in this component; auth token handling is internal to `jacLogin`.

`NavBar` is a `def:pub` client component (no server route of its own) that renders auth-aware navigation. On render it calls `jacIsLoggedIn` to compute `isLoggedIn`. When logged in it shows a Logout button whose `onClick` runs `handleLogout`, which calls `jacLogout` to clear the session (a follow-up redirect to login is left as a comment); when logged out it renders an anchor to "/login". Returns a `JsxElement`; requires no request payload and surfaces no error cases -- `jacIsLoggedIn` and `jacLogout` operate on locally stored credentials.

`GetMyData` is a `walker:pub` endpoint that returns the calling user's own data nodes. Its single ability `get` fires on `Root` entry, where `here` is the per-user root node, so the traversal is automatically scoped to the authenticated caller. It collects the outgoing neighbors of the root filtered to nodes of type `MyData` into `my_data` and reports that list as the response. Takes no parameters and performs no writes -- it is a read-only query of the user's subgraph.

`StyledComponent` returns a `JsxElement` demonstrating inline styling: the `style` prop takes a `dict` literal (note the double braces -- an expression brace containing a dict) with "color" set to "blue" and "padding" set to "10px". No parameters, no state, and no side effects; it renders static styled content.

`Card` is a `def:pub` client component, callable with no arguments and requiring no authentication context. It returns a `JsxElement`: a single div carrying the static `className` string "card card-primary" around fixed content. There is no request/response payload, no state, and no failure mode -- styling is delegated entirely to the CSS classes named in `className`.

A `cl` block whose only statement imports the stylesheet "./styles/main.css". The import has no exported symbols and no return value; its side effect is that the CSS file is picked up by the client bundler and its rules are applied globally to the rendered app. Place this in a client codespace once (typically at the app entry) rather than per component.

`Card` is a `def:pub` presentational component. Parameters: `title` (`str`), rendered inside an h2 carrying the "card-title" class, and `body` (`str`), rendered as a paragraph. Returns a `JsxElement` -- an article with `className` "card" wrapping both. Stateless and side-effect free; suitable for reuse anywhere a titled text card is needed.

`StylingExamples` is a `def:pub` component demonstrating the `cn` class-combining utility imported from "../lib/utils" (the shadcn/ui pattern). It declares three `bool` flags via `has`: `condition` (`True`), `hasError` (`False`), and `isSuccess` (`True`). `cn` is called with a base string, a short-circuit expression (`condition` and "active"), and a `dict` mapping class names "error" and "success" to `hasError` and `isSuccess`; the merged result is stored in `className` and applied to the second div. The first div shows plain static Tailwind utility classes. Returns a `JsxElement`; no inputs, no errors, no server interaction.

`JsxExamples` is a `def:pub` component showcasing core JSX expression forms. It declares reactive state via `has`: `variable` (`str`), `condition` (`bool`), `items` (`list`), and `props` (`dict`). The returned `JsxElement` demonstrates: binding `variable` to an input's `value`; conditional rendering with a short-circuit (`condition` and an element); splicing a `list` of children directly (`items`); and spreading a `dict` of props onto a button with the double-star spread of `props` plus a bare expression attribute. Purely illustrative -- no side effects.

`Profile` renders a user profile with built-in async suspense. Parameter: `user_id` (`int`), forwarded as the `id` prop to `ResolvedProfile`. The `try` / `awaiting` construct renders the `awaiting` branch (a loading paragraph) while `ResolvedProfile` is still resolving, then swaps in the resolved content inside the article. Returns a `JsxElement`; no graph side effects -- data fetching is delegated to `ResolvedProfile`.

`App` is a `def:pub` client component taking no arguments and returning a `JsxElement`: a heading plus a plain button. The block delimited by `{#*` and `*#}` is Jac's JSX comment syntax -- it documents an intended follow-up (swapping the raw button for a custom component) and produces no output in the rendered tree. No auth, no request/response shape, no error cases; the component is entirely static.

`app` is the `def:pub` entry component; it renders one `Button`, imported from "./components/Button". It passes two props: `label` set to "Click" and `onClick` set to an empty lambda handler. Returns a `JsxElement` and has no state or side effects -- it exists to demonstrate importing and instantiating a local component with props.

A `cl` block consisting solely of path-aliased imports: `Button` from "@components/Button", `formatDate` from "@utils/format", and `constants` from "@shared". The at-prefixed specifiers are bundler path aliases resolving to project directories, letting client code import shared modules without brittle relative paths. No runtime behavior beyond making the three symbols available to the rest of the codespace.

`app` is the `def:pub` root component of a Tailwind-styled client app. The codespace first imports "./assets/main.css", which pulls in Tailwind (via its own internal import), making utility classes available globally -- this import is the setup step the rest of the file depends on. `app` itself takes no arguments and returns a `JsxElement`: a full-height gray page (utility classes "min-h-screen bg-gray-100 p-8") containing a bold heading. No auth, parameters, or error cases apply.

`Form` is a controlled-input component. It keeps one piece of `has` state, `value` (`str`), bound to the input's `value` prop. Three typed event handlers are attached inline: `onChange` receives a `ChangeEvent` and writes the input text back into `value`; `onKeyPress` receives a `KeyboardEvent` and calls `submit` when the pressed `key` is "Enter"; the button's `onClick` also calls `submit`. Returns a `JsxElement`; the only side effects are the state update and whatever `submit` (defined elsewhere) does.

`TypedForm` is a `def:pub` client component (no network route) demonstrating typed DOM event handling. State via `has`: `text` (`str`) and `checked` (`bool`). The text input binds `value` to `text` and updates it in an `onChange` handler typed as `ChangeEvent`; its `onKeyDown` handler (a `KeyboardEvent`) calls `submit` when `key` is "Enter" and `shiftKey` is not held. The checkbox binds `checked` and mirrors the target's checked flag back into state. The form's `onSubmit` (a `FormEvent`) calls `preventDefault` before delegating to `handleSubmit`, so the browser never performs a native page-reload submit. Returns a `JsxElement`; failure handling is left to `submit` / `handleSubmit`.

`ConditionalComponent` demonstrates the three main conditional-rendering forms. State via `has`: `show` (`bool`) and `items` (`list`). First, an if/else picks one of two paragraphs into the local `content` variable before the return. Second, a short-circuit expression renders a paragraph only while `show` is true. Third, a list comprehension maps `items` to li elements, using each item's "id" as the React `key` and rendering its "name". Returns a `JsxElement`; no side effects.

`app` is the `def:pub` root component; it wraps the entire application (`MainAppComponents`) in a `JacClientErrorBoundary` imported from "@jac/runtime". The `fallback` prop supplies the `JsxElement` shown if any descendant throws during render -- here a generic apology div -- so a component crash degrades to a message instead of a blank page. No parameters or side effects.

`App` is a `def:pub` client component with no route, parameters, or auth requirements. It mounts `ExpensiveWidget` inside a `JacClientErrorBoundary`; if the widget throws while rendering or loading, the boundary swaps in the `fallback` element -- a div with `className` "error" reading "Component failed to load" -- instead of unmounting the whole tree. Error case: any exception in `ExpensiveWidget` is caught by the boundary; errors outside it propagate normally.

A `cl` block declaring two module-level globals with `glob`: `initialized`, a `bool` starting `False`, and `cache`, typed `any` and starting `None`. These live at codespace scope, shared across all components in the client bundle, and are typically used as one-time-setup and memoization slots. Declaring them has no immediate side effect; mutation happens wherever other code assigns them.

`search` is a walker declaration carrying only request state, with no abilities yet: `query` (`str`) is required at spawn time, and `limit` (`int`) defaults to 10. As an endpoint payload this means callers must supply `query` while `limit` is optional. Spawning it currently does nothing observable -- traversal and reporting logic remain to be added.

`_before_request` is a request-logging walker. It carries one required field, `request` (`dict`), expected to contain 'method' and 'path' keys. Its ability `log` fires on `Root` entry and prints a formatted "Request:" line from those two values via `self.request`. No traversal, no reports, and no graph mutation -- its only side effect is the log line. The leading underscore marks it as an internal helper rather than a public endpoint.

`_authenticate` is an internal auth-check walker. Field: `headers` (`dict`), the incoming request headers. Its ability `check` runs on `Root` entry, reads the "Authorization" value (defaulting to an empty string) into `token`, and rejects any value not starting with the "Bearer " scheme by reporting a `dict` with "error" "Unauthorized" and "status" 401, then returning early. If the prefix is present it (after real validation, elided here) reports {"authenticated": `True`}. Read-only -- no graph writes.

`get_users` is a public walker endpoint: the `:pub` modifier removes the authentication requirement, and the `@restspec` decorator with `HTTPMethod.GET` (imported from `http`) mounts it as a GET route instead of the default POST. Its ability `fetch` runs on `Root` entry and reports an empty `list` -- a placeholder response shape. No fields, no traversal, no side effects.

`list_users` is a public (`:pub`) walker exposed as a GET endpoint at the custom route "/custom/users" -- the `path` argument to `@restspec` overrides the default walker-derived URL. Its single ability `fetch` triggers on `Root` entry and reports an empty `list` as the response body. Stateless and read-only.

Two public GET walkers showing `@restspec` path parameters. `get_item` is mounted at "/items/{item_id}": the `{item_id}` URL segment binds to its `has` field `item_id` (`str`), and its `fetch` ability echoes it back as {"item_id": ...} via `self.item_id`. `get_user_orders` is mounted at "/users/{user_id}/orders": `user_id` (`str`) is filled from the path, while `status` (`str`, default "all") has no placeholder in the route so it arrives as an optional query parameter; `fetch` reports both. Rule illustrated: `has` fields matching a braced path segment (like `{item_id}`) become path parameters, remaining fields become query parameters.

Two public function endpoints declared with `def` plus `:pub` and mounted as GET routes via `@restspec`. `health_check` uses the default path derived from its name and returns a `dict` reporting "healthy" status. `app_status` overrides its URL with `path` set to "/custom/status" and returns a `dict` carrying "status" "running" and "version" "1.0.0". Both are side-effect-free probes -- typical liveness/status checks needing no authentication.

Entry block demonstrating public permission grants on a graph object. `perm_grant` called with a `node` and the `READ` level lets every user (all roots) read that node; calling it again with `WRITE` widens access so anyone can also modify it. Side effect: the node's access-control metadata is updated and persists with it -- these grants apply globally rather than to a specific user, so use them only for genuinely public data.

Entry block demonstrating per-user permission grants. `allow_root` gives one specific user -- identified by `target_root_id` -- access to a `node`: the first call grants the `READ` level, the second escalates the same target to `WRITE`. Unlike a global grant, other users' access is unchanged. Side effect: the node's permission records are updated to include `target_root_id` at the given levels, persisting with the node.

Entry block showing `perm_revoke`: called with a `node`, it strips all previously granted public access from that object in one step, returning it to owner-only visibility. This is the inverse of a global grant. Side effect: the node's shared-access metadata is cleared and the change persists; per-user grants made through other mechanisms are the domain of the corresponding disallow call.

Entry block showing `disallow_root`: it revokes one specific user's access to a `node`, identified by `target_root_id`, at the `READ` level. This is the per-user inverse of the corresponding allow call -- other users' grants and any public permissions are untouched. Side effect: the node's permission records are updated to drop that user's read grant, persisting with the node.

Three walkers illustrating the endpoint visibility tiers. `get_profile` has no modifier, so it gets the protected default: callers must present a JWT token, and its `fetch` ability reports the outgoing neighbors of the caller's `Root`. `health_check` is marked `:pub`, requiring no authentication -- its `check` ability reports {"status": "ok"}, the classic liveness probe. `internal_process` is `:priv`: authentication is required and execution stays isolated to the calling user's graph; its `run` ability is an empty stub. Choose the tier per endpoint -- public for probes, protected/private for anything touching user data.

`PaymentReceived` is a walker exposed as a webhook endpoint via `@restspec` with `APIProtocol.WEBHOOK` -- the shape external payment providers POST notifications to. Payload fields: `payment_id` (`str`, required), `amount` (`float`, required), and `currency` (`str`, defaulting to 'USD'). Its ability `process` runs on `Root` entry and reports an acknowledgment `dict` containing "status" "success", a message embedding `self.payment_id`, plus the received `amount` and `currency`. Actual payment-side effects are left to the elided processing step; as written it only echoes confirmation.

`EchoMessage` is an `async walker` served over a WebSocket connection (`@restspec` with `APIProtocol.WEBSOCKET`) and marked `: pub` so clients can connect without authentication. Each inbound message supplies `message` (`str`, required) and optionally `client_id` (`str`, default "anonymous"). The async ability `echo` fires on `Root` entry and reports a `dict` echoing the payload back as "echo" plus the sender's "client_id". Replies go only to the sending connection -- no broadcast, no graph writes.

`ChatRoom` is a public (`: pub`) `async walker` bound to a WebSocket endpoint with `broadcast=True` in its `@restspec`, so each report is pushed to every connected client rather than just the sender -- the core of a chat room. Message fields: `message` (`str`, required) and `sender` (`str`, default "anonymous"). The async ability `handle` runs on `Root` entry and reports the outgoing frame: a `dict` with "type" "message", the "sender", and the "content" taken from `self.message`. No persistence -- messages are relayed, not stored.

Cross-service walker invocation. The provider file defines `Greet`, a `walker:pub` with a required `name` field whose `greet` ability reports a greeting string on `Root` entry. The consumer file pulls that walker in with `sv import` from `notify_service`; when `TriggerGreet` (fields: `who`) runs its `run` ability, constructing `Greet` with `name` set to `self.who` transparently issues a POST to the provider's /walker/Greet endpoint. The returned handle `rg` exposes the remote results via `reports`, and `TriggerGreet` re-reports the first entry -- "hello, <who>". Side effects occur on the provider's graph, not the consumer's.

An in-process integration test of service-to-service calls. `sv_client` (from `jaclang.runtimelib`) is first reset with `clear_test_clients`, then `register_test_client` binds the service name "inventory_service" to `prov_client`, a `TestClient` wrapping the provider app -- from then on, cross-service calls the consumer makes to that service are routed through the in-memory client instead of the network. The test drives the consumer via `cons_client`, posting an items payload to "/function/create_order", and asserts the nested result reports "success" `True`. Side effects: registers a process-global test-client mapping, which is why the clear step comes first.

Three ways to obtain a file-storage handle with the builtin `store` factory (no imports required), each bound to a `glob` named `storage`. Bare `store()` uses defaults; passing `base_path` roots all reads/writes under "./uploads"; adding `create_dirs` set to `True` makes the backend create missing directories on demand. Side effect of construction is only handle setup -- files are touched by later method calls, not here.

File-upload API built on a shared `glob` `storage` handle rooted at "./uploads". Walker `upload_file` takes `file` (an `UploadFile` from the `http` module) and `folder` (`str`, default "documents"); on `Root` entry its `process` ability generates a collision-proof name from `uuid4`, uploads the stream via `upload` under the computed `path`, fetches `get_metadata`, and reports "success", the "storage_path", and the stored "size". Walker `list_files` takes `folder` (default "documents") and `recursive` (`bool`, default `False`); it iterates the storage listing, augments each `path` with metadata "size" and "name", and reports the collected "files" list. Side effects: `upload_file` writes bytes to the storage backend; `list_files` is read-only.

Two download-side storage operations. The entry block calls `get_url` on a `store` handle to mint a time-limited link for "profile-photos/user1.jpg" with `expires_in` of 600 seconds -- on an S3 backend this is a pre-signed URL, letting clients fetch directly without proxying bytes through the app. Walker `download_file` takes `path` (`str`); its `process` ability first guards with `exists` and reports {"error": "File not found"} then returns if the object is missing, otherwise reads the bytes via `download` and reports the "content" together with its "size". Read-only against the storage backend.

Constructing storage backends through `StorageFactory` (from `jac_scale.factories.storage_factory`) instead of the convenience helper. `StorageFactory.create` takes an explicit backend type ("local" here) plus a `config` dict -- `base_path` pointing at "./my-files" and `create_dirs` set to `True` -- and returns the handle bound to `glob` `storage`. `StorageFactory.get_default` instead resolves the backend from jac.toml, environment variables, or built-in defaults, yielding `default_storage`. Use the explicit form for tests/overrides and the default form for deployment-configured apps.

`async_processor` is an async-capable walker that sequentially processes a batch. Field: `items` (`list`), the work queue supplied at spawn. Its ability `process` is declared `async can` and fires on `Root` entry: it awaits `process_item` for each element in order (one at a time, not concurrently), accumulates the outcomes in `results`, and reports the full list. Side effects are whatever `process_item` performs; the walker itself does not modify the graph.

Entry block constructing two `kvstore` handles (from `jac_scale.lib`), showing that the same factory fronts different backends chosen by `db_type`: `mongo_db` targets a MongoDB database named 'my_app' (document-style storage), while `redis_db` targets a Redis database named 'cache' (fast key/value with TTLs). `db_name` selects the logical database in each backend. Construction only establishes the handles; no data is written here.

Document-store CRUD against a MongoDB-backed `kvstore` handle `db`. `insert_one` writes a document into the 'users' collection; `find_one` fetches the first match for a filter; `find` returns an iterable of matches -- shown with an equality filter and a Mongo-style range filter using '$gt' -- which the code materializes with `list`. `update_one` applies a '$set' modification to the first matching document, and `delete_one` removes one. Finally `set` demonstrates the key/value facade: storing a value under key 'user:123' in the 'sessions' namespace. All calls mutate or read the external database, not the Jac graph.

Entry block querying persisted graph nodes through a MongoDB-backed `kvstore`. `find_nodes` bridges the document store and the archetype layer: given the node-type name 'User' and a Mongo-style filter, it yields matching stored nodes -- here `young_users` (an '$lt' range filter on age) and `admins` (an equality filter on role), each materialized with `list`. Read-only; useful for admin-style queries across all persisted nodes of a type without walking the graph.

Redis-specific operations on a `kvstore` handle `cache` (db_type 'redis'). `set` stores a session dict under 'session:user123' with no expiry; `set_with_ttl` stores values that auto-expire after `ttl` seconds -- a 60-second token and a one-hour profile cache. `incr` atomically increments the counter at 'stats:views'; `scan_keys` returns keys matching the pattern 'session:*'; and `expire` retrofits a 1800-second TTL onto the existing session key. All calls hit the external Redis instance; nothing touches the Jac graph.

A distributed mutual-exclusion module for multi-pod deployments, built on a Redis `kvstore` handle held in the `glob` `_kv`. The single entry point is `with_repo_lock`, which serializes operations on one repository: callers pass a `repo_id` and an `action`, and the protected work itself is delegated to `run_protected_op`. The pieces relate as an acquire/execute/release pipeline. Acquire: a unique fencing value (a `uuid4` string plus the pod's HOSTNAME) is written with `set_nx_with_ttl` under a per-repo key -- set-if-absent with a 30-second TTL so a crashed holder can't wedge the system -- retried every 0.2s against a ~25-second deadline; on timeout it returns a `dict` with 'success' `False` and a 'lock contention timeout' error. Execute/release: `run_protected_op` runs inside a try whose finally calls `delete_if_equals` with the same payload, a compare-and-delete that only removes the key if this pod still owns it, making release a safe no-op when the TTL already lapsed and another pod took over.

`maybe_run_periodic_task` deduplicates a periodic job across pods using a set-if-absent debounce key. Parameter: `task_id` (`str`), identifying the task. It attempts `set_nx_with_ttl` on a per-task key with a 60-second TTL, storing a `payload` recording this pod's HOSTNAME and a timestamp; if the write wins (key was absent) it invokes `run_task` and returns `True`, otherwise another pod already ran the task within the window and it returns `False` without doing work. Side effects: one Redis key write on the winning pod plus whatever `run_task` performs.

`place_order` is a walker that emits a domain event when an order is placed. Fields: `order_id` (`int`) and `amount` (`float`). Its ability `fire` runs on `Root` entry and calls `publish` (from `jac_scale.events.publisher`) on the "orders.placed" topic, wrapping the order data in an `Event` (from `jac_scale.events.broker`) whose `data` dict carries the order fields and whose `trace_id` tags the event for correlation. Side effect: one event delivered to the broker; nothing is reported and no graph nodes are created.

`replay_all` is a subscriber that processes the topic's full history: the `start_from` argument to `@subscribe`, set to "earliest", makes the consumer begin at the oldest retained "orders.placed" event instead of only new arrivals -- a replay/backfill pattern. Parameter: `event` (`Event`); the body prints a replay note with the event's `id`. Returns `None`; side effects are limited to the print, so re-running is harmless.

`drain` performs one manual pull-based consumption cycle against an `EventStreamBroker` (from `jac_scale.events.broker`). Parameter: `broker`. It calls `consume` on the "orders.placed" topic with `max_messages` 10 and `timeout_seconds` 2.0, yielding at most one small `batch`; each event `ev` is processed (elided) and then acknowledged with `ack`, marking it consumed so it will not be redelivered. Returns the number of events handled (`int`), which is 0 when the topic is idle -- useful as a loop-termination signal. Side effect: consumer offsets advance for acked events.

`ready` is a readiness-probe walker. Its ability `check` runs on `Root` entry and verifies dependencies by calling `check_database` and `check_cache` into `db_ok` and `cache_ok`. If both pass it reports {"status": "ready"}; otherwise it reports "not_ready" along with the individual "db" and "cache" booleans so operators can see which dependency failed. Read-only -- distinguishes 'process is alive' from 'process can actually serve traffic'.

Entry block calling the builtin `allroots`, which returns every root node currently known to memory/database -- one per user in a multi-user deployment -- bound here to `roots`. This is the admin-level primitive for cross-user scans (analytics, migrations, moderation): from each element of `roots` you can traverse into that user's private subgraph. Read-only in itself, but powerful; gate any endpoint using it accordingly.

Entry block calling the builtin `commit`, which flushes all pending in-memory graph changes to the backing database in one step. Use it after a batch of mutations when you need durability at a known point (for example before returning a response or performing an external call that assumes the data is saved). Side effect: persisted state is synchronized with memory; nothing is returned.

Two ways to build a sandbox manager with `SandboxFactory` (from `jac_scale.factories.sandbox_factory`), bound to a `glob` `sandbox`. `SandboxFactory.get_default` reads the backend and its settings from jac.toml. `SandboxFactory.create` picks the backend explicitly -- "kubernetes" here -- with a config dict: `namespace` for where sandbox pods live, `base_image` as the container image, `memory_limit` per sandbox, `ttl_seconds` after which idle sandboxes expire (1800s), and `domain_template` describing per-sandbox preview URLs keyed by the sandbox id. Construction only configures the manager; cluster resources are created by later calls.

Sandbox lifecycle management on an existing `sandbox` manager. `status` returns the record for one sandbox id, whose `state` is one of pending, starting, running, stopped, or error. `list_sandboxes` enumerates every sandbox owned by a user id, each exposing `sandbox_id`, `state`, and `url`. `stop` halts a running sandbox without removing it; `destroy` tears one down and releases all its resources; `cleanup_expired` sweeps every sandbox past its TTL and returns how many were removed (bound to `cleaned`). All but `status` and `list_sandboxes` mutate real infrastructure -- schedule the cleanup call periodically.

File operations inside a provisioned sandbox, all keyed by sandbox id. `write_file` creates or overwrites a file with the given content; `read_file` returns a `result` dict whose "content" holds the text -- for binary files such as images the content comes back base64-encoded with `is_binary` `True` and a `mime_type` (e.g. "image/png") so callers know to decode it. `delete_file` removes a file, and `list_files` reports the sandbox's file listing under "files". Side effects: `write_file` and `delete_file` mutate the sandbox filesystem; reads are safe.

Entry block running a shell command inside a sandbox via `exec_command`: arguments are the sandbox id, the command string ("ls -la /app"), and a `timeout` in seconds (30) bounding execution. The returned `result` dict exposes the command's "stdout", printed here. Side effects depend entirely on the command executed -- the call itself just brokers execution inside the isolated environment.

Entry block reading a sandbox's output stream with `logs`. Arguments: the sandbox id and an `offset` (0 here, meaning read from the beginning). The `result` dict returns the log text under "content" plus an updated "offset" -- the byte position for the next call -- enabling incremental/streaming log tailing by passing each returned offset back in. Read-only.

A complete fullstack app in one file. Server side: node `Todo` declares `title` (`str`) and `done` (`bool`); the `def:pub` function `get_todos` attaches three starter `Todo` nodes to `root` and returns them as a `list` of dicts by filtering the root's children to `Todo`. Note the side effect: every invocation appends three more nodes to the persistent graph. Client side: `cl def:pub app` holds `items` state, and its async `can with entry` ability awaits `get_todos` -- transparently an HTTP call from browser to server -- then renders each item as a checkbox row keyed by `title` and checked from `done`. Returns a `JsxElement`.

A worked example of location-bound abilities reacting to a traversing walker. Node `Person` (field `name`) defines `announce`, which fires whenever a `FriendFinder` enters and prints the `visitor`; edge `Family` defines its own `announce` that fires when the walker crosses it (edge abilities run on traversal), while `Friend` is a plain marker edge.
