The first entry block wires `root` to `p1` and builds `Friend`/`Family` links among four `Person` nodes. Walker `FriendFinder` carries `started` (`bool`, default `False`): its `move_to_person` ability leaves `Root` onto outgoing nodes; `report_friend` on `Person` entry uses `started` to treat the first person as the origin (visiting all its neighbors) and prints every subsequently reached person as a friend-of-friend or family, additionally following only `Family`-typed edges from each node via the edge-filtered visit. The final entry block spawns `FriendFinder` at `root` and prints the returned walker instance.

`report_friend` is a walker ability bound to `Person` entry: it executes each time the walker steps onto a `Person` node. The body prints a friend announcement using `here.name` -- `here` being the node currently occupied. No traversal is initiated and no state is modified, so the walker stops at whatever nodes it was already queued to visit.

A small social-graph module in two parts. Schema: node `Person` carries a `name` (`str`); `Friend` and `Family` are data-less edge archetypes serving as typed relationship labels. Construction (the entry block, the module's sole entry point): three `Person` nodes are created (`p1`, `p2`, `p3`); `root` is linked to `p1` with a plain untyped edge; `p1` is connected to `p2` via a `Friend` edge; and `p2` is connected to both `p1` and `p3` in one statement via `Family` edges -- the connect operators accept a `list` target to fan out. The result is a persistent graph reachable from `root` where relationship type is encoded in the edge archetype, ready for edge-filtered traversal.

Demonstrates edge-filtered traversal. `Family` is a data-less edge archetype used as a relationship label. Walker `Visitor` defines `traverse` on `Root` entry with two visit statements: the first queues all outgoing neighbors regardless of edge type, while the second uses the edge-typed form to queue only neighbors reached through `Family` edges. Together they show the difference between unconstrained fan-out and label-constrained fan-out; the walker has no state or reports, so its effect is purely which nodes get visited.

Chess-engine constants. `Color` enumerates the two sides (`WHITE` = 0, `BLACK` = 1) and `PieceKind` the six piece types (`PAWN` through `KING`, valued 0-5) -- both use explicit integer values so they can index tables and pack into compact encodings. The `glob` castling flags are single-bit masks combinable with bitwise-or: `CASTLE_WK`/`CASTLE_WQ` for White's kingside/queenside rights, `CASTLE_BK`/`CASTLE_BQ` for Black's, and `CASTLE_ALL` (0x0F) as the union representing full castling rights at game start. `CENTER_MASK` is a bitmask (0b00111100) selecting the four center files for positional bonuses, and `BOARD_SIZE` fixes the 8x8 dimensions.

Two piece-keyed lookup tables declared as `glob` dicts over `PieceKind`. `WHITE_SYMBOLS` maps each kind to its one-letter display glyph for White ("P", "N", "B", "R", "Q", "K") for board rendering. `PIECE_VALUES` gives material worth in centipawns for evaluation -- `PAWN` 100 up through `QUEEN` 900, with `KING` at a sentinel 20000 so any line losing the king dominates every material trade. Both are read-only reference data with no side effects.

Forward declarations forming the chess module's public surface, with bodies supplied elsewhere in implementation blocks. `Board` and `Piece` are declared as `obj` stubs so signatures can reference them before definition. Three free functions are declared: `opposite_color` maps a `Color` to its opponent; `to_algebraic` converts a (row, col) `pos` tuple to algebraic notation like "e4" (`str`); and `create_piece` is the factory constructing the right `Piece` subclass for a `PieceKind` and `Color` at a given `row`/`col`. Declaration-only -- no runtime behavior in this snippet.

The piece class hierarchy. Base `obj` `Piece` carries `color` (`Color`), `kind` (`PieceKind`), `pos` (a row/col tuple), and `has_moved` (`bool`, default `False`, used for castling and pawn double-step logic). Declared methods: `row` and `col` unpack the position; `set_pos` relocates the piece; `symbol` yields its display glyph; `raw_moves` produces the piece's pseudo-legal `Move` list for a given `Board` (no check filtering); and `slide_moves` is the shared helper generating ray moves along `directions` until blocked. Six subclasses -- `Pawn`, `Knight`, `Bishop`, `Rook`, `Queen`, `King` -- each `override` only `raw_moves`, inheriting everything else, so movement rules are the single point of variation.

The program's command-line entry point. A `glob` `game` holds a `Game` instance. The entry block scans `sys.argv` (skipping the program name) for "--benchmark" or its short form "-b", setting `_benchmark_mode` to 10 when present. With the flag, it runs `benchmark` on `game` for that many self-play games; without it, it starts an interactive session via `play`. Side effects: whatever the chosen mode prints/does -- the block itself only parses arguments and dispatches.

Implementation of `raw_moves` for the `King`: single-step movement to the eight surrounding squares. It builds `adjacent` -- a comprehension over row/column offsets in [-1, 0, 1] excluding the (0, 0) stay-in-place case -- then keeps each candidate that is on the board (`valid_pos`) and either empty (`at` returns `None`) or occupied by an enemy piece (differing `color`), emitting a `Move` from `self.pos` to it. Returns the pseudo-legal `Move` list; castling and moving-into-check filtering are handled elsewhere. Pure -- no board mutation.

`postinit` hook for `Board`, run automatically after field initialization. It allocates `squares` as a `BOARD_SIZE` by `BOARD_SIZE` nested-list grid filled with `None` (empty squares), then calls `setup_pieces` to place the starting position. Side effects: the board instance goes from unconstructed to a fully initialized start-of-game state; nothing is returned.

Implementation of `attacked_squares`: computes every square the given side currently attacks. Parameter: `by_color` (`Color`). It iterates the side's pieces via `pieces_of` and unions in each piece's attack targets -- the `to_pos` of every move yielded by `raw_moves` -- using in-place set union. Returns a `set` of (row, col) tuples, used for check detection and king-safety tests. Pure query; the board is unchanged. Note it uses pseudo-legal moves, so pins are not accounted for.

Implementation of `evaluate`: a static positional score of the whole board from one side's perspective. Parameter: `color`, the side to score for. It scans every square in `squares`; each occupied one contributes its material `base` from `PIECE_VALUES`, plus a center bonus of one-tenth the base when the piece's file bit is set in `CENTER_MASK` and its rank lies in the middle rows (2-5), plus a flat 8-point development bonus for non-king pieces that have `has_moved`. Contributions add to `score` for pieces matching `color` and subtract for the opponent's. Returns an `int` in centipawns -- positive means the position favors `color`. Pure; no board mutation.

Implementation of `benchmark`: runs a batch of automated self-play games and prints a win/loss/draw tally. Parameter: `num_games` (`int`). For each iteration it constructs a fresh `Game`, calls `seed_random` with a deterministic per-game seed (i * 7919 + 42) so runs are reproducible, and plays to completion via `play_auto`, whose returned winner string increments `white_wins`, `black_wins`, or `draws`. Each game's outcome is printed as it finishes, followed by a formatted results summary. Returns `None`; side effects are console output only -- the shared game state is untouched since every game is a fresh instance.

A mixed-codespace module splitting work between the Python runtime and native compilation. `process_data` is standard Jac running on Python -- filtering a `list` of dicts to those with a truthy "active" key, with full ecosystem access available. The `na` block declares compute kernels compiled to machine code: `compute_checksum` folds a `list` of ints into a rolling polynomial hash (multiplier 31, modulo 1000000007) accumulated in a local `has` variable `result`, and `fibonacci` is the naive exponential recursion. The entry block shows the seam is invisible at the call site: both native functions are called like ordinary ones, here hashing a small list and computing the 30th Fibonacci number.

Demonstrates native-to-Python interop across codespaces. `py_double` is an ordinary Python-side function doubling an `int`. Inside the `na` block, the natively compiled `native_add_one_to_doubled` declares a local via `has`, calls straight into `py_double` -- crossing from machine code back into the Python runtime transparently -- and adds one. The entry block prints the result for input 5, yielding 11. The point: native functions can invoke Python-side functions without any bridging boilerplate.

A minimal native library module (math_utils.na.jac): the whole `.na.jac` file lives in the native codespace, so everything compiles to machine code. It exports one pure function, `square`, mapping an `int` `x` to `x * x` with no side effects -- intended to be imported by other native modules rather than run directly.

A hello-world native module (hello.na.jac) compiled to a standalone binary. `greet` takes `name` (`str`) and returns the f-string greeting -- pure, no side effects. The entry block is the binary's main: it prints the result of calling `greet` with "World". Demonstrates that `str` parameters, f-strings, and top-level entry all work in the native codespace.

Command-line argument handling in an entry block. `sys.argv` provides the argument vector as in Python: index 0 is the program name, so the loop starts at 1 and prints each user-supplied argument after reporting the count ("argc:"). A membership test on `args` detects the "--verbose" flag anywhere on the command line and prints a mode notice. Side effects: console output only. This is the minimal pattern for flag detection before graduating to structured parsing.

Native FFI usage: the import block binds two symbols directly from the system C math library at "/usr/lib/libm.so.6", declaring their C signatures with the `f64` machine type -- `sqrt` and `pow`. `hypotenuse` then uses them like ordinary functions, computing the root of the sum of squares of `a` and `b` (`float` in, `float` out; Jac's float maps onto `f64` at the boundary). The entry block prints the 3-4-5 triangle result. No Python involved -- calls go straight into the shared library.

An FFI declaration block binding a minimal windowing/drawing API from the raylib C shared library ("libraylib.so"). Each `def` states the C signature using machine types: `i32` for C ints and `c_void` for void returns. The bound surface covers the classic frame loop: `InitWindow` (width, height, title) opens the window; `WindowShouldClose` polls for exit (returns `i32` as a C boolean); `BeginDrawing` / `EndDrawing` bracket each frame; `ClearBackground` fills with a packed `i32` color; `DrawText` renders a string at a position with a font size and color; and `CloseWindow` tears down. Declarations only -- calling code elsewhere drives the loop.

A native-codespace demo (fibonacci.na.jac) of recursion compiled to machine code. `fib` is the textbook doubly recursive Fibonacci: returns `n` for the base cases at or below 1, otherwise the sum of the two preceding calls -- exponential time, deliberately compute-heavy to show off native speed. The entry block prints the first ten values via f-strings. Pure function; the only side effects are the printed lines.

A native-codespace module (animals.na.jac) demonstrating inheritance and runtime polymorphism under compilation to machine code. `Animal` is the base `obj` with a `name` field and a default `speak` returning a placeholder. `Dog` and `Cat` subclass it, each overriding `speak` to return a name-bearing bark or meow via `self.name`. The entry block is the sole entry point: it builds a heterogeneous `list` typed as the base (`list[Animal]`) holding two `Dog` instances and a `Cat`, then iterates and calls `speak` on each -- dynamic dispatch selects the subclass override, printing three different lines.

A native-codespace module (safe_div.na.jac) showing exception handling works under native compilation. `safe_divide` takes `a` and `b` (`int`), attempts floor division inside a try block, and returns a formatted result string; a `ZeroDivisionError` is caught and converted to the error message "Error: division by zero" instead of crashing. Always returns a `str`. The entry block exercises both paths -- a normal division and a division by zero.

A native CLI binary (greeter.na.jac) with argument validation. The entry block reads `sys.argv`: with no user argument it prints a usage line and terminates with exit code 1 via `sys.exit` -- the standard failure convention for shells. Otherwise `name` is taken from the first argument and the optional "--shout" flag (membership test on `args`) selects between printing the greeting uppercased (via `upper`) or as-is. Side effects: console output and the possible nonzero process exit.

A mixed module (mixed.jac) pairing ecosystem access with compiled compute. On the Python side, `serialize` wraps `dumps` (imported from the `json` standard library) to turn a `dict` into its JSON string -- the kind of library-dependent code that must stay in the Python codespace. The `na` block holds `sum_squares`, a tight loop accumulating i * i for i below `n` into a local declared with `has`, compiled to machine code. The entry block calls the native function for n=1000 and prints the result, showing both sides coexist in one file with ordinary call syntax.

A complete minimal OSP program. Schema: node `Person` carries `name` (`str`) and `age` (`int`); edge `Knows` carries `since` (`int`), giving the relationship its own data. Walker `Greeter` has two abilities: `greet` on `Root` entry steps to all outgoing neighbors, and `say_hello` on `Person` entry prints a greeting using `here.name` before continuing outward -- so it greets every person reachable along outgoing edges. The entry block builds the graph (`alice` attached to `root`, then linked to `bob` via a `Knows` edge stamped `since` 2020) and launches the walker with `root spawn`. Output: greetings for Alice then Bob; the constructed nodes persist in the graph.

A tour of node-ability dispatch on a single archetype, `SecureRoom` (field: `clearance_required`, `int`). The abilities show every trigger form. `on_enter` uses a bare untyped entry, firing for any walker that arrives. `check_clearance` is typed to `Inspector` walkers: it compares the visiting walker's clearance (via `visitor`) against `clearance_required` and halts the walker outright with `disengage` on failure -- the access-control gate. `at_root` documents the key subtlety: in node abilities the type in a typed entry names the walker archetype, not a node type, so it fires when a walker whose type is `Root` visits. `on_exit` runs as an `Inspector` leaves rather than arrives. `process` accepts a union, firing for walkers of either `Walker1` or `Walker2`. Together they map out how one node can present different behavior to different traversal types; there are no entry blocks -- this is schema meant to be visited.

Node inheritance: `Entity` is a base archetype holding the shared `created_at` timestamp field (`str`), and `User` extends it -- declared as inheriting from `Entity` -- adding `username` and `email`. A constructed `User` therefore carries all three fields, and traversal filters can match it either as a `User` or, polymorphically, as an `Entity`. Common audit-style fields live once in the base while concrete node types stay focused on their own data.

Three edge archetypes showing the range of edge declarations. `Friend` carries relationship data: `since` (`int`, required) and `strength` (`float`, defaulting to 1.0). `Follows` is data-less -- a pure typed marker whose existence is the information. `Weighted` shows edges can also have behavior: alongside its `weight` field it defines the method `get_normalized`, dividing `self.weight` by a caller-supplied `max_weight` to yield a 0-1 scaled value. Edges are therefore full archetypes: typed, data-bearing, and capable of methods.

`Road` is an edge archetype demonstrating edge-bound abilities. It stores `distance` (`float`), and its ability `on_traverse` fires when a walker of type `Traveler` crosses the edge: it adds the edge's own `distance` onto the walker's `total_distance` accumulator via `visitor`. The pattern puts per-hop bookkeeping on the edges themselves, so a traveler's total route length accrues automatically as it moves, with no logic needed in the walker or nodes.

Connection-operator basics on a data-less `Item` node. The entry block creates two instances and links them twice: `++>` builds a directed edge from `a` to `b` (traversable only outward from `a`), while `<++>` builds an undirected connection -- concretely, edges in both directions -- so each node reaches the other. Side effect: the two nodes and their edges are added to the graph (note neither is attached to `root` here, so they are floating relative to the root).

`Collector` is a bounded-gathering walker. State: `items` (a `list` accumulator, empty by default) and `max_items` (`int`, default 10) capping how many values are kept. Its `start` ability fires on `Root` entry, printing a status line and stepping to all outgoing neighbors; `collect` fires on each `DataNode` entry, appending the node's value (via `here.value`) to `self.items` only while under the cap, then continuing outward. The traversal always proceeds even once full -- only appending is gated. Results are read off the walker's `items` after the spawn; no graph mutation occurs.

A minimal end-to-end walker example. `DataNode` is a node archetype holding a single `int` `value`. Walker `Counter` accumulates a `count`: its `start` ability fires on `Root` entry, counting the root itself and stepping outward, and `count_nodes` fires on each `DataNode` entry, incrementing and continuing along outgoing edges. The entry block is the runnable demonstration: it chains two data nodes off `root`, keeps a handle to the walker in `walker_instance`, launches it with `root spawn`, and then reads the accumulated state directly off the instance -- printing 3 (root plus two nodes). The key pattern: a walker object survives its traversal, so its fields double as the result channel.

`Visitor` demonstrates the three traversal directions available in a visit statement. Its ability `go` runs on `Item` entry and queues neighbors three ways: `[-->]` follows outgoing edges, `[<--]` follows incoming edges (traversing against edge direction), and `[<-->]` follows both regardless of direction. Combined, the current node's entire neighborhood ends up queued. The walker carries no state and makes no reports -- it exists to show direction syntax; `Item` is a bare node type.

`Visitor` shows the three levels of traversal filtering from a `Person` node. `[-->][?:Person]` follows all outgoing edges but keeps only destination nodes of type `Person` (node-type filter). `[->:Friend:->]` constrains the edges themselves, traversing only those typed `Friend`. `[->:Friend:since>2020:->]` adds a field predicate on the edge, crossing only `Friend` edges whose `since` exceeds 2020 -- enabled by `Friend` declaring `since` (`int`, default 2020). Together: filter by where you land, by what you cross, or by the crossed edge's data.

A tiny module demonstrating the visit-else fallback. `Item` is a bare node archetype. Walker `Visitor` defines one ability, `traverse`, on `Item` entry: the visit statement queues all outgoing neighbors, but its attached `else` block runs when there is nothing to visit -- here printing "No outgoing edges". This gives leaf-node handling for free: interior nodes propagate the traversal while dead ends trigger the fallback, with no separate emptiness check. Entry point: spawn `Visitor` anywhere on a graph of `Item` nodes (no entry block is included).

`Visitor` shows that visit targets need not be edge queries -- any node reference works. It holds `target`, typed `Item | None` (default `None`), a node handle injectable at spawn time. Its ability `direct` on `Item` entry issues `visit here` (re-queueing the current node -- `here` is a plain node reference) and `visit self.target` (jumping straight to the stored node, regardless of whether an edge connects them). This enables teleport-style traversal driven by walker state rather than graph topology. As written the re-visit of `here` would recurse; real uses gate it with a condition.

`Visitor` demonstrates queue-position control in visit statements: the integer between colons says where newly found nodes are inserted into the walker's pending-visit queue. `visit : 0 : [-->]` pushes them to the front, so the walker descends before finishing siblings -- depth-first behavior. `visit : -1 : [-->]` appends to the end, yielding breadth-first order (and is the default). `visit : 2 : [-->]` inserts at an arbitrary index for custom priority schemes. Same traversal targets, different exploration order; the walker itself carries no state.

A module demonstrating the report channel -- how walkers stream values back to their spawner. `DataNode` holds an `int` `value` (default 0). Walker `DataCollector` fans out from the root (`start`, on `Root` entry) and, at every `DataNode`, its `collect` ability reports the node's value via `here.value` and keeps traversing -- reporting does not interrupt execution, each call just appends to the walker's output stream. The entry block ties it together: it attaches one data node to `root`, spawns the walker, and reads `reports` off the spawn `result` -- a `list` of every reported value in visit order. This is the standard pattern for collection endpoints: traverse, report each hit, let the caller consume the aggregated list.

`DataCollector` demonstrates typed report checking: declaring the `has` field `reports` with type `list[int]` constrains what the walker's report statements may emit -- each reported value is checked against `int`. Its `start` ability fans out from `Root` entry, and `collect` reports `here.value` at every `DataNode` before continuing outward. Callers read the accumulated integers from `reports` after spawning; reporting a non-int would fail the declared contract.

`Searcher` is a find-first walker. State: `target` (`str`), the name to look for. Its ability `search` fires on each `Person` entry: when `here.name` equals `self.target` it reports the matching node itself (`here`) and immediately halts the entire traversal with `disengage` -- no further queued nodes are visited; otherwise it continues outward along all edges. The result is at most one report: the first matching person found in traversal order. Read-only with respect to the graph.

`Auditor` walks accounts and reports balances of active ones only. Its ability `check`, bound to `Account` entry, first tests the node's `active` flag: when false it executes `skip`, which abandons the rest of this ability for the current node -- so neither the report nor the outward visit below runs -- and moves the walker to its next queued node. For active accounts it reports `here.balance` and continues along outgoing edges. Note the asymmetry this creates: traversal only proceeds through active accounts, since skipped nodes never issue their visit. Read-only.

The full spawn-and-collect lifecycle. `Item` nodes hold an `int` `value` (default 0). Walker `MyWalker` has a configurable field `param` (`int`, default 0) and two abilities: one on `Root` entry that steps outward, and `collect` on `Item` entry that reports `here.value` and continues, so a chain traversal reports every value in order. The entry block builds a three-node chain off `root` (`node1` through `node3`), then shows the two spawn forms -- bare construction, and construction with keyword arguments (`param` set to 10) to parameterize the run -- and finally reads the output list from `reports` on the returned `result`. Spawning returns the walker instance itself, so both its reports and any mutated fields are inspectable afterward.

Defines a minimal todo store rooted at the graph root. `Todo` is a `node` with a `title` string and a `done` flag defaulting to `False`. The `add_todo` walker takes a `title` parameter and, in its `create` ability (triggered on `Root` entry), attaches a new `Todo` to the current root via `here ++> Todo(title=self.title)`, reporting the newly created node. The `list_todos` walker's `list` ability iterates the root's outgoing children filtered to `Todo` nodes and reports each one. Side effects: `add_todo` mutates the graph by adding one node and one edge; `list_todos` is read-only.

`BaseVisitor` is a `walker` whose `log` ability fires on entry to any node, prints the current node, and continues traversal along all outgoing edges with `visit [-->]`. `DetailedVisitor` inherits from `BaseVisitor` and uses `override` on its own `log` ability to replace the parent behavior, printing the visited node's type name instead before continuing the same outgoing traversal. Neither walker takes parameters or returns values; the only side effect is console output -- the graph itself is not modified.

Demonstrates the four OSP context references. `SecureRoom` is a `node` with a `required_level` field; its `check` ability fires when an `Inspector` walker enters and compares `visitor.clearance` (the visiting walker's field) against `self.required_level`, printing an access-granted message including `visitor.name`. The `Inspector` walker carries `clearance` and `name` fields; its `start` ability on `Root` entry prints the graph root and visits all outgoing nodes, while `inspect` fires on `SecureRoom` entry and prints both the walker's own `name` (via `self`) and the room's `required_level` (via `here`). Side effects are print statements only; no graph mutation occurs.

Models a tiny social graph illustrating the three edge-creation forms. `Person` is a `node` with a `name`; `Friend` and `Colleague` are `edge` types carrying their own state (`since` defaulting to 2020 on `Friend`, `department` defaulting to an empty string on `Colleague`). The single `with entry` block is the entry point: it creates `alice` and `bob`, links them with an untyped generic edge (`alice ++> bob`), a typed directed `Friend` edge initialized with `since=2020`, and a bidirectional `Colleague` edge whose `department` is set to "Engineering". The pieces relate purely through these edges -- running the module builds the two-person graph and nothing else.

Builds two linked chains from the graph root in single expressions. Four bare `Item` nodes (`a`, `b`, `c`, `d`) are created, then `root ++> a ++> b ++> c ++> d` connects them in sequence with untyped edges -- each `++>` yields its target so the chain continues left to right. The second statement repeats the chain with typed edges, using `Start` for the first hop, `Next` for the middle hops, and `End` for the final hop via the `+>:` and `:+>` operators. Side effects: eight edges are added to the graph (four generic, four typed); nothing is returned.

Shows the three deletion forms for graph data. In the `with entry` block, `alice` and `bob` are `Person` nodes joined by a `Friend` edge; `alice del --> bob` removes just the edge between them while leaving both nodes intact, and `del bob` removes the node itself. The `Cleanup` walker demonstrates deleting the current node from inside a traversal: its `check` ability fires on `Todo` entry, and when `here.completed` is true it captures the node's id with `jid(here)`, deletes the node via `del here`, and reports a dict containing the saved id under the key "deleted". Side effects: every path mutates the graph destructively.

`DeleteWithChildren` is a private walker (`walker:priv`, so it runs against the authenticated user's own graph) that deletes a target `Todo` and its direct children in one pass. It takes one parameter, `parent_id`, the id of the node to remove. The `search` ability on `Root` entry fans out to all outgoing nodes; the `delete` ability fires on each `Todo` and removes the node with `del here` when either `jid(here)` matches `self.parent_id` (the target itself) or the node's own `parent_id` field points at the target (a child). Nothing is reported; the side effect is destructive removal of matching nodes from the graph.

Demonstrates the graph built-in helpers on freshly created `Person` nodes. Inside `with entry`, three nodes (`alice`, `bob`, `secret_node`) are constructed but never connected to `root`. `jid(alice)` returns the unique Jac identifier for the node and is stored in `id`; `save(alice)` explicitly persists the node to storage even though it is not attached to the root; `printgraph(root)` prints the current graph rooted at `root` for debugging. Side effects: one node is persisted and debug output is written to the console -- no edges are created, so none of the nodes appear under `root` in the printed graph.

`BFSWalker` traverses the graph in breadth-first order using Jac's default walker queue. Its `start` ability fires on `Root` entry, prints the starting node, and queues all outgoing neighbors with `visit [-->]`. The `traverse` ability fires on each `Person` node, prints `here.name`, and again queues every outgoing node -- because `visit` appends to the walker's queue rather than recursing, all nodes at one depth are processed before the next depth. The walker takes no parameters and reports nothing; its only side effect is console output.

Models a linear pipeline of `Step` nodes (each carrying a `label`) and a `Logger` walker that demonstrates entry/exit ability ordering. `Logger` has three abilities: `start` fires on `Root` entry and begins the traversal with `visit [-->]`; `enter` fires on each `Step` entry, printing an ENTER line before queueing the next hop; `leave` fires on `Step` exit, printing an EXIT line. As the commented trace shows for a root -> A -> B -> C chain, entry abilities run in visit order while exit abilities unwind in reverse -- the innermost node exits first, the outermost last. The commented `root spawn Logger()` line is the intended entry point.

`FilteredWalker` illustrates the filtered `visit` forms. Its `start` ability launches traversal from `Root` with an unfiltered `visit [-->]`. On each `Person` entry, the `traverse` ability shows three narrowing strategies: `visit [-->][?:Person]` restricts the targets by node type; `visit [->:Friend:->]` follows only `Friend`-typed edges; and the combined form `visit [->:Friend:since > 2020:->][?:Person]` follows `Friend` edges whose `since` field exceeds 2020 and additionally filters the destinations to `Person` nodes. The walker holds no state and reports nothing -- the snippet's purpose is traversal control, and the graph is not mutated.

`Room` is a `node` that reacts to walker traffic through two node-side abilities. `on_enter` fires when a walker of type `Visitor` enters the node and prints an entering message; `on_exit` fires when the same walker type leaves, printing an exiting message. The node declares no fields and the abilities take no parameters -- they trigger automatically, keyed on the visiting walker's type and the entry/exit phase. The only side effect is console output; the graph is untouched.

A reference catalogue of edge-traversal query expressions, organized around a `Traverser` walker whose `query` ability runs on `Person` entry. The supporting types exist purely to give the queries something to match: `Person` nodes, `EdgeType`, an `Edge` carrying filterable fields (`attr`, `a`, `b`), and `Friend`. The ability's locals map each form to its meaning: `[-->]`, `[<--]`, and `[<-->]` collect outgoing, incoming, and bidirectional neighbor nodes; `[->:EdgeType:->]` restricts by edge type; `[->:Edge:attr > 0:->]` adds an edge-attribute condition; `[-->][?:Person]` filters result nodes by type; and the `[edge -->]` and `[edge ->:Friend:->]` forms return the edge objects themselves instead of the target nodes. There is no entry point -- the module is a pattern reference, not a runnable program.

`Querier` demonstrates compound graph queries from a `Person` node inside its `complex` ability. `[here ->:Friend:-> ->:Friend:->]` performs a two-hop traversal over `Friend` edges to collect friends-of-friends; the `path` query mixes edge types, hopping first over a `Friend` edge and then a `Colleague` edge; and the `target` query combines an edge-attribute condition (`Friend` edges with `since < 2020`) with the node filter `[?:Person, age > 30]` restricting results by type and `age`. All three results are locals -- the ability reports nothing and performs no mutation.

`Processor` is a walker whose `process` ability uses a union trigger -- `with Node1 | Node2 entry` -- so the same handler fires when the walker enters either a `Node1` or a `Node2`. Both node types declare an `int` field `v` (defaulting to 0), which is why the body can safely print `here.v` regardless of which concrete type the current node is: inside the ability, `here` is typed as the union of the two. The walker carries no state, reports nothing, and does not modify the graph.

`DataNode` is a `node` holding an `int` field `value` whose `handle` ability omits a walker type -- declared `with entry`, it fires for every walker that enters the node, whether that is a `Reader` or a `Writer`. Inside the ability, `visitor` is the visiting walker, so `type(visitor).__name__` prints which walker class arrived, alongside the node's own `value` via `self.value`. `Reader` is an empty walker; `Writer` additionally carries a `new_value` field. The only side effect is the printed line -- no state changes or graph mutation occur.

`ShoppingCart` is a walker whose `process_item` ability fires on entry to any `Product` node and dispatches per-subtype presentation with typed context blocks: the `->Book` block prints the item's `title` and `author`, the `->Magazine` block prints `title` and `issue`, and the `->Electronics` block prints `name` and `warranty_years`. After the type-specific block runs, the ability accumulates `here.price` into `self.total` and continues to all outgoing nodes with `visit [-->]`. Side effects: mutates the walker's own `total` field and prints one line per item; the referenced node types (`Product`, `Book`, `Magazine`, `Electronics`) and their fields are assumed to be defined elsewhere.

A complete private CRUD surface over `Item` nodes hanging off the user's root. `CreateItem` takes `name`, attaches a new `Item` with `here ++> Item(name=self.name)`, and reports the created node (`new_item[0]`). `ListItems` fans out from `Root` with `visit [-->]`, its `gather` ability appends each visited `Item` to `self.items`, and the `finish` ability on `Root` exit reports the accumulated list in one shot. `UpdateItem` takes `item_id` and `new_name`, walks the children, and when `jid(here)` matches `self.item_id` renames the node (`here.name = self.new_name`) and reports it. `DeleteItem` matches the same way but removes the node with `del here` and reports a confirmation dict. All four are `walker:priv`, so each runs authenticated against the calling user's own graph; `CreateItem`, `UpdateItem`, and `DeleteItem` mutate the graph, while `ListItems` is read-only.

`SearchItems` is a private walker endpoint (`walker:priv`): when served, it is invoked as a POST walker route and requires an authenticated user, running against that user's own root graph. Request fields: `query` (`str`, required), the case-insensitive substring matched against each `Item` node's `name`; `matches` is internal accumulator state and should not be supplied. Behavior: the `start` ability fans out from `Root`; `check` appends a record for every matching `Item` containing its id from `jid(here)`, its `name`, and a score from `calculate_relevance(here, self.query)`; `finish` sorts `self.matches` by score descending on `Root` exit and reports the list. Response: one report -- a list of dicts with keys "id", "name", and "score" -- empty when nothing matches. No explicit error cases are handled; a missing `query` fails request validation before the walker runs.

`GetStats` is a private walker (`walker:priv`) that computes summary statistics over the caller's `Todo` nodes. It holds two counters, `total` and `completed`, both starting at 0. The `count` ability on `Root` entry fans out to all children; `tally` fires per `Todo`, incrementing `self.total` and, when `here.completed` is true, `self.completed`; `summarize` runs on `Root` exit after the traversal finishes and reports a single dict with keys "total", "completed", "pending" (the difference), and "completion_rate" (a percentage, guarded to yield 0 when `self.total` is 0 to avoid division by zero). The walker is read-only with respect to the graph; its only output is the final report.

Two public client components declared inside a `cl` block, each returning a `JsxElement`. `Greeting` is a stateless presentational component: it takes a `props` dict and renders an `<h1>` greeting interpolating `props.name`. `Counter` is stateful -- its `has count: int = 0` declaration compiles to React state, and the returned button both displays `count` and increments it through an inline `lambda` bound to `onClick`, triggering a re-render on every click. Neither component touches the server or the graph; all effects are confined to the browser UI.

Contrasts the two codespace placements for plain functions. `add` is declared with no codespace marker, so it lands in the default server codespace and runs as Python -- it takes two `int` values `a` and `b` and returns their sum. `greet` is prefixed with the single-statement `cl` marker, placing it in the client codespace where it compiles to JavaScript; it takes a `name` string and returns a greeting built by concatenation. Both are pure functions with no side effects; the marker changes only where each executes.

A minimal todo backend: `Todo` nodes carry `title` and a `done` flag defaulting to `False`, and three public walkers (`walker:pub`, so each becomes an unauthenticated REST endpoint when served) operate on the root graph. `add_todo` takes `title`, attaches a new `Todo` under the current root via `here ++> Todo(title=self.title)`, and reports a dict of the new node's `title` and `done` values. `list_todos` reads all root children filtered to `Todo` (`[-->][?:Todo]`) and reports them as a list of title/done dicts built by a comprehension. `health` reports a static status payload for liveness checks. Only `add_todo` mutates the graph; the other two are read-only.

Two public walker endpoints over `Task` nodes (`title` plus a `done` flag defaulting to `False`); both are `walker:pub`, so no authentication is required and each is served as a POST walker route named after the walker. `get_tasks`: no request fields; its `fetch` ability reads all root children filtered with `[-->][?:Task]` and reports a list of dicts, one per task, with keys "id" (from `jid(t)`), "title", and "done". An empty graph yields an empty list rather than an error. `add_task`: request body requires `title` (`str`); the `create` ability constructs a `Task`, attaches it with `root ++> task`, and reports a dict with the new node's "id", "title", and "done". Omitting `title` fails request validation before the walker runs; there are no other error paths. `add_task` mutates the graph; `get_tasks` is read-only.

`get_user` is a public walker (`walker:pub`) that looks up a single user by id. Parameter: `user_id` (`str`), compared against each candidate's `id` field. The `fetch` ability runs on `Root` entry, iterates the root's children filtered to `User` nodes (`[-->][?:User]`), and on the first node whose `user.id` equals `self.user_id` reports a dict of the user's `id`, `name`, and `email` and returns immediately. If the loop completes without a match, it reports an error dict with the message "User not found" instead of raising. The walker never mutates the graph.

Two walkers that snapshot the root graph to disk as JSON. The `save` ability of `save_state` collects the `__dict__` of every `User` and `Post` child of the root into a dict keyed "users" and "posts", writes it to "state.json" with `json.dump`, and reports a saved-confirmation dict. The `load` ability of `load_state` reads the same file with `json.load` and re-creates `User` nodes under the root via `root ++> User(**u)` for each stored record, reporting success; if the file does not exist it catches `FileNotFoundError` and reports a failure dict with the reason "No saved state" instead of raising. Side effects: file I/O in both directions and, on load, new nodes and edges added to the graph. Note the loader only restores users -- stored posts are not re-created.

`get_config` is a walker that surfaces environment-based configuration in a single report. Its `fetch` ability, on `Root` entry, reads three values via `os.getenv`: "DATABASE_URL" with a sqlite fallback default, "API_KEY" with no default (so the reported value is `None` when unset), and "DEBUG", which is compared against the string "true" to yield a `bool`. It reports one dict with keys "database_url", "api_key", and "debug". The walker takes no parameters and has no side effects beyond reading process environment variables; the graph is untouched.

`health` is a public walker (`walker:pub`) implementing a minimal liveness probe: it exposes an unauthenticated endpoint whose `check` ability fires on `Root` entry and reports the static dict `{"status": "healthy"}`. It takes no parameters, performs no traversal beyond the root, and has no side effects, making it safe to poll from load balancers or monitors.

`ready` is a readiness-probe endpoint: a public walker (`walker:pub`, no authentication) served as a POST walker route with an empty request body. On `Root` entry its `check` ability calls two helper probes, `check_database` and `check_cache` (assumed defined elsewhere), and branches on their conjunction. Success response: a single report `{"status": "ready"}`. Degraded response: `{"status": "not_ready", "db": db_ok, "cache": cache_ok}`, exposing each dependency's boolean so callers can see which one failed -- note this is still a normal report, not an HTTP error status. If either helper is undefined or raises, the walker errors before reporting anything.

Demonstrates Jac's two function homes. `factorial` is a free function computing the factorial recursively: it takes `n` (`int`), returns 1 when `n` is 0, and otherwise multiplies `n` by the recursive call -- no side effects. `Person` is an `obj` with `name` and `age` fields whose `greet` method prints a self-introduction built from both fields and returns `None`. The `with entry` block wires them together: it constructs a `Person` positionally, calls `person.greet()`, and prints `factorial(5)` (120). All side effects are console output.

Shows that Jac imports Python's data-science stack directly. The module imports `pandas` as `pd`, `numpy` as `np`, and pulls `LinearRegression` from sklearn with the `import from` form. Its `with entry` block exercises each: builds a NumPy array via `np.array` and prints its mean with `np.mean`; constructs a two-column `pd.DataFrame` and prints `df.describe()`; and instantiates a `LinearRegression` model (left unfitted). Side effects are console output only -- no data is persisted and the model is never trained.

Demonstrates the inline-Python escape hatch. The `::py::` block defines `complex_calculation`, a pure-Python function that wraps its `data` argument in a NumPy array via `np.array` and returns the tuple of its mean and standard deviation -- the block form is used so performance-critical code stays as plain Python. The `with entry` block calls it from Jac, unpacking the pair into `mean` and `std` and printing both. Side effects: console output only. Note `numpy` is imported inside the Python block, so it is only available to that code.

Main module of a small task app that composes two sibling modules. It imports `models` (providing the `Task` archetype) and `utils` (validation and description helpers). The `TaskCreator` walker takes a `title` and, on `Root` entry, gates creation behind `utils.validate_title(self.title)`: on success it constructs `models.Task(title=self.title)`, attaches it under the current node with `here ++> task`, generates a description via `utils.generate_desc(self.title)`, and prints confirmation lines; on failure it prints a too-short warning and creates nothing. The `with entry` block is the entry point, spawning `TaskCreator(title="Build API")` at `root`. Side effects: one node and edge added to the graph on the success path, plus console output.

Module holding the `Task` node definition for the task app. A `Task` has a required `title` (`str`) and a `done` completion flag (`bool`) defaulting to `False`. The module contains only this declaration -- no walkers or entry point -- so it exists to be imported by other modules that create, connect, and query `Task` nodes; as a `node` type, instances persist automatically once attached to the graph.

Utility module providing two pure helper functions for the task app. `validate_title` takes a `title` string and returns a `bool` -- true only when the title is longer than 3 characters -- serving as the gate before task creation. `generate_desc` takes the same `title` and returns a formatted placeholder description string (standing in for an AI-generated one). Neither function touches the graph or has side effects; both are intended to be imported and called by application walkers.

Application module mixing Jac with legacy inline Python. It imports `models` for the `Task` archetype and defines the Jac helper `generate_desc`, while a `::py::` block preserves two legacy functions verbatim: `validate_title` (non-trivial title validation) and `get_sample_task` (returns a sample task dict). The `TaskCreator` walker, on `Root` entry, pulls `task_data` from `get_sample_task()`, validates its title with `validate_title`, and on success creates a `models.Task`, attaches it with `here ++> task`, and prints the title plus a description from `generate_desc(task.title)`; otherwise it prints an invalid-title message. The `with entry` block spawns `TaskCreator()` at `root`. Side effects: graph mutation on the success path and console output.

Main module wiring a Jac walker to an external Python module. It imports `models` (the `Task` archetype) and `validators` -- a plain Python module whose validation function is called exactly like a Jac function. `generate_desc` is a local helper returning a formatted description string. The `TaskCreator` walker takes `title`; on `Root` entry it validates via `validators.validate_title(self.title)`, and on success creates `models.Task(title=self.title)`, connects it with `here ++> task`, and prints the created title and the generated description, or prints a too-short warning otherwise. The `with entry` block spawns `TaskCreator(title="Build API")` at `root`, mutating the graph on success.

A small importable module bundling the task domain: the `Task` node (required `title`, `done` defaulting to `False`), the `TaskCreator` walker, and the `generate_desc` helper. `TaskCreator` takes a `title` parameter; its `create` ability on `Root` entry constructs a `Task`, attaches it to the current node with `here ++> task`, and prints a confirmation. `generate_desc` is a pure function returning a formatted description string for a given `title`. There is no entry block -- the module is meant to be imported, with `TaskCreator` spawned at `root` by consumers; spawning it adds one node and one edge to the graph.

Full-stack todo service in one file. Server API (both endpoints are `def:pub`, so they are public routes auto-exposed to the client): `add_todo` accepts a todo `title`, asks the LLM-backed `categorize` function to classify it into the `Category` enum, lower-cases the enum name into the `category` string (falling back to "other (setup AI key)" if the LLM call raises), attaches a new `Todo` under `root`, and returns the created `Todo`; `get_todos` takes no arguments and returns `list[Todo]` -- every `Todo` child of `root` via `[root-->][?:Todo]`. Error cases: the only handled failure is the LLM exception fallback in `add_todo`; there are no not-found paths. The client component `app` (a `cl` `def:pub` returning `JsxElement`) holds `todos` and `text` state, loads existing todos on mount by awaiting `get_todos()`, and its `add` handler submits `text` through `add_todo` on Enter or the Add button, appending the returned todo to the list. The compiler generates the HTTP calls -- the wire shape is the typed `Todo` object itself (`title`, `category`, `done`).

Three escalating examples of Jac's meaning-typed LLM delegation. `classify_sentiment` shows the minimal form: the signature alone -- name, `text` parameter, `str` return -- is the whole specification handed to the model via `by llm`. `triage_ticket` adds output constraint: because its return type is the `Priority` enum (`LOW`, `MEDIUM`, `HIGH`, `CRITICAL`), the LLM must answer with one of those members. `plan_shopping` returns structured data -- `list[Ingredient]`, where `Ingredient` is an `obj` with `name`, `cost`, and `carby` fields -- and the accompanying `sem` declarations (`Ingredient.cost`, `Ingredient.carby`) inject extra semantic context into the prompt where field names alone are ambiguous. None of these functions have bodies; each call is an LLM invocation at runtime.

Minimal demonstration of Jac's automatic persistence. `Todo` is a `node` with a `title` and a `done` flag defaulting to `False`. The `with entry` block attaches one instance to the graph root with `root ++> Todo(title="Learn Jac")` -- and that connection is the whole persistence story: anything reachable from `root` is saved automatically across runs, with no database code, ORM, or explicit save call. Side effect: one node and one edge added to the persistent root graph.

`app` is a public client component (`def:pub` inside a `cl` block, returning a `JsxElement`) that demonstrates reading build-time environment configuration in the browser. It pulls the API base URL from `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL` -- the Vite-injected environment object available in client code -- into the local `api_url` and renders it inside a div. No state, no server calls, no side effects; the value is baked in at build time, so changing it requires a rebuild.

A client-side import manifest showing the `cl` block's npm interop forms. From `react` it pulls the hooks `useState`, `useEffect`, and `useCallback`; from the scoped package "@tanstack/react-query" (quoted because of the scope prefix) it imports `useQuery` and `useMutation`; from `lodash` it takes `debounce` and `throttle`; and from `axios` it uses the `default as axios` form to bind the package's default export. The snippet declares no components -- it exists to show that bare module names and quoted package specifiers both work with the `import from` syntax inside client code.

The minimal shape of a Jac test block: `test` followed by a quoted description ("my feature") and a braced body containing assertions. Here the body asserts a single `condition` -- a placeholder for real checks -- so the test passes or fails on that boolean. Test blocks are discovered and run by the jac test runner; they take no parameters, return nothing, and any failed `assert` marks the named test as failed.

`MyObject` is an `obj` holding a single `data` string, and its `process` method simply returns `self.data` unchanged. The "object processing" `test` block exercises it with the arrange-act-assert shape: it constructs `my_obj` with `data="test"`, calls `my_obj.process()`, and asserts the `result` round-trips the stored string exactly. No graph interaction or side effects are involved -- this is plain object unit testing.

Documents the two `assert` forms available inside a `test` block. The bare form, `assert condition`, fails the test with a generic assertion error when `condition` is falsy; the two-argument form appends a custom failure string ("Error message") that is shown when the assertion trips, making diagnosis easier. Both forms are no-ops when the condition holds, and neither has side effects.

Document this Jac code:

```jac
test "equality checks" {
    assert a == b;           # Equal
    assert a != b;           # Not equal
    assert a is b;           # Same object
    assert a is not b;       # Different objects
}
```

A `test` block cataloguing the four identity and equality assertions. `a == b` and `a != b` compare by value, while `a is b` and `a is not b` compare by identity -- passing only when both names reference the same (or, respectively, different) underlying object. The test uses free placeholders `a` and `b`; substitute real values to apply each pattern. No side effects.

Document this Jac code:

```jac
test "comparisons" {
    assert a > b;            # Greater than
    assert a >= b;           # Greater or equal
    assert a < b;            # Less than
    assert a <= b;           # Less or equal
}
```

A `test` block listing the four ordering assertions for comparable values: `a > b` (strictly greater), `a >= b` (greater or equal), `a < b` (strictly less), and `a <= b` (less or equal). The placeholders `a` and `b` stand in for real expressions; each `assert` fails the test when its comparison is false. Purely illustrative -- no side effects.

A `test` block showing three boolean assertion idioms: `assert True` always passes (useful as a reached-this-point marker), `assert not False` demonstrates negation, and `assert bool(value)` coerces an arbitrary `value` to its truthiness -- failing for empty collections, zero, empty strings, or `None`. No side effects; substitute a real expression for `value` in practice.

A `test` block covering membership assertions: `item in collection` passes when the element is present, `item not in collection` when absent, and `key in dictionary` shows that for dicts the `in` operator tests keys, not values. The names `item`, `collection`, `key`, and `dictionary` are placeholders to be replaced with real data. No side effects.

A `test` block showing the canonical null checks: `value is None` asserts the placeholder `value` holds nothing, and `value is not None` asserts it holds something. Identity comparison with `is` (rather than equality) is the correct way to test against `None`. No side effects.

A `test` block demonstrating tolerant floating-point comparison. Computing `0.1 + 0.2` yields a `result` that is not exactly 0.3 due to binary float representation, so instead of an equality check the test asserts with `almostEqual(result, 0.3, 10)` -- comparing the two values to 10 decimal places. Use this pattern whenever asserting on derived floats. No side effects.

A `test` block illustrating descriptive assertion messages. The first assertion attaches an f-string that interpolates the actual `result`, so a failure reads "Expected positive, got ..." with the real value instead of a bare assertion error; the second pins `len(items)` to 3 with a static explanation. The message argument is only shown on failure, making diagnosis faster with no cost on the passing path. `result` and `items` are placeholders for real values.

`Person` nodes carry `name` and `age`; the `FindAdults` walker's `check` ability runs on `Root` entry, iterates the root's children filtered to `Person` via `[-->][?:Person]`, and reports every node whose `age` is at least 18 -- no further traversal occurs. The "find adults" `test` block seeds three people (ages 30, 15, 25) under `root`, spawns the walker, and asserts on `result.reports`: exactly two matches, with "Alice" and "Carol" present in the collected `names` and "Bob" excluded. The walker is read-only; reports are its only output.

Models a tiny floor plan to verify graph construction in a test. `Room` is a `node` with a `name`; `Door` is a field-less `edge` connecting rooms. The single "graph connections" `test` block is the only entry point: it attaches `kitchen` under `root`, then chains `kitchen` to `living` and `living` to `bedroom` with typed `Door` edges using the `+>:` / `:+>` form. The assertions then read the structure back: per-node outgoing counts via queries like `len([root -->])` (1, 1, 1, and 0 for the dead-end `bedroom`), and typed-edge reachability via membership checks against `[kitchen ->:Door:->]` and `[living ->:Door:->]`. The module demonstrates that connection operators and traversal queries agree.

Defines a `User` object with `name` and `email` fields and a single `is_valid` predicate that returns true only when the `name` is non-empty and the `email` contains an "@". Three colocated `test` blocks -- Jac convention places them at the bottom of the module they verify -- cover the decision table: a fully valid user passes, an `email` without "@" fails, and an empty `name` fails. `is_valid` is pure (it reads `self.name` and `self.email`, mutating nothing), and each test constructs a fresh instance.

Demonstrates table-driven testing with `parametrize` from `jaclang.runtimelib.test`. `_test_square` is the test body: it receives one `pair` tuple, unpacks the input and `expected` values, squares the input, and asserts equality with a diagnostic message. The `with entry` block registers the suite: `parametrize` is called with a base name ("square"), the list of four input/expected pairs -- including zero and a negative -- and the function, generating one named test case per pair rather than one monolithic test. Side effects: test registration at module run; no graph involvement.

Shows `parametrize` (from `jaclang.runtimelib.test`) with custom test-case naming. `_test_parse` is the per-case body receiving one `raw` string from the parameter list ("500m", "2", "250"). The `with entry` block registers the cases under the base name "parse values" and supplies `id_fn` -- a typed lambda mapping each parameter `p` to an "input_"-prefixed label -- so each generated test gets a readable identifier instead of a positional index. The body is a stub here; the snippet's point is the naming hook.

Illustrates test granularity for `test` blocks. The good pattern gives each behavior its own block -- "add positive numbers" and "add negative numbers" each make a single `assert` about `add` -- so a failure pinpoints exactly which case regressed. The anti-pattern, "all math operations", bundles `add`, `subtract`, and `multiply` into one block: the first failed assertion masks the rest, and the test name cannot tell you which operation broke. Prefer one focused block per behavior.

Demonstrates test isolation for graph-backed `test` blocks. "counter increment" builds its own state from scratch -- attaching a fresh `Counter` to `root`, spawning `Incrementer`, then asserting `counter[0].count` is 1 -- rather than relying on nodes left behind by earlier tests. "counter starts at zero" likewise constructs a standalone `Counter` and checks its default `count`. The rule being illustrated: each test creates the state it needs, so tests pass or fail independently and in any order.

Boundary-value testing pattern for a `process` function over lists. Three `test` blocks probe the input-size spectrum: "empty list" asserts `process([])` returns an empty list unchanged, "single item" checks the minimal non-empty case has length 1, and "large list" feeds a thousand-element range and asserts nothing is dropped via `len(result)`. Together they pin the edges where list-handling bugs typically live; `process` itself is assumed defined elsewhere.

Contrasts failure diagnostics in `test` blocks. "calculation with message" stores the output of `calculate` in `result` and asserts against `expected` with an f-string that interpolates both -- on failure the runner shows the actual and expected values immediately. "calculation no message" makes the identical check bare: it still fails correctly but reports only that an assertion was false, forcing a debugging round-trip to learn the values. The guidance: attach an explanatory message wherever the compared values are not obvious from the test name.

Shows that a `node` behaves like a regular object until it enters the graph. `Person` declares `name` and `age` fields plus a `greet` method returning a formatted introduction built from `self.name`. In the `with entry` block, `alice` and `bob` are constructed with keyword arguments exactly like `obj` instances, methods are invoked (`alice.greet()`), and fields read (`bob.age`) -- no edges or walkers involved. Side effects: console output only; because the nodes are never connected to `root`, they are not persisted.

Builds the first edges of a graph from three detached `Person` nodes. Inside `with entry`, `alice`, `bob`, and `carol` are created, then the `++>` connect operator wires the topology: `root ++> alice` and `root ++> bob` attach two people directly under the graph's default starting node, while `alice ++> carol` hangs the third off `alice` instead -- so `carol` is reachable from `root` only via `alice`. Side effect: three untyped edges added to the persistent graph.

Models a social relationship with data on the relationship itself. `Person` is a minimal `node` carrying just a `name`; `Knows` is an `edge` type whose fields describe the connection rather than either endpoint -- `since` records the year the two met and `strength` labels the closeness ("close" vs "acquaintance"). The `with entry` block is the entry point: it creates `alice` and `bob` and joins them with the typed-edge operator `alice +>: Knows(since=2020, strength="close") :+> bob`, instantiating the edge with its data inline. The result is a two-node graph where the relationship metadata lives on the `Knows` edge and can later be filtered on during traversal.

A first complete walker program. It models people as `Person` nodes carrying a `name` and a `visited` flag (default `False`) that records walker contact. The `Greeter` walker has two abilities: `start` fires when spawned on `Root` and pushes traversal to the root's neighbors with `visit [-->]`; `greet` fires on each `Person` reached, printing a greeting and flipping `here.visited` to `True` -- but since `greet` issues no further `visit`, the walk stops there. The `with entry` block is the entry point: it chains `root` to `alice` and `alice` to `bob`, then launches everything with `root spawn Greeter()`; only `alice` is greeted, because `bob` sits a second hop out and is never queued. Side effects: node mutation (`visited`) and console output.

`Explorer` is a walker that counts rooms as it moves. It carries one piece of state, `rooms_visited`, initialized to 0. Its single `explore` ability fires on entry to each `Room` node: it increments `self.rooms_visited`, prints the current room's `name` alongside the running total, and queues all outgoing neighbors with `visit [-->]`, so the walk continues until it runs out of connected rooms. Note there is no root-entry ability, so the walker must be spawned on (or otherwise reach) a `Room` for anything to happen. Side effects: walker-state mutation and console output; the graph itself is untouched.

A complete filter-and-collect walker program. `Person` nodes carry `name` and `age`; the `FindAdults` walker starts at `Root` (its `start` ability fans out with `visit [-->]`) and, on each `Person`, the `check` ability reports the node when `here.age` is at least 18 before continuing traversal. The `with entry` block seeds three people under `root` (ages 30, 15, and 25), spawns the walker, and consumes `result.reports` -- printing the adult count and each collected person's `name`. `report` accumulates matched nodes onto the spawn result rather than returning early, so all qualifying nodes are gathered in one pass; the graph is only read, never modified.

A small social-follow graph with two query walkers. `User` nodes carry `username` and `bio`; `Follows` edges carry a `since` date and point from follower to followee. `FindFollowers`, spawned on a `User`, collects everyone with an inbound `Follows` edge via the backward-typed query `[<-:Follows:<-]` and reports each `follower`. `FindMutualFollows` computes both directions from the current user -- `following` from `[here ->:Follows:->]` and `followers` from `[here <-:Follows:<-]` -- and reports only users appearing in both, i.e. mutual follows. The `with entry` block builds the demo: `alice` and `bob` follow each other, `carol` follows `alice`, then both walkers are spawned on `alice` and their `result.reports` printed (followers: bob and carol; mutuals: bob). All walker logic is read-only.

Shows how `report` accumulates values across a walker run. `MyWalker` is private (`walker:priv`); its `do_work` ability on `Root` entry issues two `report` statements -- "first" then "second" -- and each call appends to the result rather than returning. The `with entry` block spawns the walker at `root` and reads `response.reports`, which preserves report order as a list: index 0 holds "first", index 1 "second". No parameters, no graph mutation; reports are the walker's entire output channel.

`ToggleTask` is a private walker (`walker:priv`) that flips the `done` flag of one `Task` identified by id. Parameters: `task_id` (`str`), matched against `jid(here)`; the walker also declares `reports: list[Task]` explicitly, typing the report channel so every `report` is checked against `Task` and consumers receive hydrated `Task` objects rather than raw dicts. `search` fans out from `Root`; `toggle` fires per `Task`, and on an id match negates `here.done`, reports the node, and calls `disengage` to stop immediately. The `with entry` usage shows the payoff: `result.reports[0]` can be assigned straight into a `Task`-typed variable. Side effect: exactly one node's `done` field is toggled -- or none, if the id matches nothing, in which case the report list is empty.

`ListItems` is a private walker (`walker:priv`) implementing the accumulate-then-report pattern with a typed channel. It declares `reports: list[list[str]]` (each report is a list of strings) and an internal `items` accumulator. `collect` fans out from `Root`; `gather` appends each visited `Item` node's `data` to `self.items`; and `finish`, an exit ability on `Root`, fires after the traversal completes and issues one `report` carrying the whole accumulated list. Consumers therefore read a single entry: `result.reports[0]` is the complete list, as the usage block shows. Read-only with respect to the graph; the pattern avoids producing one report per item.

`FindMatches` is a private walker (`walker:priv`) performing a typed substring search over `Item` nodes. Parameters: `search_term` (`str`); it also declares `reports: list[Item]`, so each `report` is type-checked as an `Item` and callers get hydrated node objects back. `search` fans out from `Root`; `check` fires per `Item` and reports the node whenever `self.search_term` occurs within `here.name`. Every match produces its own report, so the usage block reads the whole `result.reports` list (annotated `list[Item]`) rather than a single index. The traversal is read-only; an empty list means no matches.

`CreateItem` is a private walker endpoint (`walker:priv`) -- invoking it over HTTP requires an authenticated user, and the node it creates lands in that user's own graph. Request body: `name` (`str`, required), the label for the new `Item`; the `reports: list[Item]` declaration is a typed response channel, not an input. Behavior: the `create` ability runs on `Root` entry, attaches a node with `here ++> Item(name=self.name)`, and reports `new_item[0]` (the connect expression yields a list, so index 0 is the created node). Response: exactly one report -- the created `Item`, hydrated client-side as a typed object rather than a plain dict, as the usage shows by assigning `result.reports[0]` to an `Item`-typed variable. Error cases: a missing `name` fails request validation; otherwise the walker always succeeds, mutating the graph by one node and one edge.

Demonstrates walker composition: one walker spawning another and harvesting its state. `InnerWalker` (private) has a `result` field that its `work` ability fills with "inner data" when run at `Root`. The `work` ability of `OuterWalker` constructs `inner = InnerWalker()`, spawns it at `root` synchronously, and then -- because the walker object persists after its run -- reads `inner.result` directly, folding it into a single report dict alongside its own data. The usage block shows the combined payload arriving as `result.reports[0]`. Key point: spawned-walker attributes are the return channel between walkers; no graph mutation occurs.

`ProcessAndSummarize` is a private walker (`walker:priv`) showing deliberate multi-report structure. Parameter: `input` (`str`). Its `process` ability, on `Root` entry, first runs `do_processing` -- a helper returning the input alongside a "_processed" variant -- and reports the raw `results` list; it then issues a second `report` containing a summary dict with the item `count` (via `len(results)`) and a completion status. Consumers rely on report ordering, as the usage shows: `result.reports[0]` is the raw data, `result.reports[1]` the summary. Pure computation -- no graph reads or writes beyond entering the root.

Defensive-consumption reference for walker responses. `MyWalker` is a private endpoint (`walker:priv`, authenticated when served) whose `work` ability reports the single string "data" from `Root` -- so its response is a one-element report list. The `with entry` block documents the safe access patterns callers should use for any walker response: guard `result.reports[0]` behind a truthiness check with a `None` or empty-list fallback, since a walker that hits no matching ability reports nothing; check `len(result.reports) > 1` before indexing a second entry; and iterate with an empty-list fallback, handing each element to `process`. The error being defended against: indexing into an empty report list raises, so every access is conditional.

Contrasts response typing for a public endpoint that fetches one task by `id`. The bad variant of `get_task` declares its return as `dict` and hand-builds the payload from `jid(task)`, `task.title`, and `task.done` -- schema duplication that must be updated whenever `Task` changes. The good variant declares `-> Task` and returns the `find_task` result directly: the runtime serializes the node, and the client receives a hydrated `Task` instance with its fields intact. Both are `def:pub` (public, no auth) and read-only; prefer the typed return so the contract lives in one place.

Reference for response granularity when a private walker endpoint collects `Item` data (`walker:priv`, so callers must be authenticated and see only their own graph). `BadPattern` reports `here.data` from inside the per-`Item` ability, so a graph with N items yields a response whose report list has N entries -- callers must reassemble the collection and cannot distinguish it from N unrelated reports. `GoodPattern` is the recommended shape: `start` fans out from `Root`, `process` appends each item's `data` to the internal `items` accumulator, and `finish` (a `Root` exit ability) reports once -- the response is a single-entry report list whose element is the complete collection. Neither walker takes request parameters or mutates the graph; an empty graph produces an empty list from `GoodPattern` versus no reports at all from `BadPattern`, a difference that itself trips up clients.

Documents the positional-report contract problem. `MyWalker` (private) reports twice from `Root` -- first a list of items, then a metadata dict -- so consumers must know that index 0 is data and index 1 is metadata. The `with entry` block contrasts consumption styles: bare `result.reports[0]` / `result.reports[1]` indexing works but encodes unexplained magic numbers; the improved version documents what each slot holds and guards access -- falling back to an empty list for the data slot and checking `len(result.reports) > 1` before touching `meta`. The underlying advice: when a walker multi-reports, the index layout is part of its API and must be documented and defensively read.

A minimal full-stack round trip in one file. Server side (default codespace): `Todo` is a persisted `node` with `title` and `done`; `add_todo` is a public endpoint (`def:pub`) that attaches a new `Todo` under `root` and returns a dict of the new node's id (via `jid(todo[0])`) and `title`. Client side: the `cl` block defines the `app` component (returning `JsxElement`), holding an `items` state list; its async `add` handler awaits `add_todo("New")` -- the compiler turns this into the HTTP call -- and appends the returned record to `items`, re-rendering. The rendered UI is a single Add button wired to `add` through a `lambda` passed to `onClick`. Side effects: each click creates one persistent graph node server-side and grows the client list.

Three graph read expressions run at module entry. `[root-->]` gathers every node connected outward from `root` into the `everything` list; `[root-->][?:Task]` narrows the same result to nodes of type `Task`; and `[root-->][?:Task, done == False]` adds a field predicate, keeping only tasks whose `done` flag is `False` -- the `pending` set. All three are pure reads returning lists; nothing is created or modified. The snippet assumes `Task` nodes with a `done` field are declared and attached elsewhere.

`Scheduled` is an `edge` type carrying scheduling metadata: a required `time` string and a `priority` int defaulting to 1. The `with entry` block attaches a `Task` to `root` through one -- `root +>: Scheduled(time="9:00am", priority=3) :+> Task(title="Morning run")` creates the edge and the target node inline in a single expression. The follow-up query shows why the data lives on the edge: `[root->:Scheduled:priority>=3:->][?:Task]` traverses only `Scheduled` edges whose `priority` is at least 3, then filters the destinations to `Task` nodes, yielding the `urgent` list. Side effects: one node and one typed edge added to the persistent graph.

An LLM-delegated function with semantic annotations shaping its structured output. `Ingredient` is an `obj` whose fields the model must fill: `name`, `cost`, and `carby`. The `sem` declarations refine what the field names alone cannot convey -- `Ingredient.cost` is documented as an estimated USD amount and `Ingredient.carby` as a high-carbohydrate flag -- and these strings are injected into the runtime prompt, not mere comments. `plan_shopping` takes a `recipe` string and, being implemented `by llm()`, returns a `list[Ingredient]` the model generates; its own `sem` binding states the task ("Generate a shopping list for the given recipe."). Every call is an LLM invocation returning fully populated, typed objects.

`Foo` is a minimal `obj` -- Jac's dataclass-like archetype -- declaring a single field: `x`, an `int` defaulting to 5. Construction therefore needs no arguments, and the default can be overridden by keyword at instantiation. The object defines no methods and has no side effects; it exists as the smallest example of a `has` field declaration with a default value.

`Foo` is an `obj` pairing state with behavior: it declares an `int` field `x` defaulting to 0, and a method `my_method` that takes `val` (`int`) and returns `val + 1`. Notably the method never reads the `x` field -- it is a pure computation carried on the object, with no mutation or side effects. The snippet shows the standard inline form, where a `has` field and a `def` method with its body live together in one declaration block.

`MyWalker` is a walker with a single `process` ability that fires on entry to any `MyNode` node. On each visit it reports `here.value` -- pushing the current node's value onto the walker's results -- and then queues all outgoing neighbors with `visit [-->]`, so the walk continues until the frontier is exhausted. The walker holds no state of its own and never mutates the graph; the ordered stream of reported values is its entire output. `MyNode` and its `value` field are assumed declared elsewhere.

The declaration half of Jac's decl/impl split. `Foo` is an `obj` with an `int` field `x` (default 0) and a bodiless method signature: `my_method` takes `val` (`int`) and promises to return `int`, but the semicolon-terminated declaration defers the body to a matching implementation block in a companion file. This keeps the archetype's public surface readable while implementation details live elsewhere; the method is not callable until an implementation is provided.

The implementation half of a decl/impl split: the `impl` block supplies the body for `Foo.my_method`, which was declared signature-only in the corresponding declaration file. The header repeats the full signature -- `val` (`int`) in, `int` out -- and the body returns `val + 1`. Keeping bodies in a separate implementation file lets the declaring file read as a clean interface; the compiler stitches the two together, so callers see a normal method. Pure function of its argument, no side effects.

`Foo` is an `obj` that replaces the auto-generated constructor with an explicit `init`. The field `x` is declared via `has` with no default, and `init` takes an `x` parameter, first calls `super.init()` to run the parent chain's initialization, then assigns `self.x = x`. Use this pattern when construction needs logic beyond simple field assignment; the `super.init()` call is the important detail, ensuring inherited initialization still happens. Side effects: instance state only.

`modify` takes a `list` parameter `data` and appends the value 42 to it in place, returning `None`. Because lists are passed by reference, the mutation is visible to the caller after the call -- the function's entire purpose is this side effect on its argument. Callers should not expect a new list back; the declared `None` return makes the in-place contract explicit.

`Foo` is an `obj` whose only member is `bar`, a `static def` method: it belongs to the archetype rather than any instance, so it takes no `self` and is invoked directly on the type. It simply returns the constant 42 as an `int`. Static methods like this are the idiomatic home for instance-independent helpers; there is no state and no side effect.

`bar` is a free function taking no parameters and returning the constant 42 as an `int`. It is pure -- no inputs, no side effects, the same result every call -- serving as the minimal example of Jac's `def` syntax: typed return annotation, braced body, semicolon-terminated `return` statement.

`MyWalker` is a pure traversal walker: its single ability, `visit_node`, fires on entry to any `Node`-typed node and immediately queues all outgoing neighbors with `visit [-->]`. It carries no state, reports nothing, and never touches node data -- spawned on a graph, it simply walks every node reachable through outgoing edges from its starting point, making it a skeleton to hang real per-node logic on.

`MyEdge` is an `edge` archetype carrying its own state: a single `weight` field of type `float` defaulting to 1.0. Declaring data on the edge (rather than on either endpoint) lets each connection record its own strength; the default means edge creation without arguments still yields a valid weight, while `weight` can be set explicitly at connect time and later used in edge-condition traversal filters. No methods or side effects are defined.
