A dict literal inside a JSX expression slot: `style={{"color": "blue", "padding": "10px"}}` — string keys for the CSS properties (color, padding) mapping to string values ("blue", "10px"), applied to the `<div>` that wraps "Styled content".
According to the CSS Files excerpt, how do you include a plain CSS file such as `styles/main.css` in a client module?
With a bare import of the CSS path inside the `cl` block: `import "./styles/main.css";`. The CSS file itself just contains normal rules (the example defines `.card` with padding and border-radius).
Two components in your app both want to define a `.card` class with different styling, without the rules colliding. Which mechanism from the excerpt applies?

The scoped-CSS annex: give each component's `.cl.jac` module a `.style.css` file that shares its base name (e.g. `Card.style.css` beside `Card.cl.jac`); the two files form one logical module. The compiler hashes every class selector the annex declares with a per-module digest, rewrites the CSS rule selectors, and rewrites the module's JSX `className`/`class` literals to the same hashed form — so class names are scoped to the component automatically and two modules can both declare `.card` without colliding. Selectors that must stay global (like the example's `html` reset) are wrapped in `:global(...)`, which opts out of scoping and keeps the inner selector verbatim.
When should you rely on the scoped `.style.css` annex rewriting versus the `cn()` utility, given how each works in these excerpts?

The annex mechanism is compile-time and static: the compiler hashes declared selectors (`.card` becomes `.card-1419142b`, `.card-title` becomes `.card-title-769bf254`), rewrites matching `className` literals to agree, and auto-injects the `import "./Card.css";` side-effect — no import needed, unmatched classes are left untouched so scoped and global (e.g. Tailwind) classes can mix, and `:global(...)` escapes scoping. `cn()` is runtime and dynamic: imported from `lib/utils`, it merges conditional class values — `cn("base-class", condition and "active", {"error": hasError, "success": isSuccess})` — via `twMerge(clsx(inputs))`. So use the annex for per-module style isolation of fixed class names, and `cn()` when the class string must be computed from component state; `cn` requires `clsx` and `tailwind-merge` in `[dependencies.npm]`.
In the `StylingExamples` component, given `condition = True`, `hasError = False`, and `isSuccess = True`, which class names end up in the computed `className`?

`base-class`, `active`, and `success`. `"base-class"` is always included; `condition and "active"` yields `"active"` because condition is True; and from the dict `{"error": hasError, "success": isSuccess}`, only `success` is included since `hasError` is False. Under the hood `cn` is `twMerge(clsx(inputs))` — implementable entirely in Jac with a variadic `def:pub cn(*inputs: any) -> str`, requiring `clsx` and `tailwind-merge` in `[dependencies.npm]`.
In JSX attribute position, what is the difference between `{**props}` and the `{variable}` shorthand?

`{**props}` is a spread — it forwards every key of `props` as an attribute on the element; it is the canonical Jac form (the JS-idiomatic `{...props}` is accepted but emits warning `W0063`, "prefer `{**expr}`"). `{variable}` is the `{name}` shorthand: when an attribute's value is a variable of the same name it expands to `variable={variable}` — e.g. `<Box {title} {count} {onClick}/>` is sugar for `<Box title={title} count={count} onClick={onClick}/>` — and each shorthand attribute is still validated against the component signature.
On the `cl` target, what does a `try` slot with an `awaiting` clause lower to, and what happens to the `awaiting` body on the `sv` and `na` targets?

On `cl`, the slot is wrapped in `<JacAwaiting fallback={...}>{...}</JacAwaiting>` from `@jac/runtime` — a `React.Suspense` shim — so the `awaiting` body renders during the dispatched-but-not-joined window and the `try` body takes over once it settles. On `sv` and `na` targets the `awaiting` body is dropped with a `W2020` warning until the streaming-SSR and native-thread lowerings land. Adding an `except` arm makes the cl lowering wrap the `JacAwaiting` node in a `<JacClientErrorBoundary fallback={...}>` (re-exporting react-error-boundary's ErrorBoundary); since a JS error boundary catches every error regardless of type, per-type dispatch and `except ... as <name>` are not modeled, and `finally` is rejected via `E2022`.
You want to leave a TODO note between elements in a JSX tree. Which syntax applies, and why won't `#` or `{/* ... */}` work?

Use Jac's block comment wrapped in a JSX expression slot: `{#* TODO: replace with a custom Button component *#}`. It renders nothing and is preserved verbatim by `jac format`. A bare `#` in JSX text doesn't work because HTML allows `#` in content, so the lexer treats it as literal text. The React-style `{/* ... */}` is not supported because inside an expression slot `/` and `*` parse as Jac operators. Also note `{#* ... *#}` is the only no-op JSX slot — an empty `{}` is a parse error since a slot must contain a real expression or a block comment.
According to the inline comments in the jac.toml example, what do `base_route_app = "app"` and `cl_route_prefix = "/cl"` control?

Under `[serve]`, `base_route_app = "app"` serves the app at `/` (the comment reads "Serve at /"), and `cl_route_prefix = "/cl"` sets the client route prefix. The example also shows `[project]` metadata (name "myapp", version "0.1.0") and `[plugins.client]` with `enabled = true`.
In the excerpt, what do the entries under `[plugins.client.paths]` such as `"@components/*" = "./components/*"` define?

Import path aliases — the section maps alias patterns to real directories, so `@components/*` resolves to `./components/*` and `@utils/*` to `./utils/*`. (The excerpt then opens a `[plugins.client.configs.tailwind]` section.)
Per the excerpt, how do you route the `@mycompany` npm scope to GitHub's package registry and authenticate against it?

Map the scope under `[plugins.client.npm.scoped_registries]` with `"@mycompany" = "https://npm.pkg.github.com"`, and supply the token under `[plugins.client.npm.auth."//npm.pkg.github.com/"]` with `_authToken = "${NODE_AUTH_TOKEN}"`.
You need every npm registry request in the project to send authentication. Based on the excerpt, where does that global setting go?
Under `[plugins.client.npm.settings]` in jac.toml, set `always-auth = true` — the settings section holds global npm settings like this one.
Both `[plugins.client.npm]` and `[plugins.client.paths]` generate tooling config automatically — what does each generate, and what different problem does each solve?

`[plugins.client.npm]` solves where packages come from: its `settings` (global `.npmrc` key-values like registry, always-auth, strict-ssl, proxy), `scoped_registries` (mapping `@scope` prefixes to registry URLs), and `auth` (registry tokens, with `${NODE_AUTH_TOKEN}`-style env interpolation) are written into an auto-generated `.npmrc` in `.jac/client/configs/`, applied whenever Jac installs dependencies (`jac add --npm`, `jac start`, `jac build`) — no manual `.npmrc` management. `[plugins.client.paths]` solves how import specifiers resolve: aliases like `"@components/*" = "./components/*"` are applied to Vite's `resolve.alias`, TypeScript's `compilerOptions.paths` (with `baseUrl: "."` for IDE autocompletion), and the Jac module resolver, so `import from "@components/Button"` finds the right file. Wildcard patterns (`@alias/*`) match sub-paths; exact patterns (`@alias`) match only the alias itself.
In the Import Path Aliases example, how does the wildcard alias `"@components/*"` behave differently from the exact alias `"@shared"`?

The wildcard pattern `"@components/*" = "./components/*"` matches any sub-path under the prefix — so `import from "@components/Button"` resolves to `./components/Button`. The exact pattern `"@shared" = "./shared/index"` matches only the alias itself — `import from "@shared"` resolves to `./shared/index` and nothing else. Both are applied to Vite's `resolve.alias`, TypeScript's `compilerOptions.paths`, and the Jac module resolver, so bundling, IDE autocompletion, and compilation all agree.
In which jac.toml section do you override Vite build options, and which three options does the example set?
`[plugins.client.vite.build]` — the example sets `sourcemap = true`, `minify = "esbuild"`, and `outDir = "dist"`.
You want the dev server on port 3000, opening the browser automatically, and reachable from other machines on the network with CORS allowed. Based on the excerpt, what do you write?

Configure the Vite dev server under `[plugins.client.vite.server]` in jac.toml: `port = 3000`, `open = true`, `host = "0.0.0.0"` (so it binds beyond localhost), and `cors = true` — exactly the four options the example shows.
When do you reach for `[plugins.client.configs]` versus the `[jac-shadcn]` section?

`[plugins.client.configs]` is for tools that expect a `*.config.js` file — PostCSS, Tailwind v3, ESLint, Prettier — generating `<name>.config.js` files in `.jac/client/configs/` from TOML (e.g. `[plugins.client.configs.postcss]` with `plugins = ["tailwindcss", "autoprefixer"]` and `[plugins.client.configs.tailwind]` with content globs and theme extensions), with no standalone config files in the project root; its companion table routes Vite plugins (Tailwind v4) to `[plugins.client.vite]` instead. `[jac-shadcn]` configures the shadcn/ui component system provided by the `jac-super` plugin: visual `style`, `baseColor`, `theme`, `font`, `radius`, and menu options, all resolved offline from data bundled with jac-super — `jac create --use jac-shadcn` writes the fields, `jac retheme` regenerates `global.css` from them, and `jac add --shadcn` reads `style` to choose which Tailwind classes to emit. One generates generic tool configs; the other drives shadcn theming commands.
When overriding the generated tsconfig via `[plugins.client.ts]`, how do `compilerOptions` values behave differently from `include`/`exclude`?

`compilerOptions` values override defaults individually (the example sets `strict = false`, `target = "ES2022"`, `noUnusedLocals = false`, `noUnusedParameters = false` under `[plugins.client.ts.compilerOptions]`), whereas `include` and `exclude` replace the defaults entirely when provided — e.g. `include = ["components/**/*", "lib/**/*", "types/**/*"]` becomes the whole include list.
What does the `[plugins.client.app_meta_data]` section control, and what kinds of keys does the example include?

It sets the HTML `<head>` tags for the client app. The example includes `title`, `description`, `keywords`, `author`, `theme_color`, `robots` ("index, follow"), and Open Graph keys `og_title`, `og_description`, and `og_image` ("/assets/og-image.png").
In production, your frontend is served from one domain but the backend API lives on another. What does the excerpt say to configure?

Set the backend API base URL used by client-side requests via `[plugins.client.api]` with `base_url = "https://api.example.com"` — the excerpt notes this is useful exactly for production deployments where the API lives on a different domain than the frontend.
How do the defaults for `minify` and `base_path` differ, and what does each setting control?

`minify` (under `[plugins.client]`) controls minification in production builds and its default depends on the command: `true` for `jac build` but `false` for `jac start --dev`. `base_path` (also under `[plugins.client]`) controls the base path for asset resolution (JS/CSS) in the generated `index.html`; it defaults to `"/"` regardless of command, and is changed only deliberately — e.g. `"/myapp/"` to deploy on a subpath like `https://example.com/myapp/`, or `"./"` for relative path resolution.
When would you set `base_path = "/myapp/"` as shown in the example, and what are the other possible values mentioned?

When deploying the app on a subpath such as `https://example.com/myapp/` — `base_path` controls how the generated `index.html` resolves JS/CSS assets. It defaults to `"/"`, and can also be set to `"./"` for relative path resolution if needed.
According to the Quick Reference, which two npm packages are required for all jac-client projects, and what happens if they are missing from jac.toml?

`jac-client-node` and `@jac-client/dev-deps` are the core dependencies required for all jac-client projects. If they are missing or outdated in jac.toml, they are automatically added or updated when the config is loaded — for example during `jac start`. (npm dependencies can also be declared under `[dependencies.npm]`, e.g. lodash and axios.)
On macOS, you want to prepare your project once for building on both Android and iOS. Based on the jac setup excerpt, what command applies?

`jac setup mobile -p all` — `jac setup` is the one-time initialization for a build target, `mobile` is the target (alongside `desktop` and `pwa`), and `-p/--platform` accepts `android`, `ios`, or `all` for mobile setup.
Combining the two excerpts: which of the four build targets need a setup step, and which extended `jac start` option selects a target during development?

From the Multi-Target Architecture table, Desktop (PyTauri, requires `jac-desktop`) and Mobile (Capacitor) require setup, while Web (the default, output in `.jac/client/dist/`) and PWA do not. From the Extended Core Commands table, `jac start --client <target>` selects the client build target for the dev server; other extensions include `jac create --use client` (full-stack template), `--skip` (skip npm install), `jac add --npm` / `--npm --dev`, and `jac remove --npm`.
Per the Multi-Target Architecture table, where does each target's build output land?

Web (default, `jac build`): `.jac/client/dist/`. Desktop (PyTauri, `jac build --client desktop`): staged app under `src-pytauri/dist/`. Mobile (Capacitor, `jac build --client mobile --platform android`): Android APK / iOS build products. PWA (`jac build --client pwa`): an installable web app. Desktop and Mobile require setup (desktop needs `jac-desktop`); Web and PWA do not — all from a single codebase.
For the default web target, what does the build output directory contain and which two commands does the excerpt show?

Output goes to `.jac/client/dist/` containing `index.html`, bundled JS, and CSS. The commands are `jac build` (build for web) and `jac start --dev` (dev server with HMR); the target is standard browser deployment using Vite.
Does the desktop target require a Rust toolchain, and what does its architecture consist of?

No — the excerpt explicitly says no Rust toolchain is required. The desktop target comes from the optional jac-desktop plugin, reuses jac-client's Vite frontend pipeline, and adds a PyTauri native shell plus a PyInstaller-frozen Jac backend sidecar. The workflow is `pip install jac-client jac-desktop`, `jac setup desktop`, `jac start --client desktop --dev`, and `jac build --client desktop`; details like `[plugins.desktop]` config and sidecar bundling live in the jac-desktop Reference.
Your team wants to ship the app as a native Android APK. According to the mobile target excerpt, what approach is used and what prerequisites must be installed?

The mobile target wraps the same web bundle the web target produces in a native shell using Capacitor, producing an Android APK (or an iOS app). Prerequisites for Android: Node.js (or Bun), Java/JDK 21+, and the Android SDK (via Android Studio). iOS builds additionally require macOS with Xcode, the Xcode Command Line Tools, and CocoaPods.
What is the difference between the `jac setup mobile --platform ...` commands and the `jac start main.jac --client mobile` commands in these excerpts?

`jac setup mobile --platform android|ios|all` is the optional explicit one-time setup step, with `ios` and `all` (both platforms) available only on macOS. `jac start main.jac --client mobile` is the development command that builds and launches the app on a device/simulator — it targets Android by default, and you append `--platform ios` to launch on iOS instead. Setup prepares the platform; start runs the dev cycle.
When you run `jac start main.jac --client mobile` with no platform flag, which platform is targeted, and how do you target the other?
Android is the default; to build and launch on iOS instead, add the flag: `jac start main.jac --client mobile --platform ios`. Both commands build and launch on a device/simulator.
Where do mobile build outputs land for each platform, and which `[plugins.client.mobile]` key switches Android output from APK to AAB?

Android builds produce an APK in `android/app/build/outputs/apk/`, and iOS builds (via `jac build --client mobile --platform ios`) put Xcode build products in `ios/App/build/`. Setting `bundle = true` in `[plugins.client.mobile]` produces an AAB instead of an APK on Android (with `release = true` for release builds). The section also configures `app_name`, `app_id`, `default_platform`, `ios_sdk` (`iphonesimulator` or `iphoneos`), and `ios_destination`; notes cover `adb reverse` auto-attempts, Xcode provisioning via `npx cap open ios`, keystore config in `android/app/build.gradle`, and adding Capacitor plugins with `jac add --npm @capacitor/<plugin>` plus `npx cap sync`.
What four features does the PWA target provide according to the excerpt?

Offline support via Service Worker, installability on devices, an auto-generated `manifest.json`, and automatic icon generation (with Pillow). The PWA target delivers a Progressive Web App with a native-like experience.
You want to serve your PWA in production with custom theme colors, a named cache, custom manifest text, and your own icons. Per the excerpt, what do you run and configure?

Run `jac start --client pwa`, which builds the PWA then serves it, outputting the web bundle plus `manifest.json` and `sw.js` (the service worker). In jac.toml, set `[plugins.client.pwa]` keys `theme_color`, `background_color`, and `cache_name` (e.g. "my-app-cache-v1"), and `[plugins.client.pwa.manifest]` keys `name`, `short_name`, and `description`. For custom icons, add `pwa-192x192.png` and `pwa-512x512.png` to the `pwa_icons/` directory.
How does the automatic PWA install banner differ from the programmatic install control, and when would you use each?

The automatic banner needs no code: after `jac setup pwa`, a glassmorphic dark banner with a slide-up animation appears after a configurable delay, uses `beforeinstallprompt` for the native Chrome/Edge install flow, detects iOS Safari and shows step-by-step "Add to Home Screen" instructions, and re-prompts with exponential backoff after dismissal (7 → 14 → 28 days, max 3 prompts); it's tuned via `[plugins.client.pwa]` keys like `theme_color`/`background_color` and the banner settings. Programmatic control is for advanced use cases: import from `@jac/pwa` — the `usePwaInstall()` hook returns `(canInstall, triggerInstall)` so you can render your own button (e.g. shown only when `canInstall`, calling `triggerInstall()` on click), or use the pre-styled `PwaInstallButton` component.
In the `CustomInstallUI` example, what does `usePwaInstall()` return, and how does the component use both values?

It returns a tuple `(canInstall: bool, triggerInstall: () -> void)`, destructured as `(canInstall, triggerInstall) = usePwaInstall();` after importing from `@jac/pwa`. The component renders the "Get the App" button only when `canInstall` is truthy (`{canInstall and (...)}`), and the button's onClick lambda calls `triggerInstall()` to start the install flow. The default banner settings above it include `install_banner = true`, `install_banner_delay = 3000` ms, and `install_banner_position = "bottom"`, with customizable `install_button_text` and `install_dismiss_text`.
How does jac-client's automatic endpoint caching decide what to cache and when to invalidate, and what are the cache's size and TTL?

The compiler classifies each walker/function endpoint as a reader (no side effects) or writer (modifies state) using compiler-provided `endpoint_effects` metadata — no manual cache annotations or `jacInvalidate()` calls are needed. Reader responses go into an LRU cache of 500 entries with a 60-second TTL; concurrent identical requests are deduplicated into one network call; calling any writer endpoint automatically invalidates all cached reader responses; and auth state changes (login/logout) clear the entire cache. So spawning the same walker twice in quick succession makes only one API call, and creating/updating data automatically refreshes cached reads.
For BrowserRouter's clean URLs to work in production, what must the server do, and how does `jac start` handle it?

The server must return the SPA HTML for all non-API routes, since jac-client uses `BrowserRouter` to produce clean URLs like `/about` and `/users/123` instead of hash-based `#/about`. With `jac start` this is automatic: the server's catch-all route serves the SPA HTML for extensionless paths, excluding the API prefixes `cl/`, `walker/`, `function/`, `user/`, and `static/`. During development, the Vite dev server is configured with `appType: 'spa'` for history API fallback.
A client build fails and you see a formatted diagnostic, but you also want the raw Vite/Rollup output to dig deeper. What does the excerpt say to do?

Set `debug = true` under `[plugins.client]` in jac.toml or set the `JAC_DEBUG=1` environment variable — that shows raw error output alongside the formatted diagnostics. Note debug mode is enabled by default for a better development experience, and should be set to `debug = false` for production. The structured diagnostics themselves include error codes (`JAC_CLIENT_001` missing npm dependency → fix with `jac add --npm <package>`, `JAC_CLIENT_003` syntax error → check the source snippet, `JAC_CLIENT_004` unresolved import → verify the import path), source snippets pointing at the original `.jac` location, and actionable hints.
Comparing the two excerpts, which tool inlines build-time constants and which tool handles package management, and what format rule applies to the constants?

Build-time constants declared under `[plugins.client.vite.define]` (e.g. `"globalThis.API_URL"`, `"globalThis.FEATURE_ENABLED"`, `"globalThis.BUILD_VERSION"`) are inlined by Vite during bundling — string values must be double-quoted (JSON-encoded), like `"\"https://api.example.com\""` — and accessed in client code as `{globalThis.BUILD_VERSION}`. Package management and JavaScript bundling, per the Prerequisites excerpt, use Bun; if Bun is not installed, the CLI prompts you to install it automatically. So Vite performs compile-time value substitution, while Bun is the environment prerequisite driving installs and bundling.
Which tool does jac-client use for package management and JavaScript bundling, and what happens if it is missing?
Bun. If Bun is not installed, the CLI prompts you to install it automatically.
Which API routes are automatically proxied to the backend in dev mode?
Three route patterns: `/walker/*`, `/function/*`, and `/user/*` — all proxied to the backend automatically.
In the event handlers example, do types like `ChangeEvent` and `KeyboardEvent` need to be imported, and how are they used?

No — Jac provides ambient DOM types (`ChangeEvent`, `KeyboardEvent`, `MouseEvent`, `FormEvent`, etc.) that are available without import. In the example, the input's onChange handler is `lambda e: ChangeEvent { value = e.target.value; }` and its onKeyPress handler is `lambda e: KeyboardEvent { if e.key == "Enter" { submit(); } }`, giving type-safe event handling; the button uses a plain `lambda -> None` for onClick.
You are writing a form whose submit handler must stop the browser's default page reload, with proper typing. Which ambient type applies and how is it used?

`FormEvent` — per the event types table it fires on `onSubmit` and `onReset`, its `target` is an `HTMLFormElement`, and like all ambient DOM types it needs no import. The usage example shows exactly this: `<form onSubmit={lambda e: FormEvent { e.preventDefault(); handleSubmit(); }}>` with a `<button type="submit">` inside — `e.preventDefault()` stops the default submission before the custom handler runs. (Similarly, `ChangeEvent` handlers read `e.target.value`/`e.target.checked`, and `KeyboardEvent` handlers check keys like `e.key == "Enter" and not e.shiftKey`.)
What three conditional/list rendering techniques does the `ConditionalComponent` example demonstrate?

(1) An if/else before the return that assigns JSX to a variable — `content =

Visible

;` or `

Hidden

;` depending on `show` — then renders `{content}`. (2) Inline boolean short-circuit rendering: `{show and

Only when true

}`. (3) List rendering via a comprehension: `{[
  • {item["name"]}
    • for item in items]}`.
What does the `JacClientErrorBoundary` component do?

It is a specialized error boundary component that catches rendering errors in your component tree, logs them, and displays a fallback UI — preventing the entire app from crashing when a descendant component fails.
If jac-client already wraps the whole app in `JacClientErrorBoundary` by default, why would you still use the component manually with its props?

The built-in wrapping means you don't need to wrap your root component — errors anywhere are caught gracefully and the app displays a fallback UI instead of crashing. Manual use is for customization and granularity: the Props table shows `fallback` (a JsxElement for custom fallback UI on error), `FallbackComponent` (a Component that shows the default fallback UI with the error), and `children` (the components to protect) — so you wrap specific subtrees yourself when you want your own fallback content for just those components rather than the app-wide default.
Per the Props table, how does the `fallback` prop differ from `FallbackComponent`?

`fallback` is a JsxElement — custom fallback UI to show on error — while `FallbackComponent` is a Component that shows the default fallback UI with the error. `children` (JsxElement) are the components the boundary protects.
In the nested boundaries example, what happens to `Header` and `Footer` when `MainContent` throws an error?

They continue rendering normally. Only the inner boundary's fallback — `
Content error
` — is shown in place of `MainContent`; the outer boundary's `
App error
` fallback is not triggered. Nesting multiple error boundaries gives this fine-grained error isolation.
You are embedding a third-party micro-frontend widget in your app and don't trust its stability. Which use case from the excerpt applies?

Micro-frontend boundaries — nest error boundaries around embeddables for fault isolation. This overlaps with the first use case, isolating failure-prone widgets: protect sections that fetch data, embed third-party code, or are unstable. (The third listed use case is per-page protection: wrapping top-level pages/routes so one error can't fail the whole app.)
What are the three tiers in the memory hierarchy, and what capability does `TieredMemory` layer on top of them?

L1 is Volatile — `VolatileMemory`, in-process; L2 is Cache — `LocalCacheMemory`, TTL-based; and L3 is Persistent — `SqliteMemory`, the default. `TieredMemory` adds automatic read-through caching and write-through persistence across these tiers.
What two behaviors does `TieredMemory` provide automatically according to the excerpt?
Read-through caching and write-through persistence — both automatic, so reads populate the cache and writes propagate to persistent storage without manual handling.
What does the excerpt's example demonstrate about a `User` node created in a `with entry` block?

That objects are automatically persisted: a node type is declared as `node User { has name: str; }`, and simply constructing it — `user_node = User(name="Alice");` inside `with entry` — is enough; no explicit save step appears in the excerpt.
What four things does `ExecutionContext` manage according to the excerpt?

`system_root` (the system-level root node), `user_root` (the user-specific root node), `entry_node` (the current entry point), and `Memory` (the storage backend). Together these constitute the runtime context it manages.
You need to retrieve a specific node again after a server restart. Which mechanism from the excerpt applies?
Anchors — anchor management provides persistent object references across sessions, allowing nodes and edges to be retrieved by stable identifiers after server restarts or session changes.
Why does Jac need the `new(...)` builtin for browser objects like `Promise`, and how does the Promise example use it?

Jac has no JavaScript-style `new` keyword, so browser built-in constructors are instantiated with the ambient `new(...)` builtin, which the compiler lowers to `Reflect.construct(Cls, [args])` in the emitted JavaScript. The Promise excerpt applies this: `p = new(Promise, lambda(resolve: any, reject: any) { resolve.call(None, "done"); });` — the constructor class is the first argument, the executor lambda is passed as the constructor argument, and inside it the resolve callback is invoked via `resolve.call(None, "done")`.
In the Promise example, how is the `resolve` callback invoked inside the executor lambda?
Via `.call` with None as the receiver: `resolve.call(None, "done");`. The Promise itself is constructed with `p = new(Promise, lambda(resolve: any, reject: any) { ... });`.
How does `new(Cls, ...args)` behave differently on the server versus in `cl` blocks?

It is portable and works in any codespace: on the server it is a thin wrapper for `Cls(*args)`, while in `cl` blocks the compiler rewrites the call into `Reflect.construct(Cls, [args])` so it can drive JS class constructors that require `new` — as in the example `evt = new(CustomEvent, "my-event", {"detail": data});`.
When passing a callback that will be invoked later, what invocation form does the excerpt prescribe, and how does the WebSocket example apply it?

Use `.call(None, ...)`. In the example, the callback is stored as `handler = myCallback;`, and inside the `ws.onmessage` lambda it is invoked as `handler.call(None, JSON.parse(e.data));` — parsing the message data and passing it through the `.call(None, ...)` form.
You need a flag and a cache object shared across an entire client module, not tied to any one component. Which construct applies?

Module-level `glob` declarations inside the `cl` block: `glob initialized: bool = False;` and `glob cache: any = None;` — `glob` is used for state shared across a module (the excerpt points to the Advanced Patterns & JS Interop tutorial for more patterns).
How does what `jac start --dev` gives you differ from what `jac debug main.jac` gives you?

`jac start --dev` enables live reloading during development — changes to `.jac` files automatically reload without restart. `jac debug main.jac` is an interactive debugging mode providing step-through execution, variable inspection, breakpoints, and graph visualization. One speeds the edit-run loop; the other lets you inspect a running program's behavior.
What four capabilities does running `jac debug main.jac` provide?
Step-through execution, variable inspection, breakpoints, and graph visualization.
According to the Related Resources list, which two resources cover building desktop apps?

The "Building a Desktop App" tutorial (tutorials/fullstack/desktop.md) and the "jac-desktop Reference" (jac-desktop.md). The list also includes fullstack tutorials for setup, components, state management, npm packages & UI libraries, advanced patterns & JS interop, backend integration, authentication, and routing.
What does running `jac start` do when the jac-scale plugin is present, and what does the `--scale` flag add for production?

`jac start` turns every `:pub` or `:priv` walker into an API endpoint backed by FastAPI, with automatic Swagger docs, SQLite persistence, and built-in authentication — jac-scale generates REST endpoints from your Jac walkers and functions. For production, `--scale` automates Docker image builds and Kubernetes deployment, generating Dockerfiles, manifests, and service configurations from your code.
You are installing jac-scale for a project that only needs part of its functionality. What installation approach does the excerpt describe?
jac-scale is lightweight by default — the approach is to install only the extras you need, rather than everything, using the pip extras mechanism the excerpt introduces.
What install command does excerpt 1 recommend for production, and what does excerpt 2 say about the server's default entry point?

Excerpt 1 recommends `pip install jac-scale[all]` for production or if unsure — `[all]` includes every group (core FastAPI/uvicorn/JWT/CLI, `[data]` pymongo/redis, `[aws]` boto3, `[monitoring]` prometheus-client, `[scheduler]` apscheduler, `[deploy]` kubernetes/docker); groups are combinable like `pip install jac-scale[data,monitoring]`, you then run `jac plugins enable scale`, and using a feature without its dependency yields a clear ImportError with the exact install command. Excerpt 2 says the basic server is started with `jac start`, where `main.jac` is the default entry point — if your entry point is named differently (e.g. `app.jac`), pass it explicitly: `jac start app.jac`.
If your project's entry point is `app.jac` rather than `main.jac`, how must you start the server?
Pass the filename explicitly: `jac start app.jac`. Plain `jac start` assumes the default entry point `main.jac`.
Per the Server Options table, what is the default port and what happens if it is already in use? Also, what does `--faux` do?

The default port is 8000, with auto-fallback if it's in use (settable via `--port`/`-p`). `--faux`/`-f` prints the generated API docs only, without running a server. Other options include `--dev` for HMR mode, `--api_port` for a separate API port in HMR mode, `--no_client` to skip client bundling (API only), `--profile` for config profiles, `--scale`/`--build` for deployment, `--target` (default kubernetes), `--registry` (default dockerhub), and `--enable-tls` for HTTPS via Let's Encrypt.
What persistence backend does Jac use when running locally without `--scale`, and what flips it to MongoDB?

SQLite by default — you'll see "Using SQLite for persistence" in the server output, and no external database setup is needed for development. Persistence flips to `MongoBackend` when `MONGODB_URI` is set or when `--scale` provisions Mongo on Kubernetes. The Mongo backend has full Layer 1+2+3 schema-migration support: every persisted document is stamped with `arch_module`, `arch_type`, `fingerprint`, and `format_version`; undeserializable documents are moved to a `<collection>_quarantine` companion collection rather than silently dropped; and class-rename aliases live in `<collection>_aliases`, merged into the in-process Serializer registry on every connect. The same `jac db inspect / quarantine / alias / recover` commands work against Mongo unchanged.
In production, you renamed a persisted class and old documents can no longer resolve. Without redeploying, what does the excerpt say to run?

Register a class-rename alias and recover: `jac db alias add "old.module.LegacyName" "new.module.NewName" --app app.jac` followed by `jac db recover-all --app app.jac` — the operator-rescue path for registering a class-rename alias in production without redeploying.
In microservice mode, how do you disable CORS entirely, and what are the defaults?

Set `allow_origins = []` under `[plugins.scale.microservices.cors]` — the defaults are open (`allow_origins = ["*"]`). The section also takes `allow_methods` and `allow_headers`, and additional keys `allow_credentials`, `expose_headers`, and `max_age` are recognised. This only applies to the gateway in microservice mode; single-process `jac start` installs a permissive CORS middleware with no config knob.
How do a walker's `has` fields map onto an HTTP request, per the `search` walker example?

Walker parameters become the request body: `walker search` declares `has query: str;` and `has limit: int = 10;`, and the curl example POSTs JSON to `http://localhost:8000/walker/search` with `-d '{"query": "hello", "limit": 20}'` and a `Content-Type: application/json` header — each JSON key fills the matching `has` field (here overriding limit's default of 10 with 20).
How do the `_before_request` and `_authenticate` middleware walkers differ in the data they receive and what they do with it?

`_before_request` receives `has request: dict` and passively logs: its `can log with Root entry` prints `self.request['method']` and `self.request['path']`. `_authenticate` receives `has headers: dict` and actively gates the request: its `can check with Root entry` reads `token = self.headers.get("Authorization", "")`, and if the token doesn't start with "Bearer " it reports `{"error": "Unauthorized", "status": 401}` and returns, blocking further processing. One observes request metadata; the other inspects auth headers and can short-circuit with an error response.
In the `_authenticate` middleware example, what happens when the Authorization header is missing or lacks the Bearer prefix?

The check `if not token.startswith("Bearer ")` triggers (the header defaults to `""` via `self.headers.get("Authorization", "")`), so the walker reports `{"error": "Unauthorized", "status": 401}` and immediately `return`s — halting further processing of the request.
According to the tip in the excerpt, when should you use the `_authenticate` middleware pattern versus jac-scale's built-in auth?

Use the `_authenticate` middleware pattern when you need custom authentication logic (the example's success path reports `{"authenticated": True}`). For standard JWT authentication, use jac-scale's built-in auth endpoints — `/user/register` and `/user/login` — instead.
You want an endpoint that speaks WebSocket and pushes every response to all connected clients. Which `@restspec` options apply, and which names need imports?

Set `protocol = APIProtocol.WEBSOCKET` and `broadcast = True` — the options table notes `broadcast` (default False) broadcasts responses to all connected WebSocket clients and is only valid with the `WEBSOCKET` protocol. `APIProtocol` and `restspec` are builtins requiring no import; only `HTTPMethod` must be imported, with `import from http { HTTPMethod }`. (Other options: `method` defaults to POST, and `path` defaults to "" meaning auto-generated.)
When customizing an endpoint with `@restspec`, what does changing `method` alone do versus also supplying `path`?

Changing only the method swaps the HTTP verb while keeping the auto-generated path: `@restspec(method=HTTPMethod.GET)` on `walker :pub get_users` makes it accessible at `GET /walker/get_users` instead of the default POST (walkers are POST endpoints by default; `HTTPMethod` is imported from `http`). Supplying `path` overrides the auto-generated URL entirely: `@restspec(method=HTTPMethod.GET, path="/custom/users")` on `walker :pub list_users` makes it accessible at `GET /custom/users` — no `/walker/...` prefix at all.
At what URL and with which HTTP method is the `list_users` walker in the example accessible, and why?

`GET /custom/users`. The decorator `@restspec(method=HTTPMethod.GET, path="/custom/users")` sets the method to GET and overrides the auto-generated path with the custom `/custom/users`; the walker's `can fetch with Root entry` reports an empty list.
In what order are `@restspec` walker parameters classified, and in the `get_user_orders` example which parameter is which?

Parameters are classified as: path (matches `{name}` in the path) → file (`UploadFile` type) → query (GET) → body (other methods). In `@restspec(method=HTTPMethod.GET, path="/users/{user_id}/orders")` on `get_user_orders`, `has user_id: str` is a path parameter (it matches `{user_id}` in the path) and `has status: str = "all"` is a query parameter (a GET request field not in the path). Path parameters use the `{param_name}` syntax, as in the simpler `/items/{item_id}` example.
Does `@restspec` work on standalone functions, and what do the two examples show?

Yes — `@restspec` also works on standalone functions. The examples show `@restspec(method=HTTPMethod.GET)` on `def :pub health_check() -> dict` returning `{"status": "healthy"}`, and `@restspec(method=HTTPMethod.GET, path="/custom/status")` on `def :pub app_status() -> dict` returning status and version — the second also overriding the path to `/custom/status`.
Your users want to sign in sometimes with a username and sometimes with an email, landing in the same account either way. Which jac-scale design supports this?
The identity-based authentication system: each user can sign in through multiple identities — username, email, or an SSO provider like Google or GitHub — and all of them resolve to the same account.
What single configuration value determines whether jac-scale stores user data in SQLite or MongoDB, and where does the data live in each case?

The `mongodb_uri` setting. When it is not configured, SQLite is used: user data goes to `.jac/data/users.db` relative to the project root, via SQLAlchemy — good for development and single-instance deployments. When `mongodb_uri` is set (via jac.toml or the `MONGODB_URI` environment variable), MongoDB is used: user data goes to the `users` collection of the `jac_db` database — required for multi-instance production. Both implement the same `IdentityStorage` interface, so endpoints, walkers, and middleware are unaware of the backend.
In jac.toml, which section and key switch persistence to MongoDB?
The `[plugins.scale.database]` section with `mongodb_uri = "mongodb://localhost:27017"`.
Besides jac.toml, how else can MongoDB be enabled, and what happens when no URI is configured?
Via the environment variable: `export MONGODB_URI="mongodb://localhost:27017"`. When no MongoDB URI is configured, SQLite is used automatically with no additional setup.
You want to register a user with both a username and an email, a password, and some profile fields, then have them authenticated. Per the excerpt, what is the flow and what validation applies?

POST to `/user/register` with an `identities` array (e.g. `{"type": "username", "value": "myuser"}` and `{"type": "email", "value": "user@example.com"}`), a `credential` of `{"type": "password", "password": "secret"}`, and an optional `profile` (e.g. firstname/lastname). Success returns HTTP 201 with the `user_id` — but no token, so you must call `/user/login` afterward to authenticate. Validation: at least one identity; only `username` and `email` types; no duplicate identity types; identity values unique across all users after normalization; credential type must be `password` with a non-empty password. Profile is bounded (max 20 keys, key length 64, value length 1024 chars, 8192 bytes total JSON; values str/int/float/bool; key pattern `^[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9_]{0,63}$`) — the pattern blocks MongoDB operator injection (`$where`), dot-path traversal, and `__proto__` prototype pollution, and profile is stored under the `profile` sub-document so keys can't collide with `role`/`user_id`.
What does a successful `/user/login` return, and how is that used in the authenticated request example?

Login accepts any identity — the same user can log in with `{"type": "username", "value": "myuser"}` or `{"type": "email", "value": "user@example.com"}` plus a password credential — and returns HTTP 200 with `user_id`, `token` (a JWT like "eyJ..."), `root_id`, and `role`. The authenticated request example then presents that token on a walker call: `curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/walker/my_walker` with the header `-H "Authorization: Bearer <token>"` and a JSON body. So login mints the token; authenticated requests attach it as a Bearer header.
How does the token refresh endpoint work, and what happens with an invalid token?

POST to `/user/refresh-token` with a JSON body `{"token": "eyJ..."}` — refreshing before expiry yields a new token with a fresh expiration window; the `token` value can optionally include the `Bearer` prefix, which is stripped automatically. Success returns `{"ok": true, "data": {"token": "...(new token)...", "message": "Token refreshed successfully"}}`; an invalid or expired token returns HTTP 401.
What does the password update endpoint require, and when does it return HTTP 400?

`PUT /user/password` with an `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header and a JSON body containing both `current_password` and `new_password` — the current password is required for verification. It returns HTTP 400 if the current password is incorrect or the new password is empty; success returns ok with the user_id and "Password updated successfully".
You are deploying a jac-scale app to production. What must you change about JWT configuration and why, and why don't username changes break existing tokens?

Change the JWT secret — the default `supersecretkey_for_testing_only!` is for development only, and anyone who knows the secret can forge valid tokens for any user; set a long random secret via the `JWT_SECRET` environment variable or `[plugins.scale.jwt] secret` in jac.toml (alongside `algorithm`, default HS256, and `exp_delta_days`, default 7). Username changes don't invalidate tokens because JWTs use `user_id` (UUID) as the primary claim, not the username — claims are `user_id`, `role`, `exp`, and `iat`. Known limitations: no token blacklist or revocation (tokens stay valid until expiry) and no refresh token rotation (refresh issues a new token without invalidating the old one).
What does the curl command in the excerpt do, and what authorization does it require?

It sets a user's role via the admin API: `PUT http://localhost:8000/admin/users/{username}` with JSON body `{"role": "admin"}`, promoting the named user to admin. It requires an admin's token in the Authorization header — `-H "Authorization: Bearer <admin_token>"` — plus `Content-Type: application/json`.
Per the excerpt, what request starts a GitHub SSO login?
A GET to `/sso/github/login` — the example is `curl -L http://localhost:8000/sso/github/login`, with `-L` following the redirect to GitHub's login page.
You are upgrading an old jac-scale deployment whose MongoDB users are flat username/password documents with SHA-256 hashes. What does the excerpt say happens, and what must users do?

The MongoDB backend automatically migrates legacy users on server startup: it converts flat `username`/`email`/`password_hash` fields into the identity + credential array format, progressively rehashes old SHA-256 passwords to bcrypt on each user's next successful login (no user action required), marks a duplicate as `disabled` if normalization causes two legacy usernames to collide, and preserves existing `root_id`, `role`, and other fields. The migration runs once during `UserManager` initialization and is idempotent. SQLite deployments need no migration since they use the new format from the start. The SHA-256 migration code is marked removable once all users have logged in at least once (triggering the bcrypt rehash).
In the `[plugins.scale.auth]` configuration example, what does the `{token}` placeholder in `verify_url_template` and `reset_url_template` do, and what happens if a template is left empty?

The `{token}` placeholder is replaced with the raw token before the email is sent — e.g. `"https://app.example.com/verify?token={token}"` and `"https://app.example.com/reset?token={token}"`. Leaving a template empty makes the email contain the bare token in its body, which is useful in tests/dev. The example also sets the TTLs: `verify_token_ttl_seconds = 86400` (24h) and `reset_token_ttl_seconds = 1800` (30min). Note the endpoints share the `Emailer` plug-in; without an emailer configured, identity additions still work for non-email types but password reset is disabled.
When you add an email identity via the /user/add-identity endpoint, does the endpoint send a verification email, and what verified state is the identity stored with?

No -- the /user/add-identity endpoint never sends mail. It just adds the identity, and email identities are stored as verified=false. To dispatch a verification email afterwards you must call /user/send-verification.
What happens when you call /user/send-verification a second time on an email identity that is still unverified?

Calling it again on an unverified identity revokes the user's prior outstanding verification tokens and issues a fresh one, giving a clean retry/resend. The endpoint returns HTTP 202 with status "pending_verification" and email_sent: true. (Only if the identity is already verified does it instead return HTTP 200 with status "already_verified".)

A frontend engineer is building the page that opens when a user clicks the verification link from their email. The user may not be logged in on that device. Can the page still complete verification by calling /user/verify-identity, and what must the request contain?

Yes. /user/verify-identity requires no Bearer token -- the verification token itself is the credential. The page just POSTs a JSON body containing the token from the email ({"token": "<verification-token-from-email>"}). On success it returns HTTP 200 with status "verified" and the verified identity; if the token is expired, already-consumed, or unknown, it returns 400 INVALID_TOKEN.

In the /user/reset-password curl example, the JSON body carries "token" and "new_password" but no Authorization header. If a user submitted this request twice with the same token, what would the second call return, and what happens to the user's other reset tokens after the first success?

The second call would fail with 400 INVALID_TOKEN, because the endpoint consumes the reset token and, on success, all other outstanding reset tokens for that user are revoked. The first call succeeds with HTTP 200 and {"status": "password_reset"}; no Authorization header is needed because the token delivered to the recovery email is the credential.
What is jac-scale's Emailer abstraction used for, and how can you supply your own implementation?

The Emailer (jac_scale.abstractions.emailer.Emailer) is a thin abstraction the framework uses to send verification and password-reset emails. It ships with a built-in SMTP implementation, and you can supply any user-defined subclass via jac.toml -- no jac-scale code changes are required.
A deployment sets base_path = "/srv/files" in jac.toml's [storage] section, but the ops team also exports JAC_STORAGE_PATH=/mnt/data. Which base directory wins, and why?

/mnt/data wins. The documented configuration priority is: environment variables > jac.toml > defaults, and JAC_STORAGE_PATH is the env var that overrides the jac.toml base directory. The same override pattern applies to JAC_STORAGE_TYPE (storage type) and JAC_STORAGE_CREATE_DIRS ("true"/"false" for auto-creating directories); the TOML defaults are type = "local", base_path = "./storage", create_dirs = true.
In the emailer factory's resolution order, how is provider = "smtp" handled differently from a provider string like "pkg.module:ClassName"?

"smtp" is resolved first and maps directly to the built-in SMTPEmailer, which reads its settings (host, port, username, etc.) from the [plugins.scale.emailer.smtp] table -- as shown in the Built-in SMTP example. A "pkg.module:ClassName" string is the third resolution step: it is imported via importlib (with "pkg.module.ClassName" as a fallback form), validated as a subclass of Emailer, and instantiated with the resolved config dict. If the provider is empty or the import/validation fails, the factory returns None and email features are logged as disabled.
In the Built-in SMTP TOML example, what would break if the [plugins.scale.emailer.smtp] table were removed but provider = "smtp" were kept?

The provider = "smtp" line is what selects the built-in SMTP emailer, and the [plugins.scale.emailer.smtp] table is where its connection settings live -- host = "smtp.example.com", port = 587, and username = "apikey" in the example. Removing that table removes the SMTP server hostname, port, and username configuration, so the SMTP emailer would no longer be pointed at smtp.example.com:587 with those credentials.
According to the SMTP configuration table, what are the defaults for host, port, use_tls, and timeout, and how does the documentation recommend supplying the SMTP password?

host defaults to localhost, port defaults to 25, use_tls (STARTTLS upgrade after connect) defaults to true, and timeout defaults to 10.0 seconds. The password key defaults to "" and the docs say to prefer setting it via the EMAILER_SMTP_PASSWORD environment variable rather than in the config.
When you point the emailer provider at a custom Emailer subclass, when is the class imported and what is it instantiated with?

The factory imports the class dynamically at server startup and instantiates it with the full emailer config dict. You enable this by subclassing Emailer and pointing the provider setting at your class.

A developer wants jac-scale to send its emails through SendGrid instead of SMTP. Based on the myapp/email.py example, what is the pattern for wiring in a third-party email service, and where should the API key come from?

Subclass jac_scale.abstractions.emailer.Emailer (e.g. class SendGridEmailer(Emailer)), build the third-party client in postinit() -- the example creates sendgrid.SendGridAPIClient there -- and implement send_email(to_addr, subject, body_text, body_html=None, from_addr=None) to deliver through that client. The API key is read from the environment (os.environ["SENDGRID_API_KEY"]) rather than being hardcoded in the class.
When should you use the built-in SMTP emailer versus a custom Emailer subclass like the SendGridEmailer, and how does configuration differ between the two?

Use the built-in SMTP emailer when you already have an SMTP relay (Gmail, AWS SES SMTP interface, your own postfix) -- it requires no custom code, just TOML config. Use a custom subclass when you need a non-SMTP provider: you write a class like SendGridEmailer with send_email() and is_ready() methods and set provider = "myapp.email:SendGridEmailer" in [plugins.scale.emailer]. In the custom case the constructor receives the resolved config dict, so extra TOML keys under [plugins.scale.emailer.<your_section>] are available via self.config, and secrets like API keys should stay in environment variables read via os.environ.
According to the "Built-in SMTP (default emailer)" example's introduction, in what situation is the built-in SMTP emailer the right choice, and how much custom code does it require?

It is the right choice when you already have an SMTP relay available -- the docs list Gmail, AWS SES's SMTP interface, or your own postfix as examples. It requires no custom code at all; you configure it purely through TOML.
In the jac.toml example enabling both dashboards with custom credentials, which four credential keys are set under [plugins.scale.kubernetes]?

redis_insight_username = "admin" and redis_insight_password = "strongpassword" alongside redis_dashboard = true, plus mongo_express_username = "admin" and mongo_express_password = "strongpassword" alongside mongodb_dashboard = true -- i.e. each dashboard is switched on and given its own username/password pair.
In the registration curl example, what two top-level fields does the JSON body of POST /user/register contain, and what does each hold?

The body contains "identities" -- a list of identity objects, here one with type "email" and value "alice@example.com" -- and "credential", an object specifying the credential type ("password") and the password itself ("secret").

A script needs to kick off the password-reset flow for a user's email address. Based on the "Trigger forgot-password" example, what request should it make, and what response status should it expect regardless of outcome?

It should POST to /user/forgot-password with a JSON body containing the identity, e.g. {"identity": {"type": "email", "value": "alice@example.com"}}, and Content-Type: application/json. No auth header is needed. As the heading notes, this endpoint always returns 200, so the script should expect HTTP 200 whether or not the account exists.
Contrast the reset-password step shown in Example 1 with the motivation for Example 2's custom SendGrid emailer: what does each piece of the flow rely on to do its job?

The reset step is delivery-agnostic: the client just POSTs the token from the email plus a new_password to /user/reset-password -- it relies only on the token having reached the user. Example 2 changes how that email gets delivered: instead of SMTP, a custom emailer (written in Python) uses SendGrid's REST API, which the docs recommend when you want better deliverability stats, templates, and webhooks. In other words, the reset endpoint is the same in both cases; only the email transport behind it differs.
What reasons does the "Custom SendGrid emailer" example give for choosing SendGrid's REST API over plain SMTP?
The example says to use the custom SendGrid emailer when you want SendGrid's REST API instead of SMTP because it offers better deliverability stats, templates, and webhooks.
In the full SendGridEmailer class, what does send_email() return when the SendGrid client was never configured, and how does it decide success when the client does send?

If self._client is None (no SENDGRID_API_KEY in the environment, so postinit() left the client unset), send_email() logs a warning that it is dropping the email and returns False. When the client exists, it builds a Mail with from_email defaulting to self.from_address if from_addr is not given, sends it, and returns True only if the response status code is in the 200-299 range; any exception is logged and returns False. is_ready() reports readiness as self.enabled and self._client is not None.
A jac-scale operator needs a UI to manage users, roles, and SSO configurations without writing any admin endpoints themselves. What should they reach for?
The built-in admin portal. jac-scale includes it out of the box precisely for managing users, roles, and SSO configurations, so no custom admin tooling is needed.

The admin portal is reachable at /admin with an admin user bootstrapped automatically on first server start. How do the jac.toml options and the environment variables divide responsibility for configuring that admin account, and which wins when both are set?

jac.toml's [plugins.scale.admin] section holds the baseline settings: enabled (default true), username (default "admin"), session_expiry_hours (default 24), and require_password_reset (default true, forcing the admin to change the default password on first login). The environment variables ADMIN_USERNAME, ADMIN_EMAIL, and ADMIN_DEFAULT_PASSWORD each override the corresponding jac.toml values -- the table explicitly notes they override jac.toml. So TOML defines the defaults for the bootstrapped admin at http://localhost:8000/admin, and env vars take precedence over them.
In the example `jac.toml` monitoring configuration, what metric name prefix will exported metrics use, and what would the prefix become if the `namespace = "myapp"` line were deleted?

With the example as written, metrics use the namespace prefix `myapp` (the `namespace` option is the metrics namespace prefix). If the line were removed, the namespace would be derived from the Kubernetes namespace config (sanitized) or would fall back to the default `"jac_scale"`, per the note in the excerpt. The example also sets `walker_metrics = true`, which enables per-walker execution timing — a setting that defaults to `false`.
What are the three user roles listed in the roles table, and which one cannot be deleted?

The three roles are ADMIN (value admin, full administrative access), SYSTEM (value system, an internal system account), and USER (value user, standard user access). The SYSTEM account is the one that cannot be deleted.
According to the Admin API endpoints table, which endpoint forces a password reset for a particular user, and what HTTP method does it use?

POST /admin/users/{username}/force-password-reset. It is a POST request, alongside the other per-user admin operations like GET /admin/users/{username} for details, PUT to update role/settings, and DELETE to remove the user.
You want other users to be able to follow edges through a shared node to reach things connected to it, but not to modify the node. Which access level from the table fits, and why not READ or WRITE?

CONNECT (value 1) is the fit: it specifically means the holder can traverse edges to/from the object. READ (value 0) is read-only access to the object but is a lower level than CONNECT's traversal ability, and WRITE (value 2) grants full read/write access, which exceeds the requirement. (NO_ACCESS, value -1, would block the object entirely.)
Both perm_grant and allow_root grant access to an object -- what is the difference in who receives the access?

perm_grant grants access to everyone: it allows all users to access the object at a given level. allow_root is targeted: it grants access to one specific user's root graph. Both are shown being called inside a with entry block.
By default, what authentication do walker and function endpoints require, and how do you make one publicly accessible?

All walker and function endpoints are protected by default -- they require JWT authentication. To allow public access you must explicitly opt in with the :pub modifier. This secure-by-default design prevents accidentally exposing endpoints without authentication.
An operations team needs an uptime-monitoring service (which has no user credentials) to poll the server for liveness. Following the health_check example, how should the walker be declared?

Declare it with the :pub modifier -- walker :pub health_check -- so no authentication is required. The example's check ability runs with Root entry and reports {"status": "ok"}, which is exactly the kind of unauthenticated liveness response an external monitor can poll.
Name the three access levels a walker can have when served as an API endpoint and what each requires.

Public (:pub) -- accessible without authentication; Protected (the default) -- requires JWT authentication; and Private (:priv) -- requires JWT authentication and is per-user isolated, meaning each user operates on their own graph.
According to the permission functions reference, which function revokes all public access to an archetype, and how does its signature differ from disallow_root?

perm_revoke removes all public access and takes only the archetype: perm_revoke(archetype). disallow_root is narrower -- it revokes access from one specific root and takes three arguments: disallow_root(archetype, root_id, level).
What four capabilities does Jac-Scale provide for webhooks?

Dedicated /webhook/ endpoints for webhook walkers, API key authentication for secure access, HMAC-SHA256 signature verification to validate request integrity, and automatic endpoint generation based on walker configuration. These let external services like payment processors, CI/CD systems, and messaging platforms send real-time notifications to a Jac application.
What turns an ordinary walker like PaymentReceived into a webhook endpoint, and what walker features does the basic example still use normally?

The @restspec(protocol=APIProtocol.WEBHOOK) decorator on the walker definition is what makes it a webhook endpoint. Apart from that decorator, the PaymentReceived example is a normal walker: it declares typed has fields (payment_id: str, amount: float, and currency: str with default 'USD') and defines an ability that runs with Root entry.
In the basic webhook walker example, what would happen to the currency field if a caller's JSON payload omitted it, and why?

The walker would still work, with currency taking the value 'USD', because the has declaration gives it a default: currency: str = 'USD'. The other fields, payment_id: str and amount: float, have no defaults and must be supplied. The walker itself is made a webhook by the @restspec(protocol=APIProtocol.WEBHOOK) decorator and processes with Root entry.
At what URL is the PaymentReceived webhook walker accessible, and what fields does its report include?

It is accessible at POST /webhook/PaymentReceived. Its report includes "status": "success", a "message" built with an f-string (f"Payment {self.payment_id} received"), plus the walker's amount and currency values.
Can a webhook walker be called through the standard /walker/{walker_name} endpoint?
No. Webhook walkers are only accessible via the /webhook/{walker_name} endpoints; they are explicitly not accessible via the standard /walker/{walker_name} endpoint.
A developer worries that restarting the server will invalidate all webhook API keys their partners are using. Based on the API key management notes, is that a real risk?

No. API key metadata is stored persistently in MongoDB, in the webhook_api_keys collection, so keys survive server restarts. The docs note this replaced an older behavior where keys were held in memory only. The only prerequisite workflow is that users must create an API key first before calling webhook endpoints.

Comparing the create and list API-key operations: what do POST /api-key/create and GET /api-key/list share in their request requirements, and what extra information does creating a key require and return?

Both require the same authentication header: Authorization: Bearer <jwt_token>. Creation additionally takes a JSON body with a name (e.g. "My Webhook Key") and expiry_days (e.g. 30), and its response returns the actual api_key string, its api_key_id, the name, and created_at/expires_at timestamps. Listing needs no body -- it is a simple authenticated GET.
What endpoint and header do you use to list API keys?
Send GET /api-key/list with the required Authorization: Bearer <jwt_token> header.
Which two headers must accompany a webhook endpoint call, and what does each carry?
X-API-Key, carrying the API key obtained from /api-key/create, and X-Webhook-Signature, carrying the HMAC-SHA256 signature of the request body.
In the webhook signature scheme, what is the HMAC-SHA256 signature computed over, and what serves as the HMAC key?

The signature is computed as HMAC-SHA256(request_body, api_key) -- the request body is the message and the API key is the HMAC key. The cURL example shows this: the payload is piped through openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "$API_KEY", and the result is sent in the X-Webhook-Signature header alongside X-API-Key.

You are wiring a payment provider's server-to-server callback into your app and must choose between a regular walker and a webhook walker. Using the comparison table, which do you pick and on what grounds?

A webhook walker at /webhook/{name}. The table assigns webhook walkers the "external service callbacks" use case, with API Key + HMAC signature authentication, service-scoped access control, and HMAC-SHA256 signature verification -- which suits a payment processor that has no user JWT. Regular walkers at /walker/{name} use JWT Bearer tokens, are user-scoped, do no signature verification, and are meant for user-facing APIs.
How do the webhook execution endpoint and the API-key management endpoints differ in path shape and HTTP methods?

Webhook execution is a single POST route parameterized by walker name: POST /webhook/{walker_name}. API-key management spans three routes with three different methods: POST /api-key/create to create a key, GET /api-key/list to list the user's keys, and DELETE /api-key/{api_key_id} to revoke one -- the revoke route being parameterized by the key id rather than a walker name.
According to the required-headers table for webhook requests, under what condition is the X-Webhook-Signature header not strictly required?

X-Webhook-Signature (the HMAC-SHA256 signature) is required only if verify_signature is enabled -- the table marks it "Yes*" with that condition. Content-Type (which must be application/json) and X-API-Key (the key from /api-key/create) are always required.
What kind of communication do Jac Scale's WebSocket endpoints enable between clients and walkers?
Real-time bidirectional communication -- Jac Scale provides built-in support for WebSocket endpoints so clients and walkers can communicate in both directions in real time.

A dashboard needs to exchange many messages in both directions with the server over one long-lived connection, rather than issuing repeated request-response calls. Which Jac Scale capability fits, and what supporting features does it bring?

WebSockets. Unlike REST endpoints, which are single request-response, a WebSocket connection stays open and allows multiple messages in both directions (persistent, full-duplex). Jac Scale provides dedicated /ws/ endpoints for WebSocket walkers, persistent connections with a message loop, a JSON message protocol for sending walker fields and receiving results, JWT authentication via query parameter or message payload, connection management with automatic cleanup on disconnect, and HMR support in dev mode.
What two declaration requirements make a walker a WebSocket endpoint, and how does the EchoMessage example additionally control who can connect?

The walker must carry the @restspec(protocol=APIProtocol.WEBSOCKET) decorator and must be declared as an async walker (with an async can ability). The EchoMessage example adds : pub to make it public, so no authentication is needed to connect; it declares has message: str and client_id: str = "anonymous", echoes both back in its report, and is served at ws://localhost:8000/ws/EchoMessage.
In the EchoMessage WebSocket walker, what does a client receive back if it sends only {"message": "hi"} without a client_id?

It receives {"echo": "hi", "client_id": "anonymous"} -- the echo ability reports self.message and self.client_id, and client_id defaults to "anonymous" via has client_id: str = "anonymous". The walker is public (: pub) and reachable at ws://localhost:8000/ws/EchoMessage.
How do you convert a public WebSocket walker into one that requires JWT authentication?
Simply remove : pub from the walker definition. A private WebSocket walker -- one without : pub -- requires JWT authentication.
What does broadcast=True do on a WebSocket walker, and what use cases does the ChatRoom example call it ideal for?

With @restspec(protocol=APIProtocol.WEBSOCKET, broadcast=True), when one client sends a message, ALL connected clients of that walker receive the response instead of just the sender. The docs say this makes it ideal for chat rooms, live notifications, real-time collaboration, and game state synchronization -- the ChatRoom example reports a message dict with type, sender, and content to everyone.
A team wants a broadcast channel where only logged-in users can connect, send, and receive. How do they declare it?

Create a private broadcasting walker: keep broadcast=True but remove : pub from the walker definition. Then only authenticated users can connect and send messages, and all authenticated users receive the broadcasts.
WebSocket walkers and sv-to-sv microservice imports both move calls over the network -- how do the two mechanisms differ in connection model and code changes required?

WebSocket walkers hold a persistent connection: they must be declared async walker, are only reachable at ws://host/ws/{walker_name}, and the connection stays open until the client disconnects (with : pub controlling auth and broadcast=True fanning responses to all connected clients). sv-to-sv interop, by contrast, is request-per-call RPC between server modules: an sv import from one server module to another generates HTTP client stubs at compile time, so existing call sites become RPCs over the wire without changing the calling code.
What are the three sandbox provider implementations in jac-scale, and what isolation does each one give?

`local` isolates via a subprocess (for local development with no container runtime needed), `docker` isolates via a container (for staging, basic isolation with Docker), and `kubernetes` isolates via a pod (for production, with full isolation including resource limits and RBAC). All three implement the abstract `SandboxEnvironment` interface, and the factory instantiates whichever one the configuration selects.
What visibility must provider functions and walkers have to be reachable through sv import, and what happens if they lack it?

Provider functions must be declared def:pub and walkers must be walker:pub. Non-public functions are not exposed as endpoints, so calls into them return 404. Other preconditions: jac-scale must be installed on the consumer for automatic sibling spawning (explicit URLs and env vars work with bare jaclang), jac start <relative-path> needs a jac.toml in the current directory, and auto-spawned services must live in the same directory the consumer was started from (or be pointed at explicitly by URL).
A service wants to pass an open database handle and a node anchor to another microservice through an sv import call. Per the boundary-types rules, what is the correct approach?

Neither can cross the boundary. Anchors and closures are not wire-friendly, and live database or file handles are service-local resources. The documented pattern is to pass identifiers instead -- e.g. a jid -- and re-resolve the object on the other side. What does serialize transparently: obj types (recursively hydrated), enums (by name), primitives (int, float, str, bool, None, list[T], dict[K, V]), and walker:pub archetypes imported by name. Failures raise RuntimeError with messages like "sv-to-sv RPC '{module}.{func}' failed: {msg}".
When a consumer sv imports the Greet walker from notify_service, how does the consumer-side stub relate to the provider's walker definition?

The compiler generates a stub class on the consumer side whose name and has field shape mirror the provider's walker -- for Greet, a stub with has name: str matching walker:pub Greet on the provider (which greets with Root entry and reports f"hello, {self.name}"). Type identity is preserved, so the call site reads like a local construction of Greet even though it drives a remote spawn.
In the notify_service.jac provider example, what makes the Greet walker importable by other services, and what does it report?
It is declared walker:pub Greet -- the :pub visibility is what exposes it for import. It has a has name: str field and a greet ability with Root entry that reports the f-string f"hello, {self.name}".
When the dispatcher_service consumer evaluates Greet(name=self.who) on an sv-imported walker, how do the semantics differ from constructing that walker locally?

Locally, Greet(name="x") only constructs a walker -- you still need spawn to run it. Across the sv-to-sv boundary, instantiating the sv-imported walker is spawn-and-execute: the stub collects the keyword args into a JSON dict, the runtime POSTs it to /walker/Greet on the resolved provider URL, the provider spawns and runs the walker, and the consumer rehydrates the result into a post-execution instance with the reports list attached. So rg.reports[0] is immediately "hello, <who>", and rg.name and isinstance(rg, Greet) work -- there is no concept of an unexecuted remote walker.
When you run jac start consumer.jac, when are the sv-imported provider services brought up, and what happens if one of them fails to start?

The consumer finds every service it sv imports from -- including transitive dependencies (if A imports B and B imports C, starting A brings up all three) -- and brings them all up before it starts accepting requests. Startup is fail-fast: if any service fails to come up (missing source file, syntax error, port in use), the consumer crashes at startup with the underlying error, so you find out at deploy time rather than at first request. Note this only applies to jac start; jac run does not bring up long-running siblings and instead discovers providers lazily.
A consumer service on host A must call a provider running on host B. Given the four-step service discovery order, which mechanism should be used and why won't automatic spawning work here?

Use the JAC_SV_<MODULE>_URL environment variable (step 3, the upper-cased module name), which the docs call the knob to reach for when the provider lives on a different host. Automatic spawn (step 4) won't work across hosts because auto-spawned siblings bind to 127.0.0.1 -- reachable only from inside the consumer process, not from other machines. The full resolution order is: test client, explicit URL handed programmatically, JAC_SV_<MODULE>_URL, then automatic spawn (which assigns sibling ports in 18000-18999, so manual --port choices should avoid that range).
In the Kubernetes deployment pattern for sv-to-sv services, what replaces automatic sibling spawning, and how is the env var name derived?

Each service becomes its own Deployment + Service, and the consumer is wired to the provider with an environment variable pointing at the provider's cluster DNS name -- e.g. JAC_SV_INVENTORY_SERVICE_URL set to http://inventory-service.default.svc.cluster.local:8000 in the order-service container spec. The naming convention is JAC_SV_<UPPERCASED_MODULE_NAME>_URL, where the module name is exactly the value used in sv import from <module_name>.
In the order-service Deployment YAML, what would break if the env var were misspelled JAC_SV_INVENTORY_URL instead of JAC_SV_INVENTORY_SERVICE_URL?

The consumer would not find the provider's URL, because the convention is JAC_SV_<UPPERCASED_MODULE_NAME>_URL where the module name is the exact value used in sv import from <module_name> -- for sv import from inventory_service that is JAC_SV_INVENTORY_SERVICE_URL. The example sets it to the provider's cluster DNS name, http://inventory-service.default.svc.cluster.local:8000, on the order-service container.
For local multi-service development, what two patterns does the documentation offer, and which one is valid for multi-host deployments?

(1) Export JAC_SV_*_URL env vars per provider (e.g. JAC_SV_INVENTORY_SERVICE_URL=http://localhost:8001) in a .env file or shell, then jac start the consumer on its own port; or (2) omit the env vars and run jac start order_service.jac alone -- the consumer brings up every sv-imported service automatically, including transitive dependencies, before serving the first request. The automatic mode is supported only for single-host setups (one process, many logical services) because automatically-started services bind 127.0.0.1 only; multi-host deployments must use the JAC_SV_*_URL path.
Per the sv-to-sv troubleshooting notes, what causes '{"detail":"Invalid anchor id ..."}' 500 errors and what is the fix?

Stale anchors persisted from a previous run with a different schema. The fix is to stop the server, delete the data directory with rm -rf .jac/data/, and restart. The docs note this is not specific to sv-to-sv -- any def:pub call can hit it after a schema change. (The other listed failures: ModuleNotFoundError at startup means the provider source wasn't in the start directory, and cross-service 404s mean the provider function isn't def:pub / walker isn't walker:pub.)
You want to test that a consumer correctly calls its inventory_service provider without any real network I/O. What pattern does jac-scale provide?

Register the provider as an in-process TestClient before exercising the consumer: sv_client.register_test_client("inventory_service", prov_client) routes the consumer's calls through the registered client directly -- no sockets, no port allocation, no background threads. The example imports sv_client from jaclang.runtimelib and TestClient from starlette.testclient, and calls sv_client.clear_test_clients() at the start of the test to avoid bleed-over from previous registrations.
