Within the sv_client API, how does register_test_client differ from register, and which hygiene call does the testing section insist on between tests?

register(module_name, url) points a provider name at a real URL programmatically (taking precedence over the env var path), so calls still go over HTTP -- it is for production wiring or custom orchestrators. register_test_client(module_name, client) instead routes the consumer's calls through an in-process starlette TestClient, for tests only, with no network I/O. Between tests you must call sv_client.clear_test_clients() to drop all test-client registrations and avoid bleed-over from a previous test's registrations. (resolve_url looks up the URL from register or JAC_SV_<MOD>_URL, and unregister/unregister_test_client remove individual entries.)
According to the sv_client API reference, when do you actually need these functions, and what does resolve_url do if nothing is registered for a module?

You rarely need sv_client under normal use -- JAC_SV_<MODULE>_URL covers most production wiring and automatic startup covers single-host setups; reach for it when writing tests or a custom orchestrator. resolve_url(module_name) returns the URL the consumer would use (from register() or from the JAC_SV_<MOD>_URL env var) and raises if nothing is registered.
What contract must a plugin's override of JacAPIServer.ensure_sv_service fulfill, and under what concurrency conditions is the hook called?

The override may launch the service anywhere it wants (Docker containers, Kubernetes Jobs, systemd units, remote VMs) but must end by calling sv_client.register(module_name, <url>) so subsequent calls skip the hook. It is called during automatic startup, once per provider, in parallel up to 8 at a time, so overrides must be idempotent and safe to run concurrently -- properties the pre-existing lazy contract already required, so a plugin written against any prior version continues to work. The default implementation picks a free loopback port in 18000-18999, serves the module's def:pub endpoints on a daemon thread, waits until an HTTP probe succeeds, then registers the URL.
What does store() return with versus without jac-scale installed, and what are its two parameters and their defaults?

Without jac-scale, store() returns a LocalStorage instance; with jac-scale installed it returns a configuration-driven backend that reads from jac.toml and environment variables. Its parameters are base_path (str, default "./storage", the root directory for all files) and create_dirs (bool, default True, create the base directory if it doesn't exist). It requires no imports and is automatically hookable by plugins -- e.g. glob storage = store(base_path="./uploads", create_dirs=True).
In the line glob storage = store(base_path="./uploads", create_dirs=True), what would change if both arguments were omitted?

The defaults would apply: base_path would fall back to "./storage" as the root directory for all files instead of "./uploads", and create_dirs would still be True (its default), so the base directory would still be created if missing. What store() returns also depends on the environment: a LocalStorage instance without jac-scale, or a configuration-driven backend (reading jac.toml and environment variables) with jac-scale installed.
In the storage interface, how does download() behave differently depending on whether a destination is given, and which method produces a pre-signed or public URL?

download(source, destination=None) returns the file's bytes when no destination is given, and None otherwise (writing to the destination). get_url(path, expires_in=3600) is the method that returns a public or pre-signed URL for a file. The interface also includes upload, delete, exists, list_files(prefix="", recursive=False), get_metadata (returning size, modified, created, is_dir, name), copy, and move.
In the upload_file walker example, how is the stored file's path constructed?

The walker generates a unique filename with uuid4 -- unique_name = f"{uuid4()}.dat" -- and joins it with the walker's folder field (default "documents"): path = f"{self.folder}/{unique_name}". The walker is declared :pub, takes an UploadFile via has file, and uses a glob storage = store(base_path="./uploads") instance.
A client needs an endpoint that returns every file in a folder together with each file's size and name. Which pattern from the storage example applies?

The list_files walker pattern: iterate storage.list_files(self.folder, self.recursive) to get each path, call storage.get_metadata(path) for each, and append {"path": ..., "size": metadata["size"], "name": metadata["name"]} to a list, finally reporting {"files": files}. The walker exposes folder (default "documents") and recursive (default False) as has fields so the client controls the scope.
What flips store() from returning local storage to returning an S3Storage instance, and which configuration keys govern the S3 backend?

jac-scale's S3 integration: when configured, the store() builtin returns an S3Storage instance instead of the default local one. Configuration lives in jac.toml under [plugins.scale.storage] or env vars: type (JAC_STORAGE_TYPE, local or s3, default local), bucket (JAC_STORAGE_S3_BUCKET), region (JAC_STORAGE_S3_REGION, default us-east-1), prefix (JAC_STORAGE_S3_PREFIX, optional key prefix), endpoint_url (JAC_STORAGE_S3_ENDPOINT_URL, custom endpoint for non-AWS providers), and public_read (JAC_STORAGE_S3_PUBLIC_READ, default false; when true, direct public URLs are returned). The example sets type = "s3", bucket = "my-app-uploads", region = "us-east-1", public_read = false.
What does get_url() return for each of the three storage cases described?

For LocalStorage it returns a file:// URI to the absolute path of the file. For S3Storage with private objects it returns a secure pre-signed URL that expires after the specified time (default 1 hour). For S3Storage with public_read = true it returns a direct, permanent public URL.
In the download_file walker, what happens when the requested path does not exist in storage?

The walker guards with if not storage.exists(self.path): it reports {"error": "File not found"} and returns without attempting the download. Only when the path exists does it call storage.download(self.path) and report the content along with its size (len(content)). The excerpt also shows get_url with expires_in=600, which for S3 yields a pre-signed URL.
How does creating storage via StorageFactory.create differ from using the store() builtin?

StorageFactory is the advanced path: you import it explicitly (import from jac_scale.factories.storage_factory { StorageFactory }) and pass an explicit type and config dict -- e.g. StorageFactory.create("local", {"base_path": "./my-files", "create_dirs": True}) -- so you choose the backend and settings in code. The store() builtin is the recommended route for ordinary use; the factory is reserved for advanced use cases needing that explicit control.
In the StorageFactory example, what two settings are placed in the config dict passed to StorageFactory.create, and what backend type is requested?
The config dict is {"base_path": "./my-files", "create_dirs": True}, and it is passed with the explicit type "local": glob storage = StorageFactory.create("local", config).
Following the /traverse curl example, how would a client fetch a graph view three hops deep containing only User and Post nodes with full archetype context?

POST to /traverse with an Authorization: Bearer <token> header and a JSON body of {"depth": 3, "node_types": ["User", "Post"], "detailed": true} -- exactly as the example shows: depth controls how many hops are traversed, node_types filters to the listed node types, and detailed: true includes archetype context.
Contrast the async_processor walker with kvstore access: which works through graph abstractions and which bypasses them, and how is each set up?

The async_processor walker operates in the graph/walker layer: it is a walker with has items: list whose async can process with Root entry awaits process_item(item) per element and reports the collected results. kvstore is the opposite -- direct database operations without the graph layer abstraction. You import it from jac_scale.lib and construct handles per backend: kvstore(db_name='my_app', db_type='mongodb') for MongoDB document queries or kvstore(db_name='cache', db_type='redis') for Redis key-value with TTL/atomic ops, with the uri parameter resolving by priority: explicit → MONGODB_URI/REDIS_URL env vars → jac.toml.
In the kvstore example that creates mongo_db and redis_db, what determines which backend each handle talks to, and how is the connection URI resolved when none is passed?

The db_type argument selects the backend: kvstore(db_name='my_app', db_type='mongodb') gives MongoDB (document queries) and kvstore(db_name='cache', db_type='redis') gives Redis (key-value with TTL/atomic ops). When uri is None, resolution follows the documented priority: explicit uri first, then the MONGODB_URI/REDIS_URL environment variables, then jac.toml. The example imports kvstore from jac_scale.lib and constructs both handles inside a with entry block.
In the MongoDB kvstore example, which method updates Alice's age, and what query operators does the excerpt list as supported?

db.update_one('users', {'name': 'Alice'}, {'$set': {'age': 31}}) performs the update. The supported query operators listed are $eq, $gt, $gte, $lt, $lte, $in, $ne, $and, and $or -- the example uses $gt in db.find('users', {'age': {'$gt': 28}}). The MongoDB interface offers common methods (get, set, delete, exists) plus query methods like find_one, find, insert_one/insert_many, update_one/update_many, delete_one/delete_many, the *_by_id variants, and find_nodes.

You need to cache a user profile that should expire automatically after an hour and keep a page-view counter. Which Redis kvstore methods apply, and what happens if you call them on a MongoDB kvstore?

Use set_with_ttl for the expiring cache -- e.g. cache.set_with_ttl('cache:profile', {'name': 'Alice'}, ttl=3600) -- and incr for the counter, as in cache.incr('stats:views'). These are Redis-specific methods (alongside expire, scan_keys, set_nx_with_ttl, delete_if_equals); the docs note database-specific methods raise NotImplementedError on the wrong database type, so calling them on a MongoDB kvstore fails.
Why can't Python's threading.Lock protect a shared resource across jac-scale replicas, and what property of set_nx_with_ttl makes it a safe distributed alternative?

threading.Lock only serializes inside one process, so with multiple replicas behind a load balancer two pods can land on the same shared resource (an EFS-backed file, an external API rate limit, a row in a downstream database) at the same instant -- the lock cannot prevent that race. set_nx_with_ttl(key, value, ttl) is atomic in Redis: it sets the key only if it does not already exist (mapping to SET key value NX EX ttl), returning True to the single acquirer and False to everyone else, and its mandatory TTL means that if a holder crashes without releasing, Redis frees the lock automatically after ttl seconds so an orphan never blocks the cluster forever.
What Redis command does set_nx_with_ttl map to, what does its return value mean, and why is the TTL mandatory?

It maps to Redis SET key value NX EX ttl -- atomically setting the key only if it does not already exist, with automatic expiration. It returns True if the caller acquired the lock and False if another caller already holds it. The TTL is mandatory so that if the holder crashes without releasing, Redis frees the lock automatically after ttl seconds -- an orphaned lock never blocks the cluster forever.
In the cross-pod mutex example's with_repo_lock function, what two pieces of information go into the lock payload, and what generates the fence value?

The payload is a dict with 'fence' -- a unique token generated by str(uuid4()) -- and 'pod', taken from os.environ.get('HOSTNAME', 'local') to identify the holder. The function is built on a Redis kvstore (glob _kv = kvstore(db_name='myapp', db_type='redis')).
In the lock-acquisition loop of the cross-pod mutex example, what strategy is used when set_nx_with_ttl returns False, and what happens if the lock is never obtained?

The code retries: it sets a deadline of time.time() + 25.0 and loops, calling _kv.set_nx_with_ttl(f'repo_lock:{repo_id}', payload, ttl=30) and sleeping 0.2 seconds between attempts until it acquires the lock or the ~25-second deadline passes. If contention persists and it never acquires, it gives up and returns {'success': False, 'error': 'lock contention timeout'}. On success it runs the protected operation inside a try block so the release logic in finally always executes.
The mutex pattern releases its lock in a finally block with delete_if_equals, while the cluster-wide debounce pattern performs no release at all. Why is each choice correct?

The mutex must release so others can proceed, but safely: delete_if_equals(f'repo_lock:{repo_id}', payload) is a no-op if the TTL expired mid-operation and another pod now owns the key, because the stored value no longer matches this pod's payload. The debounce pattern intentionally skips release: set_nx_with_ttl's TTL is the window length, so letting the key expire is the mechanism -- if _kv.set_nx_with_ttl(f'task_dbnce:{task_id}', payload, ttl=60) succeeds the pod runs the task, otherwise another pod already ran it within the last 60 seconds. This collapses N pods running the same periodic task into one execution per window, the right pattern for autosave debouncing and leader-only reconciliation cycles.
In maybe_run_periodic_task, why does the function return False without running the task when set_nx_with_ttl fails, and why is there no unlock step?

A False from _kv.set_nx_with_ttl(f'task_dbnce:{task_id}', payload, ttl=60) means the debounce key already exists -- another pod already ran the task within the last 60 seconds -- so this pod skips run_task and returns False. There is no release step by design: the TTL is the window length, so the key simply expires after 60 seconds, opening the next window. This collapses N pods running the same periodic task into a single execution per window (autosave debouncing, leader-only reconciliation, any 'exactly once per window across the cluster' need).
What are the two in-tree event stream implementations, and how is one chosen at runtime?

LocalEventStream (in-memory: single-process, no persistence -- right for dev workstations, tests, and single-pod deployments) and RedisEventStream (Redis Streams: durable and cross-pod). You don't pick the broker; selection happens automatically at startup -- LocalEventStream when no Redis URL is configured, RedisEventStream when a Redis URL resolves and the [data] extra is installed. The broker itself is off by default and provides a durable log, consumer groups, replayable offsets via start_from, and at-least-once delivery with retries and a DLQ.
A developer wants to turn on event streaming with minimal configuration. Per the "Enabling" section, what is the one setting that matters and where does it go?

Add the [plugins.scale.events] section to jac.toml and set enabled = true. The docs call enabled the master switch; everything else has working defaults, so no further keys are required just to enable the feature.
In the place_order publishing example, the Event is created without an event_type. What will its event_type be, and does the walker need a try/except around publish()?

The event_type auto-defaults to the topic, "orders.placed", because it was left empty -- the docs note the topic string only needs to appear once at the call site, and you set event_type explicitly only when it differs from the topic. No try/except is needed: publish() is fire-and-forget, and errors from the broker are logged and swallowed. The example publishes Event(data={"order_id": self.order_id, "amount": self.amount}, trace_id="trace-1") from the walker's fire ability.
With @subscribe, what does the start_from argument control, what are its accepted values, and why is it called a one-time bookmark?

start_from controls where a brand-new consumer group begins reading. The default "latest" delivers only events produced after the group is created; "earliest" replays everything still retained; and a broker-specific position token (e.g. a Redis stream id like "1700000000000-0") resumes from a specific offset. It is a one-time bookmark because existing groups always resume from their stored position and ignore the argument. Handlers register at import time, the framework wires each into the active broker at server startup, and a daemon consumer thread is spawned per subscription; @subscribe also accepts group= and retry= overrides.
In the pull-consumption example, what two limits does broker.consume() take for the "orders.placed" topic?

max_messages=10 and timeout_seconds=2.0 -- consume() is called on an EventStreamBroker (imported from jac_scale.events.broker) as broker.consume("orders.placed", max_messages=10, timeout_seconds=2.0), returning a batch the drain function then iterates over.
In a pull-based consumer loop, what must happen to each event after processing, and what if it is skipped?

Each event must be acked individually via broker.ack(ev), as the drain example does after processing each event in the batch. If an event is not acked, the broker redelivers it after its visibility timeout. Also note consume() blocks up to timeout_seconds waiting for at least one event, returns up to max_messages, and accepts the same start_from= argument as subscribe() -- which only affects the first call that creates the consumer group; later calls resume from the stored position.
Connect the retry configuration keys to the reliability semantics: what happens to an event whose handler keeps failing, and which config values shape that journey?

Delivery is at-least-once, so handlers may run more than once and should be idempotent or dedupe on event.id. A failing handler is retried retry.max_attempts times (default 3) with delays taken from retry.backoff_seconds (default [1, 5, 30], clamped to the last value per attempt index; the thread sleeps responsively to the broker stop event so shutdowns aren't blocked). After retry exhaustion the event is published to the dead-letter topic formed by appending retry.dead_letter_suffix (default .dlq) to the topic name, and the original is acked so it is not redelivered indefinitely -- the DLQ is a regular topic you can consume() like any other. Other keys: enabled (default false, master switch making all calls no-ops), url (falls back to [plugins.scale.database].redis_url, else LocalEventStream), consumer_group (default jac-scale), serializer (json only).
Under the event broker's reliability semantics, what happens on process exit?

Drain on shutdown: consumer threads are signaled to stop and joined under a 10-second deadline. The other guarantees are at-least-once delivery (make handlers idempotent or dedupe on event.id), retry of failing handlers max_attempts times with backoff_seconds delays, and after exhaustion publication to the <topic><dead_letter_suffix> dead-letter topic with the original acked so it isn't redelivered indefinitely.
What delivery metadata fields does the broker expose on Event, and who sets them?

event.delivery_id, event.delivery_topic, and event.delivery_group -- first-class fields handlers can read directly for idempotency keys, structured logging, or dedup without importing broker-specific constants. They are broker-managed: producers leave them None, the broker sets them on consume() or push delivery, and they are not serialized to the wire. Related operational facts: each subscription spawns a daemon thread named jac-scale-broker-<topic>-<group> (Redis) or jac-scale-local-<topic>-<group> (Local), startup logs "Events broker enabled (kind={local|redis}, subscriptions=N)", and the wire format is CloudEvents 1.0 valid so strict CE consumers like Argo Events and Knative Eventing accept it.
On the first jac start app.jac --scale, how are database credentials for the auto-provisioned MongoDB and Redis handled in Kubernetes?

Credentials are never hardcoded in pod specs. The mongodb_root_username/mongodb_root_password and redis_username/redis_password TOML keys (defaults admin/password) are stored as Kubernetes Secret resources named {app}-mongodb-secret and {app}-redis-secret and injected via valueFrom.secretKeyRef -- kubectl describe pod shows only the secret name and key, not the value. The first deploy provisions MongoDB as a StatefulSet with a PersistentVolumeClaim and Redis as a Deployment with persistent storage (plus the app Deployment, an NGINX Ingress controller, ClusterIP services, and ConfigMaps); subsequent deployments only update the application and leave the databases untouched. To use external databases instead, set mongodb_enabled/redis_enabled = false and provide mongodb_uri/redis_url under [plugins.scale.database].
How do the database connection settings differ from the dashboard settings in their defaults and their effect on Kubernetes provisioning?

The database settings ([plugins.scale.database]) default to None and setting them turns provisioning OFF: when mongodb_uri is set the K8s MongoDB StatefulSet is not provisioned, and a set redis_url skips Redis provisioning; the MONGODB_URI and REDIS_URL env vars take precedence over the jac.toml values, and shelf_db_path (default .jac/data/anchor_store.db) covers local no-K8s jac start. The dashboards ([plugins.scale.kubernetes]) are the opposite direction: off by default (redis_dashboard, mongodb_dashboard, loki_enabled all false) and must be explicitly enabled to deploy the RedisInsight UI, Mongo Express UI, or the Loki + Alloy log pipeline.
In the dashboard configuration TOML that sets redis_dashboard = true and mongodb_dashboard = true, what does each line deploy, and what happens if the whole block is omitted?

redis_dashboard = true deploys the RedisInsight dashboard UI and mongodb_dashboard = true deploys the Mongo Express UI. If the block is omitted, neither dashboard deploys: dashboards are off by default -- both keys default to false, as does loki_enabled, which would deploy the Loki + Alloy log pipeline and add a Pod Logs dashboard to Grafana.
How are the enabled dashboards exposed and protected, and what are the default credentials?

They are served through the NGINX Ingress at fixed subpaths -- Redis Insight at http://localhost:<ingress_node_port>/cache-dashboard/ and Mongo Express at http://localhost:<ingress_node_port>/db-dashboard -- so no separate NodePorts are needed. Defaults are admin/admin for both redis_insight_username/redis_insight_password and mongo_express_username/mongo_express_password. When redis_dashboard = true, the /cache-dashboard route is always protected by HTTP basic authentication with those credentials, and the docs warn to change the defaults before deploying to a shared or public cluster.
In jac-scale's tiered memory system, where should volatile runtime state, cached data, and durable data each live?

Volatile runtime state belongs in L1, the in-memory tier; cached data belongs in L2, backed by Redis as the cache layer; and durable data belongs in L3, backed by MongoDB as persistent storage. The mermaid diagram shows the application talking to L1, which chains to L2 (Redis) and then L3 (MongoDB).
If the naming TOML example ([plugins.scale.kubernetes] app_name = "myapp", namespace = "production") were removed, what names and namespace would jac-scale use?

The defaults: app_name falls back to jaseci, which becomes the prefix for all Kubernetes resource names (deployments, services, secrets, etc.), and namespace falls back to default, the namespace resources are created in. The example exists precisely to override those two defaults to myapp and production.
Why is the domain setting mandatory when shared_ingress = true, and what does jac-scale do if it is empty?

The shared controller sees Ingress resources from all namespaces, so host-based routing is the only way to differentiate two apps -- domain becomes the Ingress host. jac-scale raises an error at deploy time if domain is empty while shared_ingress = true. Shared ingress (default false) skips deploying the per-app NGINX controller and attaches routing rules to a pre-existing controller (class named by shared_ingress_class, default "nginx"); it suits clusters that already run cluster-wide ingress-nginx or host multiple apps. Extra knobs: shared_ingress_annotations (merged onto the Ingress, needed for non-nginx controllers, caller values win) and shared_ingress_tls (set when the controller terminates TLS out-of-band, e.g. an ALB with an ACM cert).
Rate limiting and sticky sessions are both NGINX ingress features in jac-scale -- contrast what each keys on and its default state.

Rate limiting is enforced per client IP using a leaky-bucket algorithm and is on with defaults: ingress_limit_rps = 20 sustained requests/second, burst = rps x ingress_limit_burst_multiplier (default 5, queued within the burst), and ingress_limit_connections = 20 max concurrent connections per IP; excess requests get 429 Too Many Requests. Sticky sessions deliberately do NOT key on IP: NGINX sets a never-expiring route cookie on the first response and routes subsequent requests to the same pod by cookie, which survives IP changes from mobile networks, NAT, VPNs, and proxies. Session affinity is enabled by default (disable with ingress_session_affinity = false) and exists for pods holding per-user state; on pod failure NGINX re-routes and rewrites the cookie, but in-memory state on a deleted pod is lost, so true resilience requires externalizing per-user state to Redis or a database.

In the sticky-sessions section, the only TOML shown is ingress_session_affinity = false. Why is the example the disable switch rather than an enable switch, and what mechanism does the feature use when left on?

Because cookie-based session affinity is enabled by default -- the TOML line exists to turn it off if not needed. When on, NGINX sets a route cookie in the browser on the first response; every later request carries the cookie and NGINX routes it back to the same pod regardless of IP changes (mobile networks, NAT, VPN, proxies). The cookie never expires (max-age ~68 years), and on pod failure NGINX re-routes to a healthy pod and rewrites the cookie automatically. The limitation: stickiness only holds while a pod is alive -- a deleted pod's in-flight, in-memory user state is gone, so the docs advise externalizing per-user state to Redis or a database.
Why is enabling TLS in jac-scale a two-step process?

To avoid a chicken-and-egg problem: the NLB hostname is unknown until after the first deploy, so you cannot point DNS (and hence issue a certificate for the domain) before deploying. jac-scale supports custom domains with automatic HTTPS via cert-manager + Let's Encrypt, split into deploy-first, then enable TLS.
The --enable-tls step and the resource-limits settings both modify the deployment -- contrast what each changes and whether the app is redeployed.

jac start app.jac --scale --enable-tls installs cert-manager, creates a Let's Encrypt Issuer, patches the live Ingress with TLS annotations, and updates all service URLs to HTTPS (app, /grafana, /db-dashboard, /cache-dashboard) -- explicitly with no redeployment of the application; it errors if domain is unset, and cert-manager renews certificates automatically ~30 days before expiry. Resource limits, by contrast, are container-spec settings: cpu_request/memory_request are what Kubernetes reserves for scheduling and cpu_limit/memory_limit are enforced ceilings (the container is OOM-killed if memory_limit is exceeded); all four default to None and take values like "250m"/"1000m" and "256Mi"/"2Gi" with Ki/Mi/Gi or K/M/G suffixes.
In the resource-limits TOML example, what happens to the container if it exceeds memory_limit = "2Gi", and what are cpu_request = "250m" and memory_request = "256Mi" used for?

Exceeding the memory ceiling gets the container OOM-killed -- Kubernetes uses limits for enforcement. The request values are used for scheduling: cpu_request reserves CPU units and memory_request reserves memory when placing the pod. cpu_limit = "1000m" caps the maximum CPU the container may use. All four keys default to None, and values accept binary suffixes (Ki, Mi, Gi) or decimal ones (K, M, G).
What endpoint do the Kubernetes readiness and liveness probes hit, and what are the default probe timings?

Both probes issue GET <health_check_path> on the container. Defaults: readiness_initial_delay 10 seconds before the first readiness check with readiness_period 20 seconds between checks; liveness_initial_delay 10 and liveness_period 20 likewise; and liveness_failure_threshold 80 consecutive failures before the pod is restarted. The docs' tip is to set health_check_path = "/health" to use the built-in liveness and readiness endpoints.
What metric drives jac-scale's Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, what are its default bounds, and what prerequisite does the HPA have?

The HPA scales the application pod count based on average CPU utilization across all pods, with defaults min_replicas = 1, max_replicas = 3, and cpu_utilization_target = 50 (%). The prerequisite: cpu_request must be set -- without a CPU request, Kubernetes cannot compute a utilization percentage. The example shows raising the bounds to 2-10 replicas with a 70% target.
Compare overriding container images with adding additional_packages: what problem does each solve and what trade-off do the docs flag for packages?

The image keys swap base images -- python_image (default python:3.12-slim) for the application pod and busybox_image (default busybox:1.36) for the init container that runs dependency health checks -- which you override when you need a specific Python version or operate air-gapped. additional_packages (default []) instead installs extra pip packages (e.g. pandas, scikit-learn, python-dotenv) into the pod at startup, alongside the standard Jaseci stack, before the application starts. The flagged trade-off: startup-time installs slow boot, so for frequently-updated packages the docs recommend building a custom Docker image with --build to keep startup times short.
Given additional_packages = ["pandas", "scikit-learn", "python-dotenv"] in jac.toml, when are these packages installed, and what alternative do the docs suggest for frequently-updated packages?

They are installed into the pod at startup, before the application starts, alongside the standard Jaseci stack (the default is [] -- no extras). For frequently-updated packages the docs recommend building a custom Docker image with --build instead, to keep startup times short.
Under --experimental mode, where are Jaseci packages installed from, and which keys pin the source?

They are installed from the GitHub repository instead of PyPI. jaseci_repo_url (default https://github.com/jaseci-labs/jaseci.git) selects the repository, jaseci_branch (default main) the branch, and jaseci_commit (default None -- empty means latest of the branch) pins a specific commit SHA for reproducible builds, e.g. jaseci_branch = "develop" with jaseci_commit = "a1b2c3d4".
In the [plugins.scale.kubernetes.plugin_versions] table, what do the values "latest", a version string, and "none" each mean, and which packages can be pinned?

A version string like "0.1.5" pins that exact PyPI version, "latest" (the default for all packages) installs the newest from PyPI, and "none" skips installing the package entirely. The pinnable packages are jaclang (core Jac language runtime), jac_scale (the scaling plugin itself), jac_client (frontend/client support), jac_byllm (LLM integration, settable to "none" to exclude), and jac_mcp (the optional MCP server plugin).
A team wants metrics dashboards plus pod-log search in Grafana on their jac-scale deployment. Which config sections do they enable, and which components appear for logs?

Enable [plugins.scale.monitoring] enabled = true (deploying Prometheus, Grafana, kube-state-metrics, and node-exporter, and exposing the app's /metrics endpoint; k8s_metrics_enabled = true keeps the two exporters) and set loki_enabled = true under [plugins.scale.kubernetes] for logs. The log pipeline adds Loki -- a single-process log store on port 3100, ClusterIP, with filesystem/TSDB storage on an emptyDir volume so logs are ephemeral (suitable for dev/staging) -- and Grafana Alloy, a DaemonSet on every node (tolerating NoSchedule taints) that tails /var/log/pods, labels streams with namespace/pod/container, and pushes to Loki; Alloy is the OpenTelemetry-compatible successor to Promtail, which went EOL 2026-03-02. A Pod Logs dashboard (log volume plus a live log viewer) is added to Grafana automatically; Grafana is served at /grafana with admin / prometheus_admin_password (default Adminpassword123).
Both jac status and the managed: jac-scale label help you inspect a deployment -- what does each surface, and how do Degraded and Restarting differ in the status output?

jac status app.jac shows live health per component (Jaseci App, Redis, MongoDB, Prometheus, Grafana) with ready/total pod readiness counts and service URLs, using status values Running (all pods ready), Degraded (some pods ready, others not), Pending (starting up), Restarting (one or more pods crash-looping), Failed (no pods running), and Not Deployed (never provisioned) -- so Degraded means partial readiness while Restarting specifically means crash-looping pods. The managed: jac-scale label is the complementary audit mechanism: every resource jac-scale creates carries it, so kubectl can enumerate them all regardless of health.
What label does jac-scale put on every Kubernetes resource it creates, and what is it for?
The label managed: jac-scale. It exists for easy auditing -- all resources created by jac-scale carry it so they can be listed with a kubectl label selector.
What kubectl command lists every jac-scale-managed resource across all namespaces, and which resource types carry the tag?
kubectl get all -l managed=jac-scale -A. The tagged resource types are Deployments, StatefulSets, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, PersistentVolumeClaims, and HorizontalPodAutoscalers.
What does jac destroy app.jac remove, and what safeguard precedes the deletion?

You are first prompted to confirm with y before deletion proceeds. It then deletes the entire namespace and all its resources -- the application Deployment and pods, the Redis and MongoDB StatefulSets, the PersistentVolumeClaims (so the data is lost), and the Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, and HPA.
When configuring Kubernetes probes for a jac-scale app, which built-in endpoints map to the liveness and readiness probes?
/health is the built-in endpoint for the liveness probe and /ready for the readiness probe. If those aren't sufficient, you can also create custom health walkers, as the docs go on to show.
How does the simple health walker differ from the ready walker in what each verifies and reports?

The health walker is unconditional: its check ability just reports {"status": "healthy"} and is accessed at POST /walker/health. The ready walker actually verifies dependencies: it calls check_database() and check_cache(), reports {"status": "ready"} only when both are ok, and otherwise reports {"status": "not_ready"} along with the individual db and cache boolean results so you can see which dependency failed.
In the ready walker example, what does the reported payload contain when the cache check fails but the database check passes?

Since db_ok and cache_ok is false, the else branch reports {"status": "not_ready", "db": true, "cache": false} -- the walker includes each dependency's boolean (db_ok from check_database(), cache_ok from check_cache()) so the failing component is identifiable. Only when both checks pass does it report {"status": "ready"}.
According to the CLI commands table, which command enables HTTPS on a live jac-scale deployment without requiring a redeploy?

`jac start app.jac --scale --enable-tls` enables HTTPS on a live deployment with no redeploy. By contrast, `jac start app.jac --scale` deploys to Kubernetes, `--build` builds the image and deploys, and `jac destroy app.jac` removes the Kubernetes deployment (prompting for confirmation).
When the jac-scale server is running, at which three local URLs can you access the API documentation, and what does each serve?
Swagger UI is served at `http://localhost:8000/docs`, ReDoc at `http://localhost:8000/redoc`, and the raw OpenAPI JSON at `http://localhost:8000/openapi.json`.

The Prometheus Metrics overview says a `/metrics` endpoint is 'automatically registered' when metrics are enabled. What does the Configuration excerpt add about whether this happens out of the box, and how is the metrics namespace determined if you don't set one?

It does not happen out of the box: the `enabled` option under `[plugins.scale.monitoring]` defaults to `false`, so you must set `enabled = true` in `jac.toml` before metrics collection and the `/metrics` endpoint are activated (the endpoint path itself defaults to `"/metrics"` but can be changed via `endpoint`). If `namespace` is not set, it is derived from the Kubernetes namespace config (sanitized) or defaults to `"jac_scale"`.

Your Prometheus scraper hits `http://localhost:8000/metrics` and keeps receiving a 403 Forbidden response. Based on the excerpt, what is the correct way to make the scrape succeed, and why does the server behave this way?

The scrape must send the admin token as a bearer credential, e.g. `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <admin_token>" http://localhost:8000/metrics`. Unauthenticated requests receive a 403 Forbidden response by design — this protects sensitive server performance data from unauthorized access.
The `/admin/metrics` endpoint and the `[plugins.scale.secrets]` section both involve operating a jac-scale app — how do their purposes differ?

They serve entirely different concerns. `/admin/metrics` is an observability feature: it returns parsed metrics as structured JSON (a `metrics` list plus a `summary` with `total_requests`, `avg_latency_ms`, `error_rate_percent`, and `active_requests`), backing the admin portal's monitoring page that shows HTTP traffic breakdown, latency statistics, an active-requests gauge, and system metrics like GC collections, memory usage, CPU time, and file descriptors. `[plugins.scale.secrets]`, in contrast, is a deployment-configuration feature for managing sensitive environment variables securely in Kubernetes deployments.
Which section of `jac.toml` is used to manage sensitive environment variables securely in Kubernetes deployments?
The `[plugins.scale.secrets]` section.
Which environment variables can override the `[plugins.scale.sandbox]` settings from `jac.toml`, and what is the overall configuration priority?

Three environment variables override jac.toml: `JAC_SANDBOX_TYPE` (the provider type — `"kubernetes"`, `"docker"`, or `"local"`), `JAC_SANDBOX_NAMESPACE` (the Kubernetes namespace), and `JAC_SANDBOX_DOMAIN` (the domain template). The configuration priority is: environment variables > `jac.toml` > defaults.

Both the secrets deployment workflow and the `image_registry` setting read `${ENV_VAR}` values from the local environment at deploy time — but for what different purposes, and what manual step does each eliminate or still leave to you?

In the first excerpt, you `export` secret values (like `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `MONGO_PASSWORD`, `JWT_SECRET`) locally before `jac start app.jac --scale --build` so they get injected into the deployment; this eliminates the need for manual `kubectl create secret` commands after deployment. In the second, `image_registry = "${ECR_REGISTRY}"` under `[plugins.scale.kubernetes]` uses `${ENV_VAR}` interpolation just to keep registry URLs out of source control, telling jac-scale where to push the built image before manifest apply on remote clusters. Unlike the secrets flow, registry authentication is still left entirely to you (`docker login`, ECR `get-login-password`, GCR service account, etc.) — `jac-scale` does not manage registry credentials.

In the Remote Image Registry example, what would go wrong if you deployed to a remote EKS cluster with the `image_registry = "${ECR_REGISTRY}"` line removed from `jac.toml`, and why does the same omission not matter on Minikube?

For remote clusters (EKS, GKE, AKS, etc.), `image_registry` must be set — they pull images from a registry rather than loading them from a local container runtime, so without it the image cannot be tagged as `<image_registry>/<app_name>:dev-<sha12>` and pushed before `kubectl apply`. On local clusters like Minikube, Docker Desktop, k3d, or kind, an unset `image_registry` is fine because the built image is loaded directly into the cluster's runtime (`minikube image load`, `k3d image import`, `kind load docker-image`). The `<sha12>` tag suffix is a content hash of the source tree, so rebuilds change the tag and trigger an automatic rolling update.

When you set `service_account_name = "myapp-sa"` under `[plugins.scale.kubernetes]`, does jac-scale create that ServiceAccount for you? What must already exist, and what happens if the field is left unset?

No — `jac-scale` references the SA but does not create it. Both the ServiceAccount itself and any RoleBindings or ClusterRoleBindings it needs must already exist in the target namespace before deploy, typically managed by your platform layer (a Helm chart, Terraform module, or `kubectl apply` of cluster-scoped policy). When the field is unset or empty, pods fall back to the namespace's `default` ServiceAccount.
In a jac-scale shared-volumes entry, what is the `host_path` field for, and where is it safe to use?

`host_path` is the local-cluster-only alternative to PVC mode: it binds the volume to a directory on the host node instead of provisioning a PVC. It should be used only on k3d, kind, or Minikube, because it will not survive a pod move on multi-node clusters. PVC mode and hostPath mode are mutually exclusive per shared-volume entry.

A team wants each backend module of their Jac app to run as its own independently scalable workload in Kubernetes, with a single front pod routing traffic to each one. Which jac-scale configuration achieves this, and what resources are created?

They should set `[plugins.scale.microservices].enabled = true` and run `jac start --scale` against a Kubernetes cluster. In that mode, every entry in `[plugins.scale.microservices.routes]` becomes its own Deployment + Service + HPA + PodDisruptionBudget, giving each module independent scaling, while the gateway runs as a separate pod that fronts every microservice via its routes prefix.

Per-service configuration lets you merge extra env vars into a pod spec, and K-track auto-injects `JAC_SV_<MODULE>_URL` peer URLs — what happens if these two mechanisms collide, and what is the sanctioned way to point a peer at a non-cluster URL?

They cannot collide by design: in the `env` dict under `[plugins.scale.microservices.services.<name>]`, the keys `JAC_SV_NAME` and `JAC_SV_*_URL` are protected and cannot be overridden. The auto-injected peer URLs are derived by K-track from `[plugins.scale.microservices.routes]` and the configured namespace (format `http://<peer>-service.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local:<container_port>`), and a stale override would silently route sv-to-sv calls to a wrong backend. If you need a peer to point at a non-cluster URL, such as a vendor SaaS, the right way is to edit the Deployment env spec directly after deploy.

Reading the per-service configuration table, if you deploy an LLM-worker microservice without setting `rpc_timeout` and without any `hpa` settings, what behavior do you get, and what does the table recommend changing?

The service gets the defaults: `rpc_timeout` defaults to 10 seconds, which is fine for CRUD but too short for LLM workers — the table says to bump it to 120-300s for LLM workloads. It also starts with `replicas` = 1 (the HPA can scale higher) and the HPA targets 70% CPU utilization by default (`hpa.cpu_target`). To pin the replica count instead, you would set `hpa.enabled = false`, which fixes replicas at the configured `replicas` count.
In the example that scales `jac_coder_sv` hot during LLM workloads while fixing the gateway at 2, what settings does each of the two service entries receive?

`[plugins.scale.microservices.services.jac_coder_sv]` gets `rpc_timeout = 300.0` and an enabled HPA with `min = 2`, `max = 10`, and `cpu_target = 60`. `[plugins.scale.microservices.services.__gateway__]` gets `replicas = 2` with `hpa = { enabled = false }`, so the gateway stays fixed at 2 replicas instead of autoscaling.
When centralised logs are enabled in jac-scale microservice mode, what does Grafana Alloy run as, and what does it do with pod logs?

Grafana Alloy runs as a DaemonSet on every node (tolerating `NoSchedule`). It tails `/var/log/pods`, labels each stream with `namespace`, `pod`, and `container`, and pushes the logs to Loki via Kubernetes service discovery. It uses River-syntax config and supersedes Promtail, which reaches EOL on 2026-03-02.

A developer wants the simplest way to get a local Kubernetes cluster running on their laptop to try out jac-scale deployments. Which setup path does the documentation label as easiest, and what are the steps?

The Docker Desktop path, which the docs title 'Docker Desktop (Easiest)'. The steps are: install Docker Desktop, open Settings > Kubernetes, check 'Enable Kubernetes', and click 'Apply & Restart'. This gives a local cluster with no separate installation steps beyond Docker Desktop's own settings toggle.
In the two commands `kubectl logs -l app=mongodb` and `kubectl logs -l app=redis`, what does the `-l` flag accomplish, and which logs does each command retrieve?

The `-l` flag selects pods by label rather than by naming a specific pod: `app=mongodb` matches the MongoDB database pods and `app=redis` matches the Redis pods. So the first command retrieves the MongoDB database logs and the second retrieves the Redis logs.
According to the troubleshooting guidance for build failures in `--build` mode, what three things should you check?
Ensure the Docker daemon is running, verify that `.env` has the correct `DOCKER_USERNAME` and `DOCKER_PASSWORD`, and check that there is enough disk space for image building.
What command does the documentation give for checking Kubernetes events ordered by time?
`kubectl get events --sort-by='.lastTimestamp'` — it lists cluster events sorted by their last timestamp.

A team with a large existing Python codebase wants Jac's node/walker features but refuses to introduce `.jac` files, and they rely heavily on IDE autocomplete and type checking. Which deployment approach fits, and how would they define a walker?

Library Mode. It lets them use Python files with Jac's runtime as a library: all Jac features are accessible through `jaclang.lib` imports (e.g. `Node`, `Walker`, `spawn`, `root`, `on_entry`), using pure Python syntax with decorators like `@on_entry` and `@on_exit`. A walker is a Python class subclassing `Walker` with a decorated method — as in the example, `class TaskFinder(Walker)` with an `@on_entry` method `find(self, here: Task)`, launched via `spawn(TaskFinder(), root())`. It offers full IDE/tooling support (autocomplete, type checking, debugging) and zero migration friction for existing Python projects.

The two sandbox excerpts describe the same system at different levels — what does the first tell you sandboxes are for, and what does the second add about how you'd choose between the three providers?

The first excerpt covers purpose: sandboxes are isolated, ephemeral preview environments where each sandbox runs a user's Jac application in its own container or pod with resource limits, network isolation, and automatic cleanup — ideal for live preview, collaborative editing, or CI/CD preview deployments. The second covers architecture and selection: the system follows jac-scale's factory pattern (an abstract `SandboxEnvironment` interface, provider chosen via configuration, factory handles instantiation), with `local` giving subprocess isolation for local development with no container runtime, `docker` giving container isolation for staging, and `kubernetes` giving pod isolation for production with resource limits and RBAC.
To create and manage sandboxes programmatically in Jac code, what do you import and from which module?
You import `SandboxFactory` from `jac_scale.factories.sandbox_factory`, using the statement `import from jac_scale.factories.sandbox_factory { SandboxFactory }`.
You need a Kubernetes-backed sandbox that gets more memory than usual and is cleaned up after only 30 minutes. Based on the excerpt, how do you create it?

Use `SandboxFactory.create` with an explicit type and config dict, as the example shows: `SandboxFactory.create("kubernetes", {...})` passing `"memory_limit": "1Gi"` for the larger memory allowance and `"ttl_seconds": 1800` for the 30-minute lifetime, along with `"namespace": "jac-sandboxes"`, `"base_image": "python:3.12-slim"`, and `"domain_template": "{sandbox_id}.preview.example.com"`. Passing the explicit `"kubernetes"` type plus the config dict overrides the values that would otherwise apply.
Compare what `sandbox.create(...)` and `sandbox.status(...)` each take and give back in the two examples.

`sandbox.create` takes the identity and content of what to run — `user_id`, `project_id`, and `code_path` — and returns a result whose `success` flag you check before reading `result.url` (where the sandbox is ready) and `result.sandbox_id`. `sandbox.status` goes the other direction: it takes an existing sandbox id (e.g. `"jac-sbx-abc123"`, the kind of id `create` returned) and returns a status whose `state` field is one of `pending`, `starting`, `running`, `stopped`, or `error`.
What are the possible values of `status.state` when you call `sandbox.status("jac-sbx-abc123")`?
The state can be `pending`, `starting`, `running`, `stopped`, or `error`, as listed in the comment next to the `print(f"State: {status.state}")` line.
What argument does `sandbox.list_sandboxes` take in the example, and which fields are printed for each returned sandbox?

It takes a user id — `sandbox.list_sandboxes("user-123")` — and returns that user's sandboxes. The loop prints each sandbox's `sandbox_id`, `state`, and `url` (`f"{s.sandbox_id}: {s.state} - {s.url}"`).
What does `sandbox.cleanup_expired()` do, and what does its return value represent in the example?

It cleans up sandboxes that have expired beyond their TTL, and it returns the number of sandboxes it cleaned — the example stores that in `cleaned` and prints `f"Cleaned {cleaned} expired sandboxes"`.

You have a sandbox already running a user's project and need your Jac code to inspect and modify the project's files inside it without recreating the sandbox. Which capability does the documentation point to?

The sandbox File Operations API: the excerpt states you can read, write, and manage files inside a running sandbox, invoked from Jac code inside a `with entry { ... }` block. This is the right fit because it operates directly on the files of an already-running sandbox rather than requiring a new environment.
How do the signatures and results of `sandbox.write_file` and `sandbox.read_file` differ in the two examples?

`sandbox.write_file` takes three arguments — the sandbox id (`"jac-sbx-abc123"`), the file name (`"main.jac"`), and the content string to write (`"with entry { print('hello'); }"`) — and is called for its effect. `sandbox.read_file` takes only the sandbox id and file name, and returns a result you read from: the file's text is accessed as `result["content"]`, as shown by `print(result["content"])`.
When you use `sandbox.read_file` to read a binary file such as `assets/logo.png`, in what encoding is the file returned?
Binary files like images are returned as base64. The example reads the image with `sandbox.read_file("jac-sbx-abc123", "assets/logo.png")`, the same call used for text files.
What two arguments does `sandbox.delete_file` take in the example?
The sandbox id and the file to remove: `sandbox.delete_file("jac-sbx-abc123", "old_file.jac")` deletes `old_file.jac` from the sandbox identified as `jac-sbx-abc123`.

A developer calls `sandbox.list_files("jac-sbx-abc123")` and is surprised that `node_modules/` never shows up in `result["files"]`; they then try to read `/etc/passwd` and `../config` from the sandbox and both requests fail. What explains each behavior?

Both are deliberate, documented behaviors. File listing automatically skips the excluded directories `.jac/`, `node_modules/`, `__pycache__/`, `dist/`, and `.git/`, so `node_modules/` is filtered out by design. The failed reads are path security: all file paths are validated against directory traversal, absolute paths, and shell metacharacters — paths like `../`, `/etc/passwd`, or strings containing `;`, `|`, `&`, or a backtick are rejected.
`sandbox.exec_command` and `sandbox.logs` both take a sandbox id — how do their other parameters and their results differ?

`sandbox.exec_command("jac-sbx-abc123", "ls -la /app", timeout=30)` runs a specific shell command inside the sandbox with a timeout, and you read the command's output from `result["stdout"]`. `sandbox.logs("jac-sbx-abc123", offset=0)` instead retrieves the sandbox's existing log output starting from an offset, and its text is read from `result["content"]`. So one executes something new and captures stdout; the other fetches already-produced logs.
In the log retrieval example `result = sandbox.logs("jac-sbx-abc123", offset=0)`, what does passing `offset=0` request, and which key of the result is printed?

`offset=0` requests the sandbox's logs from the very beginning rather than from some later position. The retrieved log text is then printed from the `"content"` key: `print(result["content"])`. The first argument identifies which sandbox's logs to fetch (`jac-sbx-abc123`).
In the sandbox states table, what is the difference between the `pending`, `starting`, and `running` states?

`pending` means the pod/container has been created and is waiting to start; `starting` means the container is starting and installing dependencies; and `running` means the application is fully ready and serving traffic. The remaining states are `stopping` (shutdown in progress), `stopped` (container stopped), and `error` (error or crash state).
How does the `local` sandbox provider allocate ports and determine that a sandbox is ready?

It allocates a port pair from a pool (base ports 5180-5200 with a stride of 2), runs `jac start --dev -p {port}` as a child process, and checks readiness by scanning the process output for the string "Server ready". It then returns `http://localhost:{port}` as the preview URL. Because sandboxes are just subprocesses on the host, there is no isolation between them, no resource limits, the port pool caps concurrent sandboxes (10 by default), and it is for development and testing only.

A team wants sandboxes for their staging environment with real isolation and resource limits, but they don't run Kubernetes — they only have a host with the Docker daemon running. Which sandbox provider fits, and what happens when a sandbox is created?

The `docker` provider (`type = "docker"` under `[plugins.scale.sandbox]`), which runs each sandbox in an isolated Docker container with resource limits — the only requirement is a running Docker daemon on the host. On creation it builds a container from `base_image` (e.g. `python:3.12-slim`), copies project files into `/app` via tarball injection, runs `jac install && jac start --dev -p 8000`, applies memory/CPU/storage limits (e.g. `memory_limit = "512Mi"`, `cpu_limit = "500m"`), optionally creates an isolated Docker bridge network per sandbox when `network_isolation = true`, and polls container health via HTTP until ready with a 120s timeout. Containers are labeled with `jac-sandbox`, `jac-sandbox-id`, `jac-sandbox-user`, and `jac-sandbox-project`.
Step 6 of the Kubernetes sandbox provider's flow says it 'creates a Service and Ingress (unless proxy_mode = true)'. How does the Ingress Routing excerpt frame this choice?

The Ingress Routing excerpt explains that when using `type = "kubernetes"`, sandboxes need to be accessible from the browser, and there are two routing modes for achieving that. The provider excerpt describes the default of the two: each sandbox gets its own Service and Ingress created as part of the provisioning flow (after the ConfigMap is unpacked into `/app` and `jac install && jac start --dev -p 8000` runs), before pod readiness is polled and the preview URL is returned. Setting `proxy_mode = true` selects the other routing mode, in which the per-sandbox Service and Ingress creation is skipped entirely.
In the default per-sandbox Ingress mode, which two Kubernetes resources are created for each sandbox and how are they named, and what drawback does the documentation note?

Each sandbox creates a `ClusterIP` Service named `{sandbox_id}-svc` and an Ingress resource named `{sandbox_id}-ingress` with the configured hostname (from `domain_template`, e.g. `{sandbox_id}.preview.example.com`). The drawback is that creating per-sandbox Ingress resources is slow on some cloud providers — for example, AWS ALB target group registration takes 30-60 seconds. (TLS can be auto-provisioned via cert-manager when `tls_enabled = true`, which requires a `ClusterIssuer` named by `tls_issuer` to be deployed in the cluster.)
In proxy mode, how does the shared proxy decide which sandbox pod an incoming request should reach?

The proxy watches all pods labeled `jac-sandbox=true` via the Kubernetes Watch API and maintains an in-memory routing table mapping `sandbox_id` to `{ip, phase, ready}`. For each incoming request it parses the `Host` header to extract the `sandbox_id` (e.g. `jac-sbx-abc.preview.example.com` yields `jac-sbx-abc`) and forwards the HTTP request to `http://{pod_ip}:8000{path}`. WebSocket connections are bidirectionally relayed, and no per-sandbox Ingress or Service is created in this mode.

Users of your Kubernetes-based sandbox service complain that every new sandbox takes about 10 seconds to appear because of pod scheduling and image pulls. Which feature addresses this, and how does it work?

The warm pool: set `warm_pool_size` (e.g. `warm_pool_size = 3` with `type = "kubernetes"`), which pre-creates idle pods ready to accept code instantly, eliminating the ~10 seconds of pod scheduling plus image pull time. On startup the provider creates that many pods from `base_image`; each runs a wait loop (`while [ ! -f /app/.jac-start ]; do sleep 0.5; done`). When a sandbox is requested, a warm pod is claimed and relabeled with the user's sandbox ID (its `jac-sandbox-pool` label flips from `warm` to `active`), project code is injected via `kubectl exec` as a tar stream — so no ConfigMap creation is needed — and touching the `/app/.jac-start` signal file triggers `jac install && jac start`. The pool replenishes automatically in the background, and if it is exhausted the provider falls back to the standard cold-start path (ConfigMap + new pod creation).
The HMR support excerpt and the 'pod stuck in Pending' excerpt both deal with sandbox pods — at which distinct point in a sandbox's life does each apply?

The HMR excerpt applies to a sandbox that is already up and being edited: with `proxy_mode = true`, Vite HMR flows Browser ↔ Proxy (WebSocket relay) ↔ Pod, with the proxy detecting `Upgrade: websocket` requests, forwarding the `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` header (e.g. `vite-hmr`), and relaying TEXT/BINARY messages with no timeout; the pods also carry `CHOKIDAR_USEPOLLING=1` and `WATCHPACK_POLLING=true` because files written via `kubectl exec` don't trigger inotify filesystem events. The Pending excerpt applies before the sandbox ever runs — the pod fails to start — and the remedy is diagnostic: run `kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n jac-sandboxes` and check the events for scheduling failures, insufficient resources, or image pull errors.
When a sandbox pod is stuck in Pending, what does the command `kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n jac-sandboxes` let you inspect, and which three kinds of problems should you look for?

It describes the stuck pod in the `jac-sandboxes` namespace (the `-n jac-sandboxes` flag targets the namespace where sandbox pods live, and `<pod-name>` is replaced with the actual pod's name). In its output you check the events for the three documented causes: scheduling failures, insufficient resources, or image pull errors.
What command checks whether a specific sandbox's pod is running, and which label selector does it use?
`kubectl get pods -n jac-sandboxes -l jac-sandbox-id=<sandbox-id>` — it queries the `jac-sandboxes` namespace and selects the pod by the `jac-sandbox-id` label set to the sandbox's id.
According to the pod-logs troubleshooting excerpt, what are the common causes of sandbox failure, and which container do you pull logs from?

The common causes are `jac install` failing (missing dependencies), a port conflict, or an application crash. You inspect them with `kubectl logs <pod-name> -n jac-sandboxes -c sandbox`, which targets the container named `sandbox` inside the pod.
How do the 'HMR not updating the preview' excerpt and the 'Check proxy logs' excerpt relate — what does each contribute to the troubleshooting flow?

The first names the symptom and the thing to verify: when HMR is not updating the preview, you need to verify that the proxy is forwarding WebSocket traffic. The second gives the concrete diagnostic command for looking at that proxy: `kubectl logs -l app=sandbox-proxy -n jac-sandboxes`, which selects the sandbox-proxy pods by their `app=sandbox-proxy` label in the `jac-sandboxes` namespace. So one states what to check, the other shows how to check it.
What is the command to view the sandbox proxy's logs, and how does it identify the proxy pods?
`kubectl logs -l app=sandbox-proxy -n jac-sandboxes` — it selects the proxy pods via the label selector `app=sandbox-proxy` within the `jac-sandboxes` namespace.
How do you verify that the sandbox proxy is healthy, according to the excerpt?
By curling its health endpoint: `curl http://<proxy-service>:8080/_proxy/health` — the proxy service listens on port 8080 and exposes health at the `/_proxy/health` path.
What command lists every sandbox pod, and what label do all sandbox pods share?
`kubectl get pods -n jac-sandboxes -l jac-sandbox=true` — all sandbox pods carry the `jac-sandbox=true` label, so this selector in the `jac-sandboxes` namespace returns them all.
What different kinds of help do the 'Related Resources' excerpt and the 'Delete all sandboxes' excerpt offer a jac-scale user?

The Related Resources excerpt is navigational: it points to further reading — the Local API Server Tutorial, the Kubernetes Deployment Tutorial, and the Backend Integration Tutorial — rather than performing anything itself. The Delete all sandboxes excerpt is operational: it gives an immediately runnable command, `kubectl delete pods -n jac-sandboxes -l jac-sandbox=true`, which removes every pod carrying the `jac-sandbox=true` label in the `jac-sandboxes` namespace.
In the Jac vs Traditional Stack comparison, what role does each of the three Jac constructs — nodes, walkers, and the `cl { }` block — play in a full-stack app?

Nodes are your data model, walkers are your API endpoints, and a `cl { }` block (or a `.cl.jac` file) holds your UI components — all written in a single file. This replaces what a traditional full-stack web application spreads across separate projects, frameworks, and glue code: a Python backend, a React frontend, an ORM, API route definitions, and serialization logic.
In the single-file fullstack Todo example, what do `has items` and `async can with entry` inside the `cl def:pub app()` component become in the generated JavaScript?

`has items` becomes `useState` in the generated JavaScript, and `async can with entry` becomes `useEffect(() => {...}, [])` for loading data on mount. In the same file, `node Todo` defines the data model with automatic persistence to a graph database, `def:pub get_todos` creates an HTTP API endpoint, and `await get_todos()` handles the HTTP request to the backend.
Which five technologies make up the traditional-stack implementation used for comparison with Jac?
Python, FastAPI, SQLite, TypeScript, and React — the equivalent functionality is built using these instead of a single Jac program.
In the traditional-stack backend, how do the responsibilities of `backend/database.py` and `backend/models.py` differ?

`database.py` handles connection plumbing: it configures the SQLite database connection (`sqlite:///./todos.db`), creates the SQLAlchemy engine, sets up session management via `SessionLocal`, and provides the `get_db()` dependency function for database access in API endpoints. `models.py` handles data shape — and notably defines the data structure twice: once as the SQLAlchemy model `TodoModel` (table `todos`, with `id`, `title`, `done` columns) for database operations, and once as the Pydantic schema `TodoResponse` for API response serialization. So one file manages how you talk to the database, the other defines what the data looks like in the database versus in API responses.
In `backend/models.py`, how do the fields of `TodoModel` and `TodoResponse` differ, and why does the file contain two classes for the same Todo data?

`TodoModel` is the SQLAlchemy model bound to the `todos` table with three columns — `id` (Integer, primary key, indexed), `title` (String, non-nullable), and `done` (Boolean, default `False`). `TodoResponse` is the Pydantic schema with only `title: str` and `done: bool` (no `id`), plus a `Config` with `from_attributes = True`. The two classes exist because the traditional stack defines the data structure twice: once as a SQLAlchemy model for database operations, and once as a Pydantic schema for API response serialization.
In `backend/main.py`, under what condition does the `lifespan` function seed initial data, and which three todos does it insert?

On startup, after `Base.metadata.create_all(bind=engine)` creates the tables, the lifespan function seeds data only if the database is empty — `if db.query(TodoModel).count() == 0`. In that case it adds three `TodoModel` rows: "build startup", "raise funding", and "change the world", all with `done=False`, then commits and closes the session. The app also configures CORS middleware allowing the frontend origin `http://localhost:5173`.
What three npm scripts does `frontend/package.json` define, and what does each run?

`dev` runs `vite` (development), `build` runs `tsc && vite build` (TypeScript compile then Vite build), and `preview` runs `vite preview`. The manifest also lists `react` and `react-dom` as dependencies and TypeScript, Vite, `@vitejs/plugin-react`, and the React type packages as devDependencies — it's the Node.js package manifest for the JavaScript/TypeScript side of the traditional stack.

In the traditional-stack Todo app, a developer wants the frontend build to reject unused variables and handle JSX without manual React imports. Which configuration file governs this, and which options are responsible?

`frontend/tsconfig.json`, which configures the TypeScript compiler with the target JavaScript version, module resolution strategy, JSX handling, and type-checking rules. The relevant compilerOptions are `"jsx": "react-jsx"` for JSX handling and the type-checking rules `"strict": true`, `"noUnusedLocals": true`, and `"noUnusedParameters": true` (alongside `"noFallthroughCasesInSwitch": true`). The file targets `ES2020`, uses `"moduleResolution": "bundler"`, includes only `src`, and references `./tsconfig.node.json`.
Why does the frontend need both `tsconfig.node.json` and `vite.config.ts`, and what distinct job does each do?

`tsconfig.node.json` is a separate TypeScript configuration specifically for Node.js-executed files like `vite.config.ts`, which run in a different environment than browser code — it sets `composite: true`, `moduleResolution: "bundler"`, `allowSyntheticDefaultImports`, and includes only `vite.config.ts`. `vite.config.ts` itself is the build-tool configuration: it registers the React plugin (`plugins: [react()]`), sets the dev server to port 5173, and configures a development proxy that forwards `/api` requests to the backend at `http://localhost:8000` with `changeOrigin: true`. So one file type-checks the config script; the other configures how Vite serves and builds the app.
In `frontend/vite.config.ts`, what would stop working if the `proxy` block were deleted from the `server` section?

The development proxy that forwards `/api` requests from the Vite dev server (running on port 5173) to the backend server at `http://localhost:8000` would be gone, so frontend calls to `/api` paths would no longer reach the backend during development. The `changeOrigin: true` setting is part of that forwarding. The rest of the file — `defineConfig` with `plugins: [react()]` — only provides React plugin support and would be unaffected.
What two things does the `<body>` of `frontend/index.html` contain, and what is each for?

It contains `
`, the root DOM element where React mounts, and ``, which loads the TypeScript entry point. Together they make the file the HTML entry point of the app.
What does `frontend/src/types.ts` define, and what maintenance obligation does the documentation attach to it?

It defines the TypeScript interface `Todo` with two fields, `title: string` and `done: boolean`. The documentation notes these frontend type definitions must be kept in sync with the backend Pydantic schemas — a manual obligation of the traditional stack.

In the traditional-stack frontend, a React component needs the todo list from the backend, but you don't want raw `fetch` calls and error handling scattered through component code. What pattern does the codebase use for this?

An API client function, as in `frontend/src/api.ts`: `getTodos()` wraps the `fetch('/api/todos')` call, checks `response.ok` and throws `Error('Failed to fetch todos')` on failure, and returns `response.json()` typed as `Promise<Todo[]>` (importing the `Todo` type from `./types`). Components call this one function instead of dealing with HTTP requests and error checking themselves — that centralization is exactly the file's stated purpose.
How do the jobs of `frontend/src/App.tsx` and `frontend/src/main.tsx` differ in the React frontend?

`App.tsx` is the main component with the actual behavior: it manages state with `useState<Todo[]>`, loads data on mount with a `useEffect` that awaits `getTodos()` and calls `setItems`, and renders the todo list as divs with a checkbox per item (keyed by `item.title`, `checked={item.done}`, `readOnly`). `main.tsx` is only the application entry point: it calls `ReactDOM.createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!)` and renders `<App />` wrapped in `<React.StrictMode>`, mounting the App component into the DOM root element. One defines what the app does; the other bootstraps it into the page.
In `frontend/src/main.tsx`, which DOM element does the app mount into, and what wraps the `App` component in the render call?

`ReactDOM.createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!)` mounts into the DOM element with id `root`, and `<App />` is rendered wrapped in `<React.StrictMode>`. This file is the React application entry point whose sole job is mounting the App component into the DOM root element.
According to the 'What Each Approach Requires' table, what are the Jac equivalents of the traditional stack's `useState` hook, `useEffect` hook, and Pydantic serialization schema?

React state setup done with the `useState` hook becomes a `has` declaration in Jac; the data loading `useEffect` hook becomes `can with entry`; and the API serialization schema that requires Pydantic in the traditional stack is automatic in Jac. The table similarly maps the ORM model to a `node` declaration, the decorator-based API route definition to `def:pub`, and lists API client code as 'Automatic RPC' in Jac.
According to the header of the Jac Library Mode page, which part of the documentation does it belong to, and which related pages does it link?
It is part of 'Part IX: Deployment' (the jac-scale plugin section), and its related links are 'Python Integration' and 'Part III: OSP'.

An enterprise Python team adopts Jac via library mode and writes `spawn` calls that pass the bare name `root` as the starting location, mirroring what they saw in `.jac` examples. Why is that wrong in library mode, and what is the correct form?

In library mode, `root` is a Python function imported from `jaclang.lib`, so it must be called as `root()` — the bare reference is just the function object, not the root node. The same applies to the other graph builtins (`spawn`, `connect`, `get_all_root`). The convention they copied belongs to `.jac` source, where the rule is reversed: there `root` is a reserved keyword and writing `root()` emits warning W0062 (deprecated; use bare `root`). Library mode itself is exactly the fit for this team — it exposes all Jac language features as standard Python through the `jaclang.lib` package, and is designed for Python-first teams, existing Python codebases, and enterprise environments where adopting a standard Python library is more acceptable than new language syntax.
What different roles do the `jac jac2py` excerpt and the Friends Network excerpt play in learning library mode?

The `jac jac2py` excerpt describes a tool: the command transpiles Jac source files into equivalent Python code whose output provides clean, ergonomic imports from `jaclang.lib` with full IDE autocomplete, idiomatic Python with proper type hints and docstrings, and full compatibility with Python tooling, linters, formatters, and static analyzers. The Friends Network excerpt introduces a teaching example instead: a section that demonstrates Jac's object-spatial programming model through a complete example implementation in library mode. One is the conversion mechanism; the other is a worked demonstration of the result.
What does the Friends Network Example section demonstrate?
It demonstrates Jac's object-spatial programming model through a complete example implementation in library mode.
In the social network example, which two archetypes define an `announce` ability that triggers on `FriendFinder` entry, and what does each print?

The `Person` node defines `can announce with FriendFinder entry` printing `f"{visitor} is checking me out"`, and the `Family` edge defines the same ability printing `f"{visitor} is traveling to family member"`. The `Friend` edge is declared empty (`edge Friend {}`), with no ability. `Person` also carries a `has name: str` field.
You have `friends.jac` and want a pure-Python version of it that your IDE understands. What command does the documentation give, and what does the generated code look like?

Run `jac jac2py friends.jac`. The generated Python imports the needed symbols from `jaclang.lib` (`Edge`, `Node`, `OPath`, `Root`, `Walker`, `build_edge`, `connect`, `on_entry`, `refs`, `root`, `spawn`, `visit`) and re-expresses the archetypes as classes: `Person` inherits from `Node` with a `name: str` attribute and an `@on_entry` method `announce(self, visitor: FriendFinder)` printing `f"{visitor} is checking me out"`; `Friend` is an empty `Edge` subclass; and `Family` is an `Edge` subclass whose `@on_entry` `announce` prints `f"{visitor} is traveling to family member"`.
Comparing the 'Nodes and Edges' mapping excerpt with the full library-mode graph-building excerpt, what does each cover about working with the graph in Python?

The 'Nodes and Edges' excerpt covers declaration only: `node Person { has name: str; }` becomes `class Person(Node)` with the standard annotated class attribute `name: str`, and `edge Friend {}` becomes `class Friend(Edge): pass` — nodes inherit from the `Node` base class, relationships from `Edge`. The graph-building excerpt covers usage of those declarations: instances are wired with `connect(left=root(), right=p1)` and `connect(left=p2, right=[p1, p3], edge=Family)`, traversal is written as a `Walker` subclass whose `@on_entry` methods call `visit(self, refs(OPath(here).edge_out()...))` (including filtering Family edges with `edge=lambda i: isinstance(i, Family)`), and execution starts with `spawn(FriendFinder(), root())`. It also adds the note that the transpiler internally emits `from jaclang.jac0core.jaclib import ...`, while the public `jaclang.lib` API re-exports the same symbols and is the recommended import path.
In the library-mode Python version of the nodes-and-edges example, what corresponds to the Jac declaration `has name: str;`, and how are the node and edge types expressed?

The `has name: str;` field becomes a standard Python class attribute with a type annotation — `name: str` — on the class. The node type is expressed as `class Person(Node)` (graph nodes inherit from the `Node` base class imported from `jaclang.lib`) and the edge type as `class Friend(Edge): pass` (relationships between nodes inherit from the `Edge` base class).
How does the Jac walker declaration `walker FriendFinder { has started: bool = False; }` translate into library mode, and what are walkers according to the excerpt?

In library mode it becomes a Python class inheriting from the `Walker` base class imported from `jaclang.lib`: `class FriendFinder(Walker):` with the `has` field expressed as a class attribute `started: bool = False`. Walkers are graph traversal agents — they navigate through the graph structure and execute logic at each visited node or edge.
In Jac abilities, what do the `here` and `visitor` parameters represent, and which decorators mark entry and exit handlers in library mode?

`here` represents the current node or edge being visited, and `visitor` (in node/edge abilities) represents the traversing walker. In library mode, the `@on_entry` decorator marks methods that execute when a walker enters a node or edge, while `@on_exit` marks exit handlers — as in the example where `can report_friend with Person entry` becomes an `@on_entry` method `report_friend(self, here: Person)`.
Working in library mode, you need to link Susan's node to both John's and Mike's nodes with a typed Family relationship in one call. What is the right approach?

Use `connect()` with a list of targets and the `edge` parameter: `connect(left=p2, right=[p1, p3], edge=Family)` — the library-mode equivalent of the Jac statement `p2 +>: Family :+> [p1, p3];`. This works because `connect()` creates directed edges between nodes, its `edge` parameter specifies the edge type class (defaulting to a generic edge if omitted), and the function explicitly supports connecting a single source node to either a single target node or a list of target nodes.
In library mode, how does `spawn()` differ from `visit()` in when and why each is used during a walker's life?
