`spawn()` starts the whole traversal: `spawn(FriendFinder(), root())` initiates a walker at a specified node (with `root()` returning the root node of the current graph) and returns the walker instance after traversal completion — the library equivalent of `FriendFinder() spawn root`. `visit()` operates during the traversal, from inside an ability: it marks a constructed path for the walker to traverse next, e.g. `visit(self, refs(OPath(here).edge_out().visit()))` for all outgoing edges, where `OPath()` builds the path from the current node, `edge_out()` selects outgoing edges, `.edge()` can restrict the path to edges only, and `refs()` converts the path into concrete node or edge references. So `spawn()` begins the run at one node; `visit()` extends the itinerary as the walker moves.
In the library-mode traversal example, how does the second `visit` call differ from the first, and what role does the `.edge()` method play in it?

The first call, `visit(self, refs(OPath(here).edge_out().visit()))`, visits all outgoing edges — the equivalent of Jac's `visit [-->]`. The second call adds a type filter, `edge_out(edge=lambda i: isinstance(i, Family))`, so only `Family` edges are followed — the equivalent of `visit [->:Family:->]`. Its `.edge()` method filters the path to include only edges, excluding destination nodes; without it the path would not be restricted to the edges themselves. In both cases `.visit()` marks the constructed path for the walker to traverse and `refs()` converts it into concrete node or edge references.
According to the API Scope Notice, which core functions are guaranteed to be importable via `from jaclang.lib import ...`, and what caveat applies to the rest of the reference?

The core importable functions are `connect`, `disconnect`, `spawn`, `root`, `node`, `edge`, `walker`, `obj`, `Anchor`, `NodeAnchor`, `EdgeAnchor`, `WalkerAnchor`, and `Root`. The caveat is that the reference mixes these public API functions with internal runtime functions that may not be directly importable — the other listed functions may be internal to the runtime and subject to change.
In the library-mode type aliases and constants table, what is `TYPE_CHECKING` used for, and what values does the `EdgeDir` enum hold?

`TYPE_CHECKING` is a bool — the Python typing constant for type checking blocks — used in `if TYPE_CHECKING { ... }` guards to break circular imports for type-only references. `EdgeDir` is the edge direction enum with values IN, OUT, and ANY. The table also lists `DSFunc`, the object spatial function type alias.

Building a library-mode app, you need (a) a class representing an entity in the graph, (b) a class representing a typed relationship, (c) an agent that traverses the graph, and (d) a way to express a traversal path like 'outgoing edges from this node'. Which base class serves each need?

(a) Inherit from `Node`, the graph node archetype (`class MyNode(Node):`); (b) inherit from `Edge`, the graph edge archetype (`class MyEdge(Edge):`); (c) inherit from `Walker`, the graph traversal agent (`class MyWalker(Walker):`); and (d) use `OPath`, the object-spatial path builder, as in `OPath(node).edge_out()`. The table also provides `Root` as the root node type serving as the graph entry point, `GenericEdge` as the default edge type when no type is specified, and `Obj` as the generic base class for all archetypes.
What do the `edge`, `undir`, `conn_assign`, and `edges_only` parameters of the library-mode `connect()` function control?

`edge` is the optional edge class to use for the connection, `undir` is the undirected flag, `conn_assign` supplies attribute assignments, and `edges_only` makes the call return edges instead of nodes. The required `left` and `right` parameters are the source node(s) and target node(s) being connected.
In the graph traversal and walker operations table, which function stops a walker's traversal, and which converts an ObjectSpatialPath into node/edge references?

`disengage(walker)` stops the walker's traversal, and `refs(path)` converts an ObjectSpatialPath into concrete node/edge references (with `arefs(path)` listed as the async placeholder version). The table also distinguishes the public `spawn(walker, node)`, which starts a walker at a node, from the internal `spawn_call`/`async_spawn_call` execution functions that operate on anchors.
On the `OPath` class, what is the difference between `.edge_out(edge, node)` and `.edge()`?

`.edge_out(edge, node)` filters the path to outgoing edges, whereas `.edge()` restricts the path to edges only, excluding nodes. Both return Self and are chainable, like the rest of the OPath methods: `.edge_in` filters incoming edges, `.edge_any` filters any direction, and `.visit()` marks the path for visit traversal. `OPath(node)` itself creates the ObjectSpatialPath starting from a node.
Your library-mode code needs to completely sever a relationship so that neither endpoint node keeps it, not just drop it from one side. Which node/edge operation applies?

`detach(edge)`, which detaches the edge (an EdgeAnchor) from both nodes — the right choice when the relationship must be fully severed. By contrast, `remove_edge(node, edge)` only removes the edge reference from one node (it takes a NodeAnchor plus the EdgeAnchor), so it does not clear the other endpoint. The read-side counterparts in the same table are `get_edges` (edges connected to nodes), `get_edges_with_node` (edges plus their connected nodes), and `edges_to_nodes` (the nodes reached via edges).
How do the Data Access & Persistence functions differ in purpose from the Access Control & Permissions functions in library mode?

The persistence group manages the data itself and its lifecycle: `root()`/`get_all_root()` fetch root nodes, `get_object(id)` and `object_ref(obj)` translate between archetypes and ID strings, `save(obj)` persists an archetype to the database, `destroy(objs)` deletes archetypes from memory, `commit(anchor)` commits data to the datasource, and `reset_graph(root)` purges the graph from memory (returning a count of deleted items). The access-control group instead governs who may use that data: `perm_grant(archetype, level)` grants public access at an AccessLevel of READ, CONNECT, or WRITE, `perm_revoke` removes it, `allow_root`/`disallow_root` scope access to a specific root UUID, and the `check_read_access`/`check_write_access`/`check_connect_access`/`check_access_level` functions test an anchor's permissions.
Which library-mode functions list the archetypes contained in a loaded module, and what does each take?

`list_nodes(module_name)`, `list_walkers(module_name)`, and `list_edges(module_name)` list the nodes, walkers, and edges in a module respectively, each taking the module name to inspect. `list_modules()` lists the names of all loaded modules. Related functions in the same table let you fetch a specific class with `get_archetype(module_name, archetype_name)` or instantiate by name with `spawn_node`/`spawn_walker` (node/walker class name, an attributes init dict, and the source module).
The Runtime & Threading table and the Type Hints excerpt serve library-mode developers in different ways — how?

The Runtime & Threading table is an API reference for runtime plumbing: `setup()` initializes class references, `get_context()` returns the current ExecutionContext, `field(factory, init)` defines a dataclass field, `impl_patch_filename(file_loc)` patches a function's file location for stack traces, `thread_run(func, *args)` runs a function in a thread with `thread_wait(future)` awaiting its completion, and `create_cmd()` is a CLI-command placeholder. The Type Hints excerpt is instead a coding guideline: always use type hints for better IDE support, illustrated by `class Person(Node):` declaring `name: str` and `age: Optional[int] = None` with `Optional` imported from `typing`. One documents callable runtime functions; the other prescribes how you should write your own classes.
In the type-hints example, what does the declaration `age: Optional[int] = None` on `class Person(Node)` express, and why does the example annotate fields this way?

It declares `age` as an optional integer field — typed `Optional[int]` (with `Optional` imported from `typing`) and defaulting to `None` — alongside the required `name: str` field. The example annotates every field because the guidance is to always use type hints for better IDE support.
According to the Path Filtering section, what construct should you use to get flexible filtering when building traversal paths?
Lambda functions — the section's guidance is to use lambda functions for flexible filtering.
The node-attribute filtering snippet and the 'Good' import line address two different aspects of library-mode code — which aspect does each cover?

The first covers traversal logic at runtime: `visit(self, refs(OPath(here).edge_out(node=lambda n: hasattr(n, "active") and n.active).visit()))` filters by the destination node rather than the edge, following outgoing edges only to nodes that have an `active` attribute set to a truthy value. The second covers import hygiene: the line labeled 'Good' — `from jaclang.lib import Node, Walker, spawn, visit, on_entry` — shows the recommended way to pull the needed symbols from the `jaclang.lib` package.
In the import line the documentation labels 'Good', which symbols are imported and from which package?
`Node`, `Walker`, `spawn`, `visit`, and `on_entry`, all imported from `jaclang.lib` in a single statement: `from jaclang.lib import Node, Walker, spawn, visit, on_entry`.
According to the Jac-to-library-mode mapping table, what are the Python equivalents of `visit [-->]`, `visit [<--]`, and `visit [--]`?

`visit [-->]` becomes `visit(self, refs(OPath(here).edge_out().visit()))`, `visit [<--]` becomes `visit(self, refs(OPath(here).edge_in().visit()))`, and `visit [--]` becomes `visit(self, refs(OPath(here).edge_any().visit()))` — outgoing, incoming, and any-direction edges respectively. The same table maps `disengage;` to `disengage(self)` and `W() spawn root` to `spawn(W(), root())`.
What five advantages does the summary attribute to Jac's library mode?

(1) Complete Feature Parity — all Jac language features are accessible through the library interface; (2) Idiomatic Python — standard Python classes, decorators, and functions without runtime magic; (3) Full Tooling Support — generated code includes proper type hints, enabling IDE autocomplete, static analysis, and debugging; (4) Seamless Integration — the library fits into existing Python projects without build system modifications; and (5) Maintainable Output — transpiled code is readable and follows Python best practices. Overall it delivers Jac's graph-native, AI-integrated programming model through the `jaclang.lib` package while staying fully compatible with the Python ecosystem.

You want your AI coding assistant to be able to write, validate, format, and debug Jac code with real knowledge of the language rather than guessing. Which Jac plugin addresses this, and how does it work?

The `jac-mcp` plugin. It provides a Model Context Protocol server that gives AI assistants deep knowledge of the Jac language by exposing grammar specifications, documentation, code examples, compiler tools, and prompt templates through a standardized protocol. Because the protocol is standardized, any MCP-compatible AI client can then write, validate, format, and debug Jac code.
What is the difference between what the Installation excerpt and the 'Start the MCP server' excerpt have you do with jac-mcp?

The Installation excerpt is about getting the plugin onto your system: if you installed Jaseci via PyPI or the install script, `jac-mcp` is likely already included — you verify with `jac --version`, which prints all installed plugins — and only if it's missing do you run `pip install jac-mcp`. The other excerpt is about running it once installed: `jac mcp` starts the server with the default stdio transport, ready for IDE integration.
What happens when you run the bare command `jac mcp` with no additional flags?
It starts the MCP server using the default stdio transport, ready for IDE integration — no transport needs to be specified for this default behavior.
What does the command `jac mcp --inspect` do?
It prints all available resources, tools, and prompts, then exits — it does not keep a server running.
After starting the jac-mcp server, what does step 3 say you must do before your AI assistant can use Jac tools?
Add the server to your AI client's MCP configuration (the IDE Integration section covers how); once configured, you can start using Jac tools directly from your AI assistant.
Your MCP client is browser-based and must reach the jac-mcp server over HTTP instead of stdio. Per the IDE Integration docs, how do you start the server and where does the client connect?

Use the Remote/SSE setup: start the server with `jac mcp --transport sse --port 3001`, then configure the client to connect to the SSE endpoint `http://127.0.0.1:3001/sse` (event stream) and the message endpoint `http://127.0.0.1:3001/messages/` (POST). This differs from the IDE configs (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Claude Code, etc.), which all launch `jac` with args `["mcp"]` over stdio. The docs also add a tip that applies in either mode: if the `jac` binary lives in a virtualenv, put its full path (e.g. `/path/to/venv/bin/jac`, found with `which jac`) in the `command` field.
The jac-mcp server can be tuned via `jac mcp [OPTIONS]` flags or via `jac.toml` — when does each apply?

The CLI Reference describes per-invocation flags passed when launching the server: `--transport` (default `stdio`, alternatives `sse` or `streamable-http`), `--port` (default `3001`) and `--host` (default `127.0.0.1`) for the SSE/HTTP transports, and `--inspect` (default `false`) to print the inventory of resources, tools, and prompts then exit. The Configuration excerpt instead covers persistent per-project customization: you add a `[plugins.mcp]` section to your project's `jac.toml` to customize the server, so settings live with the project rather than being retyped on each command.
In the configuration example, which file and which section header do you add to customize the jac-mcp server for a project?
You add the settings to the project's `jac.toml` file, under the `[plugins.mcp]` TOML section shown in the example — that is where server customization lives.
In the jac-mcp transport settings, what are the default values of `transport`, `port`, and `host`, and which transports do the port and host apply to?

`transport` defaults to `"stdio"` (the alternatives are `"sse"` and `"streamable-http"`), `port` defaults to `3001`, and `host` defaults to `"127.0.0.1"`. The `port` and `host` settings apply to the SSE/HTTP transports — the port for serving and the host as the bind address.
What four resource-exposure flags does the jac-mcp configuration provide, and what does each expose?

`expose_grammar` exposes `jac.spec` and token definitions; `expose_docs` exposes the language documentation; `expose_examples` exposes example Jac projects; and `expose_pitfalls` exposes the common AI mistakes guide. All four are shown set to `true` in the excerpt.
An AI client connected to jac-mcp can validate, format, and convert Python code to Jac, but the `get_ast` tool never appears. Based on the tool enable/disable settings, why, and what is the fix?

`get_ast` is governed by `enable_ast`, which defaults to `false` because the tool is verbose — it is off by default. The fix is setting `enable_ast = true`. The other tools appear because their switches default to `true`: `enable_validate` covers the `validate_jac` and `check_syntax` tools, `enable_format` covers `format_jac`, and `enable_py2jac` covers the `py_to_jac` conversion tool.
How does the `project_root` setting differ in what it controls from the transport options of the jac-mcp server?

`project_root` (default `"."`) controls what the server's project-aware tools operate on — the root directory they use. The transport options instead control how clients connect to the server: `--transport stdio` is the default for IDE integration (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Claude Code); `--transport sse` serves browser-based clients and remote access via `GET /sse` for the event stream and `POST /messages/` for client messages; and `--transport streamable-http` serves advanced HTTP clients and load-balanced deployments via `POST /mcp` bidirectional streaming. None of the transports have special requirements.
Which jac-mcp transport is recommended for load-balanced deployments, and what endpoint does it use?

Streamable HTTP (`--transport streamable-http`), intended for advanced HTTP clients and load-balanced deployments; it uses a single `POST /mcp` endpoint with bidirectional streaming. By contrast, SSE (for browser-based clients and remote access) uses `GET /sse` for the event stream plus `POST /messages/` for client messages, and stdio is the default for IDE integration with Claude Desktop, Cursor, and Claude Code.

An AI assistant is onboarding a developer who has never touched Jac: the developer needs to install it, understand what makes it different, and build a first project. Which jac-mcp getting-started resources should the assistant load for each need?

`jac://docs/install` for the installation guide, `jac://docs/core-concepts` for what makes Jac different, and `jac://docs/first-app` for the 'Build an AI Day Planner' tutorial as the first project. The assistant could also pull `jac://docs/welcome` for general getting-started orientation, `jac://docs/cheatsheet` as a quick syntax reference while coding, and `jac://docs/faq` for frequently asked questions — each URI in the Getting Started table maps to one of these onboarding needs.

Object-Spatial Programming appears in both the Language Specification resources and the Language Tutorials resources — how do the two resource groups differ, and which URI would you load in each case?

The Language Specification group is reference material: `jac://docs/osp` covers Object-Spatial Programming (nodes, edges, walkers) alongside other reference pages like `jac://docs/reference-overview` (full reference index), `jac://docs/functions-objects` (archetypes, abilities, has declarations), `jac://docs/concurrency` (flow, wait, async), and `jac://docs/advanced` (comprehensions and filters). The Language Tutorials group is guided learning instead: `jac://docs/tutorial-osp` is the graphs and walkers tutorial, with `jac://docs/tutorial-coding-primer` as a coding primer for beginners and `jac://docs/tutorial-basics` for language fundamentals. So for looking up OSP semantics you load `jac://docs/osp`; for learning OSP step by step you load `jac://docs/tutorial-osp`.
Among the AI-integration resources, which URI is the byLLM plugin reference, and what do the four AI tutorials cover?

`jac://docs/byllm` is the byLLM plugin reference. The tutorials are `jac://docs/tutorial-ai-quickstart` (your first AI function), `jac://docs/tutorial-ai-structured` (structured outputs), `jac://docs/tutorial-ai-agentic` (building AI agents), and `jac://docs/tutorial-ai-multimodal` (multimodal AI).
An AI assistant is asked to help move a Jac app from a laptop demo to a production Kubernetes cluster. Which deployment-and-scaling resources should it load, and why each?

It should load `jac://docs/tutorial-production-k8s`, the Kubernetes deployment tutorial, for the cluster deployment itself, and `jac://docs/jac-scale`, the jac-scale plugin reference, for the plugin that powers deployment and scaling. If the intermediate step is serving the app as a local API server first, `jac://docs/tutorial-production-local` covers local API server deployment.
What distinguishes the Developer Workflow resource group from the Python Integration resource group in jac-mcp?

The Developer Workflow group covers day-to-day Jac tooling and project practice: `jac://docs/cli` (CLI command reference), `jac://docs/config` (project configuration), `jac://docs/code-organization` (project structure guide), `jac://docs/mcp` (the MCP server reference itself), `jac://docs/testing` (test framework reference), and `jac://docs/debugging` (debugging techniques). The Python Integration group is specifically about bridging Jac with Python: `jac://docs/python-integration` covers Python interoperability, and `jac://docs/library-mode` covers using Jac as a Python library.
What are the two Python-integration resources served by jac-mcp, and what does each describe?
`jac://docs/python-integration`, which covers Python interoperability, and `jac://docs/library-mode`, which covers using Jac as a Python library.
In the Quick Reference resource group, what content do `jac://docs/walker-responses` and `jac://docs/appendices` provide?
`jac://docs/walker-responses` provides walker response patterns, and `jac://docs/appendices` provides additional language reference material.
In the Guides & Examples resources, where do the `jac://guide/*` URIs get their content from, and what do `jac://guide/pitfalls` and `jac://examples/*` specifically provide?

The `jac://guide/*` URIs serve curated reference guides from the compiler's bundled guide store — the same guides available via the `jac guide` command. `jac://guide/pitfalls` is the guide to common AI mistakes when writing Jac (and `jac://guide/patterns` gives idiomatic Jac code patterns), while `jac://examples/*` serves example Jac projects that are auto-discovered.
An AI model connected to jac-mcp doesn't just need reference text — it needs to actually run operations like validating and formatting the Jac code it writes. Which jac-mcp capability does it use?

Tools — the server exposes 19 of them, defined as executable operations that AI models can invoke to validate, format, and analyze Jac code. Because tools are invocable operations rather than passive material, they are what the model calls when it must act on code instead of merely reading context.
When should an AI client call `check_syntax` instead of `validate_jac`, and what does each tool actually run?

`validate_jac` performs full type-check validation — it runs the complete compilation pipeline including type checking — taking required `code` plus an optional `filename` for error messages (default `snippet.jac`), and returns a `valid` flag with `errors` and `warnings` arrays (each error carrying `line`, `col`, and `message`). `check_syntax` is a quick parse-only syntax check that skips type checking, which makes it faster than `validate_jac`; it takes only the required `code` string. So use `check_syntax` when you just need a fast parse verdict, and `validate_jac` when you need the full pipeline's type-checked result.
Why is the `check_syntax` tool faster than `validate_jac`, and what parameter does it require?
It is a quick parse-only syntax check that skips type checking, which is what makes it faster than `validate_jac`. Its single required parameter is `code`, the Jac source code string to check.
In `lint_jac` output, how can you tell a style violation apart from a compiler-level error, and what does setting `auto_fix: true` add?

Style violations (warnings) have no `severity` field, while only compiler-level errors include `"severity": "error"` — as in the example where the combinable consecutive `has` declarations violation has no severity but the "Unused variable 'x'" error does. Setting `auto_fix: true` (the default is `false`) makes the tool return corrected code alongside the violations: `fixed_code` holds the corrected source and `changed` becomes `true`, whereas without it `fixed_code` is `null` and `changed` is `false`.
What does the `format_jac` tool do, what parameter does it take, and what fields does its output contain?
You have a working Python function and want the equivalent Jac source instead. Which jac-mcp tool applies, and what do you pass and get back?

The `py_to_jac` tool, which converts Python code to Jac. You pass the required `python_code` string parameter, and the tool returns a JSON object with `jac_code` containing the converted Jac source — for example a greeting function comes back as `can greet(name: str) -> str {\n    return f"Hello, {name}!";\n}` — plus a `warnings` array (empty in the example).
How does the output of `jac_to_py` differ in fidelity from the output of `jac_to_js` for the same Jac source?

`jac_to_py` returns the generated Python source that the Jac compiler produces internally — a faithful artifact, e.g. `obj Foo` becomes `class Foo(Obj)` importing from `jaclang.jac0core.jaclib` with `from __future__ import annotations`. `jac_to_js` instead performs a lighter mapping: `obj` becomes an ES6 class, `def` a JavaScript function, and `node`/`walker` only simple class stubs, and the generated output is explicitly minimal — it does not include runtime helpers or execution scaffolding. Both take a required `code` parameter, and both report failures the same way: the code field (`python_code`/`js_code`) comes back empty and error messages go into the `warnings` field, which carries both warnings and compilation errors regardless of severity.
In the `jac_to_js` example, what JavaScript does `obj Foo { has x: int = 5; }` become, and how is the default value of `x` handled?

It becomes the ES6 class `class Foo` with a `constructor(props = {})` whose body sets `this.x = (props.hasOwnProperty("x") ? props.x : 5)` — so the default `5` applies only when no `x` is supplied in `props`. The accompanying `def greet` becomes a plain JavaScript function returning the template literal `` `Hello, ${name}!` ``. On a failed conversion, `js_code` is empty and the `warnings` array carries error messages with file, line, and column information (e.g. `snippet.jac, line 1, col 13: Missing '}'`).
Is the `category` parameter of the `list_examples` tool required, and what does the tool do?
No -- `category` is an optional string parameter that acts as a category filter. The `list_examples` tool lists the available Jac example categories.
A developer wants to pull down every `.jac` file belonging to a particular example category so they can study a complete working sample. Which tool should they call and what must they pass?

They should call the `get_example` tool, which gets all `.jac` files from an example category. It has one required string parameter, `name`, which must be set to the example category name they want to retrieve.
How do `search_docs` and `get_ast` differ in what they operate on and what they return, and what required parameter does each take?

`search_docs` performs a keyword search across all documentation resources and returns ranked snippets (each result includes a `uri`, `title`, `description`, `snippet`, and `score`); its required parameter is `query`, with an optional `limit` defaulting to 5. `get_ast` instead parses Jac source code and returns AST information; its required parameter is `code`, with an optional `format` of `tree` or `json` (default `tree`). So one searches docs by keywords, while the other analyzes code -- and `get_ast`, as a compiler tool, is additionally bound by the safety limits of a 100 KB maximum input size and a 10-second timeout per operation.
According to the `run_jac` documentation, what happens when the submitted code contains no `with entry {}` block and no valid entrypoint is provided?

Execution succeeds but produces no output -- the example shows empty `stdout` and `stderr` with `exit_code` 0. (Runtime errors, by contrast, are reported in the `error` field with `exit_code` 1, while `stderr` is typically empty.)
What does `graph_visualize` always include in its returned graph, even when the executed Jac code creates no edges?

It always produces a graph rooted at `Root()` -- a graph is always returned with at least a `Root()` node, even if no edges are created. The DOT output also includes styling and metadata (colors, labels), and `program_output` captures both program stdout and CLI/tool messages.
An AI agent has just connected to the Jac MCP server and needs to figure out which documentation pages exist before diving into any specific topic. Which tool should it call first, and why?

It should call `understand_jac_and_jaseci` first. That tool takes no parameters and returns the Jac & Jaseci knowledge map -- a Markdown document listing every available resource URI by topic, with a task-to-resource lookup table. The documented workflow is to call this first to discover what documentation is available, then fetch specific pages with `get_resource`.
When should you reach for `get_resource` versus `list_commands`, and how do their inputs differ?

`get_resource` fetches the full content of a Jac/Jaseci documentation resource -- a Markdown document -- and requires a `uri` parameter (e.g. `jac://docs/osp` or `jac://guide/pitfalls`); on failure it returns an `error` field along with the requested `uri`. `list_commands` serves a different discovery purpose: it takes no parameters and lists all available `jac` CLI commands, including those added by installed plugins, grouped by category, so you can find valid command names before calling `get_command` or `execute_command`. In short, use `get_resource` to read documentation by URI and `list_commands` to enumerate CLI commands.
In the example output of `list_commands` -- `{"commands": [...], "groups": [...], "total": 34}` -- what do the three fields represent, and what extra optional field may appear?

`commands` is the list of available `jac` CLI commands (including those added by installed plugins), `groups` reflects that commands are grouped by category, and `total` (34 in the example) is the total count of commands. Additionally, an optional `extended_by` field lists plugins that add arguments to a base command.
What are the four possible values of an argument's `kind` field in the output of `get_command`, and what does each mean?

The four kinds are `POSITIONAL` (a positional argument), `OPTION` (a named option such as `--flag`), `MULTI` (accepts multiple values, e.g. repeated or space-separated inputs), and `REMAINDER` (captures all remaining arguments).
What do the exit codes 0, 1, and 2 mean in the output of `execute_command`?

Exit codes follow standard CLI conventions: `0` means success, `1` means a runtime or execution failure, and `2` means a command usage or argument error. Errors are typically reported via `stderr` rather than the `error` field, which is primarily reserved for system-level failures such as timeouts.
A developer wants a ready-made, structured system prompt for a common Jac development task that automatically brings in the pitfalls guide as context. What should they use, and why does it fit?

They should use one of the prompt templates. Prompt templates provide structured system prompts for common Jac development tasks, and each prompt automatically loads the pitfalls guide and relevant reference material as context -- so the developer gets the task-specific prompt plus the pitfalls guidance without assembling it manually.
How do the `write_module` and `write_impl` prompts differ in what they generate and what inputs they require?

`write_module` generates a brand-new Jac module with an optional `.impl.jac` file; it requires `name` (the module name) and `purpose` (what the module does), with an optional `has_impl` flag that defaults to `true` for including the `.impl.jac` file. `write_impl` instead generates only a `.impl.jac` implementation file for declarations that already exist; its single required argument is `declarations` -- the content of the existing `.jac` declaration file. So `write_module` starts from a name and purpose, while `write_impl` starts from existing declaration code.
What is the required argument of the `write_impl` prompt, and what does the prompt generate?
The required argument is `declarations`, which is the content of the `.jac` declaration file. The prompt generates a `.impl.jac` implementation file for those existing declarations.
Which three arguments does the `write_walker` prompt require, and what does each specify?

All three arguments are required: `name` (the walker name), `purpose` (what the walker does), and `node_types` (the node types the walker should traverse). The prompt generates a walker with visit logic.
What does the `write_node` prompt generate, and what are its required arguments?
`write_node` generates a node archetype with `has` declarations. It requires two arguments: `name` (the node name) and `fields` (the field definitions).
You have finished a Jac module and now want generated test blocks covering several of its functions and abilities. Which prompt applies, and what must you supply?

The `write_test` prompt applies -- it generates test blocks for a module. You must supply both of its required arguments: `module_name` (the module to test) and `functions_to_test` (the functions/abilities to test).
Contrast the `write_ability` and `debug_error` prompts: when do you use each, and what inputs do they take?

`write_ability` is for generating new code -- it produces an ability (method) implementation and requires `name` (the ability name), `signature` (the type signature), and `purpose` (what it does). `debug_error` is for fixing existing code -- it debugs a Jac compilation error and requires `error_output` (the error message or messages) and `code` (the code that caused the error). Use `write_ability` when creating a method from a spec, and `debug_error` when you already have failing code and a compiler error to diagnose.
What two required arguments does the `debug_error` prompt take?
It requires `error_output` -- the error message(s) -- and `code` -- the code that caused the error. The prompt's purpose is to debug a Jac compilation error.
What is the purpose of the `fix_type_error` prompt and which arguments must be provided?
It fixes a type checking error in Jac code. Both of its arguments are required: `error_output` (the type error message) and `code` (the code with the type error).
What does the `migrate_python` prompt do, and what is its one required argument?
It converts Python code to idiomatic Jac. Its single required argument is `python_code`, the Python source code to convert.
A user installed Jac inside a virtualenv and their MCP client fails with "command not found: jac". What is the recommended fix, and how can they find the right value to use?

The `jac` binary is not on their PATH, so they should configure the client with the full path to the binary inside the virtualenv -- e.g. `"command": "/path/to/venv/bin/jac"` with `"args": ["mcp"]`. They can find that path with `which jac` or `python -m site --user-base`.
Two failure modes are described: the server connects but shows no tools, and tools return timeout errors. How does the diagnosis and fix differ between them?

They point at different layers. "Server connects but shows no tools" is a client-side loading issue: run `jac mcp --inspect` to verify the server itself is working, and if it shows tools but the AI client does not, restart the AI client, because most clients only load MCP servers at startup. Timeout errors, by contrast, are an input-size problem: the compiler bridge enforces a 10-second timeout per operation and a 100 KB maximum input size, so if your code is very large the fix is to split it into smaller files -- restarting the client will not help.
Why can tools return timeout errors, and what should you do if your code is very large?
The compiler bridge enforces a 10-second timeout per operation, and the maximum input size is 100 KB. If your code is very large, split it into smaller files.
Where are documentation resources read from in a development install versus a PyPI install, and what is the fix if resources are missing after a PyPI install?

Resource paths are resolved relative to the jaclang package installation. In a development install (`pip install -e`), resources are read directly from the repository's `docs/` directory; in a PyPI install, bundled copies are used. If resources are missing after a PyPI install, update to the latest version with `pip install --upgrade jac-mcp`.
What prerequisites does the "Build a Chess Engine" tutorial assume, and which four things does it say you will learn along the way?

It assumes familiarity with Native Compilation basics -- `na { }` blocks (or `.na.jac` files) and `with entry {}`. You will learn: how `jac run --autonative` auto-promotes compatible `.jac` files to native execution; how `jac nacompile` produces a standalone binary with no external toolchain; how `sys.argv` enables command-line argument parsing in native programs; and how declaration/implementation separation keeps large native programs organized. The source lives at `jac/examples/chess/` as `chess.jac` (declarations) and `chess.impl.jac` (implementations).
You want the chess engine to play automated random games by itself instead of waiting for interactive input -- which of its built-in capabilities applies, and how is it driven?

The `--benchmark` mode applies: the game ships with a `--benchmark` mode that plays automated random games. It is driven through command-line argument parsing via `sys.argv`, which is one of the engine's listed features alongside the full 8x8 board, legal move generation and validation, check/checkmate/stalemate detection, castling, en passant, pawn promotion, and position evaluation with center-control and development bonuses.

Step 1 of the tutorial says there are three ways to run the chess engine, each demonstrating a different part of the native pathway. What does Option A specifically demonstrate, and what are its execution characteristics?

Option A is standard Jac execution: `jac run jac/examples/chess/chess.jac`. Unlike the other options that showcase the native pathway itself, Option A runs the program on the Python backend, offering full compatibility and standard execution -- it is the baseline against which the other native run options are contrasted.
When you run the example command `jac run jac/examples/chess/chess.jac`, what backend executes the program and what properties does that give you?
The program runs on the Python backend, which gives full compatibility and standard execution.
With `jac run --autonative`, which compiler pass decides whether a program can be promoted to native execution, and what happens when the check fails?

The `NativeCompatCheckPass` walks the AST and verifies the program uses only native-supported constructs. If it passes, the compiler generates LLVM IR, JIT-compiles it, and executes natively. If it fails -- for example, the file uses walkers or `by llm()` -- execution falls back to Python transparently. The chess engine is fully native-compatible, so it gets JIT-compiled to machine code with no changes to the `.jac` file.
You want the chess engine to run automated random games instead of starting an interactive session. Based on how the engine accepts input, what do you pass and through what mechanism does it arrive?

Pass `--benchmark` (or its short form `-b`) on the command line. The chess engine accepts command-line arguments via `sys.argv`, so this flag switches it from interactive play to running automated random games.
How does invoking the chess benchmark differ between the autonative route and the compiled-binary route?

With autonative you run it through the Jac CLI, passing the program's flag after a `--` separator: `jac run --autonative jac/examples/chess/chess.jac -- --benchmark`. With the compiled binary you first build it with `jac nacompile jac/examples/chess/chess.jac -o chess` and then invoke the executable directly with the flag: `./chess --benchmark`. Both paths produce the same benchmark run -- e.g. `Running 10 games...` followed by per-game results and a summary such as White wins: 4, Black wins: 3, Draws: 3.
In the compiled-binary example, after running `jac nacompile jac/examples/chess/chess.jac -o chess` and then `./chess --benchmark`, what does the printed results summary show for the 10 games?

The output starts with `Running 10 games...`, lists each game's outcome (e.g. `Game 1: Black wins`, `Game 2: White wins`, `Game 3: Draw`), and ends with a `--- Results (10 games) ---` summary showing White wins: 4, Black wins: 3, and Draws: 3.
In the chess engine's project structure, what is the division of responsibility between `chess.jac` and `chess.impl.jac`, and how are the two files combined?

The project uses Jac's declaration/implementation separation -- the same pattern as header files in C, but built into the language. `chess.jac` holds the declarations (types, signatures, entry point) and defines *what* exists; `chess.impl.jac` holds the implementations (all method bodies) and defines *how* it works. The compiler links them together automatically, keeping the architecture scannable at a glance.
Which two enums open the chess engine's declaration file, and what members does each define?
The declaration file starts with `enum Color { WHITE = 0, BLACK = 1 }` and `enum PieceKind { PAWN = 0, KNIGHT = 1, BISHOP = 2, ROOK = 3, QUEEN = 4, KING = 5 }`.

In the chess engine, you need `Color.WHITE` to behave as a real `int` -- usable for arithmetic, indexing, or `int`-typed APIs -- rather than just as a dictionary key. Which enum form should you use and why?

Use the typed-base form: `enum Color: int { WHITE = 0, BLACK = 1 }`. The plain form `enum Color { WHITE = 0, BLACK = 1 }` works in the engine only because the members are used as dictionary keys (in globals like `WHITE_SYMBOLS` and `PIECE_VALUES`), where identity matters more than numeric value. The `: int` typed base desugars to Python's `IntEnum`, making members act as real ints (and `: str` desugars to `StrEnum`).
In the chess declaration file, what different roles do forward declarations (like `obj Board;`) and the Piece hierarchy declarations play?

Forward declarations such as `obj Board;` and `obj Piece;` let types reference each other before they are fully defined -- e.g. function signatures like `create_piece(kind: PieceKind, color: Color, row: int, col: int) -> Piece` can mention `Piece` early. The Piece hierarchy declarations, by contrast, lay out the actual type structure with clean signatures and no method bodies: the base `obj Piece` declares fields (`color`, `kind`, `pos`, `has_moved`) and method signatures like `raw_moves(board: Board) -> list[Move]`, while each subclass (`Pawn(Piece)`, `Knight(Piece)`, etc.) uses `override def raw_moves` to declare it replaces the base method, with the compiler generating vtables so the correct implementation runs based on the object's actual runtime type.
In the chess engine's entry point, what is `sys.argv`, and does its behavior differ between `jac run --autonative` and a compiled binary?

`sys.argv` is a `list[str]` where `argv[0]` is the program/binary name. The entry point loops over `range(1, len(_args))` looking for `--benchmark` or `-b` to set benchmark mode (10 games) versus interactive `game.play()`. It works identically whether you run with `jac run --autonative` or as a compiled binary.
According to Step 4 of the chess tutorial, where do all the method bodies of the chess engine live?
All method bodies live in the `impl` file, `chess.impl.jac`.
You are implementing move generation for the Bishop and the Rook in the chess engine. Rather than duplicating the ray-casting loop in each piece, what pattern does the codebase use?

The base `Piece` provides a shared `slide_moves(board, directions)` method, and each sliding piece just passes its own direction vectors: `Bishop.raw_moves` returns `self.slide_moves(board, [(-1, -1), (-1, 1), (1, -1), (1, 1)])` (diagonals) and `Rook.raw_moves` returns `self.slide_moves(board, [(-1, 0), (1, 0), (0, -1), (0, 1)])` (ranks and files). `slide_moves` itself walks each direction with tuple unpacking `(dr, dc) = d`, appending moves while squares are empty, appending a capture and breaking when it hits an enemy piece (`target.color != self.color`), and breaking immediately on a friendly piece.
Both `King.raw_moves` and `Board.postinit` use comprehensions in the chess engine -- but for different purposes. How does each use them?

`King.raw_moves` uses a list comprehension with nested loops and a filter to compute candidate squares: `[(row + dr, col + dc) for dr in [-1, 0, 1] for dc in [-1, 0, 1] if not (dr == 0 and dc == 0)]`, then checks each adjacent position for validity and whether the target square is empty or holds an enemy piece. `Board.postinit`, by contrast, uses a nested list comprehension to build the empty board -- `self.squares = [[None for _ in range(BOARD_SIZE)] for _ in range(BOARD_SIZE)]` -- inside a `postinit` hook that then calls `self.setup_pieces()`. One generates move candidates at query time; the other initializes the data structure when the Board object is constructed.
How does `Board.attacked_squares` compute the set of attacked squares, according to the excerpt?

It uses set comprehensions and set union: starting from an empty `set[tuple[int, int]]`, it iterates over `self.pieces_of(by_color)` and for each piece merges in the destinations of its raw moves with the union-assignment `attacked |= {m.to_pos for m in piece.raw_moves(self)}`, then returns the accumulated set.
Which bitwise operations does the chess engine use to manage castling rights?
Castling rights use bitwise flags manipulated with AND, OR, and NOT.
In the chess engine, when a king moves, both castling rights for that side must be removed at once. What bitwise pattern accomplishes this?

The code checks `piece.kind == PieceKind.KING` and then clears both flags for the moving side with an AND-NOT mask: for white, `self.castling_rights &= ~(CASTLE_WK | CASTLE_WQ);` and for black, `self.castling_rights &= ~(CASTLE_BK | CASTLE_BQ);`. OR-ing the two flags builds a combined mask, `~` inverts it, and `&=` clears exactly those bits while leaving the other side's rights untouched.
Compare what `Board.evaluate` and `Game.benchmark` each compute in the chess engine and how their outputs differ.

`Board.evaluate(color)` scores a single position: it scans every square, and for each piece sums a base material value from `PIECE_VALUES`, a center bonus of `base // 10` when the piece sits on center files (tested via `(1 << c & CENTER_MASK) != 0` with rows 2-5), and a development bonus of 8 for moved non-king pieces -- adding the total for pieces of the given color and subtracting it for opponents, returning a single `int` score. `Game.benchmark(num_games)` operates at a whole-games level: it runs N automated games, seeding each with `seed_random(i * 7919 + 42)` and calling `g.play_auto()`, tallies `white_wins`, `black_wins`, and `draws` from the returned result strings, and prints per-game lines plus a final results summary rather than returning a score.
In `Game.benchmark`, why does each iteration call `seed_random(i * 7919 + 42)` before `g.play_auto()`, and how does the method decide which counter to increment?

Each iteration constructs a fresh `Game()` and seeds the random generator with a value derived from the game index (`i * 7919 + 42`), so each of the `num_games` automated games runs with its own seed. The result string returned by `g.play_auto()` drives the tally: `"White"` increments `white_wins`, `"Black"` increments `black_wins`, and anything else counts as a draw (`draws += 1`). It prints a per-game line -- `f"Game {i + 1}: {result} wins"` unless the result is `"Draw"`, in which case it prints `f"Game {i + 1}: Draw"` -- and finishes with a `--- Results ---` block listing white wins, black wins, and draws.
What important property of Jac's native pathway does the chess engine demonstrate, according to Step 5?
The same `.jac` source file works across all three execution modes -- no changes to the source are needed to switch between them.
During development of a Jac program you want native speed when possible but zero code changes and a safe fallback if the code uses unsupported features. Which run mode fits, and why?

Use `jac run --autonative` (e.g. `jac run --autonative jac/examples/chess/chess.jac -- --benchmark`). The compiler analyzes the program at build time: if all code is native-compatible it JIT-compiles to machine code and runs natively; if not, it falls back to Python. No code changes are required -- the same `.jac` file works either way -- which is exactly why the excerpt calls it ideal during development: write normal Jac, add `--autonative` when you want native speed.
What does `jac nacompile` produce for the chess engine, and which of the features from the Feature Recap does the resulting program still exercise?

`jac nacompile jac/examples/chess/chess.jac -o chess` produces a self-contained standalone executable -- no Python needed at runtime and no external compiler or linker in the build; the binary includes everything from the LLVM-compiled machine code to the final ELF/Mach-O packaging. The program it packages exercises the full range of native Jac features listed in the recap, including declaration/impl separation (`chess.jac`/`chess.impl.jac`), enums, global dicts like `PIECE_VALUES`, hex/binary literals, single inheritance with vtables, forward declarations, comprehensions, union types (`Piece | None`), bitwise castling operations, the `postinit` hook, `import sys`/`sys.argv` for `--benchmark` parsing, and `input()` for interactive move entry.
According to the Feature Recap table, where does the chess engine use forward declarations, and which native feature powers the `Pawn(Piece)` and `Knight(Piece)` subclasses?
Forward declarations are used where `obj Board;` appears before `Piece` references it. The subclasses `Pawn(Piece)`, `Knight(Piece)`, etc. use single inheritance plus vtables (virtual dispatch).
What follow-up steps does the chess tutorial suggest after completing it?

Add a minimax AI opponent using the existing `evaluate()` method; run the benchmark with `./chess --benchmark` and compare Python vs native speed; explore C Library Interop to add a graphical interface using a library like raylib; and read the full source in `chess.jac` and `chess.impl.jac` on GitHub.

You are building a CLI utility that must run on machines without Python installed, and separately you have one numeric hot loop inside a larger Python-backed Jac app. Which of the two native-compilation usage modes fits each case?

For the CLI utility, use a standalone `.na.jac` file compiled with `jac nacompile` -- it produces a self-contained binary with no Python runtime, no external compiler, and no external linker, matching the doc's "standalone tools" and "single-binary deployment" use cases. For the hot loop, use an inline native section -- drop the native-compiled function into the application alongside Python-backed code using a `na { }` block (or `to na:` section header / `na` statement prefix); the compiler generates the interop layer automatically. Native compilation targets performance-critical hot paths like numeric computation, tight loops, and data processing.
According to the Quick Reference and the Native Sections description, how do the three in-file ways of selecting the native codespace differ in scope?

The `na { ... }` braced block (recommended) compiles every element inside the braces natively -- the braces bracket exactly the tagged region, and it also works inside inner scopes. The `to na:` section header makes every following module-level element compile native until the next `to X:` header or end of file, which is convenient for a module that is mostly native. The `na` single-statement prefix tags just one declaration. All three live inside a regular `.jac` file, as the Quick Reference notes, while a fully native program instead uses the dedicated `.na.jac` extension with `with entry { }` as the entry point for standalone binaries.
In a `.jac` file that mixes codespaces, what happens to functions inside a native section versus the rest of the file, and which of the three tagging forms is recommended?

Functions in a native section compile to native machine code while the rest of the file runs on Python as usual. The recommended form is the `na { ... }` braced block, where every element inside the braces compiles native and the braces bracket exactly the tagged region; the alternatives are the `to na:` section header (everything after it compiles native until the next `to X:` header or end of file) and the `na` single-statement prefix (tags one declaration).
In the mixed-codespace example, what is the signature of the standard Jac function that runs on Python?
`def process_data(items: list[dict]) -> list[dict]` -- it takes a list of dicts and returns a list of dicts, and per the heading it is standard Jac that runs on Python.
The example's native codespace contains `compute_checksum` and `fibonacci`. Why are these two functions good candidates for the native block?

Both are pure computation with no Python dependencies. `compute_checksum` is a tight loop over a `list[int]` accumulating `result = (result * 31 + val) % 1000000007` into a local declared with `has result: int = 0;`, and `fibonacci` is a recursive numeric function (`return fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2);` with the `n <= 1` base case). Per the heading, code in this section compiles to machine code, so hot numeric loops and recursion benefit from native execution.

The example shows `with entry` calling both `compute_checksum` and `fibonacci` seamlessly -- what makes that work, and which kinds of code does the "When to Use Native Sections" guidance say should stay in the Python codespace?

The compiler handles everything: native functions are JIT-compiled and callable from the Python side without any manual bridging -- you write one file and each codespace compiles to its own backend. Native sections are recommended for tight loops over numeric data, recursive algorithms (e.g. tree traversal, dynamic programming), data transformation on large collections, and functions with no Python library dependencies; conversely, if you need PyPI packages, that code should stay in the Python codespace.
What does "context isolation" mean for the Python and native codespaces at compile time?

Native-tagged functions are excluded from Python codegen, and Python functions are excluded from native IR -- each codespace only sees its own definitions at compile time. Cross-codespace calls go through the interop bridge.
When a single `.jac` file contains both Python and native-tagged code, what does the compiler generate to connect them?
The compiler generates interop stubs automatically, so the Python and native code in the same file can call each other without manual wiring.
Contrast the two native interop mechanisms shown: a native function calling a Python function within one file, versus imports between native modules. What does the compiler do in each case?

In the single-file case, `native_add_one_to_doubled` calls `py_double(x)` across the codespace boundary (printing 11 for input 5); the compiler generates a Python-callable stub for each native function, a native-callable callback for each Python function referenced from native code, and handles type marshalling at the boundary (int, float, str, bool). Interop works for all Jac types -- primitives, collections, and Jac `obj` classes -- with the sole boundary being Python-style classes that rely on monkey patching or dynamic attribute injection, which should stay in the Python codespace. Between native modules, by contrast, no runtime bridge is involved: native files can simply import from other native files.
What does the "Import Between Native Modules" example demonstrate about `.na.jac` files?
It demonstrates that native files can import from other native files -- one native Jac module can pull in definitions from another native module via an import.
What function does the `math_utils.na.jac` module define, and what does it return?
It defines `def square(x: int) -> int`, which returns `x * x`.
In `app.na.jac`, how is the `square` function brought in from the other native module, and how does the compiler link imported native modules?

With `import from math_utils { square }`, after which the entry block prints `f"5^2 = {square(5)}"`. The compiler links imported native modules at the IR level -- no dynamic library loading is needed.
You need a Jac program that runs on target machines with no Python installed at all. What file type and command does the documentation prescribe?
Write the program as a `.na.jac` file and compile it with `jac nacompile` -- this is the prescribed route for programs that should run without Python entirely.
What distinguishes a `.na.jac` file from a mixed `.jac` file in terms of what gets compiled, and how does the `hello.na.jac` example designate its entry point?

A `.na.jac` file is entirely native -- every function, object, and expression in it compiles to machine code, rather than only tagged sections. The program's entry point is a `with entry {}` block, as in the `hello.na.jac` example where `def greet(name: str) -> str` returns `f"Hello, {name}!"` and `with entry { print(greet("World")); }` runs at startup.
What does the `hello.na.jac` example print when run, and which two constructs produce that output?

It prints `Hello, World!`. The `greet(name: str) -> str` function builds the string with the f-string `f"Hello, {name}!"`, and the `with entry { print(greet("World")); }` block serves as the program entry point that calls it with `"World"`.
In `jac nacompile <filename> [-o <output>]`, what is the default output binary name if `-o` is omitted, and what external compiler or linker does the pipeline invoke?

The default output name is the input filename without its extension. No external compiler (gcc, clang) or linker (ld, lld) is invoked -- Jac's built-in compilation pipeline handles everything from LLVM IR generation through to the final binary format for your platform, producing a fully linked, self-contained executable. The example run also prints compilation stats (object size, binary size, target triple), and regular `.jac` files can be auto-promoted to native compilation if they only use native-compatible features and contain a `with entry {}` block.
What are the four stages of the native compilation pipeline, and which component performs each?

(1) Parsing & semantic analysis -- the standard Jac frontend, shared with the Python backend; (2) LLVM IR generation -- the `NaIRGenPass` walks the AST and emits LLVM IR using llvmlite's builder; (3) machine code emission -- llvmlite's MCJIT compiles the IR to a relocatable object for the host architecture; (4) binary packaging -- a built-in platform-aware linker produces the final executable (ELF on Linux, Mach-O on macOS) with no external tools required.

A native Jac function stores a large sequence of whole numbers and also passes text to another routine. Based on the primitive type mappings, how are `int` and `str` values represented in the generated LLVM code?

A Jac `int` maps to LLVM `i64` -- an 8-byte, 64-bit signed integer -- so each whole number occupies 8 bytes. A Jac `str` maps to `i8*`, a pointer to a null-terminated byte string. (For comparison, `float` maps to `f64` at 8 bytes, `bool` to `i1` at 1 bit, and `None` is represented as a null pointer.)
What different purposes do the fixed-width types and the collection internal layouts serve in native Jac?

The fixed-width types (`i8`/`u8` through `i64`/`u64`, `f32`, `f64`, and the opaque pointer `c_void`) exist for C interop and precise control over sizes -- e.g. `i32` is a 4-byte signed integer and `f32` a 4-byte single-precision float. The collection internals table instead documents how ordinary Jac collections are represented as LLVM struct types: `list[T]` is `{ i64 capacity, i64 len, T* data }`, `dict[K, V]` is `{ K* keys, V* values, i64 len }`, `set[T]` is `{ T* data, i64 len }`, and `tuple[T, ...]` is an LLVM literal struct with fields packed by type. One set of types is chosen explicitly by the programmer for ABI precision; the other describes the compiler's internal layout of standard collections.
What is the internal LLVM struct layout of `list[T]` in native Jac?

`list[T]` is represented as `{ i64 capacity, i64 len, T* data }` -- a capacity, a length, and a pointer to the element data. (By comparison, `dict[K, V]` is `{ K* keys, V* values, i64 len }`, `set[T]` is `{ T* data, i64 len }`, and tuples are LLVM literal structs with fields packed by type.)
What does the typed-base enum form add over a plain enum in native Jac's supported data types, per the Data Types table?

A typed-base enum like `enum HttpStatus: int { OK=200, NOT_FOUND=404 }` makes its members real `int` values, whereas a plain enum like `enum Color { RED=0, BLUE=1 }` does not. The table lists both alongside the other supported data types: integers, floats, strings, booleans, None (`x: int? = None;`), lists, dictionaries, sets, tuples, and objects (`obj Point { has x: int; }`).
Which control-flow constructs does the native feature table list as supported, with what syntax shapes?

If/elif/else (`if x > 0 { ... } elif x == 0 { ... } else { ... }`), while loops (`while x > 0 { x -= 1; }`), for-in over a range (`for i in range(10) { ... }`), for-in over a collection (`for item in items { ... }`), `break;` and `continue;`, and the ternary expression `x = a if condition else b;`.

You are designing an object in native Jac that needs a constructor, a follow-up setup step after construction, and a helper with an optional argument. Which function features from the table cover each need?

Use the `init` constructor (`def init(x: int) { self.x = x; }`) for construction; the `postinit` hook (`def postinit() { self.setup(); }`) for the follow-up setup step; and default parameters (`def bias(x: int, b: int = 100) -> int { ... }`) for the optional argument. The table also confirms free functions, methods using `self`, and recursion (`def fib(n: int) -> int { return fib(n-1) + fib(n-2); }`) are all supported natively.
The Operators table and the String Operations table both describe native capabilities -- what does each cover, and where do they touch on strings differently?

The Operators table covers general operator categories: arithmetic (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `//`, `%`, `**`), comparison, logical (`and`, `or`, `not`), bitwise (`&`, `|`, `^`, `<<`, `>>`), membership (`in`, `not in`), identity (`is`, `is not`), and augmented assignment (`+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `//=`, `%=`). The String Operations table is specific to string values: literals (`"hello"`, `'world'`), f-strings and raw f-strings (`f"value={x}"`, `rf"value={x}"`), concatenation with `s1 + s2`, `len(s)`, indexing `s[0]`, and methods like `strip()`, `split()`, `upper()`/`lower()`, `find()`, `startswith()`/`endswith()`, `join()`, `replace()`, and `count()`. They overlap only in that string concatenation reuses the `+` operator; everything else in the string table is method- or literal-level rather than operator-level.
Besides plain f-strings, what other f-string variant does native Jac support, and name four supported string methods from the table.

Raw f-strings are supported with the `rf` prefix, e.g. `rf"value={x}"`. Supported string methods include `strip()`, `split(sep)`, `upper()`/`lower()`, `find(sub)`, `startswith()`/`endswith()`, `join()` (e.g. `",".join(parts)`), `replace()`, and `count()`; indexing (`s[0]`), `len(s)`, and concatenation (`s1 + s2`) are also listed.
Which list operations does the native feature table list for mutation and for querying?

Mutation: indexing assignment (`items[i] = 5`), `append()`, `pop()`, `insert()`, `remove()`, `clear()`, `reverse()`, and `sort()`. Querying/other: literal creation `[1, 2, 3]`, indexing `items[0]`, `copy()`, `index(val)`, `len(items)`, membership with `val in items`, and comprehensions like `[x * 2 for x in items]`.
What dictionary operations are supported in native Jac according to the Dict Operations table?

Literal creation (`{"a": 1, "b": 2}`), get/set by key (`d[key]`, `d[key] = val`), `len(d)` and membership (`key in d`), the view methods `keys()`, `values()`, and `items()`, `get()` and `pop()`, `clear()`, `copy()`, and `update(other)`, plus dict comprehensions such as `{k: v * 2 for k, v in d.items()}`.
Compare native Jac's object-oriented features with its exception-handling features: what forms of inheritance-like behavior appear in each?

In OOP, inheritance is structural: single inheritance is written `obj Dog(Animal) { ... }`, and subclass methods override parent methods with virtual dispatch via vtables; objects also support `has` fields with defaults, `init` constructors, keyword or positional construction (`Point(x=10, y=20)` or `Point(10, 20)`), and chained access like `obj.inner.method()`. In exception handling, hierarchy shows up in catching: catching a parent exception type also catches its child types. The exception system supports `try/except`, `try/except/else`, `try/except/finally`, multiple handlers (`except ValueError { ... } except KeyError { ... }`), exception binding (`except ValueError as e`), nested try blocks, and `raise ValueError("bad input");`, over supported types such as `Exception`, `ValueError`, `TypeError`, `RuntimeError`, `ZeroDivisionError`, `IndexError`, `KeyError`, `OverflowError`, `AttributeError`, `AssertionError`, and `MemoryError`.
In native Jac exception handling, when does a `try/except/else` else-block run, and what does the exception hierarchy row say about catching parent types?

The else block runs when no exception is raised (while a `finally` block always runs). The exception hierarchy row states that catching a parent type catches child types. Supported exception types include `Exception`, `ValueError`, `TypeError`, `RuntimeError`, `ZeroDivisionError`, `IndexError`, `KeyError`, `OverflowError`, `AttributeError`, `AssertionError`, and `MemoryError`.
What must an object implement to act as a custom context manager in native Jac, and what file I/O features does the table list?

A custom context manager is an object with `__enter__()` and `__exit__()` methods. File I/O features include `open(path, mode)` (e.g. `f = open("data.txt", "r");`), `f.read()` and `f.readline()`, `f.write(data)` and `f.flush()`, `f.close()`, and the `with` statement form `with open("f.txt", "r") as f { ... }`.
Which builtin functions are available in native Jac according to the Builtin Functions table?

`print()` (multiple args, mixed types), `len()` (strings, lists, dicts, sets), `range()` (for-loop iteration), the numeric builtins `abs()`, `min()`, `max()`, and `pow()`, the character conversions `chr()` and `ord()`, the type conversions `str()` and `int()`, and `input()` for reading a line from stdin.
You are writing a native Jac CLI tool that must read its command-line flags and abort with a failure status when arguments are invalid. Which `sys` features apply, and how is `sys.argv` structured?

Use `import sys;` and read `sys.argv`, a `list[str]` where `argv[0]` is the program name and subsequent elements are the arguments passed on the command line; abort with `sys.exit(1);` to exit the process with a status code. The example shows the pattern: print `len(args)` as argc, loop `for i in range(1, len(args))` over the real arguments, and test flags with membership like `if "--verbose" in args`. This works both with `jac run --autonative` and standalone binaries compiled via `jac nacompile` -- e.g. `./cli_tool hello --verbose world` prints `argc: 4`, each arg, and `Verbose mode enabled`.
In C library interop, where must fixed-width types like `f64` be used, and where should you use standard Jac types instead?

Fixed-width types (`f64`, `i32`, `c_void`, etc.) are only needed inside the `import from` declaration itself, to match the C function's ABI signature -- as in `import from "/usr/lib/libm.so.6" { def sqrt(x: f64) -> f64; def pow(base: f64, exp: f64) -> f64; }`. Everywhere else -- your own functions, variables, and call sites -- you use standard Jac types (`int`, `float`, `str`, etc.), and the compiler handles coercion automatically. The example's `hypotenuse(a: float, b: float) -> float` shows this: it is declared with plain `float` yet calls the `f64`-signatured C functions `sqrt` and `pow` directly. This works for any shared C library, whether system libraries like libc and libm or third-party ones like raylib.
In the libm interop example, `hypotenuse` is declared with plain `float` parameters while `sqrt` and `pow` are declared with `f64`. Why does this compile, and what does `hypotenuse` compute?

It compiles because fixed-width types like `f64` are only needed inside the `import from "/usr/lib/libm.so.6"` declaration to match the C functions' ABI signatures; everywhere else you use standard Jac types and the compiler handles coercion automatically. `hypotenuse(a, b)` computes `sqrt(pow(a, 2.0) + pow(b, 2.0))` -- the hypotenuse from the two side lengths -- and the entry block prints `f"hypotenuse(3, 4) = {hypotenuse(3.0, 4.0)}"`.
In the raylib interop example, how are C-string parameters declared, and how do shared-library file extensions differ between macOS and Linux?

C-string parameters use `str` in the `import from` declaration; the compiler lowers `str` to the `i8*` ABI shape, and `i8*` itself is an internal LLVM type, not part of Jac's surface syntax. Library paths are platform-specific: macOS shared libraries use `.dylib` (e.g. `libraylib.dylib`) while Linux uses `.so` (e.g. `libraylib.so`); system libraries are typically at `/usr/lib/libSystem.B.dylib` on macOS or `/usr/lib/libm.so.6` on Linux. Any library exposing a C ABI can be called this way -- point to the shared library path and declare the function signatures.
Which platform/architecture combinations does native compilation currently support, and what happens automatically on Apple Silicon?

Linux x86_64, Linux aarch64, macOS x86_64, and macOS arm64 (Apple Silicon) are all supported. The platform and architecture are auto-detected at compile time, and the correct binary format (ELF on Linux, Mach-O on macOS) is produced automatically with no external compiler or linker needed. On Apple Silicon, ad-hoc code signing is applied automatically as required by macOS.

You are choosing between two native Jac program designs: a long-running daemon that continuously allocates deeply nested structures, and a short batch tool with bounded allocation. Given the current memory-management status, which design is safe and why?

The bounded-allocation batch tool is the safe choice. Native Jac uses automatic reference counting -- heap-allocated values (objects, strings, lists, dicts, sets) carry a count incremented on copy and decremented when a reference goes out of scope, freed at zero. However, deep release of nested structures is currently disabled to prevent use-after-free in complex ownership scenarios, so certain long-running native programs may leak memory. Programs with bounded allocation are unaffected; proper ownership tracking is a planned improvement.
`JAC_DUMP_IR` and the bytecode cache both figure into compiler debugging -- how does each work, and when do you use which?

`JAC_DUMP_IR` is for inspecting output: setting the environment variable, e.g. `JAC_DUMP_IR=/tmp/output.ll jac nacompile program.na.jac`, writes the generated LLVM IR to a human-readable `.ll` file you can open in a text editor or process with LLVM tools (`llc`, `opt`, `llvm-dis`). The bytecode cache is about stale state: the compiler caches compiled bytecode at `~/Library/Caches/jac/bytecode/` (macOS) or `~/.cache/jac/bytecode/` (Linux), and when modifying the compiler itself you must clear it (`rm -rf` the cache directory) to ensure your changes take effect. One dumps fresh IR for inspection; the other must be deleted so old compiled artifacts don't mask compiler changes.
The docs show `rm -rf ~/Library/Caches/jac/bytecode/` for macOS and `rm -rf ~/.cache/jac/bytecode/` for Linux. When is running one of these commands necessary, and what problem does it prevent?

It is necessary when modifying the Jac compiler itself: the compiler caches compiled bytecode at those platform-specific locations, so clearing the cache ensures your compiler changes actually take effect instead of stale cached bytecode being reused.
Name five Jac features that are not yet available in the native codespace and the documented reason for one of them, plus the recommended workaround.

Not yet available: walkers/nodes/edges (graph-spatial constructs require the Jac runtime), async/await (no async runtime in native code), generators (`yield`), lambda expressions, inline Python (`::py::`, since there is no Python interpreter in native binaries), decorators, multiple inheritance (single inheritance only), `by llm()` (requires the Python runtime for LLM calls), and PyPI imports (no Python ecosystem in native binaries). The recommended workaround: keep code needing those features in the Python codespace and use `na { }` blocks only for the performance-critical parts -- the compiler handles the interop automatically.
In the `fibonacci.na.jac` example, what is the base case of `fib`, and what does the entry block print?

The base case is `if n <= 1 { return n; }`; otherwise it returns `fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)`. The `with entry` block loops `for i in range(10)` and prints `f"fib({i}) = {fib(i)}"` -- the first ten Fibonacci values, fib(0) through fib(9).

In `animals.na.jac`, a `list[Animal]` holds `Dog` and `Cat` instances and the loop calls `animal.speak()` on each. Which language pattern makes the right sound come out for each element, and what gets printed?

The pattern is inheritance with method overriding (virtual dispatch): `Dog(Animal)` and `Cat(Animal)` each redefine `speak()`, so even though the list is typed `list[Animal]`, each call dispatches to the subclass implementation. The base `Animal.speak()` returns "...", but the loop prints the overridden results: `Rex says Woof!`, `Whiskers says Meow!`, and `Buddy says Woof!`, each built with an f-string over `self.name`.

After compiling `greeter.na.jac` with `jac nacompile greeter.na.jac -o greeter`, why does `./greeter World --shout` print `HELLO, WORLD!` in capitals, and what happens if you run `./greeter` with no arguments?

The program sets `name = args[1]` ("World") and `shout = "--shout" in args`, which is true, so instead of printing the plain `f"Hello, {name}!"` it prints `greeting.upper()` -- `HELLO, WORLD!`. With no arguments, `len(args) < 2` is true, so it prints `Usage: greeter <name> [--shout]` and exits with status 1 via `sys.exit(1);`.
In the mixed example's Python side, how is the `dumps` function obtained and used?

It is imported with `import from json { dumps }`, and the `serialize(data: dict) -> str` function returns `dumps(data)`. Per the heading, this Python side has full ecosystem access; the excerpt then opens a `na {` block for the native part.
What does the native-side `sum_squares` function compute, and how does the entry block use it?

`sum_squares(n)` declares a local accumulator with `has total: int = 0;`, loops `for i in range(n)` adding `i * i`, and returns the total -- the sum of squares below n, compiled to machine code per the heading. The entry block calls `result = sum_squares(1000);` and prints `f"Sum of squares: {result}"`.
A developer wants one complete, end-to-end example covering `--autonative`, `nacompile`, `sys.argv`, and declaration/implementation separation together. Where does the documentation point them?

To the "Build a Chess Engine" tutorial (`tutorials/native/chess.md`) -- a complete walkthrough that covers `--autonative`, `nacompile`, `sys.argv`, declaration/implementation separation, and nearly every other native feature.
How does Object-Spatial Programming model data and computation, and how does that differ from ordinary function calls?

OSP models data as graphs and computation as mobile agents called walkers that traverse the graph. Instead of calling functions on objects, walkers visit nodes and perform operations based on location.
What four reasons does the documentation give for using OSP?

Natural graph modeling (social networks, knowledge graphs, state machines); AI agent architecture (walkers are natural representations of AI agents); separation of concerns (data in nodes/edges kept separate from behavior in walkers); and spatial context (`here` and `visitor` provide natural context).
In the complete OSP example, the `Greeter` walker must greet every `Person` node reachable from root. How do its two abilities cooperate to achieve that?

The `greet` ability, declared `with Root entry`, runs when the walker starts at root and issues `visit [-->];` to move to the outgoing nodes. The `say_hello` ability, declared `with Person entry`, runs at each `Person` node: it prints `f"Hello, {here.name}!"` using `here` to access the current node's data, then issues `visit [-->];` again to continue to further nodes. Together they form the traversal pattern: a Root-entry ability launches the walk, and a typed Person-entry ability handles each visited node and keeps the traversal going. The graph itself uses `node Person` (with `name` and `age`) and `edge Knows` (with `since`).

The build-graph snippet uses two different connection operators, `root ++> alice` and `alice +>: Knows(since=2020) :+> bob`. Relate this to what the Nodes section says makes nodes different from regular objects.

The snippet shows the two ways nodes get connected: `root ++> alice` creates a plain connection from root to a node, while `alice +>: Knows(since=2020) :+> bob` connects via a typed `Knows` edge carrying data (`since=2020`). This is exactly the capability the Nodes section highlights: unlike regular objects, nodes can be connected via edges and participate in graph traversals. Nodes are the vertices of the graph -- "smart objects" that hold data (here `Person(name="Alice", age=30)` and `Person(name="Bob", age=25)`) and can have abilities that execute when walkers visit them.
According to the Nodes section, what distinguishes nodes from regular objects?

Nodes are the vertices of the graph -- they hold data and can have abilities that execute when walkers visit them, like "smart objects" that know when they're being visited and can react accordingly. Unlike regular objects, nodes can be connected via edges and participate in graph traversals.
In the `node Person` declaration example, what fields and ability does the node define?

It defines `has name: str;` and `has age: int = 0;` (age with a default of 0), plus a `greet` ability declared `can greet with Visitor entry` that prints `f"Hello from {self.name}"` when a Visitor walker enters.
What is the event clause syntax for node entry/exit abilities, and what happens if the TypeExpression is omitted?
The syntax is `can ability_name with [TypeExpression] (entry | exit) { ... }`. The `TypeExpression` is optional -- if omitted, the ability triggers for ALL walkers.
You want a node to log a message whenever any walker at all enters it, regardless of walker type. Which event clause form applies?
Use a generic entry ability with no type filter: `can on_enter with entry { print("Someone entered"); }`. Because the type expression is omitted, this triggers for ANY walker that enters the node.
In a node body, how does `can check_clearance with Inspector entry` differ from `can at_root with Root entry` in what triggers each?

Both are typed entry abilities filtered on the *walker's* type. `check_clearance` triggers only when a walker of type `Inspector` enters -- it then compares `visitor.clearance` against `self.clearance_required` and calls `disengage` with "Access denied" if too low. `at_root` triggers when a walker of type `Root` visits the node -- the excerpt stresses that `Root` here refers to the walker type, NOT the node type. The pattern is identical; only the walker type being matched differs, and neither fires for walkers of other types.
