If `import validators;` were removed, the walker's Jac-first logic could no longer reach the Python utility module -- the pattern's whole point is implementing primary application logic in Jac while importing Python utilities from separate `.py` files, so the validation helpers in `validators.py` would be unavailable to `TaskCreator`.
What is the use case for Pattern 4 (Mostly Python), and what does its `main.py` import from `jaclang.lib`?

Pattern 4 maintains a Python-first application structure while importing `.jac` modules for graph-based and AI features; its use case is existing Python projects incorporating Jac's graph-native and AI capabilities. In the example, `main.py` imports `spawn` and `root` from `jaclang.lib` (alongside `validate_title` from `validators` and `Task`, `TaskCreator`, `generate_desc` from the `task_graph` Jac module).
Both Pattern 4 and Pattern 5 keep the application in Python -- so when does each apply, and what is the key structural difference?

Pattern 4 (Mostly Python) still includes a `.jac` module: `task_graph.jac` defines the `Task` node, the `TaskCreator` walker, and `generate_desc`, which `main.py` imports -- maintaining familiar Python syntax while accessing Jac's graph-based and AI features. Pattern 5 (Pure Python + Jac Library) has no `.jac` files at all: pure Python uses Jac's runtime as a library via `from jaclang.lib import Node, Walker, on_entry, connect, spawn, root`. Pattern 5's use case is conservative adoption paths, teams preferring Python syntax, or existing Python projects.
In the Pattern 5 example, how many `.jac` files does the project contain, and which names does `main.py` import from `jaclang.lib`?

The project contains zero `.jac` files -- the directory structure is just `main.py` and `validators.py`, since this pattern uses pure Python with Jac's runtime as a library. `main.py` imports `Node`, `Walker`, `on_entry`, `connect`, `spawn`, and `root` from `jaclang.lib`, plus `validate_title` from `validators`.
In the library-mode example, how is the `Task` class defined so it works with Jac's runtime?

`Task` subclasses `Node` (the Jac base class) and declares `title: str` and `done: bool`. Its `__init__` takes `title: str`, calls `super().__init__()`, then sets `self.title = title` and `self.done = False`.
In the pure-Python walker example, which decorator marks the walker's entry-point method, and what does that method do?

The `@on_entry` decorator marks `create(self, here)` as the entry point of the `TaskCreator` class (which subclasses `Walker`). On entry it validates the title with `validate_title(self.title)`, creates a `Task(title=self.title)`, links it with `connect(here, task)`, and prints the created task's title.
A team wants graph-based capabilities in an existing Python project but refuses to introduce any new language syntax. Which pattern from the excerpt fits, and how is the walker executed?

The excerpt's pattern fits exactly: it provides graph-based capabilities in pure Python without introducing new syntax, utilizing Jac's object-spatial model through library imports. The walker is executed by instantiating it and spawning it at the root: `creator = TaskCreator(title="Build API")` followed by `spawn(creator, root())` under `if __name__ == "__main__":`.

According to the Key Takeaways table, how do Pattern 1 and Pattern 5 trade off learning curve against feature access, and per the second excerpt how are exported functions and classes used once imported?

Pattern 1 (Pure Jac) has a higher learning curve and higher migration effort but grants 100% Jac features at low risk; Pattern 5 (Pure Python + Library) has a low learning curve and very low migration effort but only core runtime feature access, at very low risk. The takeaways also note projects can begin with Pattern 5 and progressively adopt Pattern 1 as requirements evolve. Per the second excerpt, exported items are used like ordinary code: `result = my_function(arg1, arg2)` calls an exported function and `instance = MyClass()` instantiates an exported class directly.
According to the Type Compatibility table, how do Jac's built-in types map to Python types?

They map one-to-one to the identically named Python types: Jac `int` -> Python `int`, `float` -> `float`, `str` -> `str`, `bool` -> `bool`, `list` -> `list`, `dict` -> `dict`, `tuple` -> `tuple`, `set` -> `set`, and `None` -> `None`.
Per the Welcome to Jac excerpt, what does Jac compile to, and which package ecosystems does that give access to?

Jac compiles to Python bytecode, JavaScript, and native machine code (C-ABI compatible), giving full access to every library in the PyPI, npm, and native ecosystems. The excerpt adds that Jac lets you weave AI into code, model complex domains as graphs, and deploy to the cloud without switching languages, managing databases, or writing infrastructure.

You want a todo app with persistent storage, AI-based categorization, a REST API, and a React frontend -- but no database setup and no separate frontend project. How does the excerpt's example achieve this in one file?

The single `main.jac` file does all of it: `node Todo` declares the data model and `root ++> todo` persists each todo; `def categorize(title: str) -> Category by llm();` gives AI categorization constrained by `enum Category`; `def:pub add_todo` and `def:pub get_todos` become the API (with `[root-->][?:Todo]` reading todos back); and `cl def:pub app -> JsxElement` defines the React frontend with input/button and a list rendered from state. The excerpt states this defines a persistent data model, an AI-powered categorizer, a REST API, and a React frontend -- no database setup, no prompt engineering, no separate frontend project. You run it by adding a `jac.toml` (with `base_route_app = "app"` and the byllm default_model) and running `jac start`.
What complexity does the Vision say should move out of developer code, and how does each of the Three Pillars deliver on that?

The Vision says to move complexity out of the developer's code and into the language runtime: things that can be automated -- database schemas, API serialization, client-server communication, prompt construction, deployment orchestration -- should be automated so the developer focuses on what the application does, not how the plumbing works. The Three Pillars deliver this: One Language uses the codespace system (server `sv`, browser `cl`, native `na` from the same file) with the compiler handling interop -- HTTP calls, serialization, type sharing; AI Native integrates LLMs with `by llm()`, the compiler extracting semantics from function names, types, and `sem` annotations to construct prompts automatically; Scale Native persists nodes connected to `root` automatically and `jac start --scale` deploys to Kubernetes with Redis, MongoDB, load balancing, and health checks provisioned -- zero DevOps.
What are Jac's three pillars, and what is one capability each provides?

One Language: write frontend, backend, and native code in a single language via codespaces targeting server (`sv`), browser (`cl`), or native binary (`na`), with the compiler handling interop so you never write glue code. AI Native: integrate LLMs at the language level with `by llm()`, where the compiler builds prompts from function names, types, and `sem` annotations, with first-class graphs and walkers for agentic programming. Scale Native: code doesn't change from laptop to cloud -- nodes connected to `root` persist automatically, and `jac start --scale` deploys to Kubernetes with Redis, MongoDB, load balancing, and health checks.
List Jac's three codespaces with their execution target, ecosystem, and syntax as given in the table.

Server: targets the Python runtime, uses the PyPI ecosystem (`numpy`, `pandas`, `fastapi`), written as `sv { }` or `.sv.jac`. Client: targets browser/JavaScript, uses npm (`react`, `tailwind`, `@mui`), written as `cl { }` or `.cl.jac`. Native: targets a compiled binary via the C ABI, written as `na { }` or `.na.jac`. Server definitions are visible to client sections, and when the client calls a server function the compiler generates the HTTP request, serialization, and routing automatically.
What is Jac's approach to AI integration called, and how does it change the way you work with LLMs?

It is called Meaning Typed Programming. Instead of writing prompts in strings and parsing responses manually, you declare *what* you want through function signatures and let the compiler handle the *how*.
You need an LLM-powered ticket triage function that can only ever return one of four fixed severity levels -- never free text. Which pattern from the excerpt applies?

Define an enum of the allowed values and use it as the LLM function's return type: `enum Priority { LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL }` with `def triage_ticket(description: str) -> Priority by llm();`. As the heading states, enums constrain the LLM to valid outputs, so the function can only produce one of the four Priority members.
In the two excerpts, how does the role of the return type in `plan_shopping` differ from the role of `tools=[...]` in `answer_question`?

The return type is the *output contract*: for `plan_shopping(recipe: str) -> list[Ingredient] by llm()`, `obj` means every field must be filled (with `sem` annotations like `sem Ingredient.cost = "Estimated cost in USD"` adding semantic context where names aren't enough), and `enum` means the LLM can only produce one of its values -- no parsing or validation code, the type system enforces correctness. `tools=[get_weather, search_web]` in `answer_question` instead gives the LLM *capabilities* for agentic workflows: the LLM decides which tools to call and in what order while producing the `str` answer.
In the `answer_question` example, who decides which of the two tools gets called, and when?

The LLM decides which tools to call and in what order -- that is exactly what the heading states. `answer_question(question: str) -> str` is declared `by llm(tools=[get_weather, search_web])`, so the LLM chooses among `get_weather` and `search_web` while answering.
What makes a node persistent in Jac, and which command runs the same program as a Kubernetes deployment?

Nodes reachable from the built-in `root` node are persistent -- they survive process restarts, and the runtime generates storage schemas from the node declarations so you never write database code (e.g., `root ++> Todo(title="Learn Jac")` is automatically persisted). The same program runs three ways with no code changes: `jac main.jac` runs locally with SQLite persistence, `jac start` runs an HTTP API server where walkers become REST endpoints, and `jac start --scale` deploys to Kubernetes with Redis, MongoDB, and load balancing. Note `jac start` defaults to `main.jac` if the filename is omitted, while `jac run` always needs it explicitly.
What does `pip install jaseci` install, and how do you verify the installation?

It installs the complete Jac ecosystem: `jaclang` (compiler), `byllm` (AI integration), `jac-client` (frontend), `jac-scale` (deployment), and `jac-super` (enhanced console). Verify with `jac --version`, which also warms the cache, making subsequent commands faster.
A newcomer wants the smallest possible first Jac program that prints a greeting. Based on the excerpt, what should they write?

Create `hello.jac` containing a `with entry` block: `with entry { print("Hello from Jac!"); }`. The `with entry` block is where top-level program execution goes, and the single print statement (ending in a semicolon) is the whole program.
Is there any difference between `jac hello.jac` and `jac run hello.jac`, and which learning path does the guide suggest for someone interested in graphs and OSP?

No difference -- `jac` is shorthand for `jac run`; both work identically. The tip adds that `-e all` (e.g. `jac -e all hello.jac`) shows type check diagnostics -- errors and warnings -- without needing a separate `jac check`. For graphs and OSP, the Choose Your Path grid says to read "What Makes Jac Different" for the concepts, then the OSP Tutorial for hands-on practice with nodes, edges, and walkers (whereas web-app builders are pointed to the Build an AI Day Planner tutorial).
According to the Choose Your Path section, which resource should someone building a web app jump to, and what does it cover?

They should jump to "Build an AI Day Planner" -- a complete 7-part tutorial covering backend, frontend, persistence, auth, and AI. (By contrast, those just trying Jac follow the Installation guide, AI/LLM users start with the byLLM Quickstart then Agentic AI, and graph/OSP learners read What Makes Jac Different then the OSP Tutorial.)
In the Quick Links table, which resource covers learning paths by experience level, and which covers all `jac` commands?

The FAQ covers learning paths by experience level, and the CLI Reference covers all `jac` commands. (Other links include the Syntax Cheatsheet as a comprehensive syntax reference, the Language Reference for complete language documentation, and Build an AI Day Planner as the complete 7-part tutorial.)
You hit a reproducible bug in Jac itself, and separately you have a usage question you'd like to discuss with other developers. Where does the excerpt direct each?
Report the bug as an issue on GitHub at Jaseci-Labs/jaseci. For questions and discussions, join the community's Discord server; you can also ask questions at JacGPT (jac-gpt.jaseci.org).
Which language-spec document covers the difference between `can` and `def`, and what else does it include?
Functions & Objects covers `can` vs `def`, along with function declarations, OOP, inheritance, enums, access modifiers, and impl blocks.
What topics does the byLLM Reference cover according to the excerpt?
The byLLM Reference covers `by llm()`, model configuration, tool calling, streaming, multimodal input, and agentic patterns.
Which reference covers native desktop development in Jac, and what specific topics does it list?

The jac-desktop Reference: native desktop via PyTauri, sidecar bundling, `jac desktop plugin`, and `[plugins.desktop]` config. (The jac-client Reference covers codespaces, components, state, routing, authentication, npm packages, and web/PWA/mobile targets.)
Where do you look for `jac.toml` project settings versus for using Jac features from pure Python code, per the two excerpts?

Project settings via `jac.toml` are covered by the Configuration reference under Tools & Config (which also lists CLI Commands for every `jac` subcommand and Testing for test syntax, assertions, and CLI test commands). Using Jac features from pure Python code is covered by Library Mode under Python Integration, while its sibling Interoperability page covers the reverse direction -- importing and using Python packages in Jac, plus the five adoption patterns.
What is the difference between the Interoperability and Library Mode reference pages?
Interoperability covers importing and using Python packages in Jac, including the five adoption patterns. Library Mode covers using Jac features from pure Python code.
What does the Walker Patterns quick-reference page cover, and what is in the Appendices?

Walker Patterns covers the `.reports` array, response patterns, and nested walker spawning. The Appendices contain the complete keyword reference, operator quick reference, grammar, gotchas, and migration guide.
What is the default entry point for `jac start`, and what do you do if your entry file has a different name?
`main.jac` is the default entry point. If your entry point has a different name (e.g., `app.jac`), pass it explicitly: `jac start app.jac`.
You need to look up the options and examples for every Jac subcommand -- what is your primary interface to the toolchain and where is the full reference?
The `jac` command is the primary interface to the Jac toolchain, and for the full reference the excerpt points to CLI Commands at `cli/index.md`.
How do the Execution commands differ from the Analysis commands in the CLI tables?

Execution commands actually run code: `jac run <file>` executes a Jac program, `jac enter <file> <entry>` runs a named entry point, `jac start [file]` starts a web server, and `jac debug <file>` runs in debug mode. Analysis commands inspect or maintain code without running the app: `jac check` type checks code, `jac format` formats source files, and `jac test` runs the test suite.
Which CLI command formats source files, and what do the other two analysis commands do?
`jac format` formats source files. `jac check` type checks code, and `jac test` runs the test suite.
Which command converts Python code to Jac, and what are the other two transform commands?
`jac py2jac <file>` converts Python to Jac. The others are `jac jac2py <file>` (convert Jac to Python) and `jac jac2js <file>` (compile to JavaScript).
Per the Project Commands table, what does `jac install` do compared with `jac add`, and which command purges the global bytecode cache?

`jac install` installs all dependencies (pip, git, plugins), while `jac add <pkg>` adds a single dependency (and `jac remove <pkg>` removes one; `jac update [pkg]` updates dependencies to latest compatible versions). `jac purge` purges the global bytecode cache, distinct from `jac clean`, which cleans build artifacts.
You want to see a visual rendering of your program's graph structure -- which tool command applies?
`jac dot <file>` generates a graph visualization. (The other tool commands are `jac lsp` to start the language server, `jac config` to manage configuration, and `jac plugins` to manage plugins.)
What does `jac plugins info byllm` do, and why is `jac plugins enable` sometimes a no-op?

`jac plugins info byllm` shows plugin information for byllm. `jac plugins enable` and `jac plugins disable` merely toggle the `disabled` list in `[plugins]`, so calling `enable` on a plugin that is not currently disabled is a no-op -- there is nothing to remove from the list.
Where does the Project Configuration section direct readers for the full configuration reference?
It directs readers to the Configuration reference at `config/index.md`.
Your project needs numpy and pandas at runtime, pytest only for development, React on the client, and gpt-4o as the default LLM. Where does each go in `jac.toml`, following the example?

numpy and pandas go under `[dependencies]` (e.g. `numpy = "^1.24.0"`, `pandas = "^2.0.0"`); pytest goes under `[dependencies.dev]`; React (and scoped packages like `"@mui/material"`) go under `[dependencies.npm]`; and the default LLM goes under `[plugins.byllm.model]` as `default_model = "gpt-4o"`. Project metadata -- name, version, description, entry-point -- lives under `[project]`.
How do the `[scripts]` entries in `jac.toml` relate to the `jac script` commands in the second excerpt?

`[scripts]` defines named commands -- `dev = "jac start --dev"`, `test = "jac test"`, `build = "jac build"` -- and the second excerpt shows how to invoke them: `jac script dev`, `jac script test`, `jac script build`. Each `jac script <name>` runs the command string registered under that name. (The same excerpt also shows private npm registry auth via `[plugins.client.npm.auth]` with `_authToken = "${NODE_AUTH_TOKEN}"`, which generates a `.npmrc`.)
What do the three commands in the Running Scripts example invoke?
Each invokes a project script by name: `jac script dev`, `jac script test`, and `jac script build` run the scripts registered as `dev`, `test`, and `build` in the project's configuration.
What is the configuration file loading order from lowest to highest priority, and which file is gitignored?

Lowest to highest: `jac.toml` (always loaded, git tracked), then `jac.<profile>.toml` (loaded when `--profile` or `JAC_PROFILE` is set, tracked), then `[environments.<profile>]` inside `jac.toml` (when a profile is set), and finally `jac.local.toml` (always loaded if present, NOT git tracked -- it is gitignored).
How do you run `app.jac` under the `prod` profile from the command line?
`jac run --profile prod app.jac`. The same flag works with other commands, e.g. `jac start --profile staging`.
Production must serve on port 80 with gpt-4o, while one developer wants port 9000 with caching off on their machine only, without committing that. How do the example profile files handle this?

Put the production settings in `jac.prod.toml` -- `[serve] port = 80` and `[plugins.byllm.model] default_model = "gpt-4o"` -- which is a tracked profile file. The developer-specific overrides go in `jac.local.toml`, which is gitignored and developer-specific: `[serve] port = 9000` and `[run] cache = false`. Also note `JAC_ENV` is deprecated; use `JAC_PROFILE` instead.
How does exposing environment variables differ between server-side and client-side code?

Server-side variables such as `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `REDIS_URL`, `MONGODB_URI`, and `JWT_SECRET` are ordinary environment variables. Client-side (Vite), only variables prefixed with `VITE_` are exposed to the client: you define them in a `.env` file (e.g. `VITE_API_URL=https://api.example.com`) and access them in client code inside `cl { }` via `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL`.
In the `.env` example, what does the client component render?

The `cl { def:pub app() -> JsxElement { ... } }` component reads `api_url = import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL;` and returns `
{api_url}
`, so it renders a div containing the value from the `.env` file: `https://api.example.com`.
Does Jac parse TypeScript files directly, and how do you override the generated `tsconfig.json`?

No -- Jac does not parse TypeScript files directly; TypeScript support is provided through Vite's built-in TypeScript handling in client-side (`cl {}`) code via the jac-client Vite toolchain. You override the generated `tsconfig.json` from `jac.toml` under `[plugins.client.ts]`, e.g. `compilerOptions = { target = "ES2022", strict = true }` plus `include` and `exclude` lists.
You need to persist a small string in the user's browser and read it back later. What does the excerpt's approach look like?
Use the browser's localStorage from client code: `window.localStorage.setItem("key", "value");` to store it and `value = window.localStorage.getItem("key");` to read it back.
How does the Document example differ from the Fetch example in the browser-API excerpts?

The Document example is synchronous DOM access: `element = document.getElementById("my-id");` grabs an element directly and the component returns JSX (`
{width}
`). The Fetch example is asynchronous network I/O: an `async def load_data() -> None` awaits `fetch("/api/data")` for the response and then awaits `response.json()` to get the data.
In the Fetch example, why are there two `await` expressions in `load_data`?

The first, `response = await fetch("/api/data");`, waits for the HTTP response; the second, `data = await response.json();`, waits for the response body to be parsed as JSON. Both are needed, which is why the function is declared `async def load_data() -> None`.
Why might AI coding assistants produce wrong Jac syntax, and what does the Jaseci team maintain to counter this?

Jac is a new language, so AI coding assistants may hallucinate syntax from outdated or nonexistent versions. The Jaseci team maintains an official condensed language reference designed for LLM context windows: jaseci-llmdocs, on GitHub at jaseci-labs/jaseci-llmdocs.
How does installing `candidate.txt` differ between Cursor and OpenAI Codex in the setup snippets?

For Cursor you copy it into place as its own rules file: `mkdir -p .cursor/rules && cp candidate.txt .cursor/rules/jac-reference.mdc`. For OpenAI Codex you append it to an existing context file: `cat candidate.txt >> AGENTS.md`. In both cases, when you update Jac you pull a fresh copy from the releases page to stay current.
What does `cat candidate.txt >> AGENTS.md` do, and what should you do when Jac is updated?

It appends the contents of `candidate.txt` to `AGENTS.md` (the `>>` appends rather than overwrites), adding the Jac reference to the Codex context file. When you update Jac, pull a fresh copy of `candidate.txt` from the releases page to stay current.
How does the Syntax Quick Reference page describe itself, and where should hands-on learners start instead?

It describes itself as a lookup reference, not a learning guide. For hands-on learning it directs you to the AI Day Planner tutorial, which teaches the concepts progressively (with "Try it" links for Functions, Objects, Walkers & Graphs, and AI Integration).
Where do docstrings go in Jac relative to the thing they document?
Docstrings go BEFORE the declaration they document: the object-level docstring appears above `obj Documented`, and the method docstring appears above `def method()` inside the object.
You want a block of code that runs only when the file is executed directly as the main module, not when it is imported. Which construct applies?
Use `with entry:__main__ { ... }` -- the example prints "Only when run directly", running only when the file is the main module.
What does the `global` statement do inside `use_global`, and how do the body-less method declarations in the second excerpt differ from normal definitions?

`glob` declares module-level globals (`glob MAX_SIZE: int = 100; glob greeting: str = "Hello";`); inside a function, `global greeting;` references the module-level glob so the assignment `greeting = "Hola";` rebinds the global rather than creating a local. The second excerpt shows pure declarations: `def add(n: int) -> int;` and `def multiply(n: int) -> int;` end with a semicolon and have no body -- the methods are declared here and defined elsewhere.
What is the syntax for importing from a sibling module and from a module in the parent package?
Sibling: `import from .sibling { helper_func }`. Parent package: `import from ..parent.mod { SomeClass }` -- one leading dot per level up, with the imported names in braces.
What three syntactic features of Jac function definitions does the `greet` example show?

Functions use the `def` keyword with typed parameters and a return annotation (`def greet(name: str) -> str`), braces for the body instead of indentation, and semicolons terminating statements -- the body is `return f"Hello, {name}!";`, which also shows f-string formatting.
You need one function that returns both the quotient and remainder of a division, defaulting the divisor to 2. How does the cheatsheet example structure this?

Use a default parameter and a tuple return type: `def divmod_example(a: int, b: int = 2) -> tuple[int, int] { return (a // b, a % b); }` -- `b` defaults to 2, and the two results come back together as a tuple.
In `kitchen_sink`, what do `/`, `*args`, and the parameters after `*args` signify -- and what does the second excerpt say about parentheses and braces in `if`/`elif`/`else`?

In `kitchen_sink`: `pos_only: int` before the `/` is positional-only; `regular: str = "default"` is a normal parameter with a default; `*args: int` collects variadic positional arguments; `kw_only: bool = True` after `*args` is keyword-only; and `**kwargs: any` collects arbitrary keyword arguments. The conditional excerpt shows that `if`/`elif`/`else` need no parentheses around conditions but braces are required around each branch body.
How do you iterate over a list in Jac according to the cheatsheet example?
With a for-in loop using a brace-delimited body: `for item in ["a", "b", "c"] { print(item); }`.
What does `for i = 0 to i < 10 by i += 2 { print(i); }` print, and what is the general form of this loop?
It prints 0, 2, 4, 6, 8. The general form is `for VAR = START to CONDITION by STEP { ... }` -- start at 0, continue while `i < 10`, stepping with `i += 2`.
How does `skip` differ from `break` and `continue`?

`break` and `continue` are loop control: `continue` jumps to the next iteration (in the example, when `i == 3`) and `break` leaves the loop (when `i == 7`). `skip` is not loop control at all -- it is an early return from the current function/ability (e.g. `if x > 100 { skip; }`) and is never tied to a loop.
What does the `skip` statement do in Jac?
`skip` performs an early return from the current function/ability -- in the example, `if x > 100 { skip; }`. It is never tied to a loop.
What two state fields does the DataView client component declare, and with what initial values?
Inside `cl { def:pub DataView() -> JsxElement { ... } }` it declares `has data: list = [];` (an empty list) and `has loading: bool = True;`.
Given `fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]`, how do you get the last element and the middle-to-end slice per the cheatsheet?
Negative indexing gets the last element: `fruits[-1]` is `cherry`. Slicing gets a range: `fruits[1:3]` is `["banana", "cherry"]`. Plain indexing works too: `fruits[0]` is `apple`.
How do dictionaries and tuples differ in access and mutability in the cheatsheet examples?

Dictionaries are accessed by key: `person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 25}` and `person["name"]` looks up a value. Tuples are immutable and positional: `point = (10, 20)`, and they support unpacking into variables with `(x, y) = point;`.
How does the cheatsheet unpack a tuple into separate variables?
With parenthesized targets: `point = (10, 20);` then `(x, y) = point;` performs tuple unpacking. Tuples are noted as immutable.
You want a data type with named, defaulted fields and don't want to hand-write `__init__`, `__eq__`, or `__repr__`. Which construct applies per the cheatsheet?

Use `obj`, which auto-generates `__init__`, `__eq__`, `__repr__`, etc. The `Pet` example declares fields with `has name: str = "Unnamed", age: int = 0;` and adds methods like `def bark()` that use `self.name` -- no constructor boilerplate needed.
The cheatsheet shows two static methods on `Pet` -- `make` and `species`. What do they have in common, and how do their roles differ?

Both are declared `static def` and take no `self` or `Self`. `make(name: str) -> Pet` works as a named constructor -- it returns a new instance via `Pet(name=name)`. `species() -> str` instead returns a fixed class-level value, the string "Canis familiaris", with no instance involved.
What does the static `species` method return, and why does it take no `self` parameter?
It returns the string "Canis familiaris". As a static method (`static def species() -> str`), it takes no `self` or `Self` -- it belongs to the type rather than any instance.
How does the `class Kitten` example differ from `obj`-style method definitions?

`class` follows standard Python class behavior: the method explicitly declares its receiver with a type annotation -- `def meow(self: Kitten)` -- rather than getting `self` implicitly. It still uses `has name: str = "Unnamed";` for the field and prints via f-string.
You need a reusable result container that holds either a success value of any type or an error, with the error type defaulting to Exception. How does the cheatsheet model this?

With a generic object with type parameters and a default: `obj Result[T, E = Exception]` declares `has value: T | None = None, error: E | None = None;` and a method `def is_ok() -> bool { return self.error is None; }` to test success.
How does a `by postinit` field differ from a property field with getter/setter blocks?

`has computed: int by postinit;` defers the field's initialization to the `postinit()` method, which computes it once after construction (`self.computed = self.count * 2;`). A property field instead runs code on every access: `balance: float` defines a `getter -> float` returning the backing field `self._balance`, a `setter(value: float)` that assigns it, and a `deleter` that resets it to 0.0 -- backed by `has _balance: float = 0.0` and accessed as `self._<name>`.
What three accessor blocks does the `balance` property define, and what does each do?

`getter -> float { return self._balance; }` reads the backing field; `setter(value: float) { self._balance = value; }` writes it; and `deleter { self._balance = 0.0; }` resets it to 0.0 on delete. The backing field is declared as `has _balance: float = 0.0`.
How do you make a computed, read-only property per the cheatsheet?

Define only a getter and omit the setter: `has doubled: float { getter { return self._balance * 2.0; } }` -- a pure computed property with no backing storage of its own, read-only because there is no `setter`.
What three visibility levels can `has` fields carry, and which is the default?

`has:pub` (public -- the default, as the comment on `name` notes), `has:priv` (private, used for `ssn`), and `has:protect` (protected, used for `age`). The object itself can also be marked, e.g. `obj:pub Profile`.
What does the `:priv` modifier on the `MyData` walker enforce, and how does the `Color` enum in the second excerpt attach values to its members?

`walker:priv MyData` enforces per-user auth on the walker (its ability still reports `[-->]` from Root entry, but access is private). The `Color` enum is a different kind of declaration entirely: it binds explicit values to members inside braces, comma-separated -- `RED = "red", GREEN = "green", BLUE = "blue"`.
You need a node object whose `next` field points to another instance of the same type (or nothing). How does the cheatsheet express this?

Name the enclosing archetype directly in the field type: `obj TreeNode { has value: int = 0, next: TreeNode | None = None; }` -- recursive types reference the archetype being defined, with `| None` and a `None` default for the empty case.
What is the syntax of a typed lambda with a return type in Jac?

`mul = lambda (x: int, y: int) -> int : x * y;` -- parenthesized typed parameters, a `-> int` return type, then a colon followed by the expression body. `print(mul(3, 4));` calls it like a normal function.
Why does the `@classmethod` decorator still exist in Jac, and what do the `else` and `finally` clauses in the try/except example do?

Static methods are the norm for methods in `obj`; the `@classmethod` decorator stays for Python `class` compatibility -- the example takes `cls: type` and returns `cls.__name__`. In the exception-handling excerpt, `10 // 0` is caught by `except ZeroDivisionError as e` (printing "Caught: {e}"), a broader `except Exception` handles other errors, the `else` block ("No error occurred") runs only when no exception was raised, and `finally` ("Always runs") executes regardless.
How do you open two files in a single `with` statement?
Separate the context managers with commas: `with open("a.txt") as a, open("b.txt") as b { print(a.read(), b.read()); }`.

After creating a Person node and connecting it with `root ++> p;`, you want to persist it, commit the change, get its unique identifier, and inspect the graph while debugging. Which built-ins from the excerpt apply?

Use `save(p)` to persist the node to storage, `commit()` to commit pending changes, `jid(p)` to get the unique Jac ID of the object, and `printgraph(root)` to print the graph for debugging -- exactly the four calls shown in the `with entry` block.
What does the `:=` operator do in the first excerpt, and how do the `test` blocks in the second excerpt verify the `fib` function?

The walrus operator assigns inside an expression: `if (n := len("hello")) > 3` binds `n` to 5 and tests it in the same condition, so the branch can use `n` ("Long string: {n} chars"). The `test` blocks are named top-level test constructs: `test "fibonacci base cases"` asserts `fib(0) == 0` and `fib(1) == 1`, and `test "fibonacci recursive"` loops `for i in range(2, 10)` asserting the recurrence `fib(i) == fib(i - 1) + fib(i - 2)`.
In the describe_image example, what two ways of constructing an Image are shown, and what would break if the first line were removed?

The entry block constructs an Image from a local file path -- Image("photo.jpg") -- and from a URL -- Image("https://example.com/img.png"). Removing the first line, `import from byllm.lib { Image }`, would break the example because the Image type used in the signature `def describe_image(image: Image) -> str by llm;` comes from byllm.lib.
How does the "walker test" example verify walker behavior?

It builds graph state with `root ++> Person(name="Alice", age=30);`, spawns the walker with `result = root spawn Greeter();`, and then checks the collected output with `assert len(result.reports) > 0;` -- tests can spawn walkers and check their reports.
You need an entity type that can live inside a graph rather than being a plain object. What does the cheatsheet declare?
A `node`: `node Person { has name: str, age: int; }` -- nodes are objects that can exist in a graph, with `has` fields for their state.
What triggers the `SecureRoom` node's abilities, and how does `Employee` reuse `Person`?

`SecureRoom`'s abilities are triggered by walkers: `can on_enter with Visitor entry` runs when a Visitor walker enters the node (printing "Welcome to {name}"), and `can on_exit with Visitor exit` runs when it leaves (printing "Leaving {name}"). `Employee` reuses `Person` through node inheritance -- `node Employee(Person) { has department: str; }` names the parent in parentheses and adds a new field.
What is the syntax for node inheritance in the cheatsheet?
The parent node goes in parentheses after the child's name: `node Employee(Person) { has department: str; }` -- Employee inherits from Person and adds a `department` field.
Can edges carry data and methods? What does the `Weighted` edge define?

Yes. `edge Weighted` has a field `has weight: float = 1.0;` and a method `def normalize(max_w: float) -> float { return self.weight / max_w; }` -- edges can hold state and behavior just like other archetypes.
You want to connect node `a` forward to `b`, connect `a` to `c` but writing the target first, and link `a` and `b` in both directions. Which connection operators apply?

`a ++> b;` connects a -> b; `c <++ a;` is the backward syntax that still connects a -> c while writing the target first; and `a <++> b;` creates a bidirectional connection a <-> b. (`root ++> a;` similarly connects root to a.)
How does creating typed connections differ from the traversal expressions in the second excerpt?

Typed connections attach edge data at creation time: `a +>: Friendship(since=2020) :+> b;` links the nodes with a `Friendship` edge carrying `since=2020` (and another with `since=1995` to c). The traversal expressions read the graph instead of building it: `[root -->]` returns all nodes via outgoing edges, `[root <--]` via incoming edges, and `[root <-->]` via any edges.
What do `[root -->]`, `[root <--]`, and `[root <-->]` each return?
`[root -->]` returns all nodes reachable via outgoing edges from root; `[root <--]` all nodes via incoming edges; `[root <-->]` all nodes via any edges (both directions).
How do you restrict a traversal result to only `Person` nodes?
Append a type filter to the traversal: `[root -->][?:Person]` returns only the Person nodes among root's outgoing connections.
You need only the connected nodes representing adults (age at least 18). Which filter expression applies?
An attribute filter on the traversal result: `[root -->][?age >= 18]` returns just the nodes whose `age` field is >= 18.
What does the `edge` keyword change in a traversal expression, and how does the walker ability in the second excerpt keep the traversal going?

Prefixing `edge` makes the expression return the edge objects themselves rather than the target nodes: `[edge root -->]` yields all edge objects, and `[edge root ->:Friendship:->]` yields the Friendship edge objects. The walker ability `can greet_root with Root entry` runs when the walker enters the root node, prints its greeting, and continues traversal by calling `visit [-->];` to move to the connected nodes.
When does the `greet_root` ability run, and what does its `visit [-->];` statement do?

It runs when the walker enters the root node -- that is what `with Root entry` specifies. After printing "{greeting} from root!", `visit [-->];` moves the walker on to the nodes connected by outgoing edges.
Inside a walker ability, what do `here` and `self` refer to, and what does `report` do?

`here` is the current node (e.g. `here.name`) and `self` is the walker itself (e.g. `self.greeting`). `report here.name;` collects a value that is returned as part of a list, and `visit [-->];` continues the traversal. The entry block builds the graph with `root ++> Person(name="Alice", age=25);` and Bob.
After `result = root spawn Greeter();`, what does `result.reports` contain in the example?
`["Alice", "Bob"]` -- spawning the walker at root runs the traversal, and `result.reports` holds the values reported along the way.
What does `visit [-->] else { ... }` do, and how do the indexed visit forms in the VisitDemo differ from a plain `visit [-->]`?

`visit [-->] else` runs the fallback block only when there are no outgoing nodes to visit -- the examples print "Reached a dead end" / "Dead end". A plain `visit [-->]` queues all outgoing nodes; the indexed forms narrow that: `visit : 0 : [-->];` visits the first outgoing node only and `visit : -1 : [-->];` the last one only. VisitDemo also shows direction (`[<--]`, `[<-->]`), type filters (`[?:Person]`), edge-type and edge-condition traversal (`[->:Friendship:->]`, `[->:Friendship:since > 2020:->]`), and `visit here;` to re-visit the current node.
In the "Triggers for any walker" example, what does the on_any ability print when it fires?

The on_any ability, declared as `can on_any with entry`, prints f"Someone entered {self.name}" -- that is, the text "Someone entered" followed by the node's own name via self.name, whenever any walker enters the node.
In the on_inspector ability, what happens when an Inspector walker with clearance less than 5 enters the node?
The ability `can on_inspector with Inspector entry` checks `if visitor.clearance < 5`; when true it prints "Access denied" and then executes `disengage;`, stopping the walker.
You are writing a node ability that should fire whenever either an Admin walker or an Inspector walker enters -- but no other walker types. Which trigger pattern applies?

Use a union of walker types in the ability trigger, as in `can on_multi with Admin | Inspector entry`. Per the excerpt, this single ability fires for both Admin and Inspector walkers (printing "Authorized personnel"), so you do not need two separate abilities.
How does the timing of the `on_leave` ability in the first excerpt differ from the inspecting code in the second excerpt?

`can on_leave with Inspector exit` is an exit ability: it runs when the Inspector walker is leaving the node, printing "Inspector leaving". The second excerpt runs while the walker is still at the current node -- it prints f"Inspecting: {here.name}" using `here` (the current node) and then queues further traversal with `visit [-->];` before moving on.
In the excerpt from "`self` = the walker", which statement makes the walker continue on to the outgoing connected nodes after printing?
The statement `visit [-->];` -- after printing f"Inspecting: {here.name}" (where `here` is the current node), the walker visits the nodes reachable via outgoing edges.
In the AnimalVisitor walker, what does the `->_` branch do?

`->_` is the fallback branch for any Animal that is not matched by the more specific `->Dog` or `->Cat` branches. It prints f"{here.name} is some animal", whereas `->Dog` prints the breed-specific message and `->Cat` prints the meow message.
After running `result = root spawn Greeter();`, what does `result.reports` contain?
According to the excerpt, `result.reports` is the list of reported values -- the spawn expression returns a result object, and printing `result.reports` shows everything the walker reported.
You want clients to create Todo items over HTTP by sending a title in the request body and receiving the created todo back. Which pattern from the excerpt applies?

Declare a public walker, e.g. `walker:pub add_todo`, which becomes an HTTP endpoint under `jac start`. Its `has title: str` field becomes the request body field, the ability `can create with Root entry` attaches the new node with `here ++> Todo(title=self.title)`, and `report new_todo;` becomes the response body.
How does exposing `health_check` as an endpoint differ from exposing `get_item`?

`health_check` is a plain public function -- `def:pub health_check() -> dict` -- which automatically becomes an endpoint returning its dict. `get_item` is a public walker (`walker:pub`) whose endpoint is customized with the `@restspec` decorator: `@restspec(method=HTTPMethod.GET, path="/items/{item_id}")` sets the HTTP method to GET and a custom path with an {item_id} path parameter (requiring `import from http { HTTPMethod }`), and it reports its response from `can fetch with Root entry`.
What HTTP method and path does the `get_item` walker expose, and how are they specified?

It uses the GET method at path "/items/{item_id}", specified via the decorator `@restspec(method=HTTPMethod.GET, path="/items/{item_id}")` on `walker:pub get_item`, with HTTPMethod imported via `import from http { HTTPMethod }`.
What happens when abilities are declared without names, as in `can with entry` on AutoNode?

Per the heading, abilities without names are auto-named by the compiler. The excerpt shows this on both a node (`can with entry` in AutoNode, printing the node's val) and a walker (AutoWalker's `can with Root entry` that visits [-->] and `can with AutoNode entry` that prints here.val).
How does using an enum return type differ from using an object return type when constraining LLM output?

The enum approach (`def categorize(title: str) -> Category by llm();`) constrains the LLM to output one of the valid enum values -- WORK, PERSONAL, SHOPPING, HEALTH, or OTHER. The structured-output approach (`def plan_shopping(recipe: str) -> list[Ingredient] by llm();`) makes the LLM produce a list of Ingredient objects where every declared field -- name: str, cost: float, carby: bool -- must be filled.
When plan_shopping runs, what must the LLM produce for each element of the returned list?
The return type is `list[Ingredient]`, and per the heading every field of the structured output must be filled -- so each Ingredient must have a name (str), a cost (float), and a carby flag (bool).
Which three configuration parameters are passed to llm() in the summarize example?
model_name="gpt-4", temperature=0.7, and max_tokens=2000 -- passed inside `by llm(...)` on `def summarize(text: str) -> str`.
What effect does passing stream=True to llm() have in the stream_story example?
It makes the LLM-backed function return a streaming response -- per the heading, the function returns a generator. The declaration is `def stream_story(prompt: str) -> str by llm(stream=True);`.
You need a quick one-off LLM answer inside an entry block without declaring a dedicated LLM-backed function. Which pattern applies?

Use the inline LLM expression: apply `by llm` directly to a string, as in `result = "Explain quantum computing simply" by llm;` inside `with entry`. This gets an LLM result from a prompt expression without any function definition.
What is the difference between the sem declarations in the first excerpt and those in the second?

The first excerpt attaches semantic strings to object fields (`sem Ingredient.cost = "Estimated cost in USD"`, `sem Ingredient.carby = "True if high in carbohydrates"`) and to a function as a whole (`sem plan_shopping = "Generate a shopping list for the given recipe."`). The second excerpt shows parameter-level semantics: `sem summarize.text` describes a specific parameter ("The article or document to summarize") and `sem summarize.return` describes the return value ("A 2-3 sentence summary"). Both change what the LLM sees at runtime, but at different granularities.
In the parameter-level semantics example, what does `sem summarize.return` declare?
It declares the semantic description of summarize's return value: "A 2-3 sentence summary". Similarly, `sem summarize.text` describes the text parameter as "The article or document to summarize".
What semantic description is attached to the CRITICAL value of the Priority enum?
`sem Priority.CRITICAL = "Requires immediate attention within 1 hour";` -- CRITICAL is one of the values of `enum Priority { LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL }`.
In the ReAct-loop tool functions, what do get_weather and search_web each return?

`get_weather(city: str) -> str` returns the string f"Weather data for {city}", and `search_web(query: str) -> list[str]` returns the one-element list [f"Result for {query}"]. These are functions the LLM can be given access to call.
You want answer_question to be able to look up weather data or search the web on its own while answering. Which approach from the excerpt applies?

Pass the functions as tools to the LLM: `def answer_question(question: str) -> str by llm(tools=[get_weather, search_web]);`. Per the heading, the LLM then decides which tools to call and in what order.
How does incl_info in the first excerpt differ from the Image parameter in the second as a way of giving the LLM extra input?

incl_info injects additional textual context into the call: `by llm(incl_info={"company": company_info})` passes the glob string company_info ("TechCorp, products: CloudDB, SecureAuth") alongside the question, with `sem support_agent` describing the task. The second excerpt instead passes an image as a typed function argument: `def describe_image(image: Image) -> str by llm;` takes an Image (imported from byllm.lib) constructed from a local file (Image("photo.jpg")) or a URL (Image("https://example.com/img.png")).
According to the heading, which part of a file is treated as server code?

Code before any header is server code by default. The example shows a server-side `node Todo { has title: str, done: bool = False; }` and a public function `def:pub get_todos() -> list` that returns a list comprehension over `[root -->][?:Todo]`.
What region of code do the `cl { ... }` braces bracket, and what does the app component inside do on entry?

The braces bracket exactly the client region. Inside, `def:pub app() -> JsxElement` declares `has items: list = []` and an `async can with entry` block that awaits `get_todos()` to fill items, then returns a `
` rendering a `

` per item via a JSX list comprehension.
You need exactly one import to be server-side and one to be client-side, without opening full region blocks. Which form applies?

The single-statement form with no header and no braces: prefix the individual import, as in `sv import from .database { connect_db }` for the server import and `cl import from react { useState }` for the client import.
Contrast what `has count: int = 0` does in the first excerpt with what `skip;` does in the second.

In a client component, `has count: int = 0;` becomes React useState -- reactive state that the button's `onClick={lambda -> None { count = count + 1; }}` updates, re-rendering the displayed "Count: {count}". `skip;` is different: it is a slot early-exit guard inside a JSX `{if ...}` slot -- in Greeting, when name is empty it emits `

(no name given)

` and then `skip;` ends the slot with whatever was emitted, so the slot output stops there.
In the Greeting component, what does the `skip;` statement do according to the excerpt's comment?

It is the slot early-exit guard: per the heading, `skip;` ends the slot with whatever was emitted -- here, after emitting `

(no name given)

` when `name == ""`, the slot ends with that children list.
Your component's data arrives asynchronously and you don't want to render the data view until it's ready. Which rendering pattern from the excerpt applies?

The loading-guard early return: `if loading { return

Loading...

; }` renders a placeholder while loading is true, and only afterwards does the component `return
{data}
;` with the real data.
When do `test "description" { ... }` blocks execute, and what isolation does each test get?

Test blocks are ignored during normal execution (`jac run`) and only run when you invoke `jac test`. Each test block runs in its own isolated context with a fresh graph -- state created in one test, including nodes connected to `root`, doesn't leak into another, so there is no need to worry about test ordering or cleanup. If NodeAnchor errors appear when re-running tests, clear stale persisted state with `jac clean --all`.
In the "Test with Setup" excerpt, what does MyObject's process() method return?
It returns `self.data` -- the object's `has data: str` field -- as declared in `def process() -> str { return self.data; }`, which the `test "object processing"` block is set up to exercise.
What two forms of the assert statement does the basic assert example show?
A bare assertion, `assert condition;`, and an assertion with an attached message, `assert condition, "Error message";` -- both inside a `test "basic assert"` block.
In a test you need to verify that two variables refer to the very same object, not merely objects that compare equal. Which assertion from the excerpt applies?

Use identity assertions: `assert a is b;` checks they are the same object (and `assert a is not b;` checks they are different objects), whereas `assert a == b;` / `assert a != b;` only check equality of values.
In the "boolean values" test, which of the three assertions could actually fail, and under what condition?
Only `assert bool(value);` can fail -- it fails when `value` converts to False. The other two, `assert True;` and `assert not False;`, assert constant truths and always pass.
What three membership assertions does the "membership" test show?
`assert item in collection;`, `assert item not in collection;`, and `assert key in dictionary;` -- checking presence, absence, and dictionary key membership respectively.
A function under test returns either a value or None, and you need to assert each case. Which assertions apply?
Use the None-checking identity assertions from the excerpt: `assert value is None;` for the absent case and `assert value is not None;` for the present case.
What different testing concerns do the float-comparison excerpt and the with-messages excerpt address?

The float-comparison test addresses floating-point imprecision: since `0.1 + 0.2` is not exactly 0.3, it uses `assert almostEqual(result, 0.3, 10);` instead of exact equality. The with-messages test addresses failure diagnostics: it attaches explanatory messages to asserts, like `assert result > 0, f"Expected positive, got {result}";` and `assert len(items) == 3, "Should have 3 items";`, so a failure reports what went wrong.
In the "assertions with messages" test, what does each assertion report if it fails?

The first, `assert result > 0, f"Expected positive, got {result}"`, reports a message interpolating the actual value of result via the f-string. The second, `assert len(items) == 3, "Should have 3 items"`, reports the fixed message "Should have 3 items" when the items list does not have exactly 3 elements.
According to the CLI options table, which flag makes the test run exit on the first failure, and what is its short form?

`--xit`, short form `-x`, exits on first failure. (By contrast, `--maxfail` / `-m` stops after N failures, `--test_name` / `-t` runs a specific test by name, `--filter` / `-f` filters by pattern, `--directory` / `-d` sets the test directory, and `--verbose` / `-v` enables verbose output.)
Why does the file-naming tip say to avoid a `test_` prefix on .jac files?
Because a `test_` prefix (e.g. `test_utils.jac`) can conflict with Python's module import system. The tip recommends descriptive names like `utils_tests.jac` or `my_app.jac` instead.
You run your test suite and want to confirm from the console output that everything passed. Based on the success example, what should you look for?

Each test line printed as `unittest.case.FunctionTestCase (test_name) ... ok` (here test_add and test_subtract both show "ok"), followed by the summary "Ran 2 tests in 0.001s" and the final "OK" line -- that final OK with per-test ok markers indicates a fully passing run.
What does the failure output in the first excerpt tell you, and how do the Calculator tests in the second excerpt keep their state from interfering with each other?

The failure output identifies the failing test by name (`FAIL: test_add`) and gives the cause (`AssertionError: Expected 5, got 4`), ending with `FAILED (failures=1)`. The Calculator tests each construct their own fresh instance -- `calc = Calculator();` at the start of both "calculator add" and "calculator reset" -- so the accumulated value from add(5)/add(3) in one test (value == 8) cannot affect the reset test, which adds 10, resets, and asserts value == 0.
In the "find adults" test, which Person nodes does the FindAdults walker report, and how does the test verify this?

FindAdults reports each Person with `person.age >= 18` found via `[-->][?:Person]` -- Alice (age 30) and Carol (age 25), but not Bob (age 15). The test asserts `len(result.reports) == 2`, builds `names = [p.name for p in result.reports]`, and asserts "Alice" and "Carol" are in names while "Bob" is not.
In a test you need to model rooms joined by doors so you can assert on the layout. Which construction pattern from the excerpt applies?

Declare `node Room { has name: str; }` and an edge type `edge Door {}`, then in the test build the graph: attach the first room with `root ++> kitchen;` and join rooms with typed edges using `kitchen +>: Door() :+> living;` and `living +>: Door() :+> bedroom;`.
How do the assertions in "Test connections" differ from those in "Test connectivity"?

"Test connections" checks the number of outgoing connections from each node with len over generic queries: `len([root -->]) == 1`, kitchen and living each have 1, and bedroom has 0. "Test connectivity" instead checks specific reachability through the typed Door edge using membership: `assert living in [kitchen ->:Door:->];` and `assert bedroom in [living ->:Door:->];`.
Which assertion in the connectivity test would fail if the Door edge from living to bedroom had never been created?

`assert bedroom in [living ->:Door:->];` would fail, because that query returns the nodes reachable from living via Door edges and bedroom would not be among them. The first assertion, `assert living in [kitchen ->:Door:->];`, would still pass.
How does the "divide by zero" test verify that divide raises the expected exception?

It wraps the call in a try block: it calls `divide(10, 0)` and then `assert False, "Should have raised error";` so the test fails if no exception occurs; the `except ZeroDivisionError` branch runs `assert True;` (commented "Expected"), passing when the ZeroDivisionError("Cannot divide by zero") raised by divide is caught.
In the separate-test-files project layout, where do the test files live and what are they named?
In a `tests/` directory at the project root (alongside `jac.toml` and `src/`), containing `models_test.jac` and `walkers_test.jac`; the source files `models.jac` and `walkers.jac` live under `src/`.
With this jac.toml [test] configuration, when does a test run stop early?

`fail_fast = false` means it does not stop at the first failure, but `max_failures = 10` stops the run after 10 failures. Tests are taken from the "tests" directory and run with verbose output (`verbose = true`).
What does JacTestClient provide, according to the excerpt?
An in-process HTTP client for testing Jac API endpoints without starting a real server or opening network ports.
What is the Python import statement for JacTestClient?
`from jaclang.runtimelib.testing import JacTestClient`.
Your endpoint tests must keep their storage inside a temporary directory instead of the working directory. Which construction from the excerpt applies?

Create the client with a custom base path: `client = JacTestClient.from_file("app.jac", base_path="/tmp/test")`. Per the heading, the base_path argument is useful precisely for temp directories in tests.
What is the difference between client.register_user and client.login in these excerpts?

`client.register_user("testuser", "password123")` registers (creates) a test user with that username and password, while `client.login("testuser", "password123")` logs in with those same credentials -- registration establishes the account and login authenticates against it; both return a response.
What arguments does client.login take in the example, and what does the call yield?
It takes the username "testuser" and the password "password123", and the call's result is assigned to `response`.
How does the example send a POST request with a JSON body to a walker endpoint?
With `client.post("/walker/create_user", json={"name": "Alice"})` -- the path targets the create_user walker and the json= keyword carries the request body.
What method and arguments does the PUT request example use?
`client.put("/walker/update_user", json={"name": "Bob"})` -- a PUT to the update_user walker path with the JSON body {"name": "Bob"}.
You need to send a DELETE request from JacTestClient. Based on the excerpt, which call form applies?

Use the generic request method, passing the HTTP verb as a string: `client.request("DELETE", "/walker/delete_user", json={"id": "123"})` -- the generic form covers methods like DELETE while still accepting a json body.
On a TestResponse object, what do the `ok` and `data` properties mean?

`ok` is a bool that is True if the status is 2xx, and `data` is `dict | None` -- the unwrapped data from the TransportResponse envelope. The object also exposes status_code (int), headers (dict), text (raw response body), and json() to parse the body as JSON.
In the full pytest example, how is the JacTestClient constructed inside test_task_crud?

Via `client = JacTestClient.from_file("app.jac", base_path=str(tmp_path))` -- loading app.jac and using pytest's tmp_path fixture (converted to str) as the base path, after importing JacTestClient from jaclang.runtimelib.testing.
After POSTing to /walker/CreateTask with json={"title": "My Task"}, what two things does the example assert about the response?
That `resp.status_code == 200` and that `resp.ok` is truthy.
You have created one task through the API and want the test to confirm exactly one task now exists. Based on the Read excerpt, what applies?

POST to the listing walker with `client.post("/walker/GetTasks")`, parse the body with `data = resp.json()`, and assert on the reports array: `assert len(data["reports"]) == 1` -- the walker's reported tasks arrive under the "reports" key of the JSON response.
In the HMR test, what does the first excerpt set up versus what the "Initial state" excerpt checks?

The first excerpt is the setup for testing hot module replacement behavior: it builds the client with `JacTestClient.from_file("app.jac", base_path=str(tmp_path))` and registers a user with `client.register_user("user", "pass")`. The "Initial state" excerpt then establishes the baseline before any reload: it POSTs to `/walker/get_data` and asserts `resp.ok`.
What request does the "Initial state" step make, and what does it assert?
It makes `resp = client.post("/walker/get_data")` and asserts `resp.ok`.
What does the "Verify after reload" step do at the end of the test?
It re-posts to `/walker/get_data`, asserts `resp.ok` still holds after the reload, and then closes the client with `client.close()`.
What does the parametrize() helper do?
It registers one test per parameter, similar to `pytest.mark.parametrize` -- it creates individual test cases from a list of inputs, so each case runs and reports independently.
You want to use the parametrize helper inside a .jac file. Which import applies?
The Jac import shown in the excerpt: `import from jaclang.runtimelib.test { parametrize }`.
How does the Signature excerpt's description of parametrize relate to the concrete Usage excerpt?

The Signature excerpt defines the API abstractly: `parametrize(base_name: str, params: Iterable, test_func: Callable, id_fn: Callable | None = None)` -- base name for generated tests, list of parameter values each passed to the test function, the test function to invoke, and an optional id_fn for test IDs. The Usage excerpt instantiates it: `_test_square(pair: tuple)` is the test_func, "square" is the base_name, `[(2, 4), (3, 9), (0, 0), (-1, 1)]` is params, id_fn is omitted -- so four tests are registered as square_0, square_1, square_2, square_3, called from a `with entry` block.
According to the "Custom Test IDs" excerpt, what is id_fn used for?

`id_fn` is used to generate descriptive test names for parametrized tests -- the example imports parametrize from jaclang.runtimelib.test and defines `_test_parse(raw: str)` as the test function it will name.
In this parametrize call, how are the individual test IDs generated?

Via the id_fn argument: `id_fn=lambda p: str -> str { return f"input_{p}"; }`, which prefixes each parameter with "input_". The call registers the test function _test_parse under base name "parse values" for the params ["500m", "2", "250"].
You're naming new test blocks for user signup and walker traversal features. Based on the excerpt, what naming approach applies?

Use readable, behavior-describing descriptions as the test names -- like the excerpt's `test "user creation with valid email" { }` and `test "walker visits all connected nodes" { }` -- so the test string itself states the behavior being verified.
Why is the first excerpt labeled "Good - focused tests" while the second is "Avoid - too broad"?

The good version gives each behavior its own test: "add positive numbers" asserts only add(2, 3) == 5 and "add negative numbers" asserts only add(-2, -3) == -5. The broad version crams three unrelated operations -- add, subtract, and multiply -- into one "all math operations" test, so a single test covers multiple behaviors instead of being focused on one.
In the "all math operations" test, what happens to the test result if only the subtract assertion is wrong?

The entire "all math operations" test fails, even though the add and multiply assertions are fine -- because the one test block bundles `assert add(2, 3) == 5;`, `assert subtract(5, 3) == 2;`, and `assert multiply(2, 3) == 6;` together. This is why the excerpt labels the pattern "Avoid - too broad".
In the "counter increment" test, how is fresh state created and what is asserted?
The test creates its own state by connecting a new Counter to root (`counter = root ++> Counter();`), spawns the walker with `root spawn Incrementer();`, and asserts `counter[0].count == 1;`.
You've written a process() function over lists and want your tests to be robust. Based on the "Test Edge Cases" excerpt, which cases apply?

Cover the edge cases shown: the empty list (`process([])` should return `[]`), a single item (`process([1])` yields length 1), and a large input (`process(list(range(1000)))` yields length 1000) -- three separate test blocks, one per edge case.
What distinguishes the "Good - clear what failed" test from the "Avoid - unclear failures" test?

The good version first captures the value (`result = calculate(input);`) and asserts with a diagnostic message -- `assert result == expected, f"Expected {expected}, got {result}";` -- so a failure shows the expected and actual values. The avoided version asserts inline with no message (`assert calculate(input) == expected;`), producing unclear failures with no indication of what the values were.
When the "calculation no message" test fails, what information is missing from the failure?

Any explanatory message: because `assert calculate(input) == expected;` has no message argument, the failure doesn't show what value was expected or what calculate actually returned -- which is why the excerpt labels this "Avoid - unclear failures".
According to the warning in the OSP tutorial intro, what does `jac run` persist, what symptoms can that cause, and how do you start fresh?

`jac run` persists graph state to a `.jac/` directory. Running an example multiple times can then produce duplicate nodes or `NodeAnchor ... is not a valid reference!` errors. To start fresh, clean the `.jac/` directory with `jac clean --all`.
How does Object-Spatial Programming invert the relationship between data and computation compared to traditional OOP?

In traditional OOP, objects exist in isolation and you call methods to bring data to computation. In OSP, objects exist in a graph with explicit relationships and you send computation (walkers) to the data -- walkers visit nodes and move to connected nodes. The quick reference lists the operators: `++>` creates/connects a node, `[-->]` / `[<--]` query outgoing/incoming edges, `spawn` starts a walker at a node, `visit` moves the walker to nodes, and `report` returns data from a walker.
You need an entity that carries data and behavior like a class, but that can later be wired into a graph. Which construct applies?

Declare a node -- per the excerpt, nodes are classes that can be connected in a graph. The example `node Person` carries `has name: str;` and `has age: int;` fields plus a method `def greet() -> str { return f"Hi, I'm {self.name}!"; }`, exactly like a regular class, while remaining connectable.
Taken together, what do the node-creation and node-usage excerpts show about nodes before they are connected?

The first excerpt shows nodes are created just like regular objects -- `alice = Person(name="Alice", age=30);` and `bob = Person(name="Bob", age=25);`. The second shows they are used like regular objects too -- `alice.greet()` prints "Hi, I'm Alice!" and `bob.age` is 25 -- and states the key point: nodes are full-featured classes with methods, inheritance, etc., and the graph capability is dormant until you connect them.
What do the two print statements in this example output?

`print(alice.greet());` outputs "Hi, I'm Alice!" and `print(bob.age);` outputs 25, per the inline comments -- demonstrating the key point that nodes behave as full-featured classes whose graph capability stays dormant until they are connected.
According to the "Connecting Nodes" excerpt, which operator connects nodes?
The `++>` operator. The example sets up three Person nodes (alice, bob, carol) in a `with entry` block before connecting them.
You want the relationship between two people to record the year they met and how close they are. Which construct applies?

A typed edge carrying data -- per the excerpt, edges can carry data and have types. Define `edge Knows { has since: int; has strength: str; }` where since records the year they met and strength holds values like "close" or "acquaintance", then connect Person nodes with it.
In the "Querying the Graph" setup, what connections are created before any queries run?
`root ++> alice;`, `alice ++> bob;`, and `alice ++> carol;` -- three Person nodes wired so alice hangs off root and bob and carol hang off alice, ready for navigation with spatial operators.
What does the query `[root -->]` return in this example, and what does len() of it print?
It returns all nodes connected to root; `print(len(people))` prints 1, because only alice is connected directly to root.
You want a reusable place to demonstrate graph queries over people and their Knows relationships. What setup does the excerpt use?

It declares the graph vocabulary first -- `node Person { has name: str; }` and `edge Knows { has since: int; }` -- then defines a function taking node parameters, `def query_examples(src: Person, alice: Person)`, whose body will run the queries against the passed-in nodes.
What is the difference between the basic queries in the first excerpt and the type-filtered queries in the second?

The basic queries select purely by direction: `[src -->]` returns all forward connections, `[src <--]` all backward connections, `[src <-->]` both directions. The type-filtered queries narrow the result: `[src -->][?:Person]` keeps only Person nodes, `[src ->:Knows:->]` traverses only via Knows edges, and `[src ->:Knows:->][?:Person]` combines both -- Knows edges leading to Person nodes.
What query syntax returns only the nodes reached via Knows edges that are also Person nodes?
`[src ->:Knows:->][?:Person]` -- the `->:Knows:->` part restricts traversal to Knows edges, and the `[?:Person]` filter keeps only Person nodes.
What does the chained traversal `[alice ->:Knows:-> ->:Knows:->]` produce?
Friends of friends -- per the comment, chaining two `->:Knows:->` hops traverses Knows edges twice from alice.
What is the difference between `Root` (capitalized) and `root` (lowercase) in Jac?

`Root` is the type of the root node, used in ability declarations like `can X with Root entry`; `root` is the built-in instance, used in expressions like `root ++> node` or `root spawn Walker()`. The excerpt's Greeter walker shows both: `can start with Root entry` for the declaration and `root ++> alice` / graph wiring in the entry block.
What does the first excerpt demonstrate about `visit` that the second excerpt's context-variable table then explains the vocabulary for?

The first shows that putting `visit [-->];` in both the Root-entry ability and the Person-entry ability keeps the traversal going, so Greeter reaches Alice, Bob, and Carol (output: Hello to all three). The second defines the variables available inside abilities: `here` is the current node, `self` is the walker instance, and `visitor` is an alias for `self` -- its Explorer example increments `self.rooms_visited` (walker state) while reading `here.name` (current node) before continuing with `visit [-->];`.
According to the "Reporting Results" excerpt, what two things does the report keyword do?

It prints the value to the console and stores it in `result.reports` for programmatic access. In the FindAdults example this is why the output shows the two Person lines first, then "Found 2 adults" with Alice and Carol listed from result.reports.
In the FindFirst walker, what does disengage do, and what would happen without it?

`disengage` immediately stops the walker's traversal -- here, as soon as it finds the first Person with age >= 18 (Bob, 25) it reports him and stops, so Carol is never visited. Without disengage the walker would continue on to Carol. The excerpt notes this is especially useful in search walkers that find and modify a specific node, like toggling or deleting a task by ID.
You're building a walker that must both carry input data and react differently depending on where it is in the graph. What does the Entry Points excerpt establish?

That walkers can have different entry points -- you give one walker multiple abilities, each triggered by a different location/node type -- and that a walker carries its own state via has fields, as DataProcessor does with `has data: str;` alongside the Person node it will process.
What does the process ability print, and on which node type does it trigger?
It triggers on Person entry (`can process with Person entry`) and prints f"Processing {here.name}" -- the current node's name -- before continuing with `visit [-->];`.
You need to find users who follow each other (mutual follows). Which pattern from the excerpt applies?

The FindMutualFollows approach: at a User node, collect who they follow with `following = [here ->:Follows:->];` and who follows them with `followers = [here <-:Follows:<-];`, then loop over following and `report user` whenever the user is also in followers -- membership in both directional query results means the follow is mutual.
What role does each excerpt play -- the two Follows connections versus the FindFollowers spawn?

The first excerpt creates the relationship data: two directed typed edges, `alice +>: Follows(since="2024") :+> bob;` and `bob +>: Follows(since="2024") :+> alice;`, which together make the follow mutual. The second runs the query over that data: `result = alice spawn FindFollowers();` spawns the walker at alice, then the loop over `result.reports` prints each follower's username.
In the "Find Alice's followers" excerpt, where is the walker spawned and how are the results consumed?

The walker is spawned at the alice node -- `result = alice spawn FindFollowers();` -- and the results are consumed by iterating `result.reports`, printing f"  - {user.username}" for each reported user under the header "Alice's followers:".
According to the output shown, who are Alice's followers and who is her only mutual follow?
Alice's followers are bob and carol, but her only mutual follow is bob -- the FindMutualFollows spawn reports just User(username='bob'), so the "Alice's mutual follows:" section lists only "- bob".
What is the default entry-point file for `jac start`, and what if your file has a different name?

`main.jac` is the default entry point; if the file is named differently (e.g. `app.jac`), you pass it explicitly: `jac start app.jac`. The excerpt shows the same graph code -- Todo node plus add_todo and list_todos walkers -- becoming a REST API this way.
Your Jac server is running locally and you want to create a todo from the command line. Based on the excerpt, what call applies?

A POST to the walker's endpoint with a JSON body: `curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/walker/add_todo -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"title": "Learn OSP"}'` -- the walker name appears in the /walker/add_todo path and the title field travels in the JSON payload.
Per the comparison table, when should you use def:pub functions versus walkers to expose server logic?

`def:pub` functions are best for simple stateless CRUD and quick prototyping: they access data directly ([root -->]), are stateless, and expose shared data with no user isolation. Walkers are best for graph traversal, per-user data, and production apps: they get a per-user root node (walker:priv enforces auth), access data by traversal (visit [-->], here), and carry state across nodes via has properties. The rule of thumb: start with def:pub to prototype, switch to walkers when you need authentication, per-user data isolation, or multi-step traversal -- the walker style being built from the Key Takeaways primitives like spawn, visit, here, report, and disengage.
According to the Key Takeaways table, what are the purposes of `report` and `disengage`?

`report` collects results from a walker, and `disengage` stops walker traversal immediately. (The table also lists node = objects that live in a graph, edge = typed relationships, walker = mobile computation, `++>` = connect nodes, `[-->]` = query connections, `visit` = continue traversal, `here` = current node, and `spawn` = start a walker at a node.)
Per the Next Steps section, which reference page covers understanding `.reports` patterns?

The Walker Responses reference (reference/language/walker-responses.md) -- listed under Reference alongside Graph Operations (the complete edge/node operator reference) and Part III: OSP (the full language reference).
A walker executes report twice during its run. How does the spawning code get both values, per the excerpt?

Every `report` appends its value to the `.reports` array on the response object returned by `root spawn MyWalker()`. So `report "first";` lands in reports[0] and `report "second";` in reports[1] -- report is the walker's "return channel", except it can fire multiple times, accumulating results. Note also that report prints each value to stdout as a side effect, so the values appear on the console too.
The first excerpt just reads response.reports directly -- what does the second excerpt recommend adding, and why?

The first shows untyped consumption: `response = root spawn MyWalker(); print(response.reports);` yields ["first", "second"]. The second recommends declaring `has reports: list[T]` on every walker as the default, not an opt-in optimization: it is a single-source-of-truth contract where `report X` (write side) and `(spawn W).reports[i]` (read side) both type-check against the same T, catching typos and shape drift at `jac check` time.
